body: Welcome to the GitHub repository for Layer5’s documentation website! The docs website is hosted at https://docs.layer5.io. We use Hugo with the google/docsy theme for styling and site structure, and Netlify to manage the deployment of the site. Quickstart 🔗 Here’s a quick guide to updating the docs: Fork the layer5io/docs repository on GitHub. Make your changes and send a pull request (PR). If you’re not yet ready for a review, add “WIP” to the PR name to indicate it’s a work in progress. Wait for the automated PR workflow to do some checks. When it’s ready, you should see a comment like this: deploy/netlify — Deploy preview ready! Click Details to the right of “Deploy preview ready” to see a preview of your updates. Continue updating your doc and pushing your changes until you’re happy with the content. When you’re ready for a review, add a comment to the PR, remove any holds or “WIP” markers, and assign a reviewer/approver. See the Layer5 contributor guide. If you need more help with the GitHub workflow, follow this guide to a standard GitHub workflow. Local development 🔗 This section will show you how to develop the website locally, by running a local Hugo server. Install Hugo 🔗 To install Hugo, follow the instructions for your system type. NOTE: we recommend that you use Hugo version v0.140.2, as this is currently the version we deploy to Netlify. For example, using homebrew to install hugo on macOS or linux: # WARNING: this may install a newer version than `v0.140.2` brew install hugo Install Node Packages 🔗 If you plan to make changes to the site styling, you need to install some node libraries as well. (See the Docsy setup guide for more information) You can install the same versions we use in Netlify (defined in package.json) with the following command: npm install -D Run local hugo server 🔗 Follow the usual GitHub workflow of forking the repository on GitHub and then cloning your fork to your local machine. Fork the layer5io/docs repository in the GitHub UI. Clone your fork locally: git clone git@github.com:/docs.git cd website/ Initialize the Docsy submodule: git submodule update --init --recursive Install Docsy dependencies: # NOTE: ensure you have node 18 installed (cd themes/docsy/ && npm install) Start your local Hugo server: hugo server -D You can access your website at http://localhost:1313/ Useful docs 🔗 User guide for the Docsy theme Hugo installation guide Hugo basic usage Hugo site directory structure hugo server reference Menu structure 🔗 The site theme has one Hugo menu (main), which defines the top navigation bar. You can find and adjust the definition of the menu in the site configuration file. The left-hand navigation panel is defined by the directory structure under the content/en directory. A weight property in the front matter of each page determines the position of the page relative to the others in the same directory. The lower the weight, the earlier the page appears in the section. Here is an example _index.md file: +++ title = "Getting Started with Layer5" description = "Overview" weight = 1 +++ Docsy Theme 🔗 We use the Docsy theme for the website. The theme files are managed with a git submodule in the themes/docsy directory. Do not change these files, they are not actually inside this repo, but are part of the google/docsy repo. To update referenced docsy commit, run the following command at the root of the repo: # for example, to update docsy to v0.6.0 # WARNING: updating the docsy version will require you to update our overrides # check under: `layouts/partials` and `assets/scss` git -C themes/docsy fetch --tags git -C themes/docsy checkout tags/v0.6.0 Documentation style guide 🔗 For guidance on writing effective documentation, see the style guide for the Layer5 docs. Overriding theme styles 🔗 The theme holds its styles in the assets/scss directory. Do not change these files, they are not actually inside this repo, but are part of the google/docsy repo. These files are managed as a Git submodule and may be updated or replaced when the theme is upgraded. Any changes made directly to the theme files will be lost during updates and are not preserved in version control. You can override the default styles and add new ones: In general, put your files in the project directory structure under website rather than in the theme directory. Use the same file name as the theme does, and put the file in the same relative position. Hugo looks first at the file in the main project directories, if present, then at the files under the theme directory. For example, the Layer5 website’s layouts/partials/navbar.html overrides the theme’s layouts/partials/navbar.html You can update the Layer5 website’s project variables in the _variables_project.scss file. Values in that file override the Docsy variables. You can also use _variables_project.scss to specify your own values for any of the default Bootstrap 4 variables. For adding custom CSS rules, use the _styles_project.scss file in the same assets/scss/ directory. Image styling 🔗 Link and asset paths 🔗 Use Hugo ref when linking from one documentation page to another documentation page: [About]({{< ref "about.md" >}}) For images and other assets that live next to index.md or _index.md, or inside that page bundle, use a normal relative path: ![Alt text](images/example.png) If you need HTML for custom sizing, keep the same relative path: For global shared assets that physically live under static/, use the static shortcode: ![Layer5 logo]({{< static "images/logo.svg" >}}) Do not use the static shortcode for assets under content/. By default, Markdown images are rendered with: max-width: 70% of the viewport max-height: 80vh of the viewport height centered block layout This default styling works well for most landscape (horizontal) images. Note In Hugo, a section is a directory containing an _index.md file. Overview 🔗 Contributing videos involves either:
Creating a category → subcategory → adding video markdown files, or Adding video markdown files directly under a category (these will automatically be assigned to an “ALL” subcategory) 1. Creating a Category 🔗 To create a top-level category:
Create a directory under content/en/videos (e.g., getting-started) Add an _index.md file inside this directory with the following frontmatter: title: Getting Started # Category text appearing in the /videos category tab and left sidebar description: > Getting started videos on Cloud and Kanvas weight: 2 # Order in which this category appears in the /videos page and left sidebar icon: bi-rocket-takeoff-fill # Icon for the category (supports Bootstrap icons and local/remote assets) videoGrid: true # When true, shows all child / nested videos as a grid of cards on this section's index page # When false, presents a hyperlinked list of videos/sub-sections instead draft: true # When true, previews this section on local dev server but hides from left sidebar and /videos landing page on published site 2. Adding Videos to Your Category 🔗 There are two approaches for adding videos:
Approach A: Create a Subcategory with Videos 🔗 Create a subdirectory under your category (e.g., getting-started/onboarding) Add an _index.md file with the following frontmatter: title: Onboarding # Subcategory text in the /videos subcategory tab and left sidebar videoGrid: true # Same functionality as in the category _index.md weight: 2 # Order in which this subcategory appears Create video markdown files (e.g., video1.md, video2.md) in this subdirectory with the following frontmatter: --- title: "Design Reviews: Adding Comments" # Required: title of the video card/list description: > # Required: description of the video Add comments to your designs in Kanvas's Designer Mode to enhance collaboration and streamline design reviews. videoId: "" # Required: YouTube video ID, example: bb6J--aApk8 videoType: youtube # Required: currently supports "youtube" (support for "local" is present, though currently disabled) # Categories and tags help match videos with documentation pages by scoring relevance, # see the guide at bottom to know how categories: [designer] tags: [review, collaboration, comments] # available as hyperlinked tags in the video card and individual video page duration: 2:30 # Optional: duration in minutes:seconds format ("min" is automatically added) --- # the following youtube shortcode is used for individual video page # Example: {{< youtube id=bb6J--aApk8 class="yt-embed-container" >}} # we can control the styling of resulting iframe and wrapping div by modify style of .yt-embed-container in assets/scss/_videos_project.scss {{< youtube id="videoId" class="yt-embed-container" >}} Approach B: Add Videos Directly Under a Category 🔗 Create video markdown files directly in the category directory with the same frontmatter format shown above. These videos will automatically be assigned to an “ALL” subcategory within the parent category.
Video and Documentation Page Matching 🔗 To display Related Videos carousel on documentation pages section pages and individual pages, videos are matched with the docs pages based on shared tags and categories:
Each matching tag contributes 1 point to the relevance score Each matching category contributes 2 points to the relevance score Videos with at least one matching tag or category appear in the “Related Videos” carousel Videos with higher scores appear first in the carousel Example 🔗 If a documentation page has:
categories: [designer] tags: [catalog, publishing] And there are two videos:
Video A:
categories: [designer] tags: [catalog, review] Video B:
categories: [designer] tags: [designs] Video A scores: 2 (category match) + 1 (tag ‘catalog’) = 3 Video B scores: 2 (category match) + 0 = 2 Video A will appear before Video B in the carousel on the documentation page.
Example Directory Structure 🔗 content/en/videos/ └── template-category/ # Top-level section (category) ├── _index.md # Defines the "Template Category" section └── sub-category/ # Sub-section inside the above category ├── _index.md # Defines the "Sub Category" sub-section └── video-1.md # file containing video specific data See content/en/videos/template-category/ for an example of a category with subcategories and videos. It is set to draft and is not published and is intended as a reference for adding videos.

body:
Kanvas lets you design Kubernetes and cloud infrastructure visually, validate and deploy that design to your clusters, and then operate what is running, all from one shared canvas. Teams work on the same design at the same time, so the diagram you discuss is the configuration you deploy.
What is Kanvas? 🔗 Kanvas is a web application for creating and sharing orchestratable designs of cloud native infrastructure. A design is a declarative description of infrastructure: the components it contains, the relationships between them, their configuration, and any annotations you add to explain it. You build a design by placing components on a canvas, connecting them, and configuring each one. You can also draw shapes, lines, text, and icons to document your intent; Kanvas treats those as annotations and never deploys them.
A design does not stop at the diagram. Kanvas validates a design against the schema of every component in it, dry-runs it against your target clusters without applying anything, and deploys or undeploys it on the Kubernetes contexts you select. Every save creates a new version of the design, and multiple people can edit the same design together in real time.
This matters because one artifact carries your infrastructure from whiteboard to running cluster. Reviewers read the same design that operators deploy, and every resource Kanvas deploys carries the identity of the design that produced it, so you can trace running workloads back to their source.
Two modes: Designer and Operator 🔗 Kanvas has two modes. You switch between them at any time; if the open design or resource has unsaved changes, Kanvas asks you to confirm before you leave.
Designer is for authoring. You compose designs from versioned components, define relationships, configure each component, and annotate the result. Whiteboarding is a toolset inside Designer, not a separate mode. Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy actions run from Designer. Operator is for running infrastructure. It shows the recorded state of your connected Kubernetes clusters, collected by MeshSync and served through Meshery. Operator can scope its view to the resources a single design deployed. Where each mode is available 🔗 Designer is available everywhere Kanvas runs, including the hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new. Operator mode, and every action that touches a cluster, needs a Meshery deployment that can reach your clusters.
Capability Hosted Kanvas (kanvas.new) Meshery Playground or self-hosted Meshery Designer: author and import designs Available Available Share and publish designs Requires sign-in Requires sign-in Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy Not available Available Connect clusters Not available Available Operator mode Not available Available When you invoke a cluster-bound capability on kanvas.new, Kanvas explains that it is not available there and points you to the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery deployment. Plan details live at layer5.io/pricing.
Choose your mode 🔗 Designer Designer mode is for creating and editing designs.
Compose infrastructure from a palette of versioned components, connect components with relationships, and configure each one.
Validate a design, dry-run it against your clusters, and deploy it.
Operator Operator mode is for operating your Kubernetes clusters and the infrastructure running on them.
See the recorded state of the clusters you select.
Filter the view to the resources that a specific design deployed.
How Kanvas relates to Meshery and Layer5 Cloud 🔗 Kanvas is an extension of Meshery. Its interface loads into Meshery UI, and a companion plugin runs inside Meshery Server. Meshery Server is the component that talks to your clusters: it deploys and observes infrastructure on Kanvas’s behalf. Layer5 Cloud is the remote provider behind Kanvas: it stores your designs and their versions and handles identity, sharing, the catalog, and events. How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud explains how requests move between these parts.
Where to go next 🔗 Getting Started - create your first design and reach a working result fast. Tutorials - learn Kanvas by building realistic designs end to end. How-to Guides - accomplish a specific task, such as deploying or sharing a design. Concepts - understand designs, components, relationships, and how Kanvas works. Reference - look up exact options, limits, permissions, and shortcuts.

body:
An organization is the tenant boundary in Layer5 Cloud. It decides whose resources a request can reach, whose billing it counts against, and which roles apply. Understanding how organizations isolate, nest, and resolve explains most of what a user can and cannot see.
What an organization is 🔗 The organization is the unit of multi-tenancy and the core security boundary. Everything else composes on top of it: teams and workspaces belong to one organization, and users hold roles in it. Roles, keychains, and keys are defined once for the whole provider, but resources, billing, and access control are isolated per organization, so a role held in one organization grants nothing in another.
The structure is flexible:
An organization has any number of teams. A team has any number of users, and a user can belong to any number of teams. A user can belong to any number of organizations, and holds an independent set of roles in each. Teams group users inside an organization and control access to workspaces and to workspace resources such as environments and managed and unmanaged connections. See Teams and Workspaces.
Organization types and hierarchy 🔗 Every Layer5 Cloud deployment has one provider organization and any number of tenant organizations.
Provider organization. The single top-level organization that operates the deployment. It owns the deployment’s default identity providers, which tenant organizations use unless they bring their own. The provider organization is never a child, and it cannot hold child organizations: its child list is always empty. Tenant organization. Every other organization. Each tenant is configured as Hosted, Branded, or White-Label, depending on the domain it uses and the identity provider that authenticates its users. See Organization Configuration Scenarios to choose between them. Child organization. A tenant organization created inside another tenant organization, its parent. Child organizations follow these rules:
An organization can have any number of children, and children can have children of their own. There is no depth limit. A child has exactly one parent, fixed when the child is created. The Organization Admin or Owner of a parent governs its direct children only: they can edit a child’s settings, add members to it, search its members, and delete it. Governing a grandchild belongs to the administrator of the intermediate organization. A parent administrator is not a member of the child. Workspaces, teams, connections, identity providers, and the mail server inside the child still require membership and a role in the child. An organization that still has live child organizations cannot be deleted. Delete the deepest children first. See Child Organizations for the full behavior.
The owner 🔗 The user who creates an organization is its owner. Ownership is a fixed attribute of the organization, separate from the Organization Admin role:
The owner cannot be removed from the organization. A removal request for the owner fails with “Organization owner cannot be removed”. Ownership cannot be transferred. Layer5 Cloud has no operation that reassigns the owner of an organization. No member can leave an organization on their own. Membership ends only when an authorized administrator removes the member. The owner can delete the organization. An Organization Admin who is not the owner cannot. Plan who creates each organization accordingly. For a shared or long-lived organization, have it created by the account that should remain its owner.
How a request or sign-in finds its organization 🔗 Every guarded request runs in one organization. Layer5 Cloud resolves that organization from these sources, in this order, and the first source that applies wins:
Domain. The request’s host matches an organization’s custom domain. X-Current-Orgid header. The organization an API client names. Saved preference. The default organization stored in the user’s preferences. Browser session. The organization the browser session last selected. The header, the saved preference, and the browser session must name an organization the user is a live member of. A value that names any other organization is ignored, and the request runs with no organization scope. Callers who hold View All Organizations (Provider Admin by default) are the exception: they can name any organization, or all to span every organization. Layer5 Cloud reads no organization from the query string. The Organization context section of the API reference gives the exact rules for API clients.
Why the domain wins 🔗 A custom domain identifies the tenant before the user makes any choice. A sign-in page served on an organization’s domain shows that organization’s branding, authenticates through that organization’s identity provider, and applies its open invitation, so the request belongs to that organization regardless of the user’s saved preference. Resolving by domain does not check membership; every guarded action still checks the permissions the user holds in that organization.
Domain matching follows these rules:
The host is matched exactly against organization domains, with the protocol and port removed. The deployment’s own base host, IP addresses, and the provider’s reserved domains are never treated as custom domains. A domain belongs to at most one organization. A deleted organization keeps its domain, so clear the domain before deleting if the address must be reused. Domain-to-organization lookups are cached for five minutes. Creating, editing, or deleting an organization clears its entry on the server that handled the change, so other server instances can serve the previous mapping until their entry expires. Assigning a new domain to an organization requires a Provider Admin. Organization administrators can keep the current domain or clear it. Layer5 Cloud validates the domain’s syntax when it is saved and does not perform a DNS lookup. See Organization Configuration Scenarios for how domains combine with identity providers.
The organization switcher lists only the organizations the user is a member of; holders of View All Organizations can also select All Organizations. See Switching Between Organizations.
Lifecycle 🔗 An organization moves through three operations. Organization Management covers the procedures.
Create 🔗 An organization starts with a name (required), a country, and a region. Creating it does two things:
The creator becomes the owner. Layer5 Cloud creates a default workspace named “My Workspace”, owned by the creator. A domain is not set at creation; a Provider Admin assigns one afterward. Creating a child organization inside a parent requires Create Organization in the parent, and makes the creator a member and an Organization Admin of the child.
Edit 🔗 Administrators of the organization shape how it looks and how users join it:
Setting What it controls Name, country, region The organization’s identity in lists and the switcher. Branding Theme colors (hex values only) and four logos: desktop, mobile, dark desktop, and dark mobile, each up to 500 KB. Resetting the theme also clears the logos. Links Terms of service, privacy policy, support channels, and social links shown on the organization’s sign-in, sign-up, and error pages and in email footers. Unsafe values are dropped rather than rejected. Sign-in carousel Whether sign-in pages show the feature carousel. On by default. Domain The custom host that resolves to the organization. New values require a Provider Admin. Open invitation One invitation that admits any non-member who signs in through the organization’s host. The user gains the invitation’s organization, team, and role grants. The invitation’s ID is public and works as a shareable link. Teams Which teams belong to the organization. Removing a team ends the mapping; the team itself is not deleted. Identity providers The organization’s own sign-in providers, in place of the provider organization’s defaults. Mail server The organization’s own SMTP server for outgoing email. See Bring Your Own Mail Server. Delete 🔗 Deleting an organization is a soft delete:
The organization, every membership in it, and every team-to-organization mapping end. Teams, workspaces, environments, and designs are not deleted by the request, but nothing reaches them through the organization afterward. No restore operation exists. Layer5 Cloud refuses the deletion in two cases:
The organization still has live child organizations (HTTP 409). Nothing is changed. The organization is the last live organization the caller owns (HTTP 403). This check does not apply when a parent administrator deletes a child. The organization’s owner, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or Owner of the live parent can delete an organization.
Who can do what 🔗 The matrix shows which default roles hold each organization permission. It is refreshed automatically from the Layer5 permission list. See Roles and Permissions for how to read it and for every other permission area.
Organization permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Org See only organizations to which you are a member. See all other members within your membership teams. ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View Organizations See all organizations of which you are an administrator. See all members of those organizations. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View All Organizations See all organizations within a Cloud deployment. See all organizations, teams, and users. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Organization Establish new organization for organizing teams, users, and resource access. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Edit Organization Edit organiaztions and add teams to it -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Add User to Organization Directly create a new user account within an organization. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Invite User to Organization Send a request for a user to join an organization. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove User from Organization Discontinue user access to organization, teams and resources; cease billing accrual. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Promote or Demote User to Org Admin Elevate or remove organization level administrative privileges. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Roles to Organization members Assign roles to users in an organization -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove Roles from Organization members Remove roles from users in an organization -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Enforced differently from the matrix 🔗 Several organization actions check a role or ownership on the server rather than the permission alone:
Delete the organization. Allowed for the organization’s owner, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or Owner of the live parent. An Organization Admin who is not the owner cannot delete. Assign a new domain. Allowed for Provider Admins only. Any other caller receives HTTP 403 when saving the change. Edit the organization and add members. Allowed for an Organization Admin or the Owner of the organization, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or Owner of the live parent. Holding Edit Organization or Add User to Organization through another role is not enough. Adding a member adds an existing account; it does not create one. Assign organization roles. Allowed for an Organization Admin of the organization, a Provider Admin, or a holder of Assign User Roles there. The target must be a member. Role rows the caller cannot write are skipped and reported in the response; the rest are applied. List every organization. Requires View All Organizations. Without it, the organization list shows only the organizations the caller is a member of. Plan availability 🔗 Identity & Access Management Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Organizations Participate as a member of multiple organizations each with their own accounting and billing structure. Multiple organizations, multiple teams. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Organizations Establish new organization for organizing teams, users, and resource access. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included The table lists the plans that include organizations; Layer5 Cloud does not block organization actions by plan today. See Feature Availability for every capability.
Cross-organization access 🔗 Entitlements are scoped to an organization. The roles a user holds in one organization do not apply in another, even for the same person.
Cross-organization access works through resource-access mappings. A mapping is attached to one resource, such as a single design, and names the user it is shared with. Mappings deliberately cross the organization boundary: a user does not need to be a member of an organization to open a resource that has been shared with them there. This is the mechanism that makes collaboration between organizations possible.
A mapping grants access to that resource only. It does not make the recipient a member of the organization, give them a role there, or reach any of the organization’s other resources.
Info Organization membership alone does not decide what a user can see and do. For how the connected identity provider, organization-scoped roles, and resource-access mappings fit together, and what counts as a security boundary, see Identity and Security: Security Boundaries. Example: the Orbital Labs ecosystem 🔗 Organization Type Administrator Relationship Constellation Cloud Provider organization, a managed service provider Dr. Aiko Sato, Provider Admin Operates the deployment and hosts Orbital Labs and Stellar Dynamics as tenants. Orbital Labs Tenant organization, a cloud-native startup Maya Chen, Org Admin Its users belong to the Infrastructure and Development teams and work in Orbital Labs workspaces. Stellar Dynamics Tenant organization, an enterprise client of Orbital Labs Marcus Webb, Org Admin A separate tenant. Its users reach Orbital Labs content only through resource-access mappings. When Maya shares the stellar-saas-platform design with Marcus, Marcus can open that one design even though he is not a member of Orbital Labs. He sees no other Orbital Labs workspace or design, and his Org Admin role in Stellar Dynamics grants him nothing in Orbital Labs.

This guide takes you through one complete learning journey in the Layer5 Academy: you find a learning path, enroll, work through it, pass its final assessment, and receive your credential. Along the way you learn how the Academy tracks your progress and how its tests are scored, so you know what to expect from any content you take next.
You need a Layer5 Cloud account to enroll. Browsing the catalog needs no account.
Step 1: Find content in the catalog 🔗 The catalog lists every piece of content available to you as a card. Each card shows the content type, title, number of courses, and difficulty level.
Narrow the catalog with three filters:
Level limits results to one difficulty level. Content Type limits results to learning paths, challenges, or certifications. Set it alone to list every item of that type. Organization limits results to one organization’s content. It appears only on the main Layer5 Academy catalog. Filters combine, so Level plus Content Type lists, for example, every beginner learning path. Clearing the filters returns the full catalog.
What you see depends on where you are The main Layer5 Academy at cloud.layer5.io/academy spans organizations and offers the Organization filter. An organization’s own Academy on its custom domain shows only that organization’s content and hides the Organization filter. Pick the content type that matches your goal:
Type Choose it when you want to Learning path Learn a subject systematically, from start to finish Challenge Solve a specific, practical problem in a realistic scenario Certification Prove skills you already have through a formal exam For this walkthrough, choose a beginner learning path.
Step 2: Enroll 🔗 The content’s detail page describes what it covers. Enroll from this page.
Enrolling creates your registration for that content and starts progress tracking. From then on the Academy records the item you are on, the items you have completed, your quiz grades, and your time spent, so you resume exactly where you left off. Every piece of content you have enrolled in appears in My Academy.
If the content’s organization attached an invitation to it, enrolling also accepts that invitation and adds you to the team that the invitation grants.
Your registration moves through these statuses, which your instructors also see in their console:
Status Meaning Registered You enrolled and have not yet started In Progress You are working through the content Completed You passed the final test Failed You did not pass Withdrawn The registration was withdrawn, by you or by an instructor in the content’s organization Step 3: Work through the learning path 🔗 The learning interface has three areas.
Course outline (left sidebar) shows the full structure of the learning path and your current position. You can move to any course at any time. Study area (center) displays the lesson content: text, images, and videos. Tags and categories (right sidebar) link to other Academy content on related topics. Work through the courses in order. Each course ends with an assessment that checks what you just learned.
Step 4: Take an assessment 🔗 Each assessment is a test with a pass percentage set by the content’s author. The test may also set a time limit, an attempt limit, and prerequisites.
Final and practice tests 🔗 A test marked final is mandatory: passing it is what completes the content. Other tests are practice. Take them to check your understanding; passing them is not required to complete the content.
Prerequisites 🔗 A test can require you to finish specific items first. If any prerequisite is missing from your completed items, the test does not start and reports Prerequisites not completed. Finish those items and try again.
Attempts and question rotation 🔗 Every time you start a test, you begin a new attempt. If the test sets a maximum number of attempts, you cannot start an attempt beyond it; the Academy reports Maximum attempts reached for this test with the number of attempts you have used. A test with no maximum allows unlimited attempts.
Tests can draw from a question bank larger than one sitting. Each attempt serves the next set of questions from the bank, wrapping back to the start when the bank runs out, so a retake usually shows you different questions.
Time limit 🔗 If the test sets a time limit, your attempt expires that many minutes after it starts. A submission after expiry is rejected with Test submission has expired. Each attempt is submitted once; a second submission of the same attempt is rejected.
Answering and scoring 🔗 Each question carries its own marks. The test supports three question types, each scored strictly:
Single answer. Select one option. You earn full marks only when you select exactly one option and it is the correct one.
Multiple answers. Select every option that applies. You earn full marks only when you select every correct option and no incorrect option. There is no partial credit.
Short answer. Type your answer. It must match the expected answer exactly, ignoring letter case and leading or trailing spaces. A blank answer is wrong.
Unanswered questions score zero. Your percentage is your score divided by the test’s total marks, and you pass when that percentage meets or exceeds the pass percentage. Scoring happens on the server the moment you submit, and the result shows your score, your pass or fail status, and which questions you answered correctly.
Step 5: Review your result 🔗 If you do not pass, the result marks which questions you answered correctly, so you can see exactly where to improve. Revisit the relevant courses through the outline, then start another attempt if the test’s attempt limit allows it.
If you pass, the assessment is complete and you move on to the next course.
Step 6: Earn your badge and certificate 🔗 When you pass the final test, your registration becomes Completed and the Academy awards the content’s credentials.
Badges. If the content names a completion badge, you receive it immediately. Each badge is tied to one piece of content, is awarded only when you finish everything that content requires, and stays on your public Layer5 Cloud profile. Badges are free.
Certificates. If the content defines a certificate, the Academy issues one in your first and last name, with the issuing organization and the issue date, and emails it to you. Each certificate has a unique ID and a public verification page that anyone can open from its link, so you can share it on professional profiles or a resume. Learning and exams are free; issuance of the official certificate is an optional, paid feature. Certificates do not expire.
Withdrawing from content 🔗 You can withdraw your own registration at any time. Withdrawing sets its status to Withdrawn. Instructors who hold the View Academy Metrics permission in the content’s organization can also withdraw learners from that organization’s content.
Frequently asked questions 🔗 Will my progress be saved if I leave and come back later? Yes. While you are enrolled, the Academy saves your current item, completed items, and quiz grades automatically. You resume where you left off.
Can I skip courses and jump directly to the exam? You can open any course at any time from the outline. A test with prerequisites does not start until you complete those prerequisite items, and the content is complete only when you pass its final test.
Can I download content for offline study? No. Academy content is available online only.
If I fail an assessment, can I retake it? Yes, up to the test’s attempt limit. A test with no limit allows unlimited retakes. Each retake usually draws different questions from the test’s question bank.
Does my certificate expire? No. Academy certificates carry an issue date and no expiration date.
How can I share my credential? Badges appear on your public Layer5 Cloud profile. Each certificate has a public verification page; share its link on professional profiles such as LinkedIn or on your resume so anyone can confirm it.
Where can I ask questions or discuss the content? Open a new topic or join an existing one in the community discussion forum, or join the Layer5 Community Slack.

A team is a named group of users inside one organization. Teams exist so an administrator can give a set of people the same access once, instead of granting it person by person. A team carries two kinds of access: roles held by its members, and workspace assignments that give the whole team access to a workspace and the resources in it.
Organizations contain any number of teams. A team has any number of members, and a user can belong to any number of teams. Teams are flat: a team cannot contain another team.
Team owner and Team Admin 🔗 Two separate things give someone authority over a team.
The owner is the user who created the team. Ownership is recorded once at creation and cannot be transferred. Team Admin is a role. A member who holds it can add and remove other members and assign the Team Admin role within the team. The two are independent. A team created from the Teams page gives its creator both: the creator becomes owner, a member, and Team Admin. A team created through the API alone records an owner but no membership and no Team Admin role until the owner adds themselves.
Action Who can do it Create a team Holders of the Create Team permission: Organization Admin, Team Admin, Academy Admin, Provider Admin Add a member Team Admin or owner of that team, or Provider Admin Remove another member Team Admin of that team, or Provider Admin Leave a team A member who is not a Team Admin and not the owner Delete a team Organization Admin or Owner, Provider Admin, or someone who is both owner and Team Admin of the team An Organization Admin who is neither owner nor Team Admin of a team cannot add or remove its members. To change membership, assign that Organization Admin the Team Admin role in the team first, or use a Provider Admin.
The owner cannot leave the team, even to hand it to someone else. Because ownership cannot be transferred, deleting the team is the only way for an owner to exit. A Team Admin who is not the owner cannot remove themselves either; only members without the Team Admin role can leave.
How a team grants access 🔗 A member’s permissions in an organization are the union of the roles they hold in the organization and in every team mapped into it. A role held in a team therefore applies across the organization in which the team lives, not only inside the team. Grant the Team Admin role deliberately: it carries team, user-viewing, and security management permissions organization-wide. See Roles and the Roles and Permissions reference.
A team also receives access to resources through workspaces: assigning a team to a workspace gives its members read-only access to the connections in the workspace’s environments. It does not open private designs to the team. Teams are not assigned to environments directly.
Who sees which teams 🔗 The Teams page lists the teams of the selected organization with name, description, owner, and creation time. Every authenticated member of the organization receives the same list; it is not narrowed to your own teams or to teams you administer. A team’s member list is likewise visible to any member of the organization.
Membership rules 🔗 Adding a member. The Teams page only offers users who already belong to the organization. The API accepts any existing user, so treat organization membership as the intended precondition and add people to the organization first (see Manage Users). Adding is idempotent. Adding someone who is already a member changes nothing. Notification. An added member receives an email unless their notification preferences disable organization and team user-management email. Invitations. Teams have no invite link or join request of their own. To bring someone into an organization and into specific teams in one step, create an organization invitation that lists the teams and team roles (see Invite Users). Removing a member. Removing a member ends their membership and every role they held in that team. It does not touch their organization membership, organization roles, or other teams. Deleting a team 🔗 Deleting a team hides it from team lists and lookups. The user accounts of its members, and every resource they own, remain. Delete removes only the team record, so workspace assignments and the roles recorded on member rows are not cleaned up by the deletion itself. Before deleting a team, remove its members and unassign it from workspaces so no access outlives it.
What is not available 🔗 Layer5 Cloud does not provide these today:
Team invite links and team join requests. Transferring team ownership. Creating a new user account from inside a team. Create the user in the organization, or use an invitation that lists the team. Limits on the number of teams per organization or per user, and unique team names. Two teams in one organization can share a name. Plan restrictions: teams are available on every plan. For the steps, see Manage Teams.

This guide outlines methods for creating user accounts, adding users to organizations, inviting new members, and managing user access within Layer5 Cloud to maintain a secure and organized environment.
Create User Account 🔗 Seamlessly initiate new user accounts, ensuring a smooth onboarding process. Specify user details, such as email, and tailor their access by adding them to one or more organizations. Optionally assign roles, defining their scope within the platform. Complete the process by sending a personalized account setup email, streamlining the user’s introduction to Layer5 Cloud.
Permission Required for User Creation Only Provider Admins and Organization Admins can create users. For more information, see Roles. Add / Remove Existing User 🔗 This section explains how to add existing Layer5 Cloud users to one of your organizations or remove them.
Open Design Adding a User to an Organization 🔗 If someone already has a Layer5 Cloud account but isn’t part of your organization, you can add them.
Go to the Users tab in the Identity section Click the Add User button. Select the organization to which you want to add the user. Select the user from the list of available users. Assign appropriate roles within the organization. Removing Users from an Organization 🔗 You can remove users from an organization one by one or several at once. This action takes away their membership and access to that specific organization’s resources but doesn’t delete their overall Layer5 Cloud account.
Method 1: Individual User Removal (One by One) 🔗 Locate the User: Find the specific user you wish to remove from the list. Use Row Action: Click the “Remove User” icon. Confirm: When prompted, confirm your decision to remove the user from the organization. Method 2: Bulk User Removal (Multiple Users at Once) 🔗 Select Users: Use the checkboxes next to each user’s name to select all the users you intend to remove. Use Bulk Action: Click the “Delete” button. Confirm: When prompted, confirm that you want to remove all the selected users from the organization. What Removal Ends 🔗 Removing a member ends every access-bearing relationship they hold inside that organization, as a single operation:
Their organization membership, together with the organization roles attached to it. Their membership in that organization’s teams, together with the team roles attached to those memberships. Both matter, because permissions reach a user through the roles carried on those memberships. A keychain granted by a team role is revoked by the removal just as an organization role’s keychain is, so a removed member is left holding no keys in the organization by either route. Both removal methods above behave identically in this respect; removing several members at once applies the same operation to each one.
Removal does not affect:
The person’s Layer5 Cloud user account, which continues to exist. Their membership in any other organization, or in teams belonging to those organizations. Designs, environments, and other resources they created, which remain in the organization. Removal is not reversible from the Users tab. To restore someone’s access, add them to the organization again and reassign their organization roles and team memberships. Neither returns on its own.
Team Access Is Not Itemized in the Confirmation The confirmation shown after a removal reports only that the member was removed from the organization. It does not list the team memberships that ended with it. Review the member’s teams before removing them if you need a record of what their removal revoked. Organization Owners Cannot Be Removed An attempt to remove the organization’s owner is rejected. Transfer ownership to another administrator first, then remove the former owner. See Roles and Permissions. Invite User via Email 🔗 You can invite new or existing users to join one of your organizations by sending them an email invitation.
How to Invite: Click the “Invite User” button. Enter the person’s First Name, Last Name, and Email address. Assign them to a target Organization. Optionally, Team(s) and Organization Role(s) they will receive. Layer5 Cloud sends an invitation email to the user. What the User Does: The person you invited will click a link in the email to accept. If they’re new to Layer5 Cloud, they’ll need to create an account first before they can join your organization. Permissions for Role Assignment An Organization Admin can assign organization roles to users, but provider roles can only be assigned by Provider Admins. For more information, see Roles.

body:
Organizations are the basic unit of multi-tenancy inside of Layer5 Cloud. The identity structure is highly flexible: organizations can have any number of teams, teams can have any number of users, and users can belong to any number of teams and organizations.
Below is an overview of the core identity components within the Layer5 Cloud.
Identity 🔗 Organizations serve as the fundamental component of multi-tenancy within the Layer5 Cloud.
They act as the top-level parent entity. All users and teams ultimately roll up to an organization. While Free plan users are limited to a single default organization, enterprise environments can leverage organizations to strictly isolate resources, billing, and access control across entirely different business units.
Outside of grouping users together, teams offer controlled access to workspaces and to workspace resources such as environments and managed and unmanaged connections.
Administrators can create teams as child units below the top-level organization. This allows you to apply unique settings, permissions, and workspace access to a specific set of users without altering the parent organization’s settings.
Each user account represents an individual collaborator. Individual user accounts exist beyond the bounds of organizations.
Anyone who uses Layer5 Cloud signs into a user account, which acts as your sovereign identity. Your user account can independently own resources such as workspaces, designs, connections, and tokens. Any action taken on the platform is directly attributed to your individual user account, regardless of which teams or organizations you belong to.
Organizational Units 🔗 Layer5 Cloud uses a hierarchical structure to isolate resources and manage users at scale:
Provider Organizations: The top-level entity that can manage multiple tenant organizations. Tenant Organizations: Individual customer or project-specific organizations (e.g., Layer5, Intel). Teams: Logical groupings of users within an organization to facilitate collaborative management. Users: Individual accounts that are members of teams and organizations. Role and Access Control 🔗 Access is granted through Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Roles are assigned at different levels of the organizational hierarchy:
Provider Administrators: Management of provider-level settings and tenant organizations. Organization Administrators: Full control over an entire tenant organization. Organization Billing Managers: Access restricted to subscription and financial management. Team Administrators: Management of specific team resources and memberships. Workspace Administrators: Management of workspace-level resources and access. How Identity, Access, and Authorization Fit Together 🔗 It is tempting to assume that organization membership alone decides what a user can see and do. It does not. Identity, access, and authorization in Layer5 Cloud are decided by a combination of three independent mechanisms that compose on top of the organization:
Authentication - the organization’s connected identity provider (IdP). Each organization is connected to an identity provider that establishes who a user is. More than one organization can - and commonly does - share the same identity provider. An organization may instead bring its own identity provider (BYOC), in which case it authenticates against its own dedicated provider. See Identity Services. Generic authorization - keys → keychains → roles. Permission keys roll up into keychains, which are assigned to roles, which are assigned to users. This decides what operations a user may perform - and it is evaluated per organization. The same person can hold different roles, and therefore a different effective set of capabilities, in each organization they belong to. Granular access - resource-access mappings. A specific resource (for example, a single design) can be shared with an individual user. These mappings grant access to that one resource and deliberately cross organizational boundaries: a user does not need to be a member of an organization to open a resource in it when a mapping grants that access. This is by design - it is what makes cross-organization collaboration possible. The practical consequence is that the same human can be a member of several organizations and have a different set of capabilities in each, while also being able to reach individual shared resources in organizations they do not belong to at all.
Security Boundaries 🔗 Because identity and authorization are layered, “where is the boundary?” has two complementary answers, depending on which layer you mean.
The organization is the unit of tenancy and the core security boundary. Everything else - teams, workspaces, roles, keychains, keys - composes on top of the organization. Resources, billing, and access control are isolated per organization.
From the authorization perspective, an organization context is itself a boundary. Because keys, keychains, and roles are evaluated per (user, organization), a user acting in the context of one organization has an independently scoped set of capabilities from the same user acting in another - including when those organizations are reached through different per-organization subdomains. Operating “inside” one organization’s subdomain does not carry a user’s permissions from another organization with them.
From the host perspective, the authentication boundary is set by the connected identity provider - not by the shape of the URL. Layer5 Cloud organizations may be reached on the canonical host, on a custom subdomain that sits under the same parent (base) domain as that canonical host, or on a fully custom domain on a different base domain. Across all of these:
Same identity provider source means the same security boundary.
Organizations that share an identity provider - typical for the canonical host and for custom subdomains that use the shared, central provider - sit within the same authentication boundary. An organization that brings its own identity provider (BYOC) is a distinct authentication boundary, regardless of how its host is named. The DNS shape of the host is not the boundary; the identity provider behind it is. See Identity Services and Social sign-in on a custom domain for how this plays out across host types.
Keys, Keychains, Sessions, and Tokens 🔗 Four building blocks carry authorization and authentication:
Keys: The atomic permissions. A key allows one action, such as Create Team. Keychains: Bundles of keys. Roles hold keychains. Sessions: One per sign-in. A browser session lasts 24 hours by default and can be ended from the Sessions tab. API tokens: Credentials for scripts, CI/CD, and Meshery clients. A token acts as your user account and never expires, so it stays valid until you delete it. For the permission keys, lifetimes, and endpoints in one place, see the Security Reference. For tasks, see the security guides.
Need more detail? 🔗 Check out the Roles Reference for a complete matrix of permissions for each role.

body:
The invitation system gives you precise control over how members join your organization, allowing you to streamline onboarding and enhance security.
You can create highly customized invitations for any scenario, from onboarding specific individuals to launching large-scale community challenges. Each invitation can be configured with expiration dates, usage quotas, and pre-assigned roles, ensuring new members get the right access from the moment they join.
Required permission From Layer5 Cloud v1.0.293, creating, editing, and deleting invitations requires the Manage Invitations permission within your organization. That one permission also covers choosing the roles and teams an invitation grants, so anyone who can write an invitation, Academy Admins included, can specify its roles. Contact your organization administrator if you need access. Default organization state 🔗 By default, organizations are closed: there is no open registration. A user cannot join your organization simply by navigating to a URL - they must either click a valid invitation link or register through a page associated with an organization that has a default invitation configured.
When no default invitation is set, new users who arrive at your organization’s registration page are registered as platform users but are not automatically added to your organization. They will have no organization membership and no roles until an administrator adds them or they accept an invitation link.
Two ways to designate the open signup invitation An organization’s open signup invitation can be set in two places: the invitation picker in Edit Organization, or the isDefault setting on the invitation itself.
The Edit Organization selection takes precedence. The isDefault marker is used when no selection has been made there, or when the invitation that selection points at no longer exists.
Roles are not assigned automatically When a user joins an organization via invitation, they receive only the roles explicitly listed on that invitation. If the invitation has no roles configured, the user joins with no role. Use the roles field on each invitation to ensure new members receive the correct initial permissions. Key capabilities 🔗 The invitation system provides three main areas of control to help you manage access effectively.
Create custom invitations for any audience 🔗 Tailor each invitation to your specific needs with three flexible modes:
Precise invitation: Target a single user by specifying their full email address. Domain-wide invitation: Onboard an entire organization at once by allowing any email from a specific domain (e.g., @layer5.io). Public invitation: Leave the email field blank to create an open link for public events (e.g., Academy Challenge invitations). Use domain wildcards carefully Patterns like @company.com allow anyone with that domain. Verify ownership and pair with roles and teams that grant only necessary access. Control the invitation lifecycle 🔗 Manage access with settings that put you in control:
Expiration date: Set a specific date and time after which the invitation link can no longer be used to join. This prevents new signups but does not affect members who have already accepted the invitation. Usage quota: Limit the number of times an invitation can be used. The invitations table shows current acceptance count alongside the limit (e.g., 2 / 5). Blank means unlimited If expiresAt is not set, the invitation never expires. If quota is not set, the invitation has unlimited uses. Manage invitations dynamically 🔗 Instantly revoke access by switching an invitation’s status between enabled and disabled at any time. A disabled invitation can be re-enabled later without recreating it.
How to create an invitation 🔗 To create a new invitation, navigate to the Invitations page from the main menu. Click the Create New Invitation button to open the creation dialog.
Email notifications After an invitation is created, a notification email is sent only to addresses listed in the emails field that are exact email addresses. Domain-wide patterns (e.g., @layer5.io) and public invitations (empty emails field) do not trigger individual notification emails - share the invitation link directly in those cases. Invitation properties explained 🔗 Property Description emails List of email addresses or domain patterns allowed to use the invitation. Exact addresses (e.g., user@example.com) and domain patterns (e.g., @example.com) are both supported. If empty, the invitation is public: any email address can use it. roles List of roles automatically assigned to new members upon accepting the invitation. If empty, the user joins with no role. Each role must be an existing organization role. Provider-wide roles, such as Provider Admin, cannot be granted by an invitation, and an invitation listing one, or a role that does not exist, is refused when it is created or edited. teams List of teams new members are automatically added to upon accepting the invitation. If empty, the user joins no team. Each team must be an existing team of your organization; an invitation listing any other team is refused when it is created or edited. quota Number that limits how many users can accept the invitation. If not set, there is no usage limit. expiresAt Date after which the invitation link can no longer be used. Does not affect existing members. If not set, the invitation never expires. status Invitation status: enabled = active and usable; disabled = inactive (can be re-enabled later). name A human-readable name used to identify the invitation. description Additional information about the invitation’s purpose, for internal reference. acceptanceOutcome What accepting the invitation does. direct_membership (the default) makes the user a member of the inviting organization. child_organization instead creates a new organization for the user beneath the inviting organization. See Choosing what accepting does. Creating or editing a child_organization invitation requires the Create Organization permission in the inviting organization. isDefault When enabled, marks this invitation as the organization’s open signup invitation. Users who register through your organization’s registration page are automatically enrolled through this invitation, receiving the pre-configured roles and teams. Without a default invitation, the registration page does not automatically add users to the organization. Only one invitation can be designated as the default at a time - designating a new one clears the previous. Like every other change to an invitation, turning this setting on or off requires the Manage Invitations permission. An edit that does not include this setting leaves it as it was. From Layer5 Cloud v1.0.289, emails, roles, and teams can each be left empty or omitted: the invitation then accepts any email address, grants no roles, or adds no teams.
Managing existing invitations 🔗 All existing invitations are displayed in a table showing key details for each invitation: its name and description, a copyable acceptance link, the owner, expiration date, quota usage, assigned roles and teams, and current status.
You can filter the list using the filter control at the top right of the table. Available filters are:
Status - show only enabled or disabled invitations Roles - show invitations that grant a specific role Teams - show invitations that add members to a specific team From the table you can perform the following management actions on each invitation:
Copy Link: Click the copy icon next to the invitation URL to copy it for sharing. Edit Invitation: Click the pencil icon to open the edit dialog and modify any invitation properties. Delete Invitation: Click the trash icon to permanently remove the invitation. This action cannot be undone. If another administrator deletes an invitation while your edit dialog is open, saving reports that the invitation was not found rather than reporting success. Close the dialog and reload the invitations table to see the current list. Whenever an edit cannot be saved, the dialog reports the specific reason it was refused.
Tracking who has accepted an invitation 🔗 The Quota column in the invitations table always shows the number of users who have accepted an invitation alongside the configured limit - for example, 2 / 5 if a quota is set, or 2 / Unlimited if no quota is configured. This lets you monitor uptake at a glance.
To see the individual users who are now members of the organization, navigate to the User Management page. Members who joined via invitation appear there alongside their assigned roles.
What happens when a user accepts an invitation 🔗 When a user clicks an acceptance link and is logged in, the system performs the following steps in order. Steps 3 to 5 describe a direct_membership invitation, the default; a child_organization invitation replaces them, as described after the list.
Validates the invitation - confirms it exists, is enabled, has not passed its expiration date, and has not exceeded its quota. Checks email eligibility - verifies the user’s email matches the invitation’s emails list. An empty list allows any email (public invitation). Adds the user to the organization - the user immediately becomes a member of the organization that owns the invitation. Assigns roles - all roles configured on the invitation are assigned to the user in that organization. If no roles are configured, the user joins with no role. Adds the user to teams - the user is added to all teams configured on the invitation. For a direct_membership invitation, role and team assignment failures are non-blocking: the user is still added to the organization even if an individual role or team assignment fails.
For a child_organization invitation, the user is not added to the inviting organization. Instead, a child organization is created for them with the invitation’s roles and teams applied inside it, as described in Choosing what accepting an invitation does. That acceptance is all or nothing: if any part of it fails, including a single role or team, nothing is created and the acceptance is not counted against the quota.
Choosing what accepting an invitation does 🔗 Every invitation has an acceptanceOutcome that decides where the accepting user ends up.
In the Create New Invitation and Edit Invitation dialogs, choose it under When accepted. Direct membership is selected by default. Child organization appears only if you have the Create Organization permission in the current organization. If you lack that permission and edit an invitation that already uses Child organization, the option is shown selected but cannot be changed.
acceptanceOutcome Result of accepting direct_membership (default) The user joins the inviting organization with the invitation’s roles and teams, as described above. child_organization A new organization named My Organization is created as a child of the inviting organization. The user is its owner and Organization Admin, it gets the standard My Team and My Workspace, the invitation’s roles are granted in it, and teams with the same names and descriptions as the invitation’s teams are created in it with the user as a member. The user does not become a member of the inviting organization, and the inviting organization’s own teams are unchanged. A few things hold for both outcomes:
Every team listed on an invitation must belong to the inviting organization. An invitation that lists another organization’s team is refused when it is created, edited, or accepted. Accepting is counted once per person. Accepting the same invitation again does not create a second child organization or use more of the quota. When someone creates a new account through your organization’s open signup invitation, they do not also receive a separate personal organization; the invitation decides where they land. If the invitation turns out not to apply (for example, its quota is used up), a personal organization is created for them as usual. How the open signup invitation is applied at sign-in 🔗 The open signup invitation is not limited to first-time registration. It is applied whenever someone signs in through your organization’s own address, such as its custom domain, on every sign-in method that address offers, including email and password as well as social sign-in. Someone who already has a Layer5 Cloud account and has never been a member of your organization becomes a member on that sign-in, with the roles and teams the invitation configures. When the open signup invitation is a child_organization invitation, that person instead receives their own child organization beneath yours, as described in Choosing what accepting an invitation does.
It is applied only to people who are not already members, which has two consequences worth knowing:
Roles and teams are never re-applied to an existing member. If you remove a role or a team from someone who joined this way, signing in again does not restore it. Each person is counted once. Repeated sign-ins by the same person do not increase the invitation’s acceptance count or add them to the organization a second time. When open signup adds nobody A person can sign in successfully and still not join your organization. The open signup invitation is applied only when all of the following hold:
Its status is enabled. Its expiration date has not passed. Its quota has not been reached. The person’s email address matches its emails list. An empty list matches everyone. When one of them does not hold, someone who is not already a member signs in as a platform user with no membership and no roles in your organization, and no error is shown to them. Existing members are unaffected: they keep the membership, roles, and teams they already have. Check these four properties first when people who sign in at your organization’s address are not appearing under User Management.
Use cases and examples 🔗 The invitation system offers flexible configurations to fit a variety of use cases.
How invitation links handle unauthenticated users When a user who is not logged in clicks an invitation link, the system saves the invitation ID in a short-lived 30-minute cookie and redirects them to the organization’s registration page. After a successful login or signup, the system reads the cookie and automatically completes the invitation acceptance with the outcome the invitation’s acceptanceOutcome selects: membership in the organization with the configured roles and teams, or a new child organization. Scenario 1: Inviting a single team member 🔗 Goal: Provide a new employee with a secure, single-use invitation that grants the correct initial permissions. Configuration: Email: Set to the new member’s specific email address. Roles: Assign their specific role (e.g., Developer). Teams: Add them directly to their project team (e.g., Frontend-Team). Quota: Set to 1 to ensure the link is only used once. Scenario 2: Opening registration for an entire organization 🔗 Goal: Allow all employees from your company to join using their corporate email without individual invitations. Configuration: Email: Use a domain pattern to cover all employees (e.g., @yourcompany.com). Roles: Assign a default role for all new members. Scenario 3: Launching a community challenge 🔗 Goal: Create a public signup link for a limited-time community event with a maximum number of participants. Configuration: Email: Leave blank for public access. Name: Give it a clear name like “Layer5 Challenge 2025”. Expiration date: Set to the date and time the challenge registration closes. Quota: Set to the maximum number of participants (e.g., 100). Roles: Assign a temporary role like Learner. Managing learner costs The available seats for learners are determined by your organization’s subscription plan. Please be mindful of your subscription to manage costs effectively. Scenario 4: Granting temporary partner access 🔗 Goal: Give an external partner secure access to specific resources only for the duration of a project. Configuration: Email: Use the partner’s domain (e.g., @partner.com). Teams: Add them only to a shared project team (e.g., Project-X-Shared). Expiration date: Set to the project’s end date to prevent new signups after the project concludes. Description: Add a note for internal reference, such as “Temporary access for Project X contractors”. Expiration does not remove existing members Setting an expiration date prevents new users from using the invitation link after that date. It does not automatically remove partners who have already joined. When the project ends, manually remove those users from the organization or team. Public invitations Public links can be forwarded broadly. Always set an expiration date and a quota to limit unintended signups.

User Accounts 🔗 Anyone who uses Layer5 Cloud signs into a user account. Your user account is your identity on Layer5 Cloud and has a username and profile. For example, see Five’s profile.
Five - Platform Engineer Organization: Orbital Labs
Role: User (Platform Engineer)
Plan: Team
Curious, enthusiastic, and reliably the first to discover that a feature works differently than the docs say it does.
Maya Chen - Org Admin Organization: Orbital Labs
Role: Org Admin + Development Team Admin
Plan: Team
Voice of reason. Has a calendar block called “Preventing Five from touching prod” that recurs every Friday at 4:45 PM.
Your user account can own resources such as workspaces, designs, connections, credentials, tokens, Any time you take any action on Layer5 Cloud such as creating a design or reviewing a deployment request, the action is attributed to your user account.
Each user account is subscribed to a plan: Free, Team, or Enterprise. All user accounts can own an unlimited number of public and private workspaces, with an unlimited number of collaborators on those workspaces. If you use Layer5 Free, private workspaces owned by your user account have a limited feature set. You can upgrade to Layer5 Enterprise to get a full feature set for private workspaces.
Note: Free plan users are limited to a single organization - their initial default organization, typically named “My Organization”.
Info For more information, see Layer5 subscription plans. Teams allow you to organize users into groups and conveniently assign access to workspaces or to assign roles with associated keychains and keys to control permissions.
Info You need to have the default Team Admin role to assign permissions to users in your team. For more information, see Teams. Organizations may have any number of teams and teams may have any number of users. User accounts are treated as sovereign entities that are owned by individual individuals, not by corporations.
Organization and teams may have any number of users accounts. User accounts are treated as sovereign entities that are owned by individual individuals, not by corporations.
Users and their tokens may be authorized to access resources. Users can be created and managed by the Provider Admins, Organization Admins, or Team Admins. Users of one organization may be granted access to resources (e.g. Workspaces and Designs) of another organization. User entitlement, roles and permissions are org-scoped, meaning that the entitlements and permissions that a given user has in one organization does not necessarily reflect the same level of access that their membership in another oganziation does.
Info Only Provider Admins and Organization Admin can create users. For more information, see Roles. Account Linking 🔗 You can link your Layer5 account to supported social sign-in providers after signing up, and you can unlink previously added providers at any time. Layer5 Cloud can also link providers automatically during sign-in when the provider returns a verified email address that already belongs to your account. This is how it works:
You create an account with the email address alice@example.com and a password. When signing in later, click to sign in with a social sign-in provider such as GitHub or Google that returns the same verified email address alice@example.com. Layer5 Cloud recognizes that the verified email address already belongs to your existing account and automatically links that provider. You are not prompted to re-enter your password for this linking step. After the link is created, you can sign in with either your password or any linked social sign-in provider. If a provider that is already linked to your account later reports a different verified email address, Layer5 Cloud still signs you in to the same account. The email already stored on your Layer5 account is not silently replaced or automatically updated.
Rules and Limitations
You cannot link the same social sign-in to multiple Layer5 accounts If you delete your account, any linked OAuth providers (e.g., GitHub) are automatically unlinked Re-registering with the same email does not automatically re-link the OAuth provider Automatic linking depends on the provider returning a verified email address If a linked provider later reports a different verified email address, Layer5 Cloud preserves the email already stored on your account instead of replacing it automatically You may unlink a social sign-in provider at any time To link or unlink a provider, see Manage Your Account.
Account Deletion 🔗 When a user deletes their account, the following behaviors apply: To delete your own account, and for the case where deletion is refused, see Delete your account.
1. Personal Resources
Personal content (e.g., unpublished designs) is soft-deleted internally. There is currently no recovery option available to users. 2. Published Content
Published content (e.g., items in the Catalog) remains accessible to the public This ensures that published work continues to benefit the community, even after the account is deleted. 3. Organization Ownership
If you are the only Org Admin or Owner, the organization may become unmanageable after you delete your account. It is strongly recommended to assign multiple admins before deletion. 4. Organization Deletion
Organizations cannot be deleted just by leaving or deleting accounts. Only Org Owners can delete an organization, and it must be done as an explicit, manual action. Org Admins do not have this permission. 5. Re-registering with the Same Email
Signing up again with the same email address creates a new, separate account. The new account: Will not automatically regain access to resources linked to the deleted account. May, in rare cases, display inconsistent profile data (e.g., old display name in design attribution). Info This is a known issue. Future versions of Layer5 Cloud will address it through UUID-based identity linking. 6. Deployed Designs
Deployed designs are not automatically removed when a user deletes their account. This ensures that deployments remain stable unless explicitly taken down. Info While account deletion is permanent for end-users, future versions of Layer5 Cloud may introduce:
A pre-deletion flow for reviewing and exporting data The ability to transfer ownership of resources (e.g., workspaces, teams, organizations) Support for recovering accounts or restoring deleted data
