The GitHub integration connects your GitHub account to Layer5 Cloud through the Layer5 GitHub App. Once connected, you can browse the repositories you granted, pick Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Docker Compose files, and Meshery designs, and import each file as a design. The same connection can also install a pull-request snapshot workflow in your repositories.
Use it when your infrastructure already lives in Git and you want those files on the canvas without downloading and uploading them one at a time. For a one-off file, import it directly instead.
Before you start 🔗 A Layer5 Cloud account. A GitHub account that can install a GitHub App on the user or organization that owns the repositories. For an organization, an owner may have to approve the installation. The View Connections permission, which shows the Integrations area in Layer5 Cloud. See Roles and Permissions. Self-hosted GitHub App requirements 🔗 The hosted service at cloud.layer5.io provides the Layer5 GitHub App. A self-hosted deployment uses its own GitHub App, and from Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287 that App must meet every item below. See the matching values in Helm Chart Values.
Each Layer5 Cloud deployment has its own GitHub App. Do not share one App between deployments, such as production and staging. The App’s first callback URL is this deployment’s https://<host>/api/integrations/github/callback, where <host> is the deployment’s public hostname. Layer5 Cloud sends GitHub no redirect_uri, so GitHub always returns to the first callback URL. Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation is enabled. githubappid, the private key, githubAppClientId and githubAppClientSecret all come from that same App. How the connection works 🔗 The connection belongs to you, not to your organization. Each user has at most one GitHub connection. A teammate who wants to import from GitHub connects their own account. GitHub confirms which installations are yours. When you install and authorize the App, GitHub reports which installations of the Layer5 GitHub App your GitHub account can access, and only those are connected. This check ships in Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287. The App sees only what you grant. At install time GitHub asks whether the App may reach all repositories or only the ones you select. Layer5 Cloud lists exactly those repositories. Widen or narrow the grant at any time by running the setup again. Cloud reads the default branch. Scans and imports always use each repository’s default branch. Import is read-only. Importing creates designs in Layer5 Cloud. It never writes to your repository. Only the optional snapshot stages commit a file. Connect and import 🔗 The Connect wizard has seven stages. You can start it from the Integrations area of Spaces in Layer5 Cloud, or from the Extensions page of a Meshery Server by enabling the Kanvas Snapshot GitHub Action.
Stage What happens Required Connect GitHub App GitHub asks you to install the Layer5 GitHub App on a personal or organization account and to choose repository access. Yes Select Repositories Lists the repositories the App can reach. Add Repository reopens the GitHub installation page so you can change access or install on another account. Yes Import Designs Lists the files in the chosen repositories. You select files or whole directories and import them. Yes Select a design for snapshots Chooses one file per repository for pull-request snapshots. Optional Configure Secrets Generates an API token that you add to the repository as a secret. Optional Add Workflows Commits the snapshot workflow to the repository. Optional Finish Summarizes what was imported and which repositories received the workflow. Yes If you open the GitHub card’s connection count before you have connected, the GitHub Connections window reads “No GitHub connections yet”. Click Connect GitHub there to start the wizard, or follow Learn how the GitHub integration works to return to this guide.
The three optional stages are covered in Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot.
What you can import 🔗 A checkbox switches the file list between every file and only the types Layer5 Cloud can import.
Type Notes Meshery design Becomes a design immediately. Kubernetes manifest Kept as source and converted when you open it. Helm chart Kept as source and converted when you open it. Docker Compose file Kept as source and converted when you open it. Kustomize Kept as source and converted when you open it. Layer5 Cloud accepts files with these extensions: .yml, .yaml, .json, .tar, .tar.gz, .tar.tgz, .zip, and .gz. A file that fails sanitizing or identification is reported as invalid or unsupported.
What an import produces 🔗 One design per file. The design is named after the file, including its extension. Private by default. The importing user owns it. Publish or share it when you are ready. See Publish Designs. Placed in your selected workspace. From Layer5 Cloud v1.0.291, each new design is added to the workspace selected in your current organization, or to the organization’s first workspace when none is selected, so it shows in My Designs. Traceable to its source. The design records its repository, path, and branch. Renaming the design does not break that link. Directories import recursively. Selecting a directory imports every supported file beneath it. Failures are per file. An unsupported or invalid file produces an error entry and does not stop the other files. The result screen lists what succeeded and what failed. Imported designs appear in My Designs. After the import, a notification sums up the result, for example 2 designs imported, 1 updated, 3 already imported and skipped.
Import from a repository again 🔗 When you run the wizard again for a repository you have imported from, for example with Reconfigure on the GitHub card, files you already imported carry a check mark. Hover over it to see which design the file became, for example Imported as "nginx-deployment". If you have nothing new to import, click Next without importing.
A file is matched to its design by repository, path and branch, never by name. When your selection includes files you imported before, Layer5 Cloud asks what to do with them before importing. The prompt lists the files, up to five followed by “and N more”, and offers three choices:
Choice What happens to the previously imported files Import new files only (default) They are left as they are. Only files that were never imported become new designs. Update the existing designs Each design’s content is replaced with the file’s current content. The design keeps its ID, sharing and links. Edits made to it since the last import are lost. Import them again as new designs Additional designs are created alongside the existing ones. Click Import to proceed with your choice, or Cancel to change the selection. A file selected both on its own and through its directory is imported once.
See where a design came from 🔗 In the table view of My Designs, the Source column shows the repository and file path of each imported design, followed by the branch when it is not the repository’s default. Hover over it to see the full source, or click it to open the file on GitHub. The cell is empty for a design that was not imported from GitHub. The column appears on large screens.
An imported design’s details page has a Source section below the left panel that lists the repository, which links to the file on GitHub, the file path and the branch (“Default branch” when the design follows the repository’s default branch). The source stays with the design when you edit it, so later imports and refreshes still recognize it.
Large repositories 🔗 Layer5 Cloud scans a repository by reading its full file tree from GitHub and keeps the result for five minutes. GitHub truncates the tree for very large repositories. When that happens, the file list is partial and Cloud answers with HTTP status 206. If a file you need is missing, select its directory or import it directly.
Manage imported designs 🔗 From Layer5 Cloud v1.0.291, your GitHub connection lists every design you have imported from GitHub, with actions to open each one or bring it up to date with its file.
On the Integrations area of Spaces in Layer5 Cloud, click the GitHub card’s connection count to open GitHub Connections. Click your connection to expand it. Imported designs lists your imported designs, newest first: Column Shows Design The design’s name. Type The format the design was imported from, or - when it is not known. Source The repository, file path and, when it is not the default, branch the design was imported from. Click it to open the file on GitHub. Last updated When the design last changed. Actions Open design opens the design in My Designs. Open source file on GitHub opens the file in a new tab. Refresh from source updates the design from the file. The list shows only your own designs, and only you can see it on your connection. It includes every design you imported from GitHub, whatever its workspace, so designs imported before Layer5 Cloud v1.0.291 are listed here until you move them to a workspace. When you have not imported any designs yet, it reads “No imported designs yet” and offers Import designs, which reopens the wizard. If the list cannot be loaded, it reads “Imported designs could not be loaded”; click Try again.
Refresh a design from its source 🔗 When a file changes in its repository, refresh the design instead of importing the file again:
In Imported designs, click Refresh from source on the design’s row. The action appears only if your role holds Import Design. Confirm with Refresh. The design’s content is replaced with the file’s current content on GitHub, and changes made to the design since it was imported or last refreshed are lost. The refresh updates the same design, so it keeps its ID, owner, visibility, catalog data, workspace assignments and links. Only its content and source change. A design that was not imported as a Meshery design keeps its source file unconverted and is converted the next time you open it.
Check or reconfigure the connection 🔗 Layer5 Cloud verifies with GitHub that the App installation the wizard opens on still exists. If you uninstalled the App from that account in GitHub, Cloud removes only that installation from the connection and opens the wizard on the next installation your connection holds. Cloud deletes the connection only once none of its installations remain. Run the wizard again to reconnect.
To change which repositories the App can read, rerun the wizard and use Add Repository. GitHub keeps the App installed and updates its grant. When you install the App on another account, the connection is updated with every installation your GitHub account can access, so the new installation joins the ones you already had.
Re-authorize an existing connection 🔗 A connection created before Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287 opens the wizard on Re-authorize your GitHub connection, and its repositories cannot be used until GitHub confirms which installations your GitHub account can access. Click Re-authorize. GitHub returns you to the wizard, without asking again if you have already authorized the App, and your repository settings are kept.
Remove the connection 🔗 Delete the GitHub connection from the Integrations area, or from the Connections page of a Meshery Server. You can delete only a connection you own, and you need the Delete a connection permission.
Deleting the connection removes it from Layer5 Cloud. It does not uninstall the App from GitHub, delete imported designs, or remove a workflow already committed to a repository. To revoke the App’s access to your repositories, uninstall the Layer5 GitHub App in your GitHub account settings. Delete .github/workflows/kanvas.yml from a repository to stop its snapshots.
Troubleshooting 🔗 You see Cause What to do A repository is missing from the list The App is not installed on it. Use Add Repository and grant access in GitHub. invalid or unsupported file for a file The extension or content is not an importable type. Check the file against the table above. A partial file list GitHub truncated the tree of a large repository. Select the directory you need, or import the file directly. GitHub did not confirm that your GitHub account can access that installation, so it was not connected. The GitHub account you are signed in with cannot access the installation you chose. Sign in to GitHub with an account that can access it, then connect GitHub again. Your GitHub account cannot access any installation of the GitHub App. Install the app on your account or organization to connect a repository. GitHub reports no installation of the App that your GitHub account can access. Install the App on your account or organization, then connect GitHub again. GitHub authorization is not configured for this environment, so GitHub cannot be connected. Please contact support. The deployment is missing the GitHub App’s OAuth client ID or client secret. On the hosted service, contact support. On a self-hosted deployment, set env.githubAppClientId and env.githubAppClientSecret. Connect, Add Repository or Re-authorize ends anywhere other than the wizard, or shows GitHub authorization could not be completed, so GitHub was not connected. Please connect GitHub again. or This GitHub connection was not started from this session, took too long, or was already used, so GitHub was not connected. Please connect GitHub again. You declined the authorization on GitHub, took more than five minutes on GitHub, reused a return page, or are signed in to Layer5 Cloud as a different user than the one who started. Changing repository access or installing the App from GitHub’s own settings or App page, instead of the wizard, returns you without the request the wizard started. On a self-hosted deployment, the GitHub App can also miss one of its requirements. Connect GitHub again from the wizard, approve the authorization, and finish on GitHub within five minutes. Change repository access with Add Repository, not in GitHub’s settings. On a self-hosted deployment, check every item in Self-hosted GitHub App requirements. The wizard shows Re-authorize your GitHub connection The connection predates installation confirmation. Click Re-authorize. See Re-authorize an existing connection. The connection vanished The App was uninstalled from every account it was connected through. Run the wizard again. unable to create JWT for GitHub integration, please uninstall app and try again The deployment cannot sign requests as the GitHub App. On the hosted service, uninstall and reinstall the App. On a self-hosted deployment, check the GitHub App credentials in the deployment settings. Refresh from source fails because the source file no longer exists The file was moved, renamed or deleted in its repository. Import the file from its new location. Refresh from source fails because the file is not importable The file is no longer a valid Helm chart, Kubernetes manifest, Docker Compose file or Meshery design. Fix the file in its repository and refresh again. Refresh from source fails because the App cannot reach the repository The GitHub App no longer has access to the repository. Reconfigure the connection with Add Repository and grant the App access to the repository. Refresh from source fails because GitHub could not be reached GitHub was unreachable, rate-limited the request or rejected the App’s credentials. Retry in a few minutes, and reconfigure the connection if the problem persists. Workflow already exists, try deleting it first at ./.github/workflows/kanvas.yml GitHub refused to write the snapshot workflow. See the troubleshooting table in Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot. Permissions 🔗 Task Requirement See the Integrations area View Connections Run the wizard, scan, and import Signed in. The server checks no permission key for these routes. Refresh an imported design from its source Own the design and hold Import Design Delete the connection Own the connection and hold Delete a connection Connection and import permissions by role Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Connections View all connections within an environment ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Import Design Import a design ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Delete a connection Delete a connection -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Next steps 🔗 Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot finishes the optional stages. Integrations lists every connection Layer5 Cloud supports. Find and Use Catalog Designs shows how to open and clone what you imported.

body:
A learning path teaches a subject through courses and modules, with assessments that gate progress. You write it as Markdown in your organization’s Academy content repository, then publish a version. This page covers the repository, layout, front matter, assets, preview, and publishing that every Academy content type shares. For the credential and assessment differences, see Build a Challenge and Build a Certification.
Prerequisites 🔗 Git, a GitHub account, and Markdown. The Academy is built with the Hugo static site generator. Content registered in the Instructor Console, which gives you the content id and the front matter to start from. Your organization’s ID and a personal access token from Layer5 Cloud, used when you publish. Create tokens as described in Tokens. Set up the content repository 🔗 Start from the academy-example template repository published by Layer5: github.com/layer5io/academy-example. Fork it, clone your fork, and work on a branch.
The template’s Go module path must match your fork. Change the module line in its module file from the template’s path to github.com/<your-username>/<your-repo-name>, then commit and push. The publish build fails while the path still names the template.
Directory layout 🔗 Each organization’s content lives in its own directory, which is how the Academy keeps one organization’s content apart from another’s. Replace <your-organization-uuid> with your organization’s ID.
Directory Holds content/<content-type>/<your-organization-uuid>/ Everything you write. <content-type> is learning-paths, challenges, or certifications. The folder hierarchy defines the navigation. layouts/shortcodes/<your-organization-uuid>/ Optional custom Hugo shortcodes for reusable components. Learning path structure 🔗 A learning path contains courses. A course contains modules and can end with a test that serves as the course exam. A module contains pages and labs.
learning-paths/<your-organization-uuid> └── {learning-path-name}/ ├── _index.md ├── course-1/ │ └── _index.md └── course-2/ ├── _index.md ├── course-exam.md └── module-1/ ├── _index.md ├── page-1/ │ └── _index.md └── test.md The _index.md in each folder defines that level’s title, description, and type. The remaining .md files are the individual activities. Challenges and certifications use a flatter layout.
Front matter 🔗 Every _index.md uses the same front matter. Only type changes with the level.
--- type: "learning-path" # or "certification", "challenge", "course" title: "Cloud Fundamentals" description: "A learning path focused on providing the technical knowledge required for advanced topics." weight: 5 banner: "kubernetes-icon.svg" id: "<your-content-uuid>" tags: [kubernetes, infrastructure] categories: [cloud] level: "beginner" # Table of content covered in the test # Each domain can have a weightage (percentage) and subdomains (items) # Weightage should sum up to 100 across all domains ( not strictly enforced, but recommended ) competencies: - title: "Domain 1" percentage: 10 # Weightage of this domain in the test items: - "Subdomain 1" - "Subdomain 2" - title: "Domain 2" percentage: 30 items: - "Subdomain 1" - "Subdomain 2" - title: "Domain 3" percentage: 60 items: - "Subdomain 1" - "Subdomain 2" # List of resource that are recommended to complete before taking the test # Not strictly enforced, but recommended prerequisiteKnowledge: - title: "Learning Path: Cloud Computing Basics" link: "https://academy-domain.com/learning-paths/cloud-computing-basics" - title: "Basic Certification: Networking Basics" link: "https://academy-domain.com/certifications/networking-basics" - title: "Basic knowledge of Linux command line" link: "https://linuxcommand.org/" # List of additional resources for further reading relatedResources: - title: "Documentation" link: "https://docs.example.com/" - title: "Instructions" link: "https://instructions.example.com/" - title: "YouTube Channel" link: "https://www.youtube.com/c/example" # Additional attributes about the test additionalAttributes: - title: "Retake Policy" description: "One Retake allowed after 30 days" - title: "Labs" description: "Hands-on labs included" --- Field Applies to Required Behavior title All Yes Display title. description All Yes Summary shown on the catalog card. type Path, certification, challenge Yes learning-path, certification, challenge, or course (singular). Plural values are rejected. id Path, certification, challenge Yes Stable UUID that learner progress is recorded against. Never change it after learners register. Two items sharing an id are rejected. weight All No Display order, lowest first. Without it, items sort alphabetically by title. draft All No When true, the page is not published. level Path, certification, challenge No beginner, intermediate, or advanced. Default beginner. banner Path, certification, challenge No Path to an image in the same folder. badge Path, certification, challenge No The awarded badge. Its png and svg fields accept a full URL or a file in the same folder. tags All No Keywords for discovery. Several allowed. categories All No The main category. Only one. Renaming content after publication breaks nothing as long as the id is unchanged. Changing the id orphans every existing registration.
Assets 🔗 Place images and other files in the same folder as the Markdown that uses them (a Hugo page bundle) and reference them by file name:
![Pod lifecycle diagram showing Pending, Running, and Succeeded states](pod-lifecycle.png) Every image needs descriptive alt text. The Academy does not enforce a size limit, but large assets slow builds and can make them fail. Host large videos on an external platform and embed them with a <video> element that points at the hosted file. Add subtitle tracks (VTT) and a poster image to embedded video. For private videos, use signed URLs or unlisted links. The usestatic shortcode is deprecated; do not use it.
Preview locally 🔗 make setup # one time make site # start the local preview server The preview uses a generic theme, so it shows structure and content but not your organization’s branding. Branding comes from your organization settings in Layer5 Cloud. If the preview shows stale content, run make clean to delete the build cache and restart. To pick up theme improvements before a release, run make theme-update.
Publish 🔗 Publishing sends your organization’s ID and a version to Layer5 Cloud, which builds your Academy at that version.
Open Design One-time setup 🔗 Store two repository secrets that the template’s publish workflow reads. The names must match exactly.
Secret Value ACADEMY_ORG_ID Your organization’s ID. ACADEMY_TOKEN Only the token string from the token JSON, beginning eyj. Omit the braces, the "token": key, and the quotes. Release 🔗 Commit your changes to the default branch, then publish a GitHub release with a new version tag such as v1.0.2. The release starts the workflow.
The publish request is accepted only from an organization admin or owner. The request calls Layer5 Cloud with your organization ID and the version. Content reaches the staging environment in about 10 minutes and production with the next Layer5 Cloud release. If the build fails, your previous version stays live. Corrections follow the same path: push, then release a new version. Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix 401 Unauthorized or “User must be logged in” ACADEMY_TOKEN contains the whole JSON object. Store only the token string. A URL containing //, such as /api/academy//update/, The organization ID secret is missing or misnamed. Name the secret ACADEMY_ORG_ID. Content missing after a release The publish failed. Open the audit events for your organization and filter by the Academy upsert action to see each attempt and its error. Duplicate ID, invalid content type, or missing required field Two items share an id, type is plural, or title, description, type, or id is absent. Make IDs unique, use the singular type, and add the field. To see who registered for what, filter the audit events by the Academy registration action.

body:
In this tutorial you build a small web application design in Kanvas Designer: a Deployment that runs the application, a ConfigMap that holds its settings, and a Service that exposes it. You start from an empty canvas, connect the components, and save the result. The saved design is the starting point for Deploy and Observe Your First Design.
Along the way you learn what a design is made of, how relationships express the way components depend on each other, and when and how Kanvas saves your work.
Before you begin 🔗 Open Kanvas in Designer mode, either at kanvas.new or in a Meshery you run. Either works for this tutorial. If you plan to deploy the design in the next tutorial, start in a Meshery you run so the design is already where you need it. See Where do you want to work?. Work inside a specific organization. Kanvas does not create designs while the “all organizations” scope is selected. Step 1: Start an empty design 🔗 Start a new design. Kanvas opens an empty canvas and names the design “Untitled Design”.
That default name matters. Kanvas does not save a new design that has an empty canvas and no name of its own. A new design becomes saveable as soon as it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and is not “Untitled Design”.
Give the design a name that describes its purpose, such as web-app. A meaningful name makes the design easy to find later, and Kanvas also uses it to label the design’s deploy steps and its Operator view.
What you should see: an empty canvas with your design name in place of “Untitled Design”.
Step 2: Add the application components 🔗 A component is one piece of infrastructure in your design: a single, typed resource such as a Kubernetes Deployment, Service, or ConfigMap, together with its configuration. Each component comes from a model, and many components exist in more than one version. Choose the version that matches the cluster you intend to deploy to.
Add three components from the Kubernetes model to the canvas:
a Deployment, which will run the web application, a ConfigMap, which will hold the application’s settings, a Service, which will give the application a stable network endpoint. Kanvas renders each component on the canvas as soon as you place it. Arrange them so you can see all three.
Not everything on a canvas is infrastructure. Shapes, text, and drawings that you add for explanation are annotation-only: they make the design easier to read but are not resources. A connector you draw for illustration is an annotation edge for the same reason. Use annotations freely to document a design; they do not change what the design describes.
What you should see: three components on the canvas, each showing its kind.
Step 3: Configure each component 🔗 Every component carries configuration based on its schema. Open a component’s configuration panel to set its fields. The canvas updates as you change them.
Configure the three components so they refer to each other:
On the ConfigMap, set a name such as web-app-config and add one key, for example GREETING. On the Deployment, set a name, a container image (for example nginx), and a label such as app: web-app on its pod template. Reference the ConfigMap by its name so the container reads its settings from it. On the Service, add the same label (app: web-app) and set a port. These references are the same ones you would write in Kubernetes manifests. Kanvas evaluates them to work out how the components relate.
What you should see: each component shows the name you gave it.
Step 4: Connect the components with relationships 🔗 A relationship describes how two components interact or depend on each other. Kanvas draws relationships on the canvas as edges between components, or as nesting when one component contains another. Relationships fall into families:
Edge relationships describe interaction between components. A Service in front of a Deployment is a network relationship. A Deployment that reads a ConfigMap is a reference relationship: one component refers to another by name. Hierarchical relationships describe containment and inheritance, such as a Namespace that must exist before the Pods inside it. Relationships come from two sources: configuration you set, and connections you make on the canvas. Components that carry the same label form a label-match relationship automatically, so the Service and the Deployment in this design are now related. You can also drag a connection line from one component to a compatible target to create an edge relationship yourself. Relationships describes every kind and what each one means.
Check that your design shows a relationship between the Service and the Deployment, and one between the Deployment and the ConfigMap. If one is missing, compare the names and labels you set in Step 3, or drag a connection between the two components.
In large designs, Kanvas can skip drawing some relationships of one kind once that kind passes its rendering limit. When that happens it shows a warning of the form “Skipped rendering of N <kind> relationships due to limit of M”. The relationships still belong to the design; only their drawing is skipped.
What you should see: the Deployment connected to both the Service and the ConfigMap.
Step 5: Save the design 🔗 Kanvas saves for you. Once the design is saveable, Kanvas saves pending changes 3 seconds after you stop editing. If a save fails, Kanvas retries with a doubling delay (3 seconds, then 6, then 12, and so on) for up to 100 attempts.
Three things happen when a design is saved:
A new version is created. Every save increments the design’s version, so a design accumulates a history of versions as you work. A new design starts as public. The first save of a new design sets its visibility to public. Later saves keep whatever visibility the design has at that point. Designs can also be private or published; Saving designs explains each. Your plan’s component limit is checked. Each plan sets a maximum number of components per design, and Kanvas checks it on every save and import. A design over the limit is not saved; Kanvas reports “Design exceeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan”. Reduce the number of components or upgrade the plan. See Layer5 pricing for the limit on each plan. This three-component design is well within every plan’s limit.
What you should see: your design saved under its new name, with no unsaved changes pending.
Optional: Merge another design into this one 🔗 You can bring an existing design into the canvas you are working on. Kanvas merges its components and relationships into the current design and leaves the original design unchanged. Use this to assemble a larger system from designs you already have. See Merging designs.
What you built 🔗 You now have a saved design named web-app that describes a web application:
three infrastructure components, each configured from its schema, relationships that record how the Service reaches the Deployment and how the Deployment reads the ConfigMap, a version history that grows with every save. You also learned the core rules of saving: a new design needs a component or a real name before it can be saved, autosave runs 3 seconds after you stop editing, a new design starts as public, and your plan limits the number of components in a design.
Next 🔗 Take this design to a cluster in Deploy and Observe Your First Design. You will validate it, dry-run it, deploy it, and watch the resulting resources in Operator mode.
description: Build a small web application design from an empty canvas, connect its components through relationships, and save it, while learning how Kanvas models and stores designs.

body:
Your Layer5 account is your personal identity on Layer5 Cloud. One account can belong to many organizations and teams, and it is how you import and create designs, collaborate through workspaces, and connect Meshery Servers. In this tutorial you create an account, verify it, sign in, and confirm that Layer5 Cloud has prepared an organization, a team, and a workspace for you. You do not set up any of those yourself before you can start working. The Check your email page and the Import from GitHub first-run page described below arrived in Layer5 Cloud v1.0.278.
1. Create an account 🔗 Sign up at https://cloud.layer5.io/signup. The registration page offers these sign-up methods:
Method What happens next Email and password Layer5 Cloud sends a verification email. You verify your address before you can sign in with your password. GitHub You authorize with GitHub and are signed in straight after registration. No verification email is sent. Google You authorize with Google and are signed in straight after registration. No verification email is sent. Your organization’s identity provider An organization that brings its own identity provider credentials, including a generic OIDC provider, shows that provider on its own sign-up page. What the email sign-up form checks 🔗 The email sign-up form asks for your first name, last name, email address, and password. Layer5 Cloud validates each field and keeps what you typed when it shows an error, so you only correct the field at fault.
Field Rule First and last name 1 to 50 characters. Letters, combining marks, and spaces only. A spam filter also rejects blocked keywords in names. An invalid name shows “Invalid first name.” or “Invalid last name.” Email address A syntactically valid address. The spam filter also rejects disposable-email domains. An invalid or rejected address shows “Invalid email address or domain not allowed.” Password At least 8 characters. Must not appear in the Have I Been Pwned breach corpus. Must not be too similar to your email address. When the deployment has a reCAPTCHA check enabled, the submit button stays disabled until you solve it. A field-level validation failure keeps your solved captcha. If the server rejects the whole submission after the captcha was sent, the captcha resets and asks you to “Please complete the verification again.” If the network fails, the page shows “We couldn’t submit your sign-up. Check your connection and try again.”
GitHub and Google sign-up skip the spam filter and the captcha.
The sign-up form stays valid for 24 hours. If you leave it open longer, it restarts and you fill it in again.
2. Verify your email address 🔗 After an email sign-up, Layer5 Cloud sends a verification email that contains both a verification link and a verification code. Either one completes verification. Both stay valid for 720 hours (30 days). Until you verify your address, Layer5 Cloud refuses password sign-in.
Your browser lands on a Check your email page that names the address the verification email went to. You can wait on this page:
Resend email sends a new verification email without leaving the page. Once it is sent, the page also offers a form where you type the code from the new email instead of opening its link. Use a different email returns you to the sign-up form with your name kept and the email address cleared. Use it if you mistyped your address. An account cannot change its email address before that address is verified, so signing up again with the correct address is the fix. The page remembers your address only in the browser tab you signed up in. If you open Check your email in a different tab, or your browser blocks site storage, the page shows generic text instead of your address. Resend email then opens the verification page, which asks for your address before it sends a new email.
If your organization uses a custom domain, the verification link stays on your organization’s domain.
If your link has expired, request a new verification email and use the latest link.
3. Sign in 🔗 Sign in at https://cloud.layer5.io/login with the method you signed up with. If you signed up with GitHub or Google, Layer5 Cloud sends you to that provider to authenticate. The sign-in form stays valid for 12 hours; an expired form restarts.
You are not asked to name an organization or a workspace. Layer5 Cloud creates both on your first successful sign-in, as described in the next steps.
Where your first sign-in takes you 🔗 Your first sign-in normally opens your dashboard. One exception applies: if you started signing up from Kanvas, or from a Meshery Server on your organization’s custom domain, and you registered in this browser, your first sign-in opens the Import from GitHub page (titled “Get started”) once. If the sign-in carries an explicit return address, Layer5 Cloud sends you there instead.
The Import from GitHub page holds one card. It explains that connecting GitHub lets you pick repositories and import Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, and Docker Compose files as designs. It also names your organization and workspace: “Organizations own workspaces. You’re in My Organization, working in My Workspace. Rename either anytime.” From there you either start the GitHub integration wizard or skip to your dashboard.
Info Layer5 Cloud remembers where you started only for the browser session you signed up in. If you sign in from a different browser, or after closing the browser you signed up in, you land on your dashboard. The Import from GitHub page is always available at https://cloud.layer5.io/register/choose-start. 4. Your default organization 🔗 Organizations are the unit of tenancy in Layer5 Cloud, and every user belongs to at least one. On your first sign-in, Layer5 Cloud creates an organization named My Organization (description “Default Organization”), makes you its owner, and gives you the Organization Admin role in it. You can create more organizations and join existing ones.
Layer5 Cloud also creates a team named My Team (description “Default Team”), attaches it to My Organization, and gives you the Team Admin role on it.
Info For more information, see Organizations. You can rename My Organization and change its description at any time. See Editing your organization.
5. Your default workspace 🔗 Workspaces are logical groups of shared resources such as environments, connections, credentials, and designs. On your first sign-in, Layer5 Cloud creates a workspace named My Workspace (description “Default Workspace”) in My Organization, owned by you. You can create more workspaces and share access to their resources through teams. If any of your organizations ever has no workspace, Layer5 Cloud re-creates My Workspace in it.
Info For more information, see Workspaces. You can rename My Workspace and change its description at any time. See Edit a Workspace.
Everything your first sign-in sets up 🔗 Created for you Name Your access Organization My Organization Owner, Organization Admin role Team My Team, attached to My Organization Team Admin role Workspace My Workspace, in My Organization Owner Global role Kanvas Grants the Kanvas extension capabilities when a Meshery Server connects with your account Layer5 Cloud also records your primary email address so that one person signing in by a different method reuses the same account instead of creating a second one. Layer5 Cloud accepts open organization invitation links on every sign-in, not only the first.
6. Explore your dashboard 🔗 The dashboard is your normal landing page after sign-in. It is a grid of widgets whose layout you can edit; Layer5 Cloud prompts you before you leave with unsaved layout changes. Available widgets include Getting Started, Workspace Activity, Explore Playground, My Academy, Learn by Video, Help Center, Meshery Instances, Kubernetes Clusters Count, Catalog Content Count, Invite Friends, Badges, My Designs, System Version, Catalog Leaderboard, and Catalog Metrics. Academy administrators see additional widgets for Academy content statistics, metrics, test analytics, and registrations.
7. Link GitHub or Google to your profile 🔗 Whatever method you signed up with, you can later link a GitHub or Google account to your existing profile from your profile page. Once linked, either method signs you in to the same Layer5 Cloud profile. Each provider shows Link or Unlink depending on its current state. Linking sends you to the provider and then back to your profile.
Changing a password or linking a provider is a privileged action. If your sign-in is older than the privileged-session window, Layer5 Cloud asks you to authenticate again first. The window is 24 hours on hosted Layer5 Cloud and 15 minutes by default on a self-hosted chart. For every account setting, see Manage Your Account.
Check your result 🔗 Your account is ready when all of the following are true:
You can sign in at https://cloud.layer5.io/login. For an email account, a successful password sign-in also proves your address is verified. Your dashboard loads after sign-in. Your organization is My Organization, and it contains My Workspace. Next steps 🔗 Set Up Your Organization: invite a teammate, create a team, and give it a workspace. Start from a Catalog Design: clone a public design into your workspace.

body:
A design is the unit of work in Kanvas. It is a declarative description of infrastructure that you author on a canvas, save as a versioned document, share with others, and deploy to your clusters. Components are the building blocks of a design: some represent real infrastructure that Kanvas deploys, and others are annotations that only explain the design. Knowing which is which, and how a design behaves when you save, share, and deploy it, tells you exactly what Kanvas will do with your work.
What a design contains 🔗 A design holds four kinds of content:
Components - the infrastructure resources in the design, such as Kubernetes Deployments, Services, or cloud provider resources, each with its own configuration. Relationships - the connections between components and what those connections mean. See Relationships. Configuration - the settings of each component. Annotations - shapes, arrows, text, and icons that document the design. Kanvas never deploys annotations. How designs are saved 🔗 Naming and the saveability rule 🔗 A new, unsaved design is named “Untitled Design”. Kanvas saves a new design only when it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and not “Untitled Design”. An empty, unnamed canvas is not saved. Once a design has been saved, it can always be saved again, even after you remove every component.
You cannot create a design while your organization scope is set to all organizations. Select a single organization first.
Autosave 🔗 Kanvas saves pending changes automatically 3 seconds after you stop editing. If a save fails, Kanvas retries with a doubling delay (3 seconds, then 6, then 12, and so on) for up to 100 attempts.
Versions 🔗 Every save creates a new version of the design. You never overwrite a previous version by saving.
Who can see a design 🔗 A design has one of three visibility values:
Visibility Meaning Public Visible beyond its owner. Every newly created design starts as public. Private Visible to its owner. Other organization members need the “View Designs” permission to view private designs. Published Listed in the catalog. Unpublishing a design sets its visibility back to private. Saving an existing design never changes its visibility. Non-owners read private and published designs only when the design is shared with them or when they hold administrator rights.
Components 🔗 Components in Kanvas fall into two categories, distinguished by whether Kanvas can orchestrate them during deployment.
Semantic components (orchestratable) 🔗 Semantic components represent actual infrastructure resources. They map directly to real infrastructure elements, so Kanvas can create, configure, and manage their lifecycle during deployment. Examples include:
Kubernetes resources (Pods, Services, Deployments) Cloud provider resources (AWS S3 buckets, Azure Functions) Infrastructure components (load balancers, databases) Semantic components are either built in, like the Kubernetes components, or custom components that you create.
Non-semantic components (annotation-only) 🔗 Non-semantic components are visual and organizational elements that document and organize your design. They do not represent deployable resources, and Kanvas ignores them during deployment. Examples include:
Text boxes and comments Shapes and containers for grouping Arrows and lines Labels and tags Visual distinction rule Semantic components have a background, which marks them as real infrastructure resources. Non-semantic components have a transparent background, which marks them as visual aids only. Both kinds support visual customization. You can change a Kubernetes Pod’s color, modify its shape, or replace its background logo without changing what Kanvas deploys.
How components are organized 🔗 Kanvas draws semantic components from integration models. Kubernetes is the most common, and every integration model, such as KEDA, Prometheus, or AWS, provides components with the same orchestratable capabilities. Kanvas organizes them in a three-level hierarchy:
Categories - high-level groups, such as “Cloud Native Network” or “Database”. Integration models - specific technologies, such as Prometheus or Kubernetes. Components - the deployable building blocks within a model. For the full list of technologies Kanvas integrates, see the integrations directory.
Kubernetes component conventions 🔗 Kubernetes components follow a consistent visual system, so you can identify a resource kind at a glance.
Color and structure
Kubernetes component icons use a distinctive blue background. Every icon has the same structure: an outer shape filled with blue that encloses a white inner symbol. The white inner symbol identifies the specific Kubernetes kind. Shape as an indicator
The outer shape identifies the component’s role:
Triangles mark core networking resources, such as Service and APIService. Hexagons mark foundational workload controllers, such as StatefulSet. Unique polygons mark specialized resources, such as Endpoints, PriorityClass, or ValidatingWebhookConfiguration. Non-semantic palettes 🔗 Kanvas provides four palettes of annotation-only components. None of them is ever deployed.
Generic shapes cover general-purpose diagramming.
Arrows show direction or create simple visual annotations. They are static shapes for illustration only. To represent a functional relationship between semantic components, such as network traffic or a dependency, use an edge instead; see the edges shape guide.
Flowchart shapes document a design’s logic and flow with standard flowchart symbols.
Simple Line Icons add icons for annotation and visual emphasis.
One component, several representations 🔗 A semantic component looks different depending on where it appears. The Deployment component is a good example:
On the canvas, it has its distinctive shape and badge.
In a component selection panel, it appears as an icon.
In a cluster resource overview, it appears as a resource entry.
To practice reading designs, see interpreting Meshery designs in the Layer5 Academy.
Limits as shipped 🔗 The limits below describe Kanvas as it ships today. Current plans and their entitlements are listed at layer5.io/pricing.
Components per design 🔗 Kanvas enforces a maximum number of components per design whenever you save or import a design. The limit depends on your organization’s plan and is the same for monthly and annual billing.
Plan Components per design Personal 100 Team Designer 200 Team Operator 100 Enterprise 300 When a design exceeds the limit, the save or import is rejected with HTTP 403 and the message “Design exceeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan”, where N is your plan’s limit. To proceed, reduce the number of components in the design or upgrade your plan.
If your organization is not entitled to add components to a design at all, the save fails with HTTP 500 and the message “Org is not entitled to adding components to a design”.
Files dropped on the canvas 🔗 You can drop files directly onto the canvas:
Image and text files up to 500 KB are accepted. Larger files are rejected. The rejection message says “Your current plan allows files up to 500 KB”, but the 500 KB limit is the same on every plan. Infrastructure-as-code files, such as Kubernetes manifests, are imported as a design. How a design maps to deployed resources 🔗 When Kanvas deploys a design, every resource it creates carries the identity of its source design:
Metadata Key Value Label design.meshery.io/id The id of the source design Annotation design.meshery.io/version The version of the design that was deployed Annotation component.meshery.io/id The id of the component in the design A resource that carries the design id label is managed by Meshery. Because the label is a standard Kubernetes label, you can also select a design’s resources with your own tooling.
This metadata powers Operator’s per-design view. A design’s view is named “<design name>-View” and shows only the resources whose design id label matches that design, so you see exactly what one design produced across your clusters. See Operator.
description: What a Kanvas design is, how it is saved, versioned, and shared, what components are, and how a design maps to the resources it deploys.

body:
In this tutorial you build a single NGINX Pod in Kanvas, deploy it to a live cluster, expose it with a NodePort Service, and inspect the running Pod in Operator: its details, a shell inside its container, and its log stream. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, and every workload controller you meet later (Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs) exists to create and replace Pods. Working with a bare Pod first shows you exactly what those controllers automate.
The Pod in this tutorial is standalone: no controller watches it, so if it fails or is deleted, nothing recreates it. That trade-off suits learning and does not suit production.
What you will learn 🔗 A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network address and are scheduled together onto one node. A Kanvas component is a Kubernetes object in design form: its configuration is the object’s manifest, and Deploy turns it into a live object. Labels identify objects, and a Service’s selector uses labels to find the Pods it sends traffic to. Deploying a design again updates the cluster in place instead of creating duplicates. Operator shows what actually runs in the cluster, which is the ground truth when it differs from the design. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed environment. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. An environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. See Environments. Operator mode for the inspection phases. Operator reads the cluster through Meshery Operator and MeshSync, which must run in the cluster. Where Operator mode is turned off, its switch is disabled; the deploy summary still confirms each object. A unique prefix. Playground is shared with other users. Pick a short prefix, such as your handle, and use it in every name and label. This tutorial uses alex. You need basic familiarity with containers and Kubernetes manifests. You do not need to write YAML.
The scenario 🔗 You build two objects in one design:
Service alex-nginx-np type NodePort, port 80, selector app=alex-nginx | | Network relationship (traffic flows from the Service to the Pod) v Pod alex-nginx label app=alex-nginx +-- container nginx image nginx:latest, port 80 You deploy the Pod first, inspect it, then add the Service and deploy again.
Build the Pod 🔗 Create a new design and name it alex-pods. Kanvas saves the design automatically as soon as it has a name or a component; there is no Save button. Add a Pod component. The Kubernetes icon in the dock lists every Kubernetes kind, and the component palette search finds it too. The component’s configurator opens as soon as the Pod lands on the canvas. Set the Pod’s name to alex-nginx and leave the namespace as default. Add one entry to the Pod’s containers: name nginx, image nginx:latest, and a container port of 80. Containers is a list, so each entry opens in its own form. In the configurator’s Labels tab, add the label app with the value alex-nginx. What just happened. The configurator form is generated from the Pod’s schema in the Meshery registry, so its fields are the Kubernetes API fields. Required fields carry a red asterisk. Each edit is written to the design after a short pause; Kanvas then checks the changed component against its schema and marks problems beside the field. Those marks are warnings and never block you. The component you built is equivalent to this manifest:
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: alex-nginx namespace: default labels: app: alex-nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:latest ports: - containerPort: 80 Check your work. The Pod sits on the canvas without a warning badge. If a badge with an error count appears on the component, select it to see each error; it leads to the field that needs attention.
Check the design before deploying 🔗 Run Validate from the design’s Actions menu. Run Dry Run from the same menu. What just happened. Validate runs in your browser. It checks each component against its schema and never contacts the cluster, so it cannot catch cluster-side problems such as a missing namespace or a name already in use. Its errors are advisory. Dry Run sends each object to the cluster’s API server as a server-side dry run: the API server applies its full validation and admission checks and persists nothing. Dry Run from the Actions menu targets the clusters selected in Meshery’s context selector.
Check your work. Validate reports No validation errors. and Dry Run reports No deployment errors. A Pod without any container fails the dry run with a Field Value Required error on the containers field; add the container and run it again.
Deploy and verify 🔗 Run Deploy from the Actions menu. The Deploy workflow has five steps: validation, choosing deployment targets, a dry run, a final review, and a summary. Select the environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Selecting an environment targets every Kubernetes connection assigned to it. Continue past the dry run once it reports no errors, then confirm the deployment. What just happened. Meshery Server turned each component into a Kubernetes object and sent it to every selected cluster. For each object it creates the object, or replaces it in place if an object of that kind and name already exists. It labels every object it applies with design.meshery.io/id=<design id> and records the design version and component id as annotations. That label is how Operator finds the objects that came from this design.
Check your work. The summary lists Deployed Pod "alex-nginx", and a notification reads Deployment completed for design 'alex-pods'. Read the per-object rows, not only the notification: the notification reads “completed” even when individual objects failed, and failures appear only as Failed to deploy rows with an error card. If the summary spinner never finishes, the request failed before it reached the cluster, most often because your session expired; reload Kanvas, sign in, and deploy again.
Inspect the Pod in Operator 🔗 Switch to Operator, either with the mode switch or with Open In Operator on the deploy summary. With the design open, Operator shows a view scoped to this design: only objects that carry this design’s id label. Select the alex-nginx Pod to open its details panel, and switch the panel from Summary to Details to see every field. What just happened. Operator draws the objects that MeshSync reports from the cluster, not the objects in your design. For a Pod, the details panel shows its phase as a status chip, the Pod IP, the host IP of its node, its QoS class, restart count, and each container’s image, ports, start time, and image pull policy. The QoS class is BestEffort because the container sets no resource requests or limits. The view is a snapshot: Operator loads it when you open a view, change a filter, or change the selected cluster, and it does not update on its own. To see later changes, change a filter or switch back to Operator.
Check your work. The status chip reads Running. A Pending Pod is not scheduled yet or is still pulling its image; load a fresh snapshot after a few seconds. If it stays Pending, the container status shows why, for example an image pull failure caused by a mistyped image name. If the canvas reads No data available for the current view, the snapshot found no objects with this design’s label: MeshSync has not reported the Pod yet, or the deploy failed. If it reads No Kubernetes context selected, select your cluster in Meshery’s context selector.
Open a shell and stream logs 🔗 Start a terminal on the Pod with Initiate Terminal Session, which is in the Pod’s right-click menu and in the details panel header. A terminal panel opens with one tab per container in the Pod. Run hostname. It prints alex-nginx, because a Pod’s name is the hostname of its containers. Run cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html to read the page NGINX serves. Start a log stream on the same Pod with Initiate Log Session. A log tab opens in the same panel. What just happened. Kanvas asks MeshSync, inside the cluster, to open /bin/sh in the container through the Kubernetes exec API, the same mechanism kubectl exec uses. The shell runs with MeshSync’s cluster permissions. The terminal sends each line when you press Enter and Ctrl+C sends an interrupt, so line-based commands work and full-screen programs such as vim, top, and less do not. Images without /bin/sh, such as distroless images, cannot open a shell.
The log tab shows the last 1,000 lines from every container in the Pod and then follows new output. Each line starts with [alex-nginx:nginx] and a Kubernetes timestamp; stdout and stderr are combined. NGINX’s container entrypoint writes its startup messages here. Closing the panel hides it without ending the sessions; the trash icon on a tab ends that session.
Check your work. The shell prints the Pod name and the HTML page. If the terminal tab stays blank, the session did not start, and Kanvas does not display the reason. The usual causes are a container without /bin/sh, a Pod that is not Running, or MeshSync not connected. When a Pod is deleted, its log stream stops without a notice.
Expose the Pod with a NodePort Service 🔗 Switch back to Designer and add a Service component named alex-nginx-np. Set the Service type to NodePort and add one port with port 80 and target port 80. Leave the node port empty so Kubernetes assigns a free one from the node port range (30000 to 32767 by default). On a shared cluster, a fixed node port that someone else holds fails the dry run. Set the Service’s selector to app: alex-nginx, the same label the Pod carries. Draw a Network relationship from the Service to the Pod. Edge handles appear when you hover a component; choose the network option and drag to the Pod. Compatible targets show a green outline while you drag, and releasing anywhere else creates nothing. Run Deploy again with the same environment. What just happened. Kubernetes routes Service traffic by the selector alone: every Running Pod whose labels match the selector becomes a backend of the Service. The Network relationship records the same connection in the design so that readers of the diagram see where traffic flows, and its edge shows the port values it reads from both components. Kanvas evaluates relationships after every change, and a relationship’s registry definition can copy designated fields from one component to the other. The selector you set is what Kubernetes acts on, so confirm it in the Service’s configurator after you draw the edge.
Deploying the same design again creates objects that are missing and replaces objects that already exist. The Service is created; the Pod is submitted unchanged and keeps running. Kubernetes treats almost every field of a running Pod as immutable, so changing a Pod beyond its container image means deleting it and creating it again, one of the reasons real workloads use Deployments.
Check your work. The summary lists Deployed Service "alex-nginx-np". Switch to Operator and select the Service. Its details show the service type NodePort, a cluster IP, the selector app=alex-nginx, and, under its connections, the ports including the node port Kubernetes assigned. The Service is reachable at http://<node IP>:<node port> from any machine that can reach the node; the Pod’s host IP is one such node address. In Playground, node IPs are often not reachable from your browser. The assigned node port still confirms that Kubernetes exposed the Pod.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu and select the same environment. The Undeploy workflow has the same five steps as Deploy, and its dry run checks the deletions.
Undeploy deletes each component’s object by kind, name, and namespace: here, the Pod and the Service. It matches by name, not by the design label, so an object with the same kind, name, and namespace that someone else created is deleted too. That is another reason to use unique names on a shared cluster. Namespaces are removed only when the design contains a Namespace component. If an object is already gone, the dry-run step reports it as not found; select the bypass option to continue, because the real undeploy ignores missing objects.
The design itself stays in your account. Delete it from the design’s file menu if you no longer need it. Deleting a design never removes objects from a cluster, so undeploy first.
What you learned 🔗 A Pod is one or more containers that share a hostname and network address. A standalone Pod has no controller, so nothing replaces it. Each Kanvas component maps to one Kubernetes object, and its configurator edits that object’s manifest. Validate checks schemas in the browser; Dry Run asks the cluster’s API server; Deploy creates or replaces each object and labels it with the design id. A Service finds its Pods by label selector. The Network relationship documents the connection in the design. Operator shows a snapshot of what runs in the cluster, and it is where you open a shell and stream logs. Next steps 🔗 Continue with Explore Deployments to let a controller manage your Pods. Read Deploying designs for every option in the Deploy workflow. Read Operator to understand how Operator sees a cluster, and Interactive terminal and Log streaming for the full session behavior.

Which limits Layer5 Cloud enforces 🔗 Layer5 Cloud enforces one limit today: components per design. When you save or import a design, Layer5 Cloud compares its component count with the limit of your organization’s active plan. A design that exceeds the limit is refused with the error Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan, where N is the limit. To proceed, reduce the number of components in the design or upgrade the plan. When an organization holds more than one active subscription, the highest component limit among them applies. An organization with no active subscription cannot save or import a design; the request fails with HTTP 500 and the error Org is not entitled to adding components to a design.

Availability depends on more than your plan 🔗 Your role 🔗 Authorization in Layer5 Cloud is by permission key. Each role you hold grants a set of keys, and your effective permissions are the union of the keys from every role you hold in the organization you are working in. An action your role does not grant is refused with HTTP 403, even when your plan includes the capability. See Roles and Permissions for which role holds which permission.
Where your deployment runs 🔗 Layer5 Cloud runs either as the hosted service that Layer5 operates or as a self-hosted deployment that you operate. Self-hosted Deployment is listed under the Enterprise plan in the Support and Deployment table. The difference that matters most for availability is provider administration. The Provider Admin role administers the deployment and passes every permission check; on a self-hosted deployment, your operators assign it.
Custom roles 🔗 Only Provider Admins create custom roles. Layer5 Cloud refuses a role creation request from anyone else with HTTP 403. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, an organization therefore cannot create a custom role itself; on a self-hosted deployment, the operator’s Provider Admins can. Roles are defined for the whole deployment, not per organization, so a role change applies in every organization where the role is held.
The Custom Roles and User-defined Roles rows in the Identity & Access Management table describe how those capabilities are packaged into plans. Layer5 Cloud does not check your plan when a custom role is created.
Plan rows and enforcement 🔗 The component limit is the only entitlement Layer5 Cloud enforces by plan. The capability rows in the matrix describe how Layer5 packages its plans. When an action is unavailable and the plan is not the component limit, check your role and your deployment first.
Support by plan 🔗 The support channels and response commitments each plan includes are listed in Support.

Layer5 Cloud gives you a home for your designs and the people who work on them: an account, an organization that holds your teams, and workspaces that hold shared resources. You reach first value in three short tutorials. Sign up and you already have an organization, a team, and a workspace. Invite a teammate and give your team a workspace. Clone a design from the public catalog and you have something to work on.
The tenancy model in one table 🔗 Everything in Layer5 Cloud sits inside this structure. Your first sign-in creates one of each for you, so you never start from an empty account.
Object What it is How it relates What you get by default User Your personal identity on Layer5 Cloud. One user can belong to many organizations and teams. Your account, plus the global Kanvas role. Organization The unit of tenancy. Membership in an organization decides who is in. Owns its teams and workspaces. Every user belongs to at least one. My Organization, owned by you, with the Organization Admin role. Team A named group of organization members. Belongs to the organization it is created in. Can be assigned to several workspaces. My Team, attached to My Organization, with the Team Admin role. Workspace A group of shared resources such as environments, connections, credentials, and designs. Lives in one organization. Has zero or more teams. A design belongs to at most one workspace. My Workspace, in My Organization, owned by you. Tutorials 🔗 Work through these in order. Each one builds on the last.
Create Your Layer5 Account: sign up, verify your address, sign in, and confirm what Layer5 Cloud set up for you. Set Up Your Organization: invite a teammate by email, create a team and a workspace, assign the team to the workspace, and move a design into it. Start from a Catalog Design: browse the public catalog, try a design in the Playground, and clone it into your workspace as a private copy. If you would rather start from your own repositories, GitHub integration imports Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, and Docker Compose files as designs.
Using Cloud with Meshery 🔗 Layer5 Cloud is a Remote Provider for Meshery. When you choose Layer5 Cloud as the provider in a Meshery Server, the server sends your browser to Layer5 Cloud to sign in, and Layer5 Cloud returns you to the server with a token. If your browser already holds a live Layer5 Cloud session, Layer5 Cloud skips the sign-in page and hands the token straight back. Layer5 Cloud returns tokens only to callback addresses it trusts and refuses all others.
A Meshery Server registers itself with Layer5 Cloud as a connection owned by the signed-in user. Registering the same server again updates that connection in place instead of creating a new one. Because every new account holds the Kanvas role, the Meshery Server receives the Kanvas extension capabilities when it connects with your account.
Architecture: how the sign-in handoff, trusted callbacks, and provider capabilities work. Meshery Server registration: how a Meshery Server becomes a connection in your account. Get help 🔗 If you run into issues during setup, join the Layer5 Slack community.

body:
Kanvas turns cloud native infrastructure into a design you can see, check, and deploy. This section takes you from an empty canvas to resources running in a Kubernetes cluster. Along the way you learn the four ideas that every other Kanvas page builds on, and which parts of Kanvas need a Meshery deployment of your own.
What you will learn 🔗 How a design is built from components, relationships, and configuration, and how Kanvas saves it. How Kanvas checks a design before it touches a cluster. How a design becomes running resources, and how Kanvas tracks them afterward. Which capabilities work on hosted Kanvas and which need a Meshery you run. The model in four steps 🔗 Design. In Designer mode you describe infrastructure as a design: components (such as a Kubernetes Deployment or Service), the relationships between them, and their configuration. Validate. Kanvas checks the design against each component’s schema and attaches every error to the component and field that caused it; a dry run then checks the design against a real cluster without changing it. Deploy. Kanvas applies the design to the Kubernetes clusters you select and labels every resource it creates with the design’s identity. Operate. In Operator mode you see the recorded state of your clusters and can filter it to the resources that belong to one design. Where do you want to work? 🔗 Kanvas runs in two places. Both use the same Designer, but only a Meshery you run can reach your clusters.
Capability Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new Meshery you run (Playground or self-hosted) Create and edit designs Yes Yes Share and publish designs Yes, after you sign in Yes, after you sign in, when Meshery uses Layer5 Cloud as its provider Validate a design No Yes Dry-run, deploy, and undeploy a design No Yes Connect and view Kubernetes clusters No Yes Operator mode No Yes On kanvas.new, validating, deploying, undeploying, connecting clusters, and opening Operator mode open a prompt that points you to a Meshery you run instead of performing the action. You have two choices:
Meshery Playground at playground.meshery.io is a hosted Meshery you can use without installing anything. Self-hosted Meshery runs in your own environment and connects to your own clusters. See the Meshery installation guide. A Meshery you run must use Layer5 Cloud as its remote provider for the features that live in Layer5 Cloud: sharing, the catalog, and Operator views. With the local provider, Meshery reports those features as not implemented.
Start on kanvas.new if you only want to design. Start on the Playground or your own Meshery if you plan to complete both tutorials below.
Sign in 🔗 You can open Kanvas and start designing without an account. Sharing and publishing a design require sign-in: when you are anonymous, these actions show a “Sign in to” prompt with a single Sign in action. Signing in takes you to the Layer5 Cloud sign-in page and returns you to the page you were on.
If sign-in cannot start because the provider address is malformed, Kanvas shows the notification “Sign-in could not start” followed by the reason.
Your first path 🔗 Complete these two tutorials in order. The second one starts from the design you save in the first.
Create Your First Design - build a small web application design from an empty canvas, connect its components, and save it. Deploy and Observe Your First Design - validate, dry-run, and deploy that design, then find its running resources in Operator mode and remove them. After the first design 🔗 Import designs from Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Docker Compose files, and existing Meshery designs. Create relationships between components and learn how Kanvas interprets them. Work with components to configure, copy, and arrange them on the canvas. Embed designs in your own documentation so diagrams stay in step with the design they describe. Browse the Tutorials for longer, scenario-based walkthroughs. Read the Concepts to understand designs, relationships, and the Kanvas architecture in depth.
