body:
The layer5-cloud chart installs the Layer5 Cloud server and, as subcharts from the Ory repository, Kratos and Hydra. The defaults below are those of chart version 0.2.0, which ships with Layer5 Cloud v1.0.278. Run helm show values layer5/layer5-cloud to print the defaults of the version you install. For the install procedure, see Deploy Layer5 Cloud.
How values reach the server 🔗 The chart writes env.* values into one ConfigMap and one Secret, and the server pod reads both as environment variables. Sensitive values go to the Secret. Any change to either rolls the server pods, because the pod template carries a checksum of both.
Where it lands Values Secret env.githubappkeypath (the key file content), env.githubAppClientSecret, env.stripeWebhookSecret, env.githubWebhookSecret, env.kratosWebhookApiKey, env.cloudCredentialEncryptionKey, env.cloudOidcStateHmacKey, env.providerOrgGithubSecret, env.providerOrgGoogleSecret, and all four smtp.* values ConfigMap Every other env.* value Both the Secret and the Helm release still hold your values in plaintext, so protect the release history and your values file.
Workload 🔗 Key Default Meaning replicaCount 1 Server replicas. Ignored when autoscaling is on. image.repository layer5/meshery-cloud Server image. image.tag latest Image tag. Pin it to a release such as v1.0.278. When empty, the chart uses its own appVersion. image.pullPolicy Always Image pull policy. imagePullSecrets [] Pull secrets for a private registry. updateStrategy RollingUpdate, 25% unavailable, 25% surge Deployment update strategy. resources.requests 256Mi memory, 250m CPU Requested resources. resources.limits {} No limits by default. autoscaling.enabled false Enables a HorizontalPodAutoscaler. autoscaling.minReplicas, .maxReplicas 1, 100 Autoscaler bounds. autoscaling.targetCPUUtilizationPercentage 80 Autoscaler target. nodeSelector, tolerations, affinity {}, [], {} Pod scheduling. podAnnotations, podSecurityContext, securityContext {} Pod and container settings. serviceAccount.create, .name, .annotations true, meshery-cloud, {} Service account. nameOverride, fullnameOverride "", meshery-cloud Resource naming. The Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and Secret derive their names from fullnameOverride. The container has a liveness probe on /healthz and readiness and startup probes on /readyz. See Monitoring.
Networking 🔗 Key Default Meaning service.type ClusterIP Service type. service.port 9876 Service port for the server. service.hydraAdminProxyPort 9879 Port of the internal proxy that sits between Kratos and the Hydra admin API. Set 0 to turn the proxy off. ingress.enabled true Creates the Ingress. ingress.className nginx Ingress class. ingress.annotations {} Controller annotations. ingress.hosts One empty host routing / to port 9876 Hosts and paths. You must set the host. Add /kratos and /hydra paths for the identity services. ingress.tls [] TLS secret and hosts. The chart does not create certificates. Server settings (env) 🔗 Key Default Meaning proto "" http or https. Used to build redirects to organization custom domains. Set https on a TLS deployment. serverbaseurl http://localhost:9876 Public base URL of the deployment. Also the base of the OAuth2 callback <serverbaseurl>/callback. serverHost localhost Public hostname of the deployment. port 9876 Port the server listens on. environment cloud Deployment mode. development connects to a local database at 127.0.0.1:5432, tolerates a failed migration, logs rendered email bodies, and skips reCAPTCHA. Use any other value in production. debug "false" Sets the DEBUG variable. loglevel 4 Log level: 4 info, 5 debug, 6 trace. Not in the default values; the server uses 4 when unset. db, hydradb, kratosdb In-cluster PostgreSQL URLs with sslmode=disable Connection strings for the meshery, hydra, and kratos databases. Change the user, password, host, and sslmode. minmesheryversion v1.0.55 Lowest Meshery Server version that can complete sign-in. A connecting Meshery Server below it is shown a “Meshery Deployment Incompatible” error. initConfig "" Provider initialization document. See Provider Initialization. otelConfig "" OpenTelemetry tracing configuration. See Monitoring. anonymousUserSessionsEnabled false Lets the deployment serve guest sessions, as used by kanvas.new. Leave off unless you operate that flow. ghtoken "" GitHub token the server uses to dispatch workflows. githubappid not set GitHub App identifier for the GitHub integration. githubappkeypath key.pem Path of the GitHub App private key file inside the chart. githubAppClientId, githubAppClientSecret "" OAuth client ID and a client secret from the settings page of the GitHub App that githubappid names. Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287 and later uses them to confirm which installations of the App the authorizing GitHub account can access. When either is empty, the server logs a warning at startup and no GitHub connection can be created or re-authorized. The App must also meet the Self-hosted GitHub App requirements. stripeSecretKey, stripePublicKey not set Stripe keys for payment processing. recaptchaSiteKey, recaptchaSecretKey not set Google reCAPTCHA keys. Signup verification runs only when both are set. Organizations on a custom domain with a different registrable domain are exempt. Identity connections 🔗 Key Default Meaning kratospublic none, required In-cluster address of the Kratos public service. The chart fails to render without it. May contain {{ .Release.Namespace }}. kratosadmin not set In-cluster address of the Kratos admin service. kratosbrowser not set Address browsers use for Kratos, such as https://cloud.example.com/kratos. hydrapublic http://hydra-public:4444 Address of Hydra’s public API. hydrabrowser not set Address browsers use for Hydra, such as https://cloud.example.com/hydra. hydraadmin http://hydra-admin:4445 Address of Hydra’s admin API. hydrapublicinternal "" In-cluster address of Hydra’s public API for calls the server makes to itself. Falls back to hydrabrowser when empty. May contain {{ .Release.Namespace }}. oauthclientid meshery-cloud Id of the Hydra OAuth2 client the server uses. oauthsecret secret1234567890 Secret of that client. Replace it. kratosWebhookApiKey "" Key Kratos sends in the X-API-Key header on registration hooks. When empty, the server accepts the placeholder dev_token. Set it, and set the same value in the Kratos hooks. providerOrgGithubKey, providerOrgGithubSecret "" Client id and secret of the default GitHub OAuth application. providerOrgGoogleKey, providerOrgGoogleSecret "" Client id and secret of the default Google OAuth application. Encryption keys 🔗 Key Default Meaning cloudCredentialEncryptionKey not set Base64 of 32 bytes. Encrypts stored credentials. When empty, encrypting or decrypting a credential fails. cloudOidcStateHmacKey not set Base64 of 32 bytes. Signs the state of brokered social sign-in. When empty, brokered sign-in fails. stripeWebhookSecret, githubWebhookSecret not set Signing secrets for inbound payment and GitHub webhooks. When empty, those inbound webhooks are rejected. Webhooks 🔗 Key Default Meaning webhookHelpAndSupport not set URL that receives support requests. webhookKanvasEntitlement not set URL that receives Kanvas entitlement events. webhookSignupRequest not set URL that receives signup decisions. See Customize Webhooks.
Mail (smtp) 🔗 Key Default Meaning smtp.smtphost "" Relay host. Must resolve to a public address. smtp.smtpport "" 25, 465, 587, or 2525. Port 465 uses implicit TLS; the others require STARTTLS. smtp.smtpusername "" Mailbox login. Must be a full email address, because it becomes the From address. smtp.smtppassword "" Mailbox password. Set all four or none. A partial configuration stops the server at startup. See Troubleshoot Email Delivery.
Kratos (kratos) 🔗 The kratos.kratos.config tree is passed to Kratos unchanged. The Kratos configuration reference describes every field. The values you must change for a real deployment:
Key Default Change to kratos.enabled true Keep true unless you bring your own Kratos. kratos.service.public.port, .admin.port 9010, 9011 Public and admin ports. kratos.kratos.config.dsn In-cluster URL for the kratos database Your connection string. kratos.kratos.config.secrets.cookie, .cipher [""] Long random strings. kratos.kratos.config.serve.public.base_url http://localhost:9010/ https://<host>/kratos. kratos.kratos.config.serve.public.cors.allowed_origins http://localhost:9010/ Your public origin. kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.default_browser_return_url, .allowed_return_urls http://localhost:9876 Your public URL. kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.flows.*.ui_url http://localhost:9876/... Your public URL with the same paths. kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.flows.registration.after.*.hooks web_hook to http://localhost:9876/identity/users, key dev_token https://<host>/api/identity/users and your kratosWebhookApiKey. kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.methods.oidc.config.providers GitHub and Google with empty credentials Your client_id and client_secret. kratos.kratos.config.courier SMTP courier, empty connection string Your courier. See Plan a Deployment. Other defaults you can change: password sign-in is on with a minimum length of 8, breached-password and similarity checks on; login flows last 720m, registration 24h, recovery and verification 720h; verification and recovery use codes; privileged_session_max_age is 15m; the log level is debug; automatic migration is on.
A list in a values file replaces the chart’s list as a whole. Copy the full providers or hooks list before you edit it.
Hydra (hydra) 🔗 The hydra.hydra.config tree is passed to Hydra unchanged. See the Hydra configuration reference.
Key Default Change to hydraPrefix cloud-hydra Name prefix of the Hydra resources. The services become <prefix>-public and <prefix>-admin. hydra.hydra.config.dsn In-cluster URL for the hydra database Your connection string. hydra.hydra.config.secrets.system [""] A long random string. hydra.hydra.config.urls.login, .consent, .error, .post_logout_redirect https://public.hydra.localhost/... https://<host>/login, /consent, /error, and /login. hydra.hydra.config.urls.self.public, .self.issuer https://public.hydra.localhost/hydra/ https://<host>/hydra/. hydra.hydra.dangerousForceHttp true false once Hydra is reached over TLS. hydra.hydra.config.strategies.access_token jwt Keep jwt. hydra.hydra.config.ttl.access_token, .refresh_token, .id_token, .auth_code 24h, 1000h, 1h, 1h Token lifetimes. Other defaults: automatic migration is on, the log level is debug, and the liveness and readiness probes use /health/alive and /health/ready on port 4444.

body:
Layer5 Cloud is a Meshery remote provider. Meshery Server delegates identity, tenancy, and persistence to it, and Kanvas, which runs inside Meshery, reaches it through Meshery Server. Knowing what Cloud supplies, and what it does not touch, explains why some features need an account, why a feature can appear for one user and not another, and why Meshery Server, rather than your browser, is what reaches your clusters.
Read the diagram from left to right. Providers sit on the left: Meshery runs with either a remote provider, which is the role Layer5 Cloud plays, or a local provider. The remote provider handles identity, tenancy, and the storage and sharing of designs. Meshery sits in the middle and mediates every request between the provider and your infrastructure. Your clusters sit on the right, where Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and Meshery Broker to report live state back to Meshery. Meshery, not the provider, is drawn connecting to the clusters and adapters on the right. What Cloud provides to a connected Meshery Server 🔗 When a Meshery Server uses Layer5 Cloud as its provider, Cloud supplies four things:
Identity and sign-in. Cloud authenticates the user and hands Meshery Server a token. Cloud publishes the keys that verify its tokens, as a JSON Web Key Set, at its unauthenticated /keys endpoint. Tenancy. Cloud holds the organizations, teams, workspaces, environments, and roles that decide what a user can see and do. See Concepts for how these relate. Persistence. Cloud stores designs and their versions, records who each design is shared with, hosts the catalog, and keeps the event log. A capabilities document. Cloud tells Meshery Server which features the provider offers to the current caller, and Meshery and Kanvas enable only those features. Meshery Server also registers itself with Cloud as a connection owned by the signed-in user. See Meshery Server Registration.
The sign-in handoff 🔗 A Meshery Server, or Kanvas, does not collect credentials itself. It hands the browser to Cloud and waits for a token to come back:
The client sends the browser to Cloud’s sign-in with a source: the address of its own token callback, encoded in base64url. The user signs in to Cloud. If the browser already holds a live Cloud session, Cloud skips the sign-in page. Cloud returns the browser to the source’s token endpoint with a token and the original reference in the query string. The token callback path is /api/user/token or /api/token. Older Meshery Servers send /user/login or /login, and Cloud rewrites those to the current paths, so older servers keep working.
If the user was working anonymously and the handoff carries the anonymous identity, Cloud moves the designs created under that anonymous identity to the signed-in account.
Which sources Cloud returns a token to 🔗 Cloud issues a token only to a source it trusts. A source must use https, name a host, and carry no port and no user information. Its host must then be one of three kinds:
Source host Accepted when Cloud’s own host The source uses the same scheme as Cloud’s configured base URL. A custom domain of an organization The domain is configured on a live organization and the source uses https. A loopback host The deployment runs in development mode. Outside development mode, loopback sources are refused. Every other source is refused with an error and no token is issued. That includes other schemes and any host that is not Cloud’s own host or a configured organization domain. There is no built-in list of trusted hosts beyond these rules. If Cloud cannot complete the lookup of an organization’s custom domain, it refuses the source rather than accepting it. Cloud never applies the live-session shortcut in step 2 to a source on its own host.
What a Meshery Server gets from Cloud, by caller 🔗 Meshery Server requests the capabilities document with GET /<meshery-version>/capabilities, optionally adding os and playground query parameters. The older unversioned /capabilities path is deprecated. The document Cloud returns depends on who is asking:
Caller Capabilities returned Anonymous, or no valid token Default capabilities only. Signed-in user Account capabilities: overview, profile, and tokens. Signed-in user with the Kanvas role Account capabilities, plus the Kanvas extension capabilities and the latest Kanvas extension package version for the connecting Meshery version. Provider Admin Account capabilities, plus administrative capabilities (user management, statistics, and events) and the Kanvas extension capabilities. Playground (playground=true) Playground capabilities, added to the set the caller would otherwise receive. Every new user receives the Kanvas role when their account is created, so a typical signed-in user gets Kanvas in Meshery without any extra setup. A user without that role still signs in but does not receive the Kanvas extension from Cloud.
The provider name 🔗 Meshery shows the provider’s name in its interface. When Cloud resolves the caller’s organization, the provider name is that organization’s name, which is how branded organizations appear under their own name. Otherwise Meshery shows the default provider name.
What Cloud stores and what stays with you 🔗 Cloud and your own deployment hold different things:
Held by Layer5 Cloud Held by your Meshery Server and clusters User accounts, organizations, teams, workspaces, environments, and roles The live state of each cluster, which MeshSync records in Meshery Server Designs, their versions, and who each is shared with The workloads and resources a deployed design produces The catalog and the event log The connections from Meshery Server to your Kubernetes clusters, through Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and Meshery Broker Connection registrations, including each registered Meshery Server and its metadata Meshery Server, not your browser, talks to your Kubernetes clusters, through the components it deploys into each one. Deploying, dry-running, and undeploying a design are operations Meshery Server performs against the contexts you select. When Meshery Server registers a Kubernetes connection with Cloud, Cloud records that connection and its credential.
Real-time collaboration is the one path from the browser straight to Cloud: Cloud hosts the signaling service that introduces collaborators, and edits then synchronize directly between their browsers. See How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud for that path and for the full picture from the Kanvas side.
Remote provider versus local provider 🔗 Meshery runs with either a remote provider or the local provider. In both cases, requests about your connected clusters and their resources stay within Meshery. The difference is what happens to provider-bound requests:
With Layer5 Cloud as a remote provider, Meshery Server forwards provider-bound requests, such as designs, views, the catalog, sharing, and support, to Cloud and relays the answers back. With the local provider, there is no remote service behind Meshery, so every provider-bound feature returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. Choose a remote provider for any feature that depends on accounts, sharing, or stored designs.
SaaS versus self-hosted 🔗 Layer5 Cloud runs as a hosted service and as a self-hosted deployment, and both act as a remote provider in the same way. The trusted-source rules above are relative to each deployment: a self-hosted Cloud trusts its own configured base URL and the custom domains of its own organizations, not those of the hosted service. To run your own deployment, see Self-Hosted.

body:
A self-hosted deployment is its own identity provider. Ory Kratos owns user accounts and sign-in, Ory Hydra issues OAuth2 tokens, and the Layer5 Cloud server connects the two to organizations, teams, and roles. Users can sign up with an email address and password, or with Google or GitHub. For how identity fits together as a concept, see Identity and Security.
What the chart configures by default 🔗 Capability Default Password sign-in On. Minimum 8 characters, checked against known-breached passwords, and rejected when too similar to the account identifier. Email verification Required before a password sign-in succeeds. Delivered as a code. Account recovery On, delivered as a code. Social sign-in Google and GitHub are enabled but have no credentials until you add them. Login flow lifespan A started sign-in must finish within 12 hours (720m). Recovery and verification flow lifespan A recovery or verification request stays valid for 30 days (720h). Registration flow lifespan A started sign-up must finish within 24 hours. Session lifespan Not set by the chart. Kratos applies its own default. See Sessions. Access tokens JWT, valid 24 hours. Refresh tokens are valid 1000 hours, ID tokens 1 hour, and authorization codes 1 hour. Change any of these through the kratos.kratos.config and hydra.hydra.config values. Both are passed to the Ory services unchanged, so the Kratos and Hydra configuration references apply.
Default Google and GitHub sign-in 🔗 Every organization signs in through the deployment’s default providers until the organization registers its own. You supply those defaults as two OAuth applications, one for Google and one for GitHub, and the deployment uses them in two places:
Where Used for Configured with Kratos Social sign-in and sign-up on the deployment’s own hostname, and social sign-up on every hostname client_id and client_secret of the github and google entries under kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.methods.oidc.config.providers Layer5 Cloud server Social sign-in on organization custom domains env.providerOrgGithubKey, env.providerOrgGithubSecret, env.providerOrgGoogleKey, env.providerOrgGoogleSecret Use the same OAuth application for both. Register these redirect addresses on it, replacing <host> with your deployment hostname:
Provider Addresses to register Google https://<host>/kratos/self-service/methods/oidc/callback/google and https://<host>/oidc/callback/google. Google matches redirect addresses exactly. GitHub https://<host>/. GitHub matches by path prefix, so the host root covers both callbacks. You register addresses on your deployment hostname only. A custom-domain organization that uses the default providers completes the exchange on your hostname and returns to its own domain.
How the defaults are stored 🔗 At every start, the server reads the env.providerOrg* values and stores each pair it finds, encrypted with env.cloudCredentialEncryptionKey, as a credential and connection in an administrative environment of the provider organization. Three behaviors follow:
A provider needs both its key and its secret. A provider with only one set is skipped, and the log says so. The server needs an administrator first. The seed records which user created the rows, so it waits until the provider organization has a member. On a new deployment, provider initialization creates that member on first start, and the seed runs on the same start. Stored credentials are not overwritten. After the first successful seed, changing env.providerOrg* and redeploying does not change what the server uses. There is no self-service rotation of the defaults today: replacing them means replacing the stored credential directly in the database, so plan their lifetime before you go live and ask Layer5 support for guidance when you must rotate. The seed never blocks startup. When it fails, the server starts and sign-in on custom domains that rely on the defaults fails until a later start succeeds. Search the startup log for IdP seed messages.
Bring your own credentials 🔗 An organization can register its own Google or GitHub OAuth application, or an OIDC provider, so that the consent screen carries its own brand and the whole exchange stays on its own domain. The organization’s administrators do this themselves; Provider Admins can do it for any organization. See Configuring Identity Providers.
Bringing your own credentials is always optional. Social sign-in works on every custom domain with the deployment’s defaults, including a custom domain on a different registrable domain from your deployment. An organization brings its own credentials for its brand, its own rate limits and audit trail, or a separate authentication boundary, never to make social sign-in available.
Organization’s domain Default providers Own credentials None, or a subdomain of the deployment’s base domain (team.example.com on a cloud.example.com deployment) Work out of the box Optional A different registrable domain (meshery.yourcompany.com pointed at your deployment) Work out of the box Optional For the named combinations and when to choose each, see Organization Configuration Scenarios.
The identity provider is the security boundary 🔗 Organizations that sign in through the same identity provider sit inside the same authentication boundary. An organization that brings its own credentials is a distinct boundary. The shape of the host name does not decide this; the identity provider behind it does.
Host class Example Identity provider Authentication boundary Canonical host cloud.example.com The deployment’s default providers The shared boundary Subdomain of the same base domain partner.example.com The default providers The shared boundary Different base domain meshery.yourcompany.com The default providers, unless the organization brings its own The shared boundary, unless it brings its own Any host, with own credentials Any of the above The organization’s own provider A distinct boundary The authentication boundary combines with authorization: each organization context scopes what a user may do through keys, keychains, and roles. See Security Boundaries for the full picture.
Custom domains 🔗 Setting up a custom domain for an organization is a Provider Admin task. See White-label Layer5 Cloud for the steps and Social sign-in on a custom domain for how sign-in behaves there.

body:
Import turns an existing configuration into an editable design. Kanvas identifies the format from the file content, converts it to a Meshery design, and saves it as a new design in your account. A File Upload or URL Import does not keep the original file, so exporting later produces a new file from the current design. A GitHub import is different: the design stays bound to its source, as described in Where the imported design lands.
Import works in Designer mode. The import action is hidden in Operator mode.
Choose how to import 🔗 Method Accepts Result Import dialog, File Upload One local file New design, or merge into the open design Import dialog, URL Import One direct http or https URL to a single file New design, or merge into the open design Drag or paste onto the canvas One or more files One new design per file, or a merge prompt if the canvas is not empty Catalog clone or open A published design Copy of the design, see Clone a Design GitHub integration in Layer5 Cloud Files and folders in a connected repository One private design per valid file The URL must point at a file, not a repository, a chart repository, or a directory. Folders cannot be imported directly: compress a Kustomize project or Helm chart into a single archive first.
The import dialog takes a name (1 to 255 characters, default “Untitled Design”). Names are not required to be unique. If you leave the name empty, Kanvas uses the name inside the file, and drops use the file name.
Supported formats 🔗 Kanvas accepts .yml, .yaml, .json, .tar, .tar.gz, .tgz, .gz, and .zip. Any other extension is rejected. Archives are extracted safely and entries that try to escape the archive directory are refused.
Kanvas decides the format by content, not by the file name, and takes the first match in this order:
Meshery design. A YAML or JSON design file, or an OCI image archive (.tar, .tgz, .zip) whose layers contain a design file. Only the first design in an archive is taken. An OCI archive without a design file fails. Kubernetes manifest. A .yml or .yaml file with one or more documents. Unknown resource kinds are kept as generic objects. Helm chart. A packaged chart archive. An uncompressed .tar is reported as needing gzip compression. Individual chart files such as Chart.yaml cannot be imported, and values overrides are not an import option. Docker Compose. Compose services are first converted to Kubernetes resources, so the design contains Kubernetes components. Kustomize. A single kustomization file, or an archive that contains kustomization.yaml and every file it references. The full matrix is in Supported Import and Export Formats.
Import a file as a new design or merge it 🔗 When the canvas is empty, import loads the new design. When a design is open, the dialog offers Import as new and Merge into current.
Import as new saves the file as a design and opens it. If the open design has unsaved changes, the browser asks you to confirm before leaving. Declining cancels the load, but the imported design stays saved in your account. Merge into current saves the file as its own design, then appends its components and relationships to the open design. Files dropped on a non-empty canvas raise a Merge Design prompt that names the incoming design and its component count. It offers Cancel, Open as new, and Merge into current. Cancel does not delete the design the import already saved.
Dropping several files imports each as a separate design. The import dialog processes a single file at a time.
How a merge behaves 🔗 Merging happens in the editor and changes only the open design.
Identity. Every component and relationship in the incoming design receives a new identifier. Kanvas does not match or de-duplicate against existing components, so merging the same design twice doubles its components. Preserved. Names, kinds, configuration, styles, and the internal layout of the incoming block. Placement. The block’s top-left corner moves to the drop position when you dropped a file. Otherwise it lands 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down from its original coordinates, and it can overlap existing components. Not carried over. The incoming design’s name, id, version, visibility, catalog data, layer preferences, and workspace. The open design keeps its own. After the merge. Relationship evaluation runs as for any edit, and autosave persists the result after three seconds. If the merged design exceeds your plan’s component limit, the save fails and the merged components remain unsaved on the canvas. See Save Designs. Merging needs no permission key, but the incoming design must be one you can read: your own, public, published, or shared with you.
Where the imported design lands 🔗 The imported design is owned by you, placed in your selected workspace, public, at version 0.0.1, and records its detected source type. Imports from a GitHub repository are the exception: each file becomes a private design named after the file. The design records the repository and file path it came from, and the imported file itself is stored with the design. Re-importing, refreshing, and viewing that source are covered in Connect GitHub. GitHub imports read each file from the repository’s default branch. The stored file is not offered for download, so exporting still produces a new file from the current design. Invalid files in a selection are reported per path and do not stop valid files from importing.
The components-per-design plan limit applies to URL imports and to every save. GitHub imports are not checked at import time. They are checked the first time the design is saved.
URL import limits 🔗 The server fetches a URL under these limits:
Only http and https, checked again on every redirect, with at most 5 redirects. 10 seconds to connect and 30 seconds for the request. 16 MiB maximum body. Destinations that resolve to loopback, private, or link-local addresses are refused. Failures 🔗 Every failed import shows the same message, Failed to import design "<name>", whether the cause is an unrecognized format, an invalid archive, a plan limit, or an unreachable server. Nothing is saved when the server rejects the file. A failed merge shows Failed to merge design: <reason>.
Files dropped on the canvas follow separate rules. Images and .txt files become canvas objects, not designs, and files over 500 KB are rejected whatever your plan. Archive types RAR and 7Z pass the drop check but fail at import. Other file types are ignored without a message.
Related 🔗 Save Designs covers plan limits and failures after an import. GitHub Integration covers connecting a repository.

body:
An organization is the tenant boundary in Layer5 Cloud: teams, workspaces, roles, resources, and billing all attach to one. This guide covers the administrator tasks for an organization: create it, edit its branding and sign-in settings, manage its members, move between organizations, and delete it. For what an organization is and how it relates to teams and roles, see Organizations.
Who can do what 🔗 The Organizations page opens for members who hold View Org or View All Organizations. Each task needs its own permission, and a few tasks are enforced more tightly than the permission matrix shows.
Organization permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Org See only organizations to which you are a member. See all other members within your membership teams. ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View Organizations See all organizations of which you are an administrator. See all members of those organizations. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View All Organizations See all organizations within a Cloud deployment. See all organizations, teams, and users. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Organization Establish new organization for organizing teams, users, and resource access. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Edit Organization Edit organiaztions and add teams to it -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Add User to Organization Directly create a new user account within an organization. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove User from Organization Discontinue user access to organization, teams and resources; cease billing accrual. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Promote or Demote User to Org Admin Elevate or remove organization level administrative privileges. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Roles to Organization members Assign roles to users in an organization -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove Roles from Organization members Remove roles from users in an organization -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Task Who is admitted Create an organization Holders of Create Organization (Organization Admin and Provider Admin by default) Edit an organization, add or remove its teams, add a member Organization Admin or Owner of that organization, Provider Admin, or Organization Admin or Owner of its parent Set a domain to a new value Provider Admin only Clear a domain or keep the stored one The administrators who can edit the organization Remove a member Holders of Remove User from Organization Delete an organization Its Owner, a Provider Admin, or Organization Admin or Owner of its parent. An Organization Admin who is not the Owner cannot delete it. Creating an Organization 🔗 Create an organization to give a project, customer, or business unit its own teams, users, and resource access.
How to create an Organization 🔗 An organization takes these details:
Field Required Notes Organization Name Yes The form keeps Create disabled until you enter a name. Country No Picked from a list. Region No A time zone, picked from a list. Members No Existing Layer5 Cloud users to add at creation. What creation does:
You become the Owner. The creator is recorded as the organization’s owner. Ownership cannot be transferred or removed (see Limits). Members are added. The form adds you and any users you picked as members. A default workspace is created. Every organization starts with one workspace named My Workspace, owned by you. The event is recorded. Layer5 Cloud logs a success or failure event for the creation. The Add Organization control is disabled when your role lacks Create Organization. A new organization does not carry a domain. To give it one, see Organization Configuration Scenarios.
Child Organizations 🔗 An organization can have child organizations of its own, to any depth. A parent’s Organization Administrator or Owner can edit a child’s settings and membership, or delete it, without joining the child. Anything inside the child still requires membership in the child. A parent that still has children cannot be deleted. See Child Organizations for details.
Editing Your Organization 🔗 Editing changes how the organization looks, how its members sign in, and how it is reached.
What you can edit 🔗 Setting What it controls Name, country, region The organization’s identity in lists and switchers. Domain The address that routes users to the organization. See Domain. Open Org Invitation The invitation that admits non-members who sign in through the organization. See Using the Open Organization Invitation Link. Theme and logos Colors and four logos shown to members. See Branding. Links Legal, support, and social links on sign-in pages and email footers. Feature carousel Whether the sign-in pages show the feature carousel. On by default. Teams Which teams belong to the organization. See Teams. Identity Providers The OAuth applications that power sign-in. See below. Email The mail server the organization sends through. See below. Every successful update is recorded as an event.
Branding 🔗 Branding applies to the signed-in experience and, on an organization with its own domain, to the sign-in, sign-up, and error pages.
Theme colors. Every color must be a hex value (#rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb, or #rrggbbaa). Layer5 Cloud rejects any other value with a 400 error that names the color. Resetting the theme also clears the logos. Logos. Four slots: desktop, mobile, dark desktop, and dark mobile. Each image can be at most 500 KB. A larger file fails the update with image size exceeds the maximum limit. Links. Terms of Service and Privacy Policy accept an http or https URL, a mailto: or tel: link, or a root-relative path. Support entries (Discussion Forum URL, Support Email, Slack URL) accept the same forms plus plain text without a colon, such as a bare email address. LinkedIn, X, and YouTube accept an absolute http or https URL. Layer5 Cloud silently drops a value it considers unsafe, including javascript: and data: links, instead of rejecting the update. Clearing every link restores the defaults. An organization that publishes any link of its own gets an email footer without the provider’s channels for the ones it left empty. Domain 🔗 The domain field routes users who arrive at that address into the organization. Layer5 Cloud validates a changed domain when you save:
It is 3 to 253 characters long. It is made of dot-separated labels of 1 to 63 ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens. A label cannot start or end with a hyphen. Write internationalized names in Punycode (xn--). It is a hostname, not an email address, and does not start with http, https, or www. It is not one of the provider’s reserved hosts, including the canonical Layer5 Cloud address. It is unique. No two organizations share a domain, and the check includes deleted organizations (see Deleting Your Organization). Validation is syntactic. Layer5 Cloud does not look the name up in DNS when you save, so a valid name that does not resolve yet is accepted.
Only a Provider Admin can set a domain to a new value. Any other caller receives a 403 error that says a domain requires a Provider Admin. Clearing the field removes the assignment and is open to the organization’s administrators. Domain-to-organization lookups are cached for five minutes, and every organization create, update, and delete clears the affected entry immediately. Changing a domain can break routing for users who rely on the old address, so plan the change with the provider.
Teams in the organization 🔗 Adding a team to an organization maps the team into it, and removing a team ends that mapping only. The team itself is not deleted. Adding a team requires an Organization Admin or Owner of the organization, or a Provider Admin. Removing a team also admits someone who is both Team Admin and Team Owner of that team. Removing a team that does not belong to the organization returns a 404 error.
Configuring Identity Providers (Bring-Your-Own Credentials) 🔗 The Identity Providers tab controls which OAuth applications power sign-in for your organization. This is most useful when your organization uses a custom domain and you want your own brand, not Layer5’s, shown on the Google, GitHub, or OIDC consent screen.
By default, your organization uses Layer5’s shared OAuth applications. To override them, add your own provider. There is no separate enable step:
Use Add Google, Add GitHub, or Add OIDC to register a provider. Each walkthrough displays the exact redirect URI to add to your OAuth application. Saving your first provider switches the organization to its own identity providers automatically. Use Edit to rotate a provider’s credentials, or Remove to delete a single provider. Removing your last provider reverts the organization to Layer5’s defaults. Use Delete All Identity Providers to remove every configured provider at once. This deletes the environment that Layer5 Cloud provisioned to hold them, and the organization reverts to Layer5’s default identity providers. Every removal asks you to confirm and explains the consequences before it proceeds.
Who can configure this Organization Administrators and Owners can add, rotate, and remove their organization’s identity providers themselves. Provider Administrators can additionally manage the identity providers and the other settings of any organization, whether or not they are members of it. Switching identity providers does not affect existing user accounts or login history. Users who signed in through a provider you later remove may need to re-authenticate.
Configuring Your Own Mail Server 🔗 The Email tab lets your organization send application mail such as invitations and notifications through its own SMTP server, from its own domain, instead of through Layer5’s shared mail server. Nothing about the message then points to a shared provider.
Setup has three steps: register the server and its credentials, prove control of the sending domain by publishing a DNS TXT record, and pass a connection test. Completing them changes nothing on its own. Mail keeps leaving through Layer5’s shared server until an administrator turns the server on, which switches routing over. The tab reports delivery health afterwards, and a fallback setting decides what happens to a message your server does not accept.
The full walkthrough, with a worked example for Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Amazon SES, SendGrid, and Postmark, and a troubleshooting table for every failure the tab reports, is in Bring Your Own Mail Server.
Who can configure this Organization Administrators and Owners can configure, test, turn on, turn off, and remove their organization’s mail server, under the same gate as the Identity Providers tab. Using the Open Organization Invitation Link 🔗 An organization can designate one of its invitations as its open invitation. The open invitation admits people without a per-person invite, so you can onboard many users at once or run public sign-ups.
You designate it in either of two places: the Open Org Invitation setting of the organization, or the Set as open signup invitation option on the invitation itself. When both are set, the organization’s setting wins as long as it names a live invitation of that organization.
When to use it 🔗 Bulk onboarding. Onboard many users without sending individual emails. Public sign-ups. Let people sign up openly, for example from a community page. Cross-organizational collaboration. Make it easy for outside collaborators to join. How it works 🔗 On sign-in. Every time someone signs in through the organization’s domain, or through a request that names the organization, Layer5 Cloud accepts the open invitation for them if they are not yet a member. Acceptance adds the organization, team, and role grants that the invitation carries. It never removes anything. New users. A person without an account is directed to sign up, and the invitation is applied when they first sign in. Existing users. A person with an account joins with it. Failure. If acceptance fails, Layer5 Cloud logs the failure and the sign-in still succeeds. Visibility. The organization record publishes the open invitation’s id, and the id is also its invitation code. Treat an open invitation as a shareable link, not a secret. Inviting users to specific teams To place invited users into teams, list the teams on an invitation. See Manage Teams. For individual invitations and their expiry, see User Invitations. Managing Members 🔗 Membership decides which organizations a person can enter, and roles inside it decide what they can do there.
Add a member. Adding a member attaches an existing Layer5 Cloud account to the organization. It does not create an account. Adding someone who is already a member changes nothing. The caller must be an Organization Admin or Owner of the organization, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or Owner of its parent. Remove a member. Removal ends the person’s organization membership and their membership in every team of that organization in one step. Their account stays. Removal needs Remove User from Organization. The Owner cannot be removed. An attempt to remove the Owner fails with the error Organization owner cannot be removed. Removing someone with no membership returns a 404 error with no organization membership to remove. Repeating a removal is harmless. Assign or remove an organization role. The caller must be an Organization Admin of that organization, a Provider Admin, or hold Assign User Roles in it. The target must be a member of the organization, except when a Provider Admin makes the change. A row the caller may not change is skipped and reported in the response as unauthorized to assign org roles, and the rest of the request still applies. Only a Provider Admin can assign provider roles. Promoting or demoting a user to Organization Admin is the same operation. Every addition and removal is recorded as an event that states what ended.
Switching Between Organizations 🔗 Your current organization decides which resources you see, where new resources land, and which permissions apply.
The switcher lists only the organizations you are a member of. Members who hold View All Organizations, a Provider Admin by default, can also select All Organizations. If you need an organization you are not in, ask its administrator or use an invitation link.
Order of precedence 🔗 Layer5 Cloud decides your organization for each request from these sources, first match wins:
Domain. If the address you reached maps to an organization, that organization applies. This outranks every selection you make. X-Current-Orgid request header. API clients set it per request. Saved preference. The organization you last selected is stored in your user preferences. Browser session. The organization saved in the session cookie. Layer5 Cloud ignores a header, preference, or session value that names an organization you do not belong to, and runs the request with no organization scope. Holders of View All Organizations are exempt and can name any organization. There is no query-string or URL-parameter source. The API request format, including the header name, is in the API reference.
What changes when you switch 🔗 Area Behavior Designs, workspaces, environments, connections Only the selected organization’s resources appear. New resources Created in the selected organization. Resources do not follow you between organizations, so check the selection before you create anything important. Roles and permissions Scoped to the organization. The same person can hold different roles in different organizations, and administrative rights in one organization grant nothing in another. Team memberships The memberships and permissions of the selected organization apply. For role details, see the roles concept.
Deleting Your Organization 🔗 Deleting an organization retires it and every membership in it. The operation has no undo.
What deletion does 🔗 The organization is marked deleted and no longer appears in any list or switcher. Every user membership in the organization ends. User accounts are not deleted. Every mapping between the organization and its teams ends. The teams themselves are not removed. The organization’s domain stops routing. The deleted organization still holds the domain, so no other organization can use it. Clear the domain before you delete if the address needs to be reused. The request does not delete the organization’s workspaces, environments, or designs, and nothing reaches them through the organization afterwards. Layer5 Cloud has no restore operation, so treat the deletion as permanent. The confirmation dialog states that the action is irreversible.
Deletion is permanent Once you confirm, the organization and its memberships cannot be restored. When deletion is refused 🔗 Condition Result The organization still has child organizations 409 conflict. Nothing is deleted. Delete the children first, starting with the deepest. It is the last organization you own 403 with you can't delete your last organization. The refusal does not apply when a parent’s administrator deletes a child. You are an Organization Admin but not the Owner Refused. Only the Owner, a Provider Admin, or the parent’s administrator can delete. When to delete 🔗 Delete an organization when it was created for a temporary project or in error, when consolidation made it redundant, or when you must retire it for compliance. Do not delete it when you only need to change memberships, when other users or services still depend on it, or when you are unsure what it holds. Remove members or teams instead.
How to delete your organization 🔗 Select the organization, choose Delete, and type the confirmation word the dialog asks for.
Limits today 🔗 These actions do not exist in Layer5 Cloud today:
Transfer ownership. The creator stays the Owner. No operation reassigns ownership. Leave an organization. A member cannot leave on their own. An administrator removes a member. Restore a deleted organization. Move a child organization to a different parent. Related 🔗 Organizations (concept) Child Organizations Organization Configuration Scenarios Roles and Permissions

body:
A workspace is the unit you use to organize designs and to decide which teams can reach an organization’s environments and connections. This guide covers every task on a workspace. For what a workspace is and how it relates to teams, environments, and designs, read the Workspaces concept.
Each task names the permission it needs. Layer5 Cloud checks the permission in the organization that owns the workspace. A custom role or a team role can hold any of these permissions; the default holders are below.
Workspace permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Workspace See all workspaces within an organization ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Workspace Create new workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Edit Workspace Edit workspace and it's team and environment membership -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Delete Workspace Dissolve workspace and all team and environment memberships. Leave associated resources intact -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign team to workspace Add new team to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove team from workspace Remove team from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign environment to workspace Add new environment to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove environment from workspace Remove environment from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Designs to Workspaces Assign designs to workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove Designs from Workspaces Remove designs from workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Views to Workspace Add new views to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Unassign Views from Workspace Remove views from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Find workspaces 🔗 Needs: View Workspace to see the Workspaces page. The API lists workspaces for any signed-in member of the organization.
Every member of an organization can list every workspace in it. Team membership does not narrow the list. A list request names one organization. A user who holds View All Organizations can ask for every organization at once.
You can search by name or description, order by creation or update time, and page through results.
Create a workspace 🔗 Needs: Create Workspace in the organization that will own the workspace.
A workspace takes a name, a description, and an organization. The workspace stays in that organization for its whole life; Layer5 Cloud ignores a later request to change it.
The Workspaces page requires a name and an organization. The API does not check that the name is non-empty. Name and description are each limited to 255 characters. A longer value fails with Unable to create workspace. Names do not have to be unique. Two workspaces in one organization can share a name, so choose names you can tell apart. You become the owner of record. Creating a workspace does not assign any team or environment, and an empty workspace gives nobody access to anything. Edit a workspace 🔗 Needs: Edit Workspace.
You can change the name and the description. An update changes only the fields you send. A request with an empty body fails. A workspace that is not in one of your organizations answers workspace not found.
Give a team access to a workspace 🔗 Needs: Assign team to workspace to add a team, Remove team from workspace to take it away.
The team and the workspace must belong to the same organization. A team from another organization is refused with HTTP 403. Assigning a team that is already assigned changes nothing and returns the existing assignment.
What a team assignment grants is narrower than it sounds:
It grants It does not grant Read-only access to the connections, and their credentials, in every environment attached to the workspace Access to private designs in the workspace The ability to see the workspace (all organization members see all workspaces) Permission to create, edit, or delete anything Removing the team ends the access at once. To give a team access to a private design, share the design with the people who need it. See Share Designs.
Attach an environment to a workspace 🔗 Needs: Assign environment to workspace to attach, Remove environment from workspace to detach.
Attaching an environment makes its connections readable to every member of the workspace’s teams. The environment and the workspace must belong to the same organization; a cross-organization attachment is refused with HTTP 403.
Some environments are provisioned by Layer5 Cloud itself to hold organization configuration such as the mail server or sign-in providers. Layer5 Cloud refuses to attach one to a workspace: this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be added to a workspace.
Attaching an environment that is already attached returns the existing attachment. Detaching one that was never attached answers no such environment assignment. Detaching an environment that was already detached returns the earlier record without error.
The same environment can sit in any number of workspaces. Creating and filling environments is covered in Manage Environments.
Place designs and views in a workspace 🔗 Needs: Assign Designs to Workspaces and Remove Designs from Workspaces for designs. Assign Views to Workspace and Unassign Views from Workspace for views.
A design or view belongs to at most one workspace. Placing it in a workspace moves it: Layer5 Cloud removes every earlier workspace assignment, then adds the new one. There is no copy.
Ownership does not change. The user who created a design stays its owner after any move. The workspace decides the organization. A design is listed under the organization of the workspace that holds it, and the Share Design permission is checked in that organization. Moving a design into a workspace in another organization moves it into that organization. Workspace membership is not design access. A private design stays private. Only the owner, provider administrators, and users the design was shared with can open it, wherever it sits. Private, public, and published designs can all live in one workspace. Removing a design from its workspace leaves it with no workspace. The design and its owner are unaffected. The permission is checked in the destination workspace’s organization only. Layer5 Cloud does not check that you own the design or that the design is in your organization.
The unassigned list for a workspace shows only designs you own.
Review workspace activity 🔗 Needs: View Workspace.
Each workspace keeps an event log. It records the creation, update, and deletion of the workspace, and every assignment and unassignment of a team, environment, design, or view, with the email of the person who acted. Failed attempts are recorded as error events. The log is paged and searchable.
Delete a workspace 🔗 Needs: Delete Workspace.
Deleting a workspace ends, in one step, every team, environment, design, and view assignment it holds. It deletes none of those resources: the teams, environments, connections, designs, and views all remain. Designs and views that were in the workspace have no workspace afterwards, and team members lose the connection access the workspace gave them.
An organization must keep at least one workspace. Layer5 Cloud refuses to delete the last one with cannot delete workspace: at least one workspace must exist for the organization. The check holds under concurrent requests, so two simultaneous deletes cannot empty an organization. The refusal arrives as HTTP 500.
Create the replacement workspace first, then delete the other.
Patterns that work 🔗 One workspace per project. Attach the project’s team and environments, and keep its designs together. One workspace per stage. Give a production workspace only the production environment and the platform team. Members of other teams cannot read production connections through it. See Promote a Design from Staging to Production. One workspace per team. Attach the team and the environments it works with. Questions 🔗 Can other workspace members edit or delete my design? Workspace membership grants no design access. People you shared the design with can read, edit, and clone it. Only the owner or a provider administrator can delete it.
How do I make a design read-only for everyone? Publish it. See Publish Designs.
Does a workspace have size limits? No. Layer5 Cloud enforces no space or file-count limit on workspaces, and no plan check on workspace actions.

body:
Your profile belongs to you, not to an organization. A change applies in every organization you belong to. This guide covers the four things you can change about your account: the profile, the password, the linked sign-in providers, and the account itself.
Before you start 🔗 You need the View Profile permission to open the profile. The default user role holds it. Changing your password needs Reset Password. Deleting the account needs Delete Account. The default user role holds both. Layer5 Cloud signs you in through an identity service. Password changes and account deletion need a live browser sign-in. A script that holds only an API token cannot do either. Changing a password or linking a provider is a privileged action. If your sign-in is older than the privileged-session window, Layer5 Cloud asks you to sign in again first. The window is 24 hours on hosted Layer5 Cloud and 15 minutes by default in the self-hosted chart. A user’s profile can also be edited by an administrator who holds Update User Profile in an organization you share with them. Only a Provider Admin can change another user’s email address. Edit your profile 🔗 The profile form saves itself. About one second after you stop typing, Layer5 Cloud saves the change and confirms it with a short message. There is no Save button, and edits made during a save are queued, not lost.
Field Behavior First Name, Last Name Free text. An empty value never overwrites the stored name. Username Read-only. It is the identifier assigned to the account and cannot be edited. E-mail Must look like an address (name@host.domain). An invalid value blocks saving and shows “Please enter a valid email address”. Country, Region Optional. Pick a country, then a region of that country. Avatar URL Optional. A public URL to a JPEG, PNG, GIF, SVG, or WEBP image. Layer5 Cloud loads the image before it saves. An address that does not load as an image is rejected. Avatar color The background color shown when you have no avatar image. Saved as a user preference. Tagline A short public line about you. Social Links Up to 5 links, each with a type (GitHub, LinkedIn, X, Company or Organization, or Personal Website) and a URL. An empty URL is allowed; a malformed one is rejected. Your avatar, tagline, and social links appear on your public profile.
Change your email address 🔗 Changing the email address changes the identifier you sign in with. Layer5 Cloud marks the new address as unverified and sends it a verification message. The confirmation reads “Profile updated. Please check your new email address to verify it.” Verify the new address before you rely on it. If the verification message cannot be sent, the change still completes.
Layer5 Cloud writes the change to the identity service first and to your profile second, so a rejected address never leaves the two out of step.
Change your password 🔗 Use the Reset Password control on the profile. Enter the new password twice. The two entries must match, or the form reports “Your new passwords do not match”.
The identity service enforces the password policy:
At least 8 characters. Not a password found in known breaches. Not too similar to your email address. A strength bar (Very weak to Strong) shows how guessable the password is. It is advice only and does not block you; the policy above does. A rejected password returns the identity service’s reason. A successful change shows “Password updated”.
Changing your password does not end your other sessions or revoke your API tokens. To cut off a device or script, end the session or revoke the token yourself with Review and Sign Out Sessions and Create and Use an API Token.
If you forgot your password, use the recovery flow from the sign-in page instead. It emails a one-time code and link that stay valid for 30 days.
Link or unlink a sign-in provider 🔗 Link GitHub or Google to sign in with whichever you prefer. Either method opens the same account, with the same organizations, designs, and roles. GitHub and Google are the only supported providers.
The profile lists a Link option for each provider you have not linked and an Unlink option for each provider you have linked. The provider you used to create the account appears in neither list: you cannot unlink it, and it is already linked.
Linking sends you to the provider to approve access, then returns you to Layer5 Cloud. Layer5 Cloud asks GitHub for your profile and email address and Google for your email and profile. Unlinking removes the provider from your account. Your password and the other linked provider keep working.
A provider account can be linked to one Layer5 Cloud account only. Linking depends on the provider reporting a verified email address. For how Layer5 Cloud resolves sign-ins that share an email address, read Account Consolidation and the Account Linking rules.
Delete your account 🔗 Deletion is permanent. Layer5 Cloud asks you to confirm, and then does not offer recovery.
What deletion does:
Hands any credential you hold on behalf of an organization to that organization’s successor, so the organization keeps working. The successor is the organization’s owner, or else its longest-standing Organization Admin. Marks your account as deleted and removes your memberships in every organization and team, which removes your roles with them. Records the deletion in the audit trail. Removes your sign-in identity, including linked GitHub and Google sign-in, and signs you out. What deletion leaves behind:
Published content, such as items you published to the catalog, stays public. Organizations you own continue to exist. Deleting your account does not delete or transfer them. The audit trail keeps its entries. Re-registering with the same email address does not restore the old account or re-link a provider.
When deletion is refused 🔗 Layer5 Cloud refuses the deletion, and changes nothing, when you are the only owner or Organization Admin of an organization that holds credentials designated to it. The message begins “Refusing to delete your account” and names the organization. Without a successor, those credentials would be orphaned.
Resolve it, then retry:
Promote another member of that organization to Organization Admin. An organization’s ownership cannot be transferred, so a second Organization Admin is the way to give it a successor. Or release the credentials from the organization, or delete them. See also 🔗 Users explains accounts, memberships, and sign-in methods. Set Notification Preferences controls the email you receive. Security covers sessions and API tokens.

body:
The interactive terminal opens a shell inside a running container without leaving the Operator canvas. Use it for last-mile diagnosis that logs and status cannot answer: testing connectivity from inside a pod, reading a mounted file, or checking an injected environment variable. It is a browser-based equivalent of kubectl exec, scoped to the resource you selected.
Before you start 🔗 Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. See How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud. A connected cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and a message broker in the cluster. MeshSync executes the shell, and Meshery Server relays input and output through the broker. If any of the three is unavailable, the terminal does not connect (see Failure modes). A running container whose image contains /bin/sh. Distroless images have no shell and cannot be used. Open a session 🔗 The action is named Initiate Terminal Session and is offered on Pod and Container resources only. Right-click the resource on the canvas, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel. The session starts immediately and the terminal panel opens at the bottom left of the canvas. There is no separate connect step.
What opens depends on what you selected:
You select Sessions opened A pod One session per container in the pod’s containers list, each in its own tab. Init and ephemeral containers are not included. There is no prompt to choose a container. A container One session for that container. A node with an active session shows a terminal badge. Selecting the badge reopens the panel.
Work in the terminal 🔗 Each tab is one shell session. The panel is draggable, minimizable to a dock icon with a session count, and keeps its scrollback (10,000 lines). Closing the panel with the close button hides it and leaves the sessions running. The trash icon on a tab ends that tab’s session and removes the tab. Leaving Operator mode closes the panel.
The terminal edits your input in the browser and sends it to the container when you press Enter:
Key Behavior Printable keys, Backspace Edit the current line locally. Enter Sends the whole line to the shell. Up, Down Walk the history of lines typed in this tab. Ctrl+C Sends an interrupt to the running command. Tab Inserts four spaces. It does not trigger shell completion. Other Ctrl, Alt, and Meta combinations Ignored. Because input is line-based and the remote terminal is not resized when you resize the panel, commands that take over the screen, such as vim, top, and less, do not work. Use commands that print and exit: ls, cat, env, ps aux, curl, nslookup.
The search icon in the panel header opens a search field with next and previous controls for finding text in the scrollback.
Limits and scope 🔗 Item Behavior Sessions per container One live session per container per user. Starting a second session for the same container does nothing and opens no new tab. Concurrent sessions overall No limit is enforced. Different users Each user gets an independent session, even on the same container. Shell Fixed to /bin/sh with a terminal attached. No bash fallback and no shell selection. Identity in the container The exec call runs with MeshSync’s own Kubernetes access, not a per-user Kubernetes identity. Anyone who can open a terminal has the reach of the workload’s container, so treat access to this action as access to the container. Idle timeout, maximum duration None. Reconnect None. If the connection between your browser and Meshery Server drops, the tab stays on screen but is dead. Close the tab and start a new session. Who can use it 🔗 Kanvas does not hide or disable the action based on role or plan. The permission model lists View Interactive Terminal as an Operator capability for the Team Operator plan and above. See Permissions by Role and Feature Availability for the current role and plan matrix.
Failure modes 🔗 Symptom Cause and fix Panel shows Failed to create terminal session with a reason The Kanvas extension could not be loaded by Meshery. The reason names the cause, for example a plugin built for a different Meshery version than the one you run. Install matching versions. Toast No container found to create term session The selected component lists no containers. Empty tab, no prompt Meshery Server could not reach MeshSync. Confirm the cluster shows as connected and that the broker is connected. Kanvas does not display the server’s error text for terminal sessions. Prompt never appears, or the shell prints an error The container has no /bin/sh, is not in the Running phase, or was deleted. Errors raised while MeshSync opens the shell print in the terminal itself. Session goes quiet after exit or a pod restart The session ended on the cluster. Kanvas shows no closed message. Close the tab and start a new session. For cluster connection problems, see Troubleshoot Kanvas.
Related 🔗 Stream Container Logs opens in the same panel as terminal sessions. Operator explains where this data comes from. Resource Details lists the actions available for every resource kind.

Layer5 Cloud starts with unsafe placeholder values for every secret and with localhost for every URL. Settle the decisions below first, so the install is a single helm install with a complete values file.
Decisions to make 🔗 Decision What to settle Where it is configured Database A PostgreSQL server that hosts three databases: meshery, kratos, and hydra. env.db, env.kratosdb, env.hydradb, and the subchart dsn values Hostname and TLS One public hostname, a certificate for it, and the scheme (https). ingress.*, env.serverbaseurl, env.serverHost, env.proto Secrets Replace every placeholder before first start. See Secrets to generate. env.*, kratos.*, hydra.* Identity providers The Google and GitHub OAuth applications that act as the default sign-in providers. See Identity Services. env.providerOrg* Mail A relay on a public address that offers STARTTLS (or implicit TLS on 465), and how identity mail leaves. See Mail. smtp.*, Kratos courier values First administrator The Provider Admin account and the provider organization. See Provider initialization. env.initConfig Network paths What must be reachable between components and from users. See Networking. Ingress, network policy, egress rules Observability Where logs and traces go. See Monitoring. env.loglevel, env.otelConfig Database 🔗 Layer5 Cloud creates and migrates its own schema. The server applies migrations every time it starts, and exits if a migration fails, so give the database user the rights to create tables and the uuid-ossp extension in the public schema of the meshery database. Kratos and Hydra run their own migrations when the chart’s automigration setting is on, which is the default.
The chart does not install a database. Size it for your user count and design volume. Run PostgreSQL with persistent storage that survives pod rescheduling, and back it up: organizations, designs, credentials, and identities all live in it.
Hostname and TLS 🔗 Users, Meshery Servers, and API clients reach everything through one hostname. The ingress must route three paths:
Path Backend Notes / Layer5 Cloud server, port 9876 The chart’s default ingress route. /kratos Kratos public service, port 9010 Browsers load sign-in and account flows from here. Strip the prefix when your controller supports it. /hydra Hydra public service Browsers use this for the OAuth2 sign-in redirect. Pass WebSocket upgrades on /collaboration. Set the same public URL in env.serverbaseurl, env.kratosbrowser, env.hydrabrowser, and the Kratos and Hydra urls values, or sign-in redirects point at the wrong host. On a TLS deployment, set env.proto to https: the server builds redirects to organization custom domains from that value and uses http for anything else.
The chart does not create or request a certificate. Terminate TLS at the ingress with a secret or a certificate manager of your choice.
Secrets to generate 🔗 Generate each value once, store it in your secret manager, and pass it to Helm. A change to a value that the chart writes into the Layer5 Cloud ConfigMap or Secret rolls the server pods.
Value Purpose Notes env.oauthsecret Secret of the OAuth2 client that Layer5 Cloud uses against Hydra. Must match the Hydra client you create. The default is a public placeholder. env.cloudCredentialEncryptionKey Encrypts stored identity-provider and mail credentials. Base64 of 32 random bytes. When empty, credential encryption fails. Losing it makes stored credentials unreadable. env.cloudOidcStateHmacKey Signs the state of the brokered OIDC sign-in. Base64 of 32 random bytes. When empty, brokered sign-in fails. env.kratosWebhookApiKey Shared key Kratos presents when it calls the registration hooks. Must equal the value in the Kratos registration web_hook configuration. The shipped default is the placeholder dev_token on both sides. kratos.kratos.config.secrets.cookie and .cipher Kratos session cookie and data encryption. Long random strings. The shipped value is empty. hydra.hydra.config.secrets.system Hydra system secret. Long random string. The shipped value is empty. env.providerOrgGithubSecret, env.providerOrgGoogleSecret Client secrets of the default OAuth applications. See Identity Services. smtp.smtppassword Password of the shared mail relay. Stored in a Kubernetes Secret, but also visible in the release’s stored Helm values. Generate a 32-byte key with openssl rand -base64 32. The server logs an error at startup when the credential encryption key is not a valid key, and keeps running without it.
Mail 🔗 Two kinds of mail leave a deployment, and they take different paths.
Application mail (invitations, notifications, welcome mail) is sent by the Layer5 Cloud server through the shared relay in smtp.*, unless an organization has registered its own relay. Identity mail (email verification and account recovery) is sent by Kratos through its courier. The chart ships the SMTP courier with an empty connection string, so set kratos.kratos.config.courier.smtp.connection_uri, or switch the courier to the HTTP strategy that posts to /api/identity/flow/emails on Layer5 Cloud. The HTTP strategy renders each message with the signup organization’s branding and rewrites the link onto its custom domain, and sends it as application mail. It has no SMTP fallback: when Layer5 Cloud rejects a message, Kratos retries and then abandons it without a visible error. Choose it when you use custom domains; choose the SMTP courier when you want identity mail independent of the application.
The shared relay is screened at startup. A relay on a non-submission port, an internal address, or without STARTTLS stops the server. See Troubleshoot Email Delivery.
Outbound dependencies 🔗 Destination Used for Required Your SMTP relay All mail For any mail Google and GitHub Social sign-in, when you register OAuth applications Only if you offer social sign-in reCAPTCHA Signup verification when you set both reCAPTCHA keys Only when configured Your webhook receivers Support requests, signup decisions, Kanvas entitlement events Only when configured OpenTelemetry collector Traces Only when env.otelConfig is set Public STUN and TURN hosts (from browsers) Direct co-editing between browsers For real-time collaboration Next step 🔗 Deploy Layer5 Cloud with the decisions above written into a values file.
