body:
A pipeline is only as trustworthy as its boundaries. In this tutorial you build two stages of one in a single organization: a staging workspace and a production workspace, each with its own team and its own environment. You put a design in staging, promote it to production, deploy it to the production environment from Kanvas, and read the production workspace’s activity log to confirm every change and who made it.
By the end you know what each object controls:
A workspace is a boundary. It decides where a design lives and which teams reach which connections. An environment is a deploy target: a named group of connections. A team assignment gives read-only access to connections. It does not give access to designs. Before you begin 🔗 You have a Layer5 Cloud account and work in an organization where your role holds the permissions below. Organization Admin and Workspace Admin hold all of them. The organization has at least one connection, such as a Kubernetes cluster. Two connections, one per stage, make the separation clearer, but one works: a connection can belong to more than one environment. The organization has a team for each stage, or one team you assign to both. To create teams, see Manage Teams. To complete step 7, you run a Meshery Server that holds the cluster connection. The hosted kanvas.new site does not deploy designs. You own a design. If you do not, clone one with Start from a Catalog Design. Each step needs a specific permission. The table shows which built-in roles hold each one:
Permissions used in this tutorial Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin Create Workspace Create new workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign team to workspace Add new team to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Environment Create a new environment -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign connections to environment Add new connections to environments -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign environment to workspace Add new environment to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Designs to Workspaces Assign designs to workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Confirm that the organization switcher shows the organization you intend. Every workspace and environment you create belongs to that organization permanently.
1. Create the staging and production workspaces 🔗 Create two workspaces in your organization and name them staging and production. Layer5 Cloud does not require unique names, so check the workspace list first and pick names nobody else in the organization uses.
Each new workspace starts empty: no teams, no environments, no designs. Every member of your organization can already see both workspaces in the list. Visibility is organization-wide; what a workspace grants comes from what you assign to it next.
2. Create an environment for each stage 🔗 Create two environments named staging and production. Assign a connection to each: your staging cluster to the staging environment and your production cluster to the production environment. If you have one connection, assign it to both.
An environment is the unit you deploy to. Grouping connections this way means that later, choosing where a design runs is one choice, not a list of clusters.
3. Give each workspace its environment 🔗 Assign the staging environment to the staging workspace and the production environment to the production workspace.
A workspace never holds connections directly. It holds environments, and the environments hold connections. This step makes each stage’s connections reachable from its workspace.
4. Assign a team to each workspace 🔗 Assign your staging team to the staging workspace and your production team to the production workspace. Each team must belong to the same organization as the workspace.
Assigning a team completes a chain: team member, to team, to workspace, to environment, to connection. Every member of the production team can now read the production connection and its credential. That access is read-only; only the connection’s owner can modify or delete it. Remove any link in the chain and the access ends.
5. Put your design in staging 🔗 Assign your design to the staging workspace. When you look for designs to add, the list offers only designs you own that are not already in the workspace.
The design is now listed under your organization through the staging workspace. The staging team cannot open it, though. A team assignment grants connection access, not design access, so a private design stays private. Keep that in mind for step 8.
6. Promote the design to production 🔗 Assign the same design to the production workspace.
Now look at the staging workspace: the design is gone. A design lives in at most one workspace, so assigning it to production moved it there. Promotion is a move, not a copy, which means there is exactly one current version and one place to find it.
Layer5 Cloud checks one permission for this move: Assign Designs to Workspaces in the production workspace’s organization. Anyone who holds it can promote, so grant it only to the people who should decide what reaches production.
7. Deploy to the production environment 🔗 Open the design in Kanvas and deploy it. The deploy action offers environments from your organization’s whole list at the moment you deploy. It does not limit the list to the design’s workspace, so select the production environment yourself. For the deploy options, see Deploy a Design.
The workspace decided where the design lives. The environment you choose now decides where it runs. Those are two separate decisions, and keeping them separate is what lets one design move through stages.
8. Let the production team read the design 🔗 The production team can reach the production connection but still cannot read your private design. To give them access, share the design with the people who need it. See Share a Design.
9. Confirm who did what 🔗 Open the production workspace’s recent activity. It lists each change recorded against the workspace, including the environment assignment, the team assignment, and the design assignment from this tutorial, each with the email address of the person who made it. Reading the activity log requires the View Workspace permission.
Use this log whenever you need to answer who promoted a design and when.
Roll back 🔗 To roll back, assign the design to the staging workspace again. It leaves production the same way it left staging, and the staging workspace’s activity log records the assignment.
What you built 🔗 Object Staging Production Workspace staging production Environment (deploy target) staging, with the staging connection production, with the production connection Team access Read-only access to the staging connection Read-only access to the production connection Design Lived here first Lives here now, deployed to the production environment Next steps 🔗 Workspaces explains the full access chain and lifecycle rules. Environments explains deploy targets and connection access. Manage Workspaces covers editing, removing members, and deleting workspaces.
description: Build staging and production workspaces, promote a design between them, deploy it to a production environment, and confirm who did what.

Sharing opens a private design to the people you name. Each grant is for one person, and it has no access level: a person who can open the shared design can also edit it and comment on it. You can also change a design’s visibility to make it open to everyone, and you can copy a link that points people to it.
This guide covers the task. For the reasoning behind the access model, read Collaboration Model. For a worked example with two people, follow Collaborative Editing.
Before you start 🔗 Requirement Detail Signed-in account Anonymous visitors to kanvas.new can design without signing in, but sharing asks them to sign in first. Layer5 Cloud also refuses a share from an anonymous session. Share Design permission Kanvas hides the Share action without it, and Layer5 Cloud checks it again when the request arrives. Layer5 Cloud checks it in the organization that owns the design’s workspace. A design that is in no workspace is checked in an organization the design’s owner belongs to. View All Users permission The people picker searches users through this permission. Without it the search is rejected, and the dialog does not find anyone. A loaded, non-empty design Share is unavailable while a design is empty, and while it is still loading. A new design has no link until its first save assigns it an id. An unpublished design Share is hidden for a published design. A remote provider Under the local provider, sharing returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. See Feature Availability by Plan. Views use the same dialog and the same grant model. Sharing a view needs the Share Views permission instead of Share Design. See Views.
Visibility levels 🔗 Visibility decides who can open a design without a grant.
Visibility Who can open it Who can edit it Private The owner, provider administrators, and people you grant access The same people Public Anyone with the link or the design id, including anonymous visitors Any signed-in user Published Everyone, through the Layer5 Cloud catalog The owner, provider administrators, and people with a grant A newly saved design is public, whatever visibility the client requests. Make a design private before you put sensitive architecture in it. A design cannot change visibility while it is published. See Publish Designs for the published state.
Changing visibility saves like any other edit: it raises the design’s version and counts against the plan’s components limit.
Give people access 🔗 Open Share for the design. It is in the design’s top bar, and in the menu of a design in your list of recent designs. Search for the person and add them. The search covers every user on Layer5 Cloud your role may search, not only your organization. It returns ten matches at a time and nothing for an empty search. Confirm the person appears in People with Access. The grant takes effect immediately. The person opens the design with the link, and it also appears in their list of designs.
What a grant allows 🔗 A grant carries no access level. It lets a person open a private design, edit and save it, comment on it, clone it, and download it. What else they can do depends on their own permissions, not on the grant: deploying, validating, and sharing each check the person’s role.
Action Owner Person with a grant Open and edit the design Yes Yes Comment, resolve, and reopen threads Yes Yes Clone and download Yes Yes Share it onward With the Share Design permission With the Share Design permission Change visibility Yes Layer5 Cloud does not restrict it to the owner Revoke access Yes With the Share Design permission Delete the design Yes, and provider administrators No Transfer ownership Not supported Not supported Most accounts hold the Share Design permission, because the default Organization Admin role includes it. Expect a collaborator to be able to share the design onward unless your organization has changed its roles. See Permissions by Role.
Rules for grants 🔗 The owner cannot be granted access, and the owner’s access cannot be revoked. A person can be granted access once. A second grant for the same person is rejected. Grants and revokes in one request are applied independently. If one half fails, the other half stays in place, and the failure names the half: “access could not be granted” or “access could not be revoked”. Layer5 Cloud sends an invitation email to a newly granted person only when the request asks for one. The email links to the design in the Meshery Playground. Each share request is recorded as an event. Grant access to people in another organization 🔗 A grant does not compare the person’s organization with the design’s. You can share a design with a user from any organization on the same Layer5 Cloud. There is no provider setting that enables or blocks this. The cross-organization tutorial walks through it.
Share a link 🔗 Copy Link produces a link that opens the design in Kanvas. It works for private and public designs.
Public design: anyone with the link can open it and, if signed in, edit it. Private design: the link only points to the design. The person also needs a grant, or an administrator role. Without one, Layer5 Cloud refuses the request, and an anonymous visitor cannot open it. The link carries the design’s id. Anyone who learns the id of a public design can open it.
Revoke access 🔗 Remove the person from People with Access. The change applies at once. Their clones and any copies they made stay theirs. Comments they wrote remain in the design, because comments are part of the design.
Deleting a design removes every grant for it.
What does not grant access 🔗 Teams. The dialog finds individual users only. Layer5 Cloud accepts a grant for a team through its API, but no access check honors it, so team members gain nothing from it. Workspaces. Adding a design to a workspace, and assigning teams to that workspace, does not open a private design to those teams. Layer5 Cloud checks the owner, provider administrators, and the design’s own grants. See Workspaces for what a workspace does control. Organization membership. Being in the owner’s organization does not open a private design. To give a whole team access, grant each member.
Messages and failures 🔗 Message Cause What to do Unable to share: this design could not be loaded. Try again once it has loaded. Share was opened while the design was still loading, or after its load failed. Wait for the design to load, or reopen it, and open Share again. Failed to load the list of people with access. The owner or the access list could not be fetched. Kanvas shows this error instead of an empty list. Close and reopen Share. An empty list does not mean nobody has access while this error shows. Failed to update visibility. The visibility change was rejected. Retry. Changing visibility is not supported for this kind of item. The item has no visibility control. Keep its current visibility. A single error naming the parts that failed A grant, a revoke, or the invitation email did not complete. Parts that succeeded stay in place. Reopen Share, check People with Access, and repeat the missing part. After any grant or revoke, check People with Access before you rely on the change.
The Share dialog: add people, review who has access, set visibility, and copy the link. Related 🔗 Collaboration Model explains how access, live editing, and comments fit together. Review a Design with Comments covers feedback on a shared design. Delete a Design explains who can delete and what disappears with a design.
description: Give specific people access to a design, set its visibility, share a link, and revoke access. Covers who can share, what a grant allows, and what fails.

body:
Validation checks the configuration of each component in a design against the schema of that component’s definition. It runs in your browser, needs no cluster, and changes nothing. Run it while you build to catch missing or malformed fields before a dry run or a deployment spends time on them.
Before you start 🔗 Environment. Validation runs in a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run it and shows a self-hosted-feature prompt instead. A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled while the design has no components. An unsaved design validates; Kanvas validates the design as it is on the canvas. Permission. On mobile, the Validate Design permission gates the action. See Permissions by Role. What validation checks 🔗 Checked Not checked Each component’s configuration against the JSON schema of its registered definition, with all errors collected per component Relationships between components Required fields, types, and formats, including 32-bit and 64-bit integers and integer-or-string values Dependencies, namespaces, and cross-references Anything in the target cluster Annotation components (text, shapes, and other visual elements) carry no infrastructure and are skipped. They are counted separately in the summary.
Two cases pass silently, so a clean result does not prove every component was checked:
A component whose definition cannot be fetched from the registry is skipped as valid. A design whose schema version is not a supported design version reports 0 components, 0 annotations, and no errors. Read the results 🔗 The results show a summary line, <N> component(s) and <M> annotations, and an error count. With no errors the result reads No validation errors.
With errors, each component that has them appears as an expandable row with its name and error count. Each error names the field by its dotted path, for example Field "spec.ports" must have required property 'apiGroup'. When the path is empty, the line shows the message alone. Errors are warnings: they never block you from continuing.
To fix an error, open the component and go to the field named in the path. A missing required property names the field you need to fill in.
Validation runs fresh each time you open it, so results always reflect the current design.
Results on the canvas 🔗 Validation also marks the canvas. A component with errors shows a circular badge at its lower left holding the total number of errors, schema and dry-run errors combined. Selecting the badge expands it to two counts: a yellow triangle for schema errors and a red octagon for dry-run errors. Each opens the matching results, scrolled to that component.
Badges appear only when the Validation Warnings and Deployment Errors entries in the Layers panel are on and the render mode is Full. They are hidden in Wireframe, Medium, and View-only modes. A new validation or dry run replaces them, and loading another design clears them. Editing a component does not clear its badge, so run validation again after you fix something.
The event it records 🔗 Validating the whole design records an informational event in the event log:
Validation completed for ‘’ with error(s) found.
The event carries the design name, the total error count, and per-component results. Validating a single component records nothing.
Validate and dry run compared 🔗 Validate Dry run Checks against Each component’s schema The Kubernetes API of each target cluster Needs a cluster No Yes Catches Missing or malformed configuration Everything the cluster’s admission and schema checks reject Speed Immediate One request per cluster Validate is the fast loop while you build. Run a dry run before you deploy, because it is the only check that involves the cluster you are deploying to. The deploy and undeploy flows run validation as their first step.

body:
Kanvas Snapshot posts a picture of your infrastructure as a comment on each GitHub pull request. Reviewers see which components a Kubernetes manifest, Docker Compose file, or Helm chart defines, and how they connect, before they read the YAML. The comment updates on every push to the pull request.
The snapshot runs in a GitHub Actions workflow on GitHub-hosted runners. It never touches your cluster. For how a snapshot is built and what it can and cannot do, see Kanvas Snapshot.
You can set it up two ways. The Layer5 GitHub App path installs the workflow for you. The direct path has you add the action to a workflow you own. Both produce the same comment.
Before you start 🔗 A Layer5 Cloud account. A repository on github.com that holds the infrastructure file. GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab, and Bitbucket are not supported. Permission to install a GitHub App on the repository, and to add repository secrets and commit to the default branch. A plan that includes GitOps Snapshots. See availability by plan. Set up with the Layer5 GitHub App 🔗 The Connect wizard for GitHub in Layer5 Cloud walks through seven stages. Running it again later updates the connection.
Stage What happens Connect GitHub opens so you can install the Layer5 GitHub App on your user or organization and choose repositories. Select repositories Lists only repositories where the App is installed. To add one, install the App on it again. Import designs Scans the selected repositories for Helm charts, Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files, and Meshery designs, and imports what you pick. Import failures are counted per repository. Select a design for the snapshot You choose at most one file per repository. Cloud stores its path for that repository. At least one repository needs a selection to continue. Configure secrets Cloud generates a Layer5 Cloud API token and shows it once. You add it to each repository as a secret named MESHERY_TOKEN. Configure workflows Cloud commits the workflow to each selected repository. Clear the checkbox to skip this stage and install nothing. Finish Shows which repositories received the workflow. Cloud never writes the secret for you. Add MESHERY_TOKEN to each repository yourself, with that exact name, and confirm the checkbox in the wizard. The wizard generates a new token each time the secrets stage opens, and it cannot show an earlier one again. Generate tokens in Layer5 Cloud and revoke them there; see Tokens.
What the installed workflow does 🔗 The wizard commits .github/workflows/kanvas.yml to the default branch of each repository, with the commit message Install Kanvas workflow. If that file already exists, the wizard replaces it.
Setting Value Name Kanvas Screenshot Service Triggers pull_request when opened, synchronized, or reopened. Also workflow_call, with an optional fileName input that overrides the stored path. Runner ubuntu-latest Token permissions actions: read, contents: write, security-events: write, statuses: write, pull-requests: write, id-token: write Authentication secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to comment, secrets.MESHERY_TOKEN for Layer5 Cloud Input file The path you selected for that repository Input type Kubernetes Manifest, always Two behaviors matter after install:
The input type is always Kubernetes Manifest. If the file you chose is a Docker Compose file or a Helm chart, edit application_type in the committed workflow to Docker Compose or Helm Chart. The workflow is built from the latest template at install time. Installing the same repository twice on different days can produce a different workflow. Review the committed file before you rely on it. Per-repository install results are:
Result Meaning Workflow added with a commit link The file was committed. Workflow already exists, try deleting it first at ./.github/workflows/kanvas.yml GitHub rejected the write because of the existing file. Delete or edit the file in the repository, then run the stage again. unable to install workflow in <repository> The request failed or timed out after 30 seconds. Run the stage again. repository must be in "owner/name" form The repository identifier is malformed. If you uninstall the App 🔗 Uninstalling the App from one account removes only that installation from your GitHub connection. See Check or reconfigure the connection.
Use the action in your own workflow 🔗 Skip the wizard when you want to choose the triggers, run snapshots from a workflow you already maintain, or authenticate with a personal access token instead of the App.
Generate a Layer5 Cloud API token and store it as a repository secret, for example MESHERY_TOKEN. Add a workflow. The action needs its own repository checked out to a folder named action, and the same token permissions the installed workflow uses. name: Kanvas Snapshot on: pull_request: types: [opened, synchronize, reopened] permissions: actions: read contents: write security-events: write statuses: write pull-requests: write id-token: write jobs: snapshot: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: path: action repository: layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot - uses: layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot@v0.2.44 with: githubToken: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} mesheryToken: ${{ secrets.MESHERY_TOKEN }} prNumber: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} application_type: "Kubernetes Manifest" filePath: manifests To snapshot a file that is hosted at a public URL, such as a packaged Helm chart, replace filePath with application_url and set application_type to Helm Chart. Pin the action to the latest release tag; v0.2.44 is current at the time of writing.
Action inputs 🔗 Input Required Default Behavior githubToken Yes - Posts the pull request comment. The built-in GITHUB_TOKEN or a personal access token that can write pull request comments. mesheryToken Yes - Layer5 Cloud API token. application_type Yes - Kubernetes Manifest, Docker Compose, or Helm Chart. filePath No - A file, or a directory of manifests, in the checked-out repository. application_url No - A public URL of the source file. designID No - The id of an existing design. Overrides filePath and application_url. prNumber No 0 The pull request to comment on. With 0, no comment is posted. skipComment No false Set to true to render without commenting, for manual or scheduled runs. assetLocation No - Where the rendered image is stored. email No - See known limitations. When you give filePath a directory, the action merges the .yaml and .yml files directly inside it into one document. It does not read subfolders. Point it at the folder that holds the manifests, or at a single file.
The action outputs resource_url, the URL of the rendered image. When no image URL comes back, the action does not post a comment.
Choose other triggers 🔗 The comment needs a pull request number, so only pull request runs post one. Use any other workflow event, such as push, schedule, or workflow_dispatch, to render a snapshot without a comment and read resource_url in a later step. Leave prNumber at 0 or set skipComment to true for those runs.
What the pull request comment contains 🔗 The comment shows the rendered image, linked to itself, with links to the generated design in the catalog and to an editable copy in the Playground. The workflow keeps one comment per pull request and replaces its content on each run.
Alongside the comment, each run uploads debug logs, screenshots, and a video of the render as workflow artifacts, whether the run succeeds or fails. Open them from the workflow run when a snapshot looks wrong.
Change or remove snapshots 🔗 To Do this Snapshot a different file Run the wizard again and select another file, or edit filePath in the workflow. Add a repository Install the App on it, then run the wizard again. Upgrade the action Change the version tag after layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot@ in the workflow. Check the release notes when application_type or input names change. Rotate the token Generate a new API token, update the MESHERY_TOKEN secret, and revoke the old token. Remove snapshots Delete .github/workflows/kanvas.yml, delete the MESHERY_TOKEN secret, and revoke the token. Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause and fix The workflow runs and no comment appears The run had no pull request number, skipComment is true, or the render produced no image URL. Open the uploaded workflow artifacts to see why the render failed. The snapshot shows nothing, or only some resources A directory path reads only the YAML files directly inside it. Point filePath at the folder that holds them. The snapshot treats a Helm chart or Compose file as a manifest The wizard sets application_type to Kubernetes Manifest. Edit it in the workflow. Authentication fails MESHERY_TOKEN is missing, misspelled, or revoked, or the repository does not share the secret with the workflow. The wizard lists no repositories The App is not installed on them. Install it, then run the wizard again. Known limitations 🔗 Email delivery. The email input does not deliver mail today. The action sends its request in a shape the Layer5 Cloud endpoint rejects, and the workflow continues without a failure. Use the pull request comment or resource_url. No diffs. A snapshot shows the current file only. It does not compare against the base branch. Single design per repository in the wizard. To snapshot more than one file, add the action to a workflow of your own for each file. GitHub.com only. The App and the install flow work against github.com.

Your account is your identity across every organization you belong to. These guides cover the settings that belong to you, and the subscription that belongs to the organization you administer. For how accounts relate to organizations, sign-in methods, and roles, read the Users concept.
The account area has four tabs: Profile, Preferences, Subscription, and Plans. Each tab opens only for a user who holds its permission. Without the permission, the tab shows a permission-denied view.
I want to Go to Permission needed Update my name, email, avatar, tagline, or social links Manage Your Account View Profile Change my password Manage Your Account Reset Password Sign in with GitHub or Google as well as my password Manage Your Account View Profile Delete my account Manage Your Account Delete Account Choose which emails I receive Set Notification Preferences View Profile See, start, upgrade, or cancel my organization’s subscription Manage Subscriptions and Billing View Subcription, plus Organization Owner or Organization Admin The default user role holds View Profile, Reset Password, and Delete Account, so every member can manage their own account. The permission is spelled “View Subcription” in the permission list; use that spelling when you search for it.

In Layer5 Academy, a Challenge is a hands-on, scenario-based task. Where a Learning Path teaches a subject from the ground up and a Certification tests knowledge a learner already has, a Challenge gives them a concrete problem and asks them to solve it.
When to use a challenge 🔗 Choose a challenge when the learner should build, break, or fix something real and is scored on the result. Compare the content types in Create Academy Content.
Challenge: Focus on Doing, Not Reading Choose a Challenge when the point is for the learner to build, break, or fix something real. If most of your material is explanation, it belongs in a Learning Path instead. How to Create Your Challenge 🔗 Challenges are authored the same way as every other Academy content type: as Markdown in your organization’s Academy content repository, published through a Git-native workflow. If you have not set that repository up yet, start with Creating Content for the Academy, which covers the repository setup once for all three content types.
Get your identifiers 🔗 Register the challenge in the Instructor Console and choose Challenge as the content type. The console generates the challenge id and a ready-to-paste front matter block. Use your organization’s ID in the directory path. See Create Academy Content.
1. Set Up the Directory Structure 🔗 All challenges live under content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid>, each in its own folder named with a descriptive, URL-friendly slug. The final URL follows this pattern:
https://cloud.layer5.io/academy/content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid>/<challenge-folder-name>/
A challenge is typically one scenario broken into a few sections:
content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid> └── keda-autoscaling-challenge/ <-- The <challenge-name> directory ├── _index.md <-- Defines the challenge's metadata ├── keda-icon.svg <-- Banner image, referenced from the front matter └── autoscaling-with-keda/ <-- The task itself ├── _index.md <-- The objective and prerequisites └── content/ ├── description/ <-- What the challenge is about, and the steps ├── getting-started/ <-- How to set up and begin └── faq/ <-- Common questions A challenge that ships an interactive lab and a graded exam adds them as their own sections alongside the task:
content/challenges/<your-organization-uuid> └── heal-the-mesh/ ├── _index.md ├── lab/ │ └── _index.md <-- The hands-on lab └── exam/ └── _index.md <-- The assessment that closes the challenge Sections Are Yours to Name description, getting-started and faq are a convention, not a fixed structure - the folder hierarchy you create is what the Academy renders as the challenge’s navigation. Use the sections your scenario actually needs. 2. Define the Challenge with Front Matter 🔗 The _index.md at the root of the challenge folder carries its metadata. Here is a complete example, taken from a published challenge:
--- title: "CNCF Autoscaling Challenge" description: "Learn event-driven autoscaling in Kubernetes. Work with scaled objects in KEDA, monitoring with Prometheus, OpenTelemetry & CloudEvents and advanced KEDA configurations." banner: "keda-icon.svg" id: "<your-challenge-uuid>" weight: 1 tags: [meshery, keda, open source] level: "advanced" categories: [platform] prerequisite_knowledge: - title: "Access to Meshery" children: - title: "Self-hosted Meshery" link: "https://docs.meshery.io/installation" - title: "Meshery Playground" link: "https://play.meshery.io" additional_attributes: - title: "Retake Policy" value: "3" description: "Up to three retakes allowed per exam" --- Front Matter Fields Reference 🔗 Fields marked ✅ are required; those marked - are optional.
Field Required Description id ✅ Crucial. A stable UUID used to track learner progress. Do not change it once learners have enrolled. title ✅ The human-readable title shown to learners. description ✅ A summary of the scenario. This is the text learners read on the catalog card. weight - Controls display order (lower numbers appear first). Items are sorted alphabetically by title if not specified. banner - Path to a banner image in the same folder (Page Bundle). tags - Keywords for discovery. Learners can browse by tag. level - Intended difficulty: beginner, intermediate or advanced. Default: beginner. categories - Assigns the challenge to a category. badge - Defines the digital badge awarded on completion. Its png and svg fields accept a full remote URL or a local file path in the same folder. prerequisite_knowledge - What a learner needs before starting, rendered as a list with optional links. additional_attributes - Free-form title/value/description rows, used for things like retake policy and scoring. Where `type` Comes From You do not set type: "challenge" on every file. The content/challenges/_index.md at the top of the section declares it once and cascades it to everything beneath, so each challenge inherits the right type - and therefore the right template - automatically. 3. Write the Scenario 🔗 The task’s own _index.md is where you state the objective and the prerequisites, and the sections beneath it carry the detail:
Description - what the challenge is about, and the numbered steps a learner must follow to complete it. Getting Started - how to get an environment ready, including any Meshery access the scenario needs. FAQ - the questions learners predictably ask. Write the steps so that success is unambiguous. A challenge is scored, so a learner needs to know exactly what “done” looks like before they start.
4. Add the Assessment 🔗 Most challenges close with an exam that validates the learner’s work. Exams in a challenge follow the same unified Academy assessment standard as every other content type.
How to Create and Configure Exams For question types, scoring, passing percentages, question pools and retry settings, see the Integrating Assessments in the Academy guide. 5. Publish 🔗 Publishing a challenge is the same two-stage release process as the rest of your Academy content: a GitHub Release on your content repository, followed by a Layer5 Cloud release. Until both have happened, your changes will not be live. See Publishing Your Content.
Monitor your challenge 🔗 The Instructor Console reports on challenges alongside your other content:
Learners lists registrations. Filter by content type Challenge and by status to follow who is Registered, In Progress, Completed, Failed, or Withdrawn. Curricula shows registrations, completion rate, and pass rate for each published challenge. Overview shows pass rates per assessment. A low pass rate separates a hard challenge from unclear instructions only when the attempt count is high enough to mean something. Academy Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Academy Theoretical Learning A comprehensive learning management system for creators and instructors on how to build, manage, and extend educational content like learning paths, challenges, and certifications. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Academy Practical Learning An inclusive, collaborative, hands-on learning environment for students. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Learner outcomes 🔗 Completing all the required components of a challenge earns the learner a digital badge - a verifiable credential they can share on their professional profiles. Unlike a Certification, a Challenge does not issue a paid Certificate of Completion; its outcome is the score, the rank, and the badge.
The badge is awarded when the learner passes the final test of the challenge. See the Learner Guide for the learner’s side of this.
Frequently Asked Questions 🔗 Can a challenge have more than one task? Yes. The folder hierarchy beneath the challenge’s _index.md is what defines its structure, so a challenge can hold several sections. Most challenges are a single scenario because that keeps the objective sharp, but nothing prevents a longer one.
Does a challenge have to include an exam? No. An exam is the usual way to validate that the learner solved the problem, but a challenge whose completion is judged by a lab does not need one.
Can I change a challenge after learners have started it? You can edit its content freely - but never change its id. That UUID is what learner progress is recorded against, and changing it orphans every registration made against the old value.
How do learners find my challenge? Through the Academy catalog, filtered by Content Type → Challenge. See Exploring the Content Catalog.

A child organization is an organization created inside another organization, called its parent. A child is otherwise an ordinary organization: it has its own members, teams, workspaces, invitations, domain, and credentials. The parent relationship adds one thing, which is that administrators of the parent can manage the child’s settings and membership from the parent.
Permissions Required Creating a child organization requires the Create Organization permission in the parent. Seeing the list of a parent’s children requires View Organizations in the parent. Editing, deleting, or adding members to a child from the parent requires the Organization Administrator or Owner role in the parent. To understand the specific roles needed for each action, please refer to the Roles and Permissions reference. How Organizations Nest 🔗 An organization can have any number of child organizations. A child can have child organizations of its own, and those can have children of their own. There is no limit on depth. Every top-level organization sits directly under the provider organization of your Layer5 Cloud deployment. The provider organization is never itself a child, and it does not appear in the child organizations section. A child belongs to exactly one parent. A child cannot be moved to another parent after it is created. A parent administers its direct children only. An administrator of a grandparent does not administer a grandchild by virtue of that role; the administrator of the intermediate organization does.
Creating a Child Organization 🔗 Any member holding the Create Organization permission in the parent can create a child. The creator becomes an Organization Administrator of the new child.
Select the parent organization, then create the child from the Child organizations section of the Organizations page. The form asks for the same details as any organization: name (required), country, region, and description.
The parent is always the organization you have selected, so there is no parent field to fill in. If you do not see a create control, your role in the parent does not include Create Organization.
Viewing Child Organizations 🔗 The Child organizations section on the Organizations page lists the direct children of the selected organization, showing each child’s name, description, and domain. It appears for anyone holding View Organizations in the selected organization, and it does not appear when you have the provider organization or all organizations selected.
Seeing a Child Is Not Joining It Being able to see the list of children does not make you a member of any child. You do not see a child’s members, invitations, or other settings from the list, and the child does not appear in your organization switcher unless you are a member of it. What a Parent Administrator Can Do 🔗 An Organization Administrator or Owner of the parent can manage a direct child from the parent, without joining the child. From the parent, they can:
Edit the child’s settings, using the edit action on the child’s row. Add members to the child. The Child organizations section has no add-member control, so this is done through the existing add-member API for the child. Search the child’s members. Delete the child, using the delete action on the child’s row, provided the child has no child organizations of its own (see Deleting Organizations That Have Children). This access is read from the parent administrator’s role in the parent on every request. Removing someone as an Organization Administrator of the parent ends their access to the settings of every child at once, with nothing to clean up in the children.
What a Parent Administrator Cannot Do 🔗 Governing a child does not make the parent administrator a member of it. Anything inside the child still requires membership in the child and the usual role there, including:
workspaces, environments, connections, and credentials, teams, identity providers, the mail server. To work inside a child, a parent administrator must be added to it as a member like anyone else. Holding a permission such as Edit Organization in the parent does not grant that permission in the child.
Switching into a Child 🔗 The organization switcher lists only the organizations you are a member of. A parent administrator who is not a member of a child can edit that child’s settings from the parent but cannot switch into it. The creator of a child is a member of it from the start, so the creator can switch into it right away. Other members of the parent do not appear in the child until someone adds them to it. See Switching Between Organizations for how the switcher and the active organization work.
Deleting Organizations That Have Children 🔗 An organization that still has child organizations cannot be deleted. The request is refused and nothing is deleted. Delete the children first, starting with the deepest, and then delete the parent. Children are never deleted along with their parent and are never moved to another parent.
Deleting a child removes it as described in Deleting Your Organization.

Every organization in Layer5 Cloud is configured by two choices: where your users sign in (the front door) and whose identity provider authenticates them. The combinations form five named scenarios. This guide helps you pick one and then walks through the settings that implement it, including who is allowed to change each setting.
For the mechanics behind the choices, see White-labeling (themes, logos, custom domains) and Identity Services (bring-your-own-credentials and authentication boundaries).
Provider and tenant organizations 🔗 These scenarios configure a tenant organization, which is every organization except one.
Provider organization. The single top-level organization that operates the deployment. On the hosted service it is Layer5. On a self-hosted deployment it is your platform team. It owns the deployment’s default identity providers, the Google and GitHub applications every other organization falls back to. A Provider Admin manages platform-wide settings. Tenant organization. Every other organization: a customer, partner, or business unit. A tenant is what you configure into one of the scenarios below. The provider organization always signs in on the deployment’s canonical address with the default identity providers.
The two choices 🔗 Choice Options Front door: where users sign in Shared: the deployment’s own address, such as cloud.layer5.io. Branded subdomain: a subdomain of the deployment’s base domain, such as acme.layer5.io. Custom domain: your own domain, such as cloud.acme.com. Identity provider: who runs sign-in Shared: the deployment’s Google and GitHub applications. Your own (BYOC): your own Google, GitHub, or OIDC single sign-on. Email-and-password sign-in and the Google and GitHub buttons work in every scenario, including on a custom domain that uses the default identity providers. The scenarios differ in whose identity provider authenticates users and whose brand appears on the consent screen, not in whether social sign-in is available.
The scenarios at a glance 🔗 Scenario Front door Identity provider Branded sign-in pages Consent screen shows Setting needed Hosted Shared Shared No (shared page) Platform name None. This is the default. Branded Branded subdomain Shared Yes Platform name Domain (Provider Admin) Branded + BYOC Branded subdomain Your own Yes Your brand Domain (Provider Admin) and identity providers White-Label Custom domain Shared Yes Platform name Domain (Provider Admin) White-Label + BYOC Custom domain Your own Yes Your brand Domain (Provider Admin) and identity providers One combination does not exist: the shared front door always uses the shared identity provider, so there is no “Shared + your own identity provider”. To use your own identity provider, give the organization a branded subdomain or a custom domain first.
Choose a scenario 🔗 Do you need a branded address? No: use Hosted. Nothing to configure. A subdomain of the platform is fine: continue with Branded. It must be your own domain: continue with White-Label. Do you need your own identity provider? You need one for your own consent-screen branding, your own OAuth rate limits and audit trail, corporate single sign-on, or a distinct authentication boundary. On a subdomain: no means Branded, yes means Branded + BYOC. On your own domain: no means White-Label, yes means White-Label + BYOC. Bringing your own identity provider is always optional, whatever the domain.
What each scenario means for your users 🔗 Hosted 🔗 Users sign in at the deployment’s address and pick your organization in the organization switcher. Theme colors and logo appear inside the app. The sign-in page itself is the platform’s, shared by every organization on that address. This is the default and needs no configuration.
Branded 🔗 The organization has its own subdomain of the deployment’s base domain. Sign-in, sign-up, and error pages carry your colors, logo, and links. Social buttons use the platform’s applications, so the consent screen shows the platform’s name.
Branded + BYOC 🔗 A branded subdomain plus your own OAuth clients or OIDC provider. The consent screen shows your brand, and the organization becomes a distinct authentication boundary. See The identity provider is the security boundary.
White-Label 🔗 The organization runs on your own domain, on a different base domain from the deployment, with the platform’s identity providers. Social sign-in works without extra setup and shows the platform’s name on the consent screen.
White-Label + BYOC 🔗 Your domain and your identity provider. The organization is branded end to end. This is the usual choice for a partner or reseller that offers the platform under its own name.
Set up a custom domain 🔗 A domain routes users who arrive at that address into your organization. The scenarios other than Hosted all depend on it.
Who can set it 🔗 Only a Provider Admin can set a domain to a new value. An Organization Admin sees the domain field in the organization settings, but the save fails with a 403 error that says the domain requires a Provider Admin. Organization administrators can keep the stored value and can clear it. Ask the provider to set the domain, and tell them the exact hostname.
What a valid domain looks like 🔗 Layer5 Cloud checks the domain when it changes:
Rule Detail Length 3 to 253 characters. Labels Dot-separated, each 1 to 63 ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens, not starting or ending with a hyphen. Format A hostname. Email-shaped input with @ is rejected. The value cannot start with http, https, or www. Internationalized names Write them in Punycode (xn--). Reserved hosts The provider’s own hosts, including the canonical Layer5 Cloud address and the Layer5 marketing and documentation hosts, are rejected. Uniqueness One organization per domain. Deleted organizations keep their domain, so clear the domain before you delete an organization if the address must be reused. The check is syntactic. Layer5 Cloud does not resolve the name when you save, so a valid hostname whose DNS is not ready yet is accepted. Point the domain’s DNS at your Layer5 Cloud deployment, as described in White-labeling.
How the domain is used 🔗 Exact match. Layer5 Cloud compares the host of each request, with the protocol and port removed, to organization domains. The match is exact, so cloud.acme.com and www.cloud.acme.com are different hosts. The domain wins. A request that arrives on an organization’s domain runs in that organization, ahead of the request header, the saved preference, and the browser session. See Switching Between Organizations. Never custom. The deployment’s own address, IP addresses, and reserved hosts are never treated as custom domains. Cache. Lookups, including misses, are cached for five minutes. Creating, updating, or deleting an organization clears the affected entry on the server that handled the change, so the change is visible there immediately and everywhere within the cache window. Clearing. Emptying the field removes the assignment. Users who arrive on the old address no longer land in the organization. Open invitation. When an organization has an open invitation, a non-member who signs in on its domain joins through it. Changing a domain that users already rely on can break their routing and bookmarks. Announce the change first.
Verify the assignment 🔗 The by-domain lookup is public and needs no credentials. It returns the organization record when the domain is assigned and null with a 200 status when it is not:
curl "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/orgs/by-domain?domain=cloud.acme.com" Substitute your deployment’s address and your hostname. A null result means the domain is unassigned, mistyped, or still inside the cache window for a recent change.
Add your own identity provider 🔗 Organization Admins and Owners add, rotate, and remove identity providers without the provider’s help. The procedure is in Configuring Identity Providers. The first provider you save switches the organization to its own identity providers. Removing the last one returns it to the platform’s defaults.
Membership policy is independent 🔗 The scenario controls where and how users sign in. It does not control who may join. Membership is governed by invitations, open sign-up, and the roles and teams an invitation grants. Any scenario pairs with any membership policy. See Using the Open Organization Invitation Link and User Invitations.

Academy content is written as Markdown in your organization’s own Git repository and published as a numbered version. Layer5 Cloud holds the record of each piece of content (its identity, access rules, and badge) and every learner’s registration, progress, and test results. This guide covers the workflow end to end. The pages beneath it cover each content type in depth.
Prerequisites 🔗 The View Academy Metrics permission in your organization (Academy Admin, Organization Admin, or Provider Admin). See the Instructor Console. An organization with the Academy configured, so the console is not in its “not configured” state. Comfort with Git and Markdown. The workflow 🔗 Register the content in the console. The content creation flow creates the content record and generates the identifiers and front matter you paste into your repository. Write the content in your repository, following the layout for its type. Preview locally to check structure and links. Publish by releasing a version of your repository. The release asks Layer5 Cloud to build your organization’s Academy at that version. Monitor registrations, completion, and pass rates in the console. Register content in the console 🔗 The creation flow collects the following. Only the content type is required to create the record. The record starts with status not ready, public visibility, and beginner level. Cloud generates the slug from the content type plus three random words.
Step Field Behavior Basic Information Content Type Learning path, challenge, or certification. Basic Information Title, Description Appear on the catalog card. Content Details Difficulty Level beginner, intermediate, or advanced. Content Details Categories, Tags Used for discovery in the catalog. Content Details Banner Image Optional. A path to an image in the same folder as the content’s index file. Content Access Workspace An existing workspace, or a new one. Content Access Team The team whose members can access the content. Content Access Status Enabled or Disabled. Content Access Content Access End Date When the invitation behind the content expires. Recognition Badge The badge awarded when a learner completes the content. Generate Template Front matter and setup guide The YAML to place at the top of the content’s index file, with your identifiers. Registering content also creates an invitation for it. When a learner registers, the invitation is accepted at the same time, which adds the learner to the content’s team. Content owned by the provider organization has no invitation.
You can change the team, access status, end date, workspace, and badge later from the Curricula view. Changing the content’s id in your repository after learners register orphans their progress, because progress is recorded against that identifier.
Choose a content type 🔗 Learning path Challenge Certification Goal Teach a subject from the ground up Solve a hands-on scenario Validate existing knowledge Structure Path, courses, modules, pages One scenario with lab and exam sections A flat set of exams Assessment Quizzes and exams, mandatory or optional An exam closes most challenges One or more exams Credential Badge Badge Badge, and an optional paid certificate In this section 🔗 Create a Learning Path: repository setup, structure, front matter, preview, and publishing, which apply to every content type. Build a Challenge Build a Certification Add Assessments: quiz, test, and exam files, question types, scoring, and attempt limits. Use the Content Template Creator: the registration flow, the front matter it generates, and the invitation behind each content item. Extend the Academy: HTML, CSS, custom shortcodes, embedded designs, and award emails. Platform Development: local preview, theme development, and end-to-end builds.

Relationships record how components connect, and Kanvas keeps related configuration in sync once they exist. You create some relationships by hand and Kanvas creates others when it evaluates the design. This guide shows which is which, how to create each kind, and how to remove or hide them.
Relationships work only in Designer mode. For what each kind means, read Relationships.
Kind You create it by You remove it by Edge (network, mount, reference, and other edge subtypes) Picking an edge from a component’s handle and dragging to a target Selecting the edge and choosing Delete Hierarchical, inventory Dropping a component onto a compatible parent Dragging it out, or choosing Move Out of Parent Hierarchical, wallet Dropping a component onto a compatible host Deleting the component, or choosing Move Out of Parent Hierarchical, alias Kanvas creates it during evaluation Deleting the alias component TagSets (shared labels) Giving components matching labels Changing the labels so they stop matching Annotation edge Drawing with the Pen tool Selecting the edge and choosing Delete Create an edge relationship 🔗 Edge relationships connect components that exchange traffic or depend on one another, such as a Service and a Deployment.
Hover a component to reveal arrow handles on its bottom, left, and right sides, then select one. A circular menu opens. Pick a relationship from the menu. It lists every edge relationship in the registry that can start from this component, with the subtype in a tooltip. A binding relationship lists one item per component that can sit between the two ends. Drag from the source to a target. Compatible targets in view get a green outline, and incompatible components dim to half opacity. Kanvas checks only the components visible in the viewport. Release on a compatible target. Releasing on an incompatible component, a non-component, or empty canvas cancels the creation without a message. A binding relationship also places its binding component between the two ends.
The edge shows an arrow and a label. Network edges label the source and target ports and protocols, read from the configuration the relationship manages.
Nest components in a parent 🔗 Drag a component onto another and release. Valid targets are the components that form an inventory or wallet relationship with it, and Kanvas outlines them in green while you drag. The same drop works when you drag a component from the palette onto an existing component.
Inventory. The child is drawn inside the parent. For example, a Pod dropped on a Namespace becomes its child. You can collapse and expand parents. Wallet. The child is absorbed into the host and shown as a green badge at the host’s bottom-right corner with the item count. Select the badge to list the items, then select an item to open its configurator. A sidecar attached to a workload is an example. A component has at most one parent. Dropping it into a new parent replaces the old relationship, and dropping it on empty canvas removes it.
Let labels form TagSets 🔗 You never draw a TagSet. When components carry labels or annotations that match under a registry relationship definition, the next evaluation creates a TagSet and draws a translucent region around the group. See Work with Tags.
Remove a relationship 🔗 Edge. Select the edge and choose Delete in its toolbar. Kanvas marks the relationship deleted, and the next evaluation reverses its effects on configuration. Inventory. Drag the child out of the parent, or right-click it and choose Move Out of Parent. Wallet. No control deletes a wallet relationship by itself. Delete the component, or choose Move Out of Parent. TagSet. No control deletes a TagSet. Change the labels so they no longer match, or hide the layer. Style an edge 🔗 Select an edge to open its toolbar. It offers line color, line style (solid, dashed, or dotted), curve and arrow style, a label, and an animation (none or marching ants). Styling changes only appearance.
Hide a kind of relationship 🔗 The Layers panel lists eight relationship kinds, each with a count and a show or hide toggle: hierarchical inventory, wallet, and alias; TagSets; and edge mount, network, annotation, and reference. Open the panel with the backslash key or from the design toolbar.
Hiding a kind removes it from the canvas. It does not stop evaluation. Kanvas still evaluates the whole design, so configuration that a hidden relationship manages keeps syncing. The toggles are stored in the design, so they are saved with it, restored when it reopens, and shared with collaborators. Everything is visible by default.
Configuration sync 🔗 When two components are related, the registry definition names which fields on each side are linked, and Kanvas writes values across them each time it evaluates the design. For example, changing a Service’s port updates the matching container port on a related Deployment. The relationship definition decides the direction, so it can differ by kind. See Policy Evaluation.
Limits 🔗 Kanvas draws at most 30 TagSets. Beyond that, it shows the warning “Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30”. TagSets render only in Full render fidelity. No other kind has a rendering limit. See also 🔗 Add and Configure Components: the Relationships tab lists each component’s relationships.

In this tutorial, an Organization Admin at one company asks an engineer at another company to review a private design. By the end, you will have given someone outside your organization access to one design, held a review in a comment thread, and removed that access. Along the way, you will learn what a grant gives someone, where Kanvas checks permissions, and why the review itself has to happen in comments.
The cast is the same one used across these docs. Marcus Webb is the Organization Admin at Stellar Dynamics. Five is a Platform Engineer at Orbital Labs, a separate organization.
Before you begin 🔗 Marcus holds the Share Design permission in Stellar Dynamics. Kanvas checks it in the organization that owns the design’s workspace, so a grant from another organization does not count. Marcus holds the View All Users permission. The people picker in the Share dialog depends on it. Five holds View All Users as well, so he can @mention Marcus in a comment. Both accounts exist on the same Layer5 Cloud. The design is saved and private. A design gets a link only after its first save gives it an id. Kanvas hides Share for empty designs and for published designs. The scenario 🔗 Marcus owns a saved design called stellar-saas-platform. It models Stellar Dynamics’ Azure SaaS stack: an AKS cluster, Azure SQL, API Management, Azure AD, Event Hub, and the connections between them. Before his team runs it in production, he wants Five to review the architecture.
Step 1: Marcus grants Five access 🔗 Marcus opens the Share dialog on stellar-saas-platform and searches for Five by name. The search covers every user Marcus’s role lets him search, not just members of Stellar Dynamics, so Five appears even though he belongs to Orbital Labs. Marcus adds Five, and Five now appears in the list of people with access.
Here is the model to remember. A private design opens for its owner, for provider administrators, and for each person who holds a grant on it. A grant links one person to one design. It has no access level and never checks organizations. Kanvas does not compare Five’s organization with the design’s, and you do not need any provider-level trust setting.
An invitation email goes out only when the share request asks for one, so Marcus copies the design link and sends it to Five himself.
Result: Five holds a grant on stellar-saas-platform.
Step 2: Five opens the design 🔗 Five follows the link while signed in to his Orbital Labs account. The design loads with every component and connection Marcus drew. It also appears in Five’s list of designs shared with him.
Five gets this one design and nothing else. The grant does not make him a member of Stellar Dynamics. Other private designs in the same workspace remain closed to him, because each private design checks its own grants. Assigning a team to the workspace would not open them either.
Result: Five sees the design Marcus sees.
Step 3: Five comments and mentions Marcus 🔗 Five places a comment next to API Management and writes:
@Marcus Webb You’re missing a WAF in front of API Management.
Typing @ followed by part of a name brings up matching users. Choosing one stores a real mention, not plain text.
The comment is a component in the design, so it saves and travels with the design. If Marcus has the design open, the comment shows up on his canvas right away. Because Five mentioned him, Marcus also gets an email with the design’s name, a snapshot, and the thread, unless he has turned off comment emails in his account preferences.
Result: An open thread on the design names Marcus.
Step 4: Marcus responds, edits, and resolves 🔗 Marcus replies in the thread. Five wrote an earlier message in it, so Five receives an email about the reply. Marcus then adds an Azure Application Gateway in front of API Management and connects the two. Kanvas autosaves the change.
Marcus resolves the thread. The comment leaves the canvas but stays in the comments panel under the Resolved filter. Resolving sends no email. If anyone posts again in the thread, it reopens.
Result: The fix is in the design, and the thread records why it was made.
What this means for review 🔗 Kanvas has no view-only or comment-only grant. A grantee can do anything an editor can do. Five can open the design, save edits, comment, clone it, download it, and switch it between private and public. He can only re-share it if his role gives him the Share Design permission in Stellar Dynamics’ organization. Five cannot delete the design, and he cannot take over ownership.
The rules of the review therefore live in the comment thread, not in the permission system. Marcus has two tools for keeping it that way:
Remove the grant when the review ends. Access lasts exactly as long as the grant does. Offer a clone. If Five wants to experiment, a clone gives him an independent copy, and the original stays untouched. For live co-editing during a review, see Collaborative Editing.
Step 5: Marcus revokes access 🔗 Once the review is done, Marcus removes Five from the list of people with access in the Share dialog. When Five opens the link again, Kanvas refuses it, and the design leaves his shared list.
Five’s comments stay in the design. Comments are part of the design, so removing a person does not remove what they wrote. A clone is a separate design, so revoking access to the original does not affect any clone Five made.
Result: Only Marcus and provider administrators can open stellar-saas-platform.
Access at a glance 🔗 This table applies to a private design. Provider administrators can open and delete any private design.
Person Open the private design Edit it Comment Re-share Delete Marcus (owner) Yes Yes Yes Yes, with the Share Design permission Yes Five (grantee) Yes Yes Yes Only with the Share Design permission in the design’s organization No Someone with no grant No No No No No Next steps 🔗 Share a Design covers granting, revoking, and changing visibility. Review a Design with Comments covers comment threads, mentions, filters, and notifications. Collaboration Model explains how sharing, comments, and live editing fit together. Permissions by Role lists every permission that controls these actions.

In this tutorial you take the design you saved in Create Your First Design to a live Kubernetes cluster. You validate it, dry-run it against the cluster, deploy it, and then switch to Operator mode to see the running resources that belong to the design. You finish by undeploying it.
Along the way you learn the difference between checking a design against its schemas and checking it against a cluster, how Kanvas chooses where to deploy, and how Kanvas keeps track of the resources a design creates.
This tutorial needs a Meshery you run Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new cannot validate, dry-run, deploy, or undeploy designs, and it does not offer Operator mode. On kanvas.new these actions open a prompt that sends you to a Meshery you run instead. Use the Meshery Playground or install Meshery in your own environment, then open your design there. Before you begin 🔗 You need:
The web-app design from the previous tutorial, saved and open in Designer mode. A Meshery you run, either the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery, signed in with Layer5 Cloud as its provider. Operator views are stored in Layer5 Cloud, so the local provider cannot show them. A connected Kubernetes cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. Meshery Operator installs MeshSync and Meshery Broker in the cluster; MeshSync streams the cluster’s live state to Meshery Server, and that stream is what Operator mode displays. See Operator. Permissions in your organization for each action. Validate Design permits both validation and dry runs, Deploy Design permits deploying, and Undeploy Design permits undeploying. When you lack one of these permissions, the matching action is not available to you. Step 1: Validate the design 🔗 Validate the design from the design’s action toolbar. Kanvas shows “Validating design” and opens a dialog titled Validate design "web-app".
What Kanvas does: validation checks every component in the design against that component’s schema. It does not contact any cluster. Each error is attached to the component and the field that caused it, so you fix problems where they are, not in a separate list. When validation of the whole design completes, Kanvas records a validation event in your Layer5 Cloud event log.
What you should see: no errors for this design. If validation finds problems, Kanvas shows “Design validation error” and marks the affected components. Open each marked component, correct the field, and validate again.
Step 2: Dry-run the design against the cluster 🔗 Start a dry run. Kanvas opens a dialog titled Dryrun design "web-app".
What Kanvas does: a dry run sends the design to the target cluster for checking without applying anything. It catches problems that schemas cannot, the ones only the cluster knows about. Dry-run errors attach to components in the same way as schema errors, so both kinds appear side by side on the affected component.
Validation answers “is this design well formed?”. A dry run answers “would this cluster accept it?”. Run both before every deployment.
What you should see: a dry run that completes without errors. Nothing has changed in the cluster yet.
Step 3: Deploy the design 🔗 Deploy the design. Kanvas opens a dialog titled Deploy design "web-app" that walks you through the deployment.
What Kanvas does: Kanvas applies the design to the Kubernetes contexts you select. If you do not select any, Kanvas deploys to all connected clusters. Choose your target deliberately when more than one cluster is connected.
Every resource Kanvas creates carries the design’s identity:
Metadata Key Value Label design.meshery.io/id The design’s ID Annotation design.meshery.io/version The design version that was deployed Annotation component.meshery.io/id The ID of the component the resource came from The label is what makes a resource “managed by Meshery”. It also lets you find the design’s resources with your own tools, for example kubectl get all -l design.meshery.io/id=<design-id>.
What you should see: the deployment completes, and the Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap exist in the cluster.
Step 4: Observe the design in Operator mode 🔗 Switch from Designer to Operator mode.
If the design has unsaved changes, Kanvas asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?” before it switches. Confirm only if you are ready to lose those changes; otherwise stay, let the design save, and switch again.
What Kanvas does: Operator mode shows the recorded state of your clusters through views. A view is a saved set of filters. A new, empty view shows Nodes and Namespaces across the clusters you select. A design’s view is named after the design, web-app-View, and filters on the design’s design.meshery.io/id label, so it shows only the resources this design created.
What you should see: in the design’s view, the running Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap from your design, and nothing else from the cluster.
Step 5: Undeploy the design 🔗 Return to Designer mode and undeploy the design. Kanvas opens a dialog titled Undeploy design "web-app".
What Kanvas does: undeploy removes the design’s resources from the Kubernetes contexts you select. As with deploy, selecting no context targets all connected clusters. You can dry-run an undeploy first to see what it would do.
What you should see: the undeploy completes and the resources are removed from the cluster. The design itself stays saved, ready to deploy again.
If something goes wrong 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix A prompt says Operator mode is not available on kanvas.new. Hosted Kanvas cannot validate, deploy, undeploy, connect clusters, or open Operator mode. Open the design in the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery. Validate, dry run, deploy, and undeploy are disabled. The design is empty. These actions need at least one component. Add components to the design, or open the saved web-app design. One of the actions is not available to you. Your role in the organization lacks the matching permission: Validate Design, Deploy Design, or Undeploy Design. Ask an organization administrator to grant the permission. “Design validation error” appears. One or more components fail their schema. Open each marked component, correct the field the error is attached to, and validate again. A dry run reports errors on components. The target cluster would reject part of the design. Correct the marked components, then run the dry run again before you deploy. Kanvas asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?” The design has changes that are not saved yet. Cancel, let autosave finish or save the design, then switch modes. Resources appeared in clusters you did not intend. No Kubernetes context was selected, so the action targeted all connected clusters. Undeploy from the unintended clusters, then select contexts explicitly before you deploy again. What you learned 🔗 Validation checks a design against component schemas; a dry run checks it against a cluster. Neither changes the cluster. Deploy and undeploy act on the contexts you select, and on every connected cluster when you select none. Every deployed resource is labeled with the design’s ID, which is how Operator mode filters the cluster inventory down to one design. Switching modes with unsaved changes asks for confirmation. Each action is gated by its own permission. Next 🔗 Validating designs Dry-running a design Deploying designs Undeploying designs Operator, to explore views and live cluster state beyond a single design.
