body:
This guide installs the layer5-cloud chart, which deploys the Layer5 Cloud server together with Kratos and Hydra. It assumes you have made the decisions in Plan a Deployment. The commands use the release name layer5-cloud in the namespace layer5-cloud.
Prerequisites 🔗 A Kubernetes cluster and Helm 3. An ingress controller that supports WebSocket upgrades, and a TLS certificate for your hostname. A PostgreSQL server you can create databases on. An SMTP relay that satisfies the mail constraints, or the decision to run without mail. The OAuth applications for Google and GitHub, if you offer social sign-in. Install 🔗 1. Prepare the database 🔗 Create one role and three databases on your PostgreSQL server, then create the uuid-ossp extension in the meshery database. The server creates the schema itself.
CREATE ROLE meshery LOGIN PASSWORD '<password>'; CREATE DATABASE meshery OWNER meshery; CREATE DATABASE kratos OWNER meshery; CREATE DATABASE hydra OWNER meshery; \c meshery CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "uuid-ossp"; Any PostgreSQL deployment works, including an operator such as CloudNativePG, a managed service, or a server outside the cluster. The chart reaches it only through the connection strings you set in the next step.
2. Create the namespace and add the chart repository 🔗 kubectl create namespace layer5-cloud helm repo add layer5 https://docs.layer5.io/charts helm repo update helm show values layer5/layer5-cloud > values.yaml helm show values prints every value of the chart version you are about to install. Keep that file as the baseline and edit it. The chart values reference explains each value.
3. Write the values file 🔗 Set at least the following. The kratospublic, kratosadmin, and hydraadmin addresses and the ingress backend names are the in-cluster service names of the Kratos and Hydra subcharts. Run kubectl -n layer5-cloud get svc after the first install and correct them to match your release. The chart defaults for these addresses (hydra-admin, hydra-public) do not match the names the subcharts create. The /(.*), /kratos/(.*), and /hydra/(.*) paths with the rewrite annotation strip the prefix before the request reaches each service; use your controller’s equivalent if it is not NGINX.
env: proto: https serverbaseurl: https://cloud.example.com serverHost: cloud.example.com db: postgres://meshery:<password>@<db-host>:5432/meshery?sslmode=require kratosdb: postgres://meshery:<password>@<db-host>:5432/kratos?sslmode=require hydradb: postgres://meshery:<password>@<db-host>:5432/hydra?sslmode=require kratospublic: http://layer5-cloud-kratos-public.layer5-cloud.svc.cluster.local:9010 kratosadmin: http://layer5-cloud-kratos-admin.layer5-cloud.svc.cluster.local:9011 kratosbrowser: https://cloud.example.com/kratos hydrapublic: https://cloud.example.com/hydra hydrabrowser: https://cloud.example.com/hydra hydraadmin: http://cloud-hydra-admin.layer5-cloud.svc.cluster.local:4445 oauthclientid: layer5-cloud oauthsecret: <generated> cloudCredentialEncryptionKey: <base64 32 bytes> cloudOidcStateHmacKey: <base64 32 bytes> kratosWebhookApiKey: <generated> initConfig: | organization: name: "Example Corp" user: first_name: "Ada" last_name: "Admin" email: "admin@example.com" password: "<initial password>" ingress: className: nginx annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-regex: "true" nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$1 nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600" nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "3600" hosts: - host: cloud.example.com paths: - path: /(.*) pathType: ImplementationSpecific backend: service: name: meshery-cloud port: number: 9876 - path: /kratos/(.*) pathType: ImplementationSpecific backend: service: name: layer5-cloud-kratos-public port: number: 9010 - path: /hydra/(.*) pathType: ImplementationSpecific backend: service: name: cloud-hydra-public port: number: 4444 tls: - secretName: cloud-example-com-tls hosts: - cloud.example.com smtp: smtphost: smtp.example.com smtpport: "587" smtpusername: no-reply@example.com smtppassword: <password> Then set the Kratos and Hydra values. Helm replaces a list as a whole, so copy the lists you change from values.yaml and edit them in place:
Replace every http://localhost:9876 and http://localhost:9010 URL under kratos.kratos.config with your public URL. That covers serve.public.base_url (https://cloud.example.com/kratos), serve.public.cors.allowed_origins, selfservice.default_browser_return_url, selfservice.allowed_return_urls, and each ui_url and default_browser_return_url under selfservice.flows. Point the registration web_hook entries at https://cloud.example.com/api/identity/users. Add a hook to https://cloud.example.com/api/identity/signup/validate before it on the password method if you use signup validation or reCAPTCHA. Set each hook’s X-API-Key value to env.kratosWebhookApiKey. The chart default URL omits the /api prefix, which the server does not serve. Set kratos.kratos.config.secrets.cookie and .cipher, and hydra.hydra.config.secrets.system. Set the Kratos dsn and Hydra dsn to the same database URLs as env.kratosdb and env.hydradb. Set the Hydra urls (login, consent, error, and self.public and self.issuer) to https://cloud.example.com/..., with self.public and self.issuer ending in /hydra/. Set hydra.hydra.dangerousForceHttp to false once Hydra is reached over TLS. Add the Google and GitHub client_id and client_secret under the Kratos oidc providers, and the matching env.providerOrg* values. Choose the identity mail courier. See Mail. Route /kratos and /hydra on the ingress to the Kratos and Hydra public services, as described in Plan a Deployment.
4. Install the chart 🔗 helm install layer5-cloud layer5/layer5-cloud \ --namespace layer5-cloud \ --values values.yaml Kratos and Hydra run their database migrations when they start, and the Layer5 Cloud server applies its own before it reports ready. Pods can restart once or twice while the databases fill. Wait for them:
kubectl -n layer5-cloud rollout status deploy/meshery-cloud 5. Create the OAuth2 client in Hydra 🔗 Layer5 Cloud authenticates to Hydra as an OAuth2 client whose id and secret you set in env.oauthclientid and env.oauthsecret. Create that client in Hydra with the matching values and the redirect address <serverbaseurl>/callback. The server does not create it, and sign-in does not work until it exists.
kubectl -n layer5-cloud exec deploy/cloud-hydra -- hydra create client \ --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4445 \ --id layer5-cloud \ --secret '<the value of env.oauthsecret>' \ --grant-type authorization_code,refresh_token,client_credentials,implicit \ --response-type token,code,id_token \ --scope openid,offline,offline_access \ --redirect-uri https://cloud.example.com/callback \ --skip-consent The command uses the flag names of the Hydra version in the chart’s subchart. If your Hydra is older, its command is hydra clients create with --grant-types, --response-types, and --callbacks.
Confirm the deployment works 🔗 GET https://cloud.example.com/readyz returns 200. The server log contains Server is up and running! and no Failed to initialize Provider Admin line. You can sign in as the administrator you defined in env.initConfig. That user holds the Provider Admin role. See Provider initialization. Send a test email through POST /api/system/email/test. See Troubleshoot Email Delivery. If you registered Google or GitHub, sign in with each. Once sign-in works, remove env.initConfig from your values file and run helm upgrade, so the initial password does not stay in your release history and logs.
Connect a Meshery Server 🔗 Meshery Server is a separate deployment. Install it by following the Meshery documentation, then point it at your deployment as its remote provider. See Meshery Server registration and the Meshery guide to remote providers. The server rejects sign-in from a Meshery Server older than env.minmesheryversion.
Upgrade 🔗 Run helm upgrade with the new chart version and your values file. The server applies pending database migrations when it starts, and exits if one fails. Take a database backup first.

A dry run submits every component in the design to the Kubernetes API server of each target cluster as a server-side dry-run request. The API server validates the object exactly as it would on a real apply, including schema, field values, and admission, and then discards it. Nothing is created, updated, or persisted, so you can repeat a dry run as often as you like.
Before you start 🔗 A connected cluster. Meshery must hold at least one connected Kubernetes context. With none, the request fails with error meshery-server-1096, Kubernetes cluster is unavailable. A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled for an empty design. Permission. Dry run is gated by the Validate Design permission. See Permissions by Role. A Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run dry runs. Meshery Server performs the dry run with the kubeconfig it holds. Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and the broker are not required.
Run a dry run 🔗 You reach a dry run in two ways.
On its own. Choose Dry Run from the design’s Actions menu. This opens Dryrun design "<name>" and runs a deploy-type dry run against your current cluster selection, or against all connected clusters when none is selected. There is no cluster-selection step.
Inside a deploy or undeploy. Step 3 of both steppers is a dry run against the environments you chose in step 2. In the deploy stepper it simulates creating the resources. In the undeploy stepper it simulates deleting them. See Deploy a Design and Undeploy a Design.
On mobile, Dry Run runs without a modal and shows its results as badges on the canvas.
What the server does 🔗 Stage Behavior Components Annotation components are dropped. Each remaining component becomes a Kubernetes object. Clusters The object goes to every selected cluster. Deploy-type A create with strict field validation and field manager meshery. Undeploy-type A delete by name. Namespace The component’s own metadata.namespace. Otherwise default for namespaced kinds, and none for cluster-scoped kinds. Persistence None. The dry run does not create namespaces. Read the results 🔗 The summary shows <N> component(s) and <M> annotations and the error count. With no errors it reads No deployment errors.
Each failing component is an expandable row, <name> (<count>). A component fails when any selected cluster returns a Kubernetes failure for it. Each error shows a bold type and field path, then the message the API server returned:
The type is the Kubernetes cause in words: Field Value Required, Field Value Invalid, Field Value Not Supported. Anything else shows as Failure. The path reads <component> > settings > <field>. Metadata name, namespace, labels, and annotations map to those names. When Kubernetes names no field the path is unknown. When the API gives no causes, its status messages appear as plain text. If the whole call fails rather than a component, a structured error block appears with the entry type RequestError, not a per-component row.
Selecting an error closes the results and opens the component’s configuration at the field. Errors also feed the red octagon badge on the canvas. See Validate a Design for where badges appear.
Each dry run records an event: Dry Run completed for design '<name>'. at informational severity, even when components failed, or Failed to dry-run design '<name>'. at error severity when the call itself failed. A dry run does not change the design’s deployment count.
Common errors 🔗 Error Cause Fix Field Value Invalid A value is outside what Kubernetes accepts, for example a Service port of 0 where 1 to 65535 is required. Correct the value in the component’s configuration. Field Value Required A required field is empty. Fill in the field. Resource not found for a component of a kind with an irregular plural See the limits below. Bypass the error if the kind is correct. Missing custom resource definition The design uses a custom resource whose definition is not on the cluster. Install the definition on the cluster first, then run the dry run again. Limits of a dry run 🔗 Irregular plurals. Dry run builds each resource name from the lowercase kind plus “s”. Kinds with irregular plurals, such as Ingress, NetworkPolicy, StorageClass, and Endpoints, can return a not-found error even when the component is correct. Namespaces the design creates. A dry run never creates a namespace. A component placed in a namespace that the same design would create reports an error, because the namespace does not exist yet. Undeploy-type runs. Deleting an object that is absent returns NotFound. Dry-running the undeploy of a design that was never deployed, or is already removed, shows an error for every component. A real undeploy ignores objects that are already absent. The Include Dependencies option. The dry-run step shows an Include Dependencies checkbox. It has no effect on the dry run. Bypass errors 🔗 In the deploy and undeploy steppers, when a dry run reports errors, the step shows a checkbox, Bypass errors and initiate deployment. Next stays disabled while the dry run is running, or while errors exist and the checkbox is off. Use the bypass when you know the errors are false positives from the limits above. The cluster raised each of them, and the real deployment may fail for the same reason.

body:
In this tutorial you build an NGINX Deployment with two replicas, deploy it, scale it to three, and roll it to a new image version, inspecting the result in Operator after each change. A Deployment is the controller most stateless applications run under: you declare how many Pods you want and what they look like, and Kubernetes keeps that many running and replaces them gradually when the template changes. Seeing the ReplicaSets and Pods appear and change shows you what the controller does on your behalf.
What you will learn 🔗 A Deployment owns ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet owns Pods built from one version of the Pod template. The Deployment’s selector must match its Pod template’s labels, and Kubernetes never lets you change the selector afterward. Scaling changes how many Pods run without creating a new ReplicaSet; changing the template starts a rolling update with a new ReplicaSet. Deploying a changed design from Kanvas replaces the object in place, which is how you update a running workload. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed environment. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. An environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. See Environments. Operator mode for the inspection phases, which needs Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster. Where Operator mode is turned off, its switch is disabled; the deploy summary still confirms each object. A unique prefix. Playground is shared. Use your own prefix in every name and label; this tutorial uses alex. The Pods tutorial. Explore Pods introduces the configurator, Validate, Dry Run, Deploy, and Operator, which this tutorial uses without re-explaining. The scenario 🔗 Deployment alex-web replicas 2, selector app=alex-web, label app=alex-web | +-- ReplicaSet alex-web-<template hash> (created by Kubernetes) +-- Pod alex-web-<template hash>-<id> (created by Kubernetes) +-- Pod alex-web-<template hash>-<id> You design only the Deployment. Kubernetes creates the ReplicaSet and Pods from it.
Build the Deployment 🔗 Create a new design named alex-deployments and add a Deployment component. The configurator opens as soon as the component lands on the canvas. Set the name to alex-web and leave the namespace as default. Set replicas to 2. Set the selector’s match labels to app: alex-web. In the Pod template, set the template’s metadata labels to app: alex-web, the same pair as the selector. In the Pod template’s spec, add one container: name web, image nginx:1.27, container port 80. In the configurator’s Labels tab, add the label app: alex-web to the Deployment itself. You use it later to find everything the Deployment owns. What just happened. The Deployment’s configuration mirrors its manifest. The selector tells the Deployment which Pods belong to it, and the template is the blueprint for those Pods. Nested objects such as the selector and the template open in their own forms. The component is equivalent to:
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: alex-web labels: app: alex-web spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: alex-web template: metadata: labels: app: alex-web spec: containers: - name: web image: nginx:1.27 ports: - containerPort: 80 Check your work. Run Validate and then Dry Run from the Actions menu. Validate checks the schema in your browser; Dry Run asks the cluster’s API server, which also checks rules the schema cannot express. If the selector and the template labels differ, the dry run fails with a Field Value Invalid error on the template labels, stating that the selector does not match the template labels. Fix the pair and run the dry run again.
Deploy and see what Kubernetes created 🔗 Run Deploy from the Actions menu, select the environment that holds your cluster’s connection, and confirm once the dry run reports no errors. Switch to Operator. With the design open, Operator shows a view scoped to this design: the objects that carry this design’s id label. Select the alex-web Deployment and switch its details panel to Details. Select the app=alex-web label chip in the details panel. This adds the label to the view’s filter, and the view reloads. What just happened. Kanvas sent one object, the Deployment, and labeled it with the design id. The Deployment controller then created a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet created two Pods. Those objects come from the controller, not from Kanvas, so they carry the template’s labels (plus a pod-template-hash label that Kubernetes adds) instead of anything Kanvas applies. Label filters in a view match objects that carry any of the listed labels, so adding app=alex-web brings the ReplicaSet and the Pods into the view alongside the Deployment.
The names show the ownership chain: the ReplicaSet is named after the Deployment plus a hash of the Pod template, and each Pod is named after its ReplicaSet plus a random suffix.
Check your work. The Deployment’s details show pods 2 / 2 (available out of desired), the selector app=alex-web, and the image nginx:1.27. The view holds one ReplicaSet and two Running Pods. Operator shows a snapshot, so if Pods are still starting, change a filter or switch back to Operator to load a fresh one. If the summary reported Failed to deploy Deployment "alex-web", open its error card; on a shared cluster the most common cause is a name another user already deployed.
Scale the Deployment 🔗 Switch to Designer and change replicas from 2 to 3. Run Deploy again with the same environment. Switch to Operator to load a fresh snapshot. What just happened. Deploy replaced the existing Deployment in place with your new configuration; it did not create a second one. The controller saw that the desired count rose to three and told the existing ReplicaSet to create one more Pod. Scaling does not touch the Pod template, so no new ReplicaSet appears.
Check your work. The Deployment shows pods 3 / 3, and the same ReplicaSet now owns three Pods. Two Pods keep their original names and ages; the new one is younger.
Roll out a new image 🔗 Switch to Designer and change the container image from nginx:1.27 to nginx:1.28. Run Deploy again. Switch to Operator and look at the ReplicaSets and Pods. What just happened. Changing the Pod template gave it a new hash, so the controller created a new ReplicaSet and shifted Pods to it gradually. With the default rolling update strategy, Kubernetes starts new Pods before removing old ones and keeps at least three quarters of the desired Pods available throughout. The old ReplicaSet stays at zero replicas so that Kubernetes can roll back to it.
Check your work. The view holds two ReplicaSets: the new one owns three Pods with fresh names, and the old one owns none. The Deployment’s details show the image nginx:1.28. A snapshot taken mid-rollout shows Pods under both ReplicaSets; load a fresh snapshot to see the finished state. If you mistype the image tag, the new Pods cannot pull it and stay not ready, the rollout stalls, and the old Pods keep serving. Correct the tag and deploy again.
A change to a field Kubernetes treats as immutable, such as the Deployment’s selector, does not apply, and the Deploy summary still reports Deployed. To change the selector, undeploy the Deployment and deploy it again.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu and select the same environment. Undeploy deletes the alex-web Deployment by kind, name, and namespace; Kubernetes garbage collection then removes the ReplicaSets and Pods it owns. Undeploy matches by name, not by the design label, so a same-named Deployment created by someone else in the same namespace is deleted too. If the dry-run step reports the Deployment as not found, it is already gone; select the bypass option to finish.
The design stays in your account until you delete it from the design’s file menu. Deleting a design never removes cluster objects.
What you learned 🔗 You declare a Deployment; Kubernetes creates the ReplicaSets and Pods and keeps the desired count running. The selector must match the template labels and is immutable once deployed. Scaling reuses the existing ReplicaSet; a template change creates a new ReplicaSet and rolls Pods over to it, keeping the old one for rollback. Deploying a changed design replaces the object in place, and a label filter in Operator reveals objects that Kubernetes created on your behalf. Next steps 🔗 Continue with Explore Services to put a stable address in front of these Pods. Read Deploying designs for every option in the Deploy workflow. Read Operator to understand views, filters, and snapshots.

A design is a single record in Layer5 Cloud. It has one owner, lives in one workspace, and carries a visibility (private, public, or published) and a version. These guides cover each way a design enters, changes state, and leaves that record.
Two defaults shape everything below. A design saved for the first time is public, whatever visibility the client requests. Every save of an existing design raises its patch version by one (0.0.1, 0.0.2, and so on).
Goal Guide Bring in a manifest, Helm chart, Compose file, Kustomize project, or design, or merge one design into another Import and Merge Designs Understand autosave, the save indicator, Save as, and plan limits Save Designs Start from a public or published design Clone a Design Back up a design or hand it to other tools Export Designs Show a design on another site Embed Designs Make a design available in the catalog Publish Designs Remove a design permanently Delete a Design For the exact formats Kanvas accepts and produces, see Supported Import and Export Formats. To share a design with specific people, see Share Designs.
Where designs go 🔗 Every new design lands in exactly one workspace: the workspace you have selected for the current organization, or the first workspace you can see in that organization. If the organization has no workspace, saving, importing, and cloning fail. Creating a design is refused while the organization selector is set to all.
Anonymous users on kanvas.new can create, save, and import designs. Those designs move to the account when the user signs in. Sharing and publishing require an account.

An environment groups connections into a deploy target and is the means by which a workspace exposes those connections to its teams. This guide covers every task on an environment. For the model behind it, read the Environments concept.
Each task names the permission it needs. Layer5 Cloud checks the permission in the organization that owns the environment.
Environment permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Environment See all environments within an workspace. ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Environment Create a new environment -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Edit Environment Edit environment and it connection membership -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Delete Environment Dissolve environment and all connection memberships. Leave associated resources intact. -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign connections to environment Add new connections to environments -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove connections from environment Remove connections from environment, -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View Connections View all connections within an environment ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed The feature matrix lists environments under the Enterprise plan. Layer5 Cloud does not refuse environment actions because of the plan.
Find environments 🔗 Needs: View Environment to see the Environments page. The API lists environments for any signed-in member of the organization.
Every member of an organization can list every environment in it, whether or not the environment is attached to a workspace they belong to. A list request names one organization; View All Organizations widens it to every organization. You can search by name or description, order by creation or update time, and page through results.
Environments that Layer5 Cloud provisions for itself appear in the list too. See Environments you cannot change.
Create an environment 🔗 Needs: Create Environment in the organization that will own the environment.
An environment takes a name, a description, and an organization. The organization is required; without it the request fails with organizationId is required. The environment stays in that organization for its whole life.
The Environments page requires a name and an organization. The API does not check that the name is non-empty or unique. Name and description are each limited to 255 characters. A new environment is empty and attached to no workspace. It is an ordinary environment, which means you can edit and delete it and manage its connections. Edit an environment 🔗 Needs: Edit Environment.
An update replaces both the name and the description with the values you send. A field you leave out becomes empty, so send both every time. Editing never changes the organization and never changes the connections.
Assign connections to an environment 🔗 Needs: Assign connections to environment.
Assigning a connection places it in the environment, whether the connection is managed or discovered. One connection can be in any number of environments, and an environment can hold any number of connections.
Assigning a connection also makes its credentials reachable. Who can use it follows the access rules for connections: the owner, members of teams assigned to a workspace that holds the environment, and holders of View All Organizations.
Layer5 Cloud answers an assignment this way:
Condition Result The environment exists and is ordinary The connection is assigned No live environment has that identifier HTTP 404, no environment with the requested id The environment is provisioned by the platform HTTP 403, this connection cannot be assigned to this environment Layer5 Cloud checks the permission in the environment’s organization. It does not compare the connection’s organization with the environment’s, and it does not check who owns the connection.
View the connections in an environment 🔗 Needs: View Environment.
The connection list of an environment defaults to the connections assigned to it. Switch the filter to see the connections not yet in it, which is the pick list for an assignment. You can search, order by creation time, update time, or name, and page through results.
Remove connections from an environment 🔗 Needs: Remove connections from environment.
Removing a connection takes it out of this environment only. The connection and its credential remain, and so does its membership in any other environment. Team members who reached the connection only through this environment lose that access.
Condition Result The connection is in the environment It is removed The connection was never assigned HTTP 404, no such connection assignment The environment is provisioned by the platform HTTP 403, this connection cannot be detached from this environment See the environments in a workspace 🔗 The environments attached to a workspace default to the list of its environments. Switch the filter to list the organization’s environments not yet attached, which is the pick list for an attachment. Attaching and detaching are workspace tasks. See Attach an environment to a workspace.
Delete an environment 🔗 Needs: Delete Environment.
Deleting an environment ends every connection assignment and every workspace attachment it holds. It deletes no connection, credential, or workspace. Connections that also belong to other environments stay in those. Team members lose the access the environment gave them through workspaces.
Condition Result The environment is ordinary and live It is deleted No live environment has that identifier HTTP 404, no environment with the requested id The environment is provisioned by the platform HTTP 403, this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be deleted here Any other failure HTTP 400, unable to delete environment Environments you cannot change 🔗 Layer5 Cloud provisions some environments itself to hold organization configuration, such as the mail server or sign-in providers. They show in the environment list like any other. The controls on this page refuse them:
You cannot delete one. You cannot assign connections to one or remove connections from one. You cannot attach one to a workspace. An existing attachment of one to a workspace can still be removed. Manage the configuration they hold through the organization guides: Bring Your Own Mail Server and Organization Configuration Scenarios.

Layer5 Cloud is a Meshery remote provider. When a Meshery Server uses Layer5 Cloud, hosted or self-hosted, the server registers itself with Cloud on behalf of the signed-in user. Registration is what makes that Meshery Server known to Cloud: it appears as a meshery connection owned by that user. This page explains what the server sends, how Cloud tells a new server from one it already knows, what survives re-registration, and what each failure means.
For where registration fits in the overall relationship between Cloud and Meshery, see How Layer5 Cloud Works with Meshery and Kanvas.
Why registration exists 🔗 Registration answers two questions for Cloud:
Which Meshery Server is calling? Many Meshery deployments can work with the same Cloud deployment, and Cloud must keep them apart. Who owns it? Every registration is owned by exactly one user, the user whose session made the request. A registration record answers both. It ties a stable server identifier to an owner and survives Meshery Server restarts.
How Cloud identifies a Meshery Server 🔗 A Meshery Server generates a stable server identifier on its first start and keeps it locally. It sends that identifier as serverId inside the connection’s metadata.
Cloud recognizes an existing registration by three values together:
the connection kind, meshery the owner, which is the authenticated user metadata.serverId Each owner and serverId pair maps to exactly one connection. Cloud places no limit on either side of that pair: one user can register any number of Meshery Servers, and one Meshery Server can be registered by any number of users, with one connection per user.
Connections are owned by a user, not by an organization. Each user sees their own connections, including the Meshery Servers they registered.
The registration request 🔗 A Meshery Server registers by sending a connection to:
POST /api/integrations/connections The request must be authenticated with a Cloud session or a bearer token. Cloud takes the owner from that authentication, never from the request body.
Field Required Description kind Yes The connection kind. Case-insensitive. Accepted values are meshery, kubernetes, prometheus, and grafana. A Meshery Server registers itself with meshery. metadata.serverId Yes, for meshery The stable identifier the Meshery Server generated. The key is camelCase. name No A display name. When omitted, Cloud names the connection <kind>-<random>, for example meshery- followed by a random suffix. metadata (other keys) No Additional details about the server, such as its version. Cloud refreshes them on every registration. On success, Cloud responds with HTTP 201 and a one-item page of connections containing the registered connection. Every registration call, first or repeat, records a “registered” event for the connection in the account’s event log.
First registration 🔗 When no connection matches the owner and serverId, Cloud creates a new meshery connection owned by the authenticated user.
Re-registration 🔗 A re-registration is any later call from the same Meshery Server, carrying the same serverId, for the same user. It typically follows a Meshery Server restart, a new sign-in, or a reconnect.
Cloud updates the existing connection in place:
Kept from the stored connection Refreshed from the request ID, name, kind, type, sub-type, status, owner, and creation time Metadata and the last-updated time Two consequences follow:
Re-registering never renames a server. A request that omits name, and would otherwise get a random name, cannot replace the name the connection already has. Re-registering never resets status. A Meshery Server you disconnected or ignored stays disconnected or ignored when it registers again. Status changes through connection lifecycle actions Connection status changes through the dedicated connection lifecycle actions, such as connect, disconnect, ignore, and delete, not through registration. Registration carries the stored status forward, so a restarting server cannot undo a status you set. Other connection kinds 🔗 The same endpoint registers the other accepted kinds, with their own identity rules:
Kubernetes. Cloud derives the connection’s ID from the cluster and the owner, so registering the same cluster again updates the existing connection instead of creating another. Cloud stores the cluster’s credential once and keeps the stored status. Prometheus and Grafana. Cloud creates the connection or updates the existing one in place. Validation and errors 🔗 Condition Result The request carries no Cloud session or bearer token Rejected. The endpoint requires authentication. The authentication does not resolve to a user Rejected before anything is stored, with the error “cannot register meshery connection: missing owner in authenticated session”. kind is not one of the accepted values HTTP 500 with the error “connection kind: <kind>, not implemented yet”. metadata.serverId is missing or empty on a meshery registration HTTP 500 with the error “empty server id; cannot check for existence”. No connection is created. Operator guidance 🔗 If you operate a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud, these symptoms map to the most common causes:
Registration fails with “missing owner in authenticated session”. The request reached Cloud with authentication that does not resolve to a user. Look at the request in your logs and confirm that it carries a valid session or bearer token for an existing account. Registration fails with “empty server id; cannot check for existence”. The client did not send serverId in metadata. Cloud does not fall back to creating an unidentified connection. Confirm that the client sends the identifier under the camelCase key serverId. Registration fails with “not implemented yet”. The client sent a kind other than meshery, kubernetes, prometheus, or grafana. A Meshery Server appears under the wrong user. The owner comes from the session, not from the request body. The server was registered while a different account was signed in. The same Meshery Server appears more than once. Each owner and serverId pair is a separate connection, so a server registered by two users appears once for each of them. If one user sees the same server twice, the server presented a different serverId, which happens when it loses the identifier it stored locally and generates a new one. A Meshery Server’s name or status in Cloud does not change when it reconnects. This is intended. Re-registration preserves the stored name and status; change them through the connection’s own actions.

Plan these network paths before you deploy. Most are ordinary HTTPS traffic through your ingress. Real-time co-editing is the exception: it connects browsers directly to each other, and the deployment only introduces them.
Required network paths 🔗 From To Protocol Purpose Browsers, Meshery Servers, API clients Ingress, public hostname HTTPS UI, API, sign-in (/kratos), and OAuth2 (/hydra) Browsers Ingress, /collaboration WebSocket over HTTPS Co-editing signaling Layer5 Cloud server Kratos and Hydra services HTTP, in cluster Account and token operations. Default ports: Kratos public 9010 and admin 9011, Hydra public 4444 and admin 4445 Kratos Layer5 Cloud server HTTP, in cluster Registration hooks, and identity mail when the HTTP courier is selected Layer5 Cloud server, Kratos, Hydra PostgreSQL TCP 5432 Databases meshery, kratos, hydra Layer5 Cloud server SMTP relay SMTP on 25, 465, 587, or 2525 Mail. The relay must resolve to a public address Layer5 Cloud server Webhook receivers HTTPS Optional webhooks Layer5 Cloud server OpenTelemetry collector OTLP gRPC Optional traces Browsers Public STUN and TURN hosts UDP and TCP Direct connections between co-editing browsers The ingress must support WebSocket upgrades. A controller or load balancer that closes idle connections shorter than the signaling keep-alive (below) disconnects users from their co-editing session.
How co-editing connects people 🔗 When two people open the same design, their browsers exchange edits directly over WebRTC. Layer5 Cloud takes part only at the start and for presence:
Each browser opens a WebSocket to /collaboration on the provider that signed the user in and joins a room named after the design. The server tells each browser who else is in the room. The browsers ask public STUN servers how to reach each other, and fall back to a public TURN relay when a direct path is blocked. Edits then travel browser to browser. They do not pass through Layer5 Cloud or Meshery Server. A self-hosted provider is its own signaling host. Users connected to your deployment never signal through Layer5’s hosted service.
In short: the WebSocket carries introductions and presence, WebRTC carries the work, and STUN and TURN help the browsers find each other.
What the signaling endpoint does and enforces 🔗 Authentication. A connection must present the user’s access token. The server answers an unauthenticated connection with 401. Rooms. The endpoint creates a room when someone joins and tracks who is in it. It accepts any room name from a signed-in user and does not check that the user may open the design the room belongs to. Design identifiers are random, and the content of a design stays on the peers, so treat the identifier as the secret that gates a room. Messages. The server relays join, leave, and broadcast messages, and pushes the member list of each room to its members, with each person’s name and avatar. Keep-alive. The server pings each connection every 27 seconds. A client that does not answer within 30 seconds is dropped. Persistence. The server stores nothing from a session. The person who made an edit saves it through the normal design save; a person who opens the design later loads the last saved version. Origins. The endpoint accepts WebSocket connections from any origin. What peers see 🔗 Each participant is shown to the others with their name, avatar, cursor, and selected component. Presence colors are random per session, so two people can share a color. A second browser tab with the same account appears as another collaborator.
Sizing and limits 🔗 Layer5 Cloud enforces no cap on the number of people in a room, on document size, or on session length. Because every browser connects to every other browser, connection count grows with the square of the room’s size, and a very large room degrades before the server does. Plan for design reviews and pairing, not broadcast to large audiences.
When co-editing cannot connect 🔗 Kanvas keeps working as a single-user editor and writes the reason to the browser console. There is no on-screen indicator and no automatic retry. Check these in order:
Symptom Likely cause The WebSocket to /collaboration fails with 401 The user’s session has expired. Signing in again fixes it. The WebSocket never upgrades The ingress or an intermediate proxy does not pass WebSocket upgrades on /collaboration. The WebSocket connects, but people do not see each other’s changes Browsers cannot reach the public STUN and TURN hosts, or a firewall blocks WebRTC. The STUN and TURN hosts are set by the Kanvas client and are not configurable in the deployment. People see each other’s presence but not edits The same cause: signaling works and the peer connection does not.

Layer5 Cloud sends email when something happens that involves you: you earn a badge, your role changes, someone comments on your design. Notification preferences decide which of those emails reach you. Preferences belong to your account, so they apply in every organization you belong to.
Email is the only channel. Layer5 Cloud has no per-event choice between email and another channel.
Before you start 🔗 You need the View Profile permission, which the default user role holds. The preferences are on your own account, and you cannot set them for anyone else.
How preferences work 🔗 Everything is on until you turn it off. A new account receives every notification. You opt out of the ones you do not want, and a notification added later is on for you until you turn it off. Preferences save themselves. About one second after your last change, Layer5 Cloud saves it and confirms with “Notification preferences updated”. There is no Save button. Preferences are grouped. The preferences appear under categories and sub-categories. Each category has a switch that turns every preference in it on or off at once. To opt out of all email, turn every category off. A preference suppresses email, not the event. The event still happens and still appears in the audit trail. Only the email is skipped. Preferences you can set 🔗 The categories below are the ones the account page lists. Layer5 Cloud reads the list of available preferences from its own configuration, so a deployment can list more or fewer.
Category Preference Emails you when Acknowledgment Badge assignment and updates A badge is awarded to you or changed. Organization Activity Organization update An organization you belong to is updated. Workspace Activity Team, user, and organization management A team you belong to is updated, or you are added to a team. Workspace Activity Role assignment and updates Your roles change. Workspace Activity Comments on your designs Someone comments on a design you own. Turning this off silences email about comments on your designs. Workspace Activity Participating and @mentions in comments You are mentioned in a comment, or a thread you took part in gets a reply. To stop email from one thread without turning the preference off, mute that thread. See Mute a thread.
Preferences that do nothing yet 🔗 Three preferences appear greyed out and unchecked, and cannot be changed: Changes to designs, Deployments in environments, and Weekly summary. Layer5 Cloud does not send those emails today. Do not rely on them.
Edge cases 🔗 Anonymous accounts never receive organization update email. Layer5 Cloud checks the preference when it is about to send the email. Turning a preference back on does not resend email that was skipped while it was off. If saving fails, the page shows the reason, and your previous setting stays in force. See also 🔗 Review and collaborate on designs describes who receives comment email. Manage Your Account covers your profile and sign-in.

This page tells you which Kanvas actions require a permission, which default roles grant each permission, and which actions are limited by something other than a permission. Use it to find out why an action is missing for a user and which role grants it.
How permissions work 🔗 A permission is a named key, such as Deploy Design, that allows one action. Keys are grouped into keychains, and a role bundles one or more keychains. Your organization assigns roles to users. Before Kanvas offers certain actions, it checks whether the user holds the matching key. Kanvas uses the shared Layer5 permission set and defines no permissions of its own. See Roles and Keychains.
Where Kanvas checks a permission 🔗 Kanvas checks a permission before it offers each of the following actions:
Action Permission checked Also note Validate and Dry run Validate Design One permission controls both actions. Disabled while the design is empty. Deploy Deploy Design Disabled while the design is empty. Undeploy Undeploy Design Disabled while the design is empty. Share Share Design Also hidden while the design is empty or published. Publish Publish Design Anonymous users get a sign-in prompt instead. Operator mode None The provider enables Operator mode. When the provider does not enable it, the Operator switch is disabled. When a user does not hold the permission, Kanvas does not offer the action: the toolbar hides it or shows it disabled, and the action sheet on small screens omits it.
Layer5 Cloud also enforces permissions when it receives a request, independently of the Kanvas interface. It checks Share Design when a design is shared, View Designs when a user reads other members’ private designs, the workspace permissions when designs or views are assigned to or removed from a workspace, and Share Views when a view is shared.
Default role access 🔗 The tables below show which default roles grant each design and view permission. They are refreshed automatically from the Layer5 permission list.
A check mark means the role grants the permission. A check mark with an asterisk means the role grants the permission only on resources the user owns. A dash means the role does not grant the permission. Design lifecycle Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin Validate Design Validate a design ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Deploy Design Deploy a design -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Undeploy Design Retract all resources used in a Meshery design from the cluster -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Share Design Share design with anyone within your organization, and make your design easily accessible to all relevant team members. ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Publish Design Publish a design ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Unpublish Design Unpublish a design ✓*Allowed on resources the user owns ✓*Allowed on resources the user owns ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Clone Design Clone any published design to customise it according to your use cases ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View Designs View all public and published designs of other team members and private of signed-in user ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Designs to Workspaces Assign designs to workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove Designs from Workspaces Remove designs from workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Views and clusters Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Views See all views within a workspace ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Views to Workspace Add new views to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Unassign Views from Workspace Remove views from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Add cluster Add Kubernetes cluster -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View All Kubernetes Clusters View all configured Kubernetes clusters ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Org Admin is the Organization Admin role. The roles not shown, Org Billing Manager and the Academy roles, hold none of these permissions. Provider Admin holds every permission.
Anonymous users 🔗 A user is anonymous when no one is signed in or the signed-in account has anonymous status. An anonymous user authors and edits designs. Sharing or publishing a design opens a sign-in prompt that names the feature and offers a single Sign in action.
Anonymous users receive the anonymous role. It holds the same canvas permissions as the User role, plus Screenshot Canvas and View help center. It does not hold the Operator terminal, metrics, or component details permissions.
On kanvas.new, Validate, Dry run, Deploy, Undeploy, connecting a cluster, and Operator mode open a prompt that directs the user to the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery deployment. This applies to signed-in users on kanvas.new as well. See Feature Availability by Plan.
What is not gated per action 🔗 Canvas editing 🔗 Kanvas does not check a permission for individual canvas edits: adding, deleting, cloning, copying, locking, and styling components, shapes, text boxes, sections, and comments; undo and redo; and the pen and pencil tools. Roles carry permissions with these names, but removing them from a role does not prevent the edit. Three things limit canvas editing instead:
Mode. Designer mode allows authoring. Operator mode does not. Node kind. Live nodes, the resources Kanvas reads from a connected cluster, are read-only in every mode. Design ownership and sharing. A user edits a design they own or one that is shared with them. Operator mode 🔗 Operator mode blocks canvas authoring: dropping, editing, duplicating, deleting, and renaming nodes are not allowed. Operator mode is not read-only, though. From Operator, a user still opens terminal and exec sessions and generates load.
Terminal, log streaming, and performance tests 🔗 The Kanvas interface does not check a permission before it opens a terminal session, streams container logs, or runs a performance test. Layer5 Cloud defines the permissions Stream container logs, Perform performance test in Operator, and Select performance profile in Operator. By default, only Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold them.
Customizing access 🔗 A custom role bundles keychains that the default roles do not combine, so a group can receive exactly the permissions it needs, such as Validate Design without Deploy Design. Only a Provider Admin creates a custom role. On hosted Layer5 Cloud an organization cannot create one itself; on a self-hosted deployment the operator’s Provider Admins can. In the Kanvas interface, a custom role changes what is offered only for the actions listed in Where Kanvas checks a permission; Layer5 Cloud applies its own checks to sharing, private designs, and workspace assignments. See Roles.

A new deployment has no users, so nobody can sign in to administer it. Provider initialization solves that: when the server starts with INIT_CONFIG set, it creates the provider organization and its first Provider Admin. From that account, you create organizations, assign roles, and manage the deployment. See Roles and Permissions for what a Provider Admin can do.
Format 🔗 INIT_CONFIG holds a YAML document. In Helm, set it as a multiline string in env.initConfig, or load it from a file with --set-file env.initConfig=provider-init.yaml.
organization: name: "Example Corp" description: "The provider organization for Example Corp." country: "United States" region: "North America" user: first_name: "Ada" last_name: "Admin" email: "admin@example.com" username: "admin@example.com" password: "<initial password>" Field Required Meaning organization.name Yes Name of the provider organization. organization.description No Description. organization.country No Country. organization.region No Region. user.first_name Yes First name of the administrator. user.last_name Yes Last name of the administrator. user.email Yes Email address. It is the sign-in identifier. user.username No Defaults to the email address. user.password Yes Initial password. The provider organization always has the fixed identifier 11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111. Every deployment uses the same one.
What happens at startup 🔗 The server evaluates INIT_CONFIG on every start, after database migrations and before it reports ready.
Not set. Initialization is skipped. Set but invalid. A missing required field or YAML that does not parse is logged as an error. The server keeps starting, with no provider administrator. The provider organization already exists. Initialization is skipped, and any change to INIT_CONFIG is ignored. The provider organization does not exist. The server runs these steps in order: Creates a Kratos identity with the password and the email marked verified. Creates the user and marks the account active. Grants the user the Provider Admin role and the Kanvas role. Creates the provider organization with the fixed identifier, owned by that user. Adds the user to the organization with the Organization Admin role. The first administrator can sign in as soon as the server is ready. They never see an email verification step, because the address is created verified.
After the organization exists, the server also seeds the deployment’s default Google and GitHub sign-in credentials from env.providerOrg*. See Identity Services.
Failure modes 🔗 Condition Result A step fails after earlier steps succeeded The server logs the error and keeps starting. The steps are not wrapped in one transaction, so rows from earlier steps remain. Fix the cause and restart. A restart repeats the whole sequence for as long as the provider organization does not exist. Kratos rejects the identity (for example, the password is too weak or the identity exists) The server logs a warning and continues with the remaining steps. INIT_CONFIG removed after the first successful start No effect. The organization exists. INIT_CONFIG changed after the first successful start No effect. Change the administrator through the product. Handling the password 🔗 The initial password is stored in the Helm release, in the pod environment, and in the server log, because the server logs the configuration it reads. Treat all three as secret. After you have signed in and changed the password, remove env.initConfig and run helm upgrade. The administrator account is unaffected.
When to use it 🔗 Use INIT_CONFIG for every new self-hosted deployment, and keep the file in your secret manager next to the other values. It makes a deployment reproducible: a rebuilt cluster with the same values and a restored database comes up with the same administrator, and a rebuilt cluster with an empty database creates it again.

body:
A relationship records how two components connect: one runs inside the other, one sends traffic to the other, one mounts the other’s storage, or both carry the same label. Relationships do more than draw lines. Each relationship definition names the configuration fields on both sides that must agree, so Kanvas can write values from one component into the other and keep the design consistent as you edit. The definitions come from the Meshery registry, not from Kanvas, so the set of relationships available to you depends on the models you use.
Kinds of relationship 🔗 The Layers panel lists eight kinds of relationship, which fall into three families.
Edge relationships 🔗 An edge is a line between two components that interact. You draw it by hand. Kanvas lists the edges the registry allows from the component you start on, and highlights the targets that are compatible.
Subtype Meaning Example Network Traffic can flow between the components. The edge labels source and target ports and protocols. A Service gives a stable endpoint to a Deployment’s replicas. Mount One component gives storage or files to another, through a binding component placed between them. A PersistentVolume mounted into a Pod. Reference One component points to another by name, identifier, or scope. It declares a dependency and does not itself grant access or carry traffic. A Pod that references a ConfigMap or a Secret. Annotation A line you draw with the Pen tool to explain flow. It has no effect on configuration. A traced request path on a diagram. The registry can define other edge subtypes. They appear in the edge picker when they can start from the selected component.
Hierarchical relationships 🔗 A hierarchical relationship nests one component in another. A component has at most one parent.
Inventory. The child is drawn inside its parent, as a Pod sits inside a Namespace. Because the Namespace’s name is the Pod’s namespace, the parent’s configuration flows to the child. Wallet. The child is absorbed into its host and shown as a count badge on the host, as a sidecar is attached to a workload. Alias. The child stands for one field inside its parent. Editing the alias edits that field of the parent. TagSets 🔗 Components that carry matching labels or annotations form a TagSet. Kanvas never asks you to draw one. It appears when the labels match and disappears when they stop matching. See Work with Tags.
How relationships form 🔗 Three mechanisms create relationships:
Mechanism Kinds You create them: drag an edge, drop a component into a parent, or draw with the Pen Edge, inventory, wallet, annotation Evaluation creates them from the registry definitions TagSets, alias, and any relationship the definitions say should exist Paste or duplicate copies them with the components Any relationship whose two ends are both in the copied set Deleting a component marks the relationships that touched it as deleted. The next evaluation then reverses their effects on configuration.
Relationships keep configuration in sync 🔗 Evaluation is the process that applies relationship definitions to a design. It runs shortly after a change, writes values across related fields, and can add or remove components and relationships. The direction of a write depends on the definition and the kind.
Kind Typical direction Example Inventory Parent to child The child takes its namespace from the parent Namespace. Edge Source to target A Service’s port is written into the related Deployment’s container port. Wallet Attached item to host The host takes the item’s configuration. Treat these as typical. The relationship definition is the authority, and Kanvas does not hard-code a direction. Policy Evaluation explains when evaluation runs and why results can change after you stop editing.
What relationships mean at deploy time 🔗 Annotation edges, TagSets, and the drawing of any relationship never change what Kanvas deploys by themselves. What gets deployed is the configuration of each component. Relationships matter because they decided what that configuration is.
Related pages 🔗 Create Relationships: create, remove, and hide relationships. Designs and Components: what a design contains.

A comment is a note on the canvas that holds a threaded conversation. Use comments to give feedback, record the reason behind a configuration choice, or ask a teammate a question next to the component it concerns. A comment is part of the design: it saves with the design, appears live to everyone who has the design open, and travels with clones and exports.
For how comments fit with live editing and access, read Collaboration Model.
Who can comment 🔗 Anyone who can open a design can comment on it. The role catalog lists separate permissions for adding, resolving, deleting, and styling comments, but Kanvas does not enforce them. Whoever can edit a design can do every comment action. Comments work in Designer mode only.
Because new designs are public, a comment on a public design is visible to anyone who opens it. To limit who sees your review, make the design private and share it with the reviewers. See Share a Design.
A comment thread on the canvas. Add a comment 🔗 Add a comment in any of three ways:
Drag the Comment tool from the dock onto the canvas, or click it to drop a comment near the center. Right-click the canvas and choose Add Comment. The comment lands where you clicked. Press M. The comment appears near the center of the canvas, and you can drag it into place. A comment is an annotation component, so it moves, locks, groups, copies, and deletes like other annotations. See Canvas Objects. The Annotations toggle in the Layers panel hides all annotations, comments included, on your canvas. Hidden comments still sync.
Hold a conversation 🔗 Each comment holds one thread. Type a message and press Enter to send it. Press Ctrl or Cmd with Enter to add a line break. A message cannot be empty. A thread shows its first message and offers to show the rest when it has more than one.
A message can contain:
Mentions. Type @ and the start of a name. The picker searches every user on the platform, not only people with access to the design, and shows up to seven matches. A bare @ shows none. The search needs the View All Users permission. If it fails, Kanvas shows an error instead of “no users”. Links. URLs become links. Emoji. Type : and part of an emoji name to pick one. Messages cannot be edited, and a single message cannot be deleted. Deleting a comment removes the whole thread. Resolve a thread instead of deleting it when you want to keep the record.
Resolve and reopen 🔗 Resolve a thread when the discussion is done. A resolved comment leaves the canvas but stays in the design with all its messages. Reopen it to bring it back. Adding a message to a resolved thread reopens it. Resolving and reopening send no notification.
Find threads in the comments panel 🔗 The Comments panel lists every comment that has at least one message, newest activity first. Filter it by:
Filter Shows All Every comment with a message Open Threads that are not resolved Resolved Resolved threads For me Threads where any message mentions you The panel uses the same thread control as the canvas, so you can read, reply, resolve, reopen, and mute from it.
Reuse a comment 🔗 Copy, paste, and duplicate create a new comment with the original’s messages, timestamps, and name. The new comment is independent: editing or deleting the original does not change it. Copying or duplicating sends no notification. A reply to the copy notifies participants in the copy’s thread. Pasting a comment into another design does not change who can open that design, so participants from the original thread may be unable to open the copy’s design.
Notifications 🔗 Kanvas sends comment notifications by email when a message is added. Resolving and reopening a thread send nothing.
Kanvas emails these people, after removing the author of the new message:
Recipient Receives email when Mentioned users The new message mentions them Thread participants They wrote an earlier message in the thread, or an earlier message mentioned them The design owner Someone other than the owner added the message A request is sent only when the message mentions someone, or the thread already has an earlier message by or mentioning another person. A first comment that mentions nobody emails nobody, including the design owner. Mention the owner when you need them to see a new comment.
An email goes out only if the recipient’s account preferences allow it. Two preferences apply: comments on your designs, which governs the owner’s email, and participating and mentions in comments, which governs the other two. See Notification Preferences.
Kanvas does not check that a recipient can open the design before it emails them. The email shows the thread and links to the design in the Meshery Playground, whichever Meshery the design is stored for.
If a message posts but the emails fail, Kanvas shows “Comment posted, but the mentioned users could not be notified” and the reason. The comment stays.
Kanvas does not track which messages a person has read. Someone who misses an email learns of the comment only from a later notification or by opening the design.
Mute a thread 🔗 Use the bell in a thread to stop mention and participant emails to you for that thread. The bell toggles your mute. The mute is stored in the thread, so it saves with the design and every collaborator can see the list of people who muted it.
Muting affects only the thread where you set it. Mentions in other threads and designs still reach you. The owner’s email is decided by the commenter’s mute list, not the owner’s: a thread the owner muted still emails the owner, and a thread the commenter muted does not.
Account preferences apply to every design. A disabled preference stops those emails everywhere.
Review practices that match how Kanvas works 🔗 Mention the person you need. Mentions are the dependable notification path. Resolve instead of delete. Resolution keeps the discussion for later. Review in a private, shared design. Everyone with access can also edit, so agree who changes the design and who comments. Use the For me filter after time away. It lists threads that mention you. Related 🔗 Collaboration Model Share a Design Collaborative Editing Canvas Objects Keyboard Shortcuts

This page tells you which permissions each default Layer5 Cloud role holds. Use it to find out why an action is missing for a user and which role grants it. For how roles, keychains, and permissions fit together, see Roles.
How permission checks work 🔗 A permission is a named key that allows one action, such as Create Team. A keychain groups keys, and a role groups keychains. Layer5 Cloud checks the key, never the role name. Before it runs a guarded action, Cloud resolves the organization the request names, then checks whether the user holds the key through a role in that organization. A user’s permissions are the union of the keys from every role the user holds there.
When a user lacks the key, Cloud refuses the request with HTTP 403 and the message “You do not hold the permission this action requires in this organization”. The response body is JSON with an error message and a code.
Provider Admin passes every permission check, in every organization.

It is not listed and cannot be assigned. See Permissions by Role for what anonymous users can do in Kanvas.
The Kanvas role holds no keychains. It makes the Kanvas extension available when a Meshery Server connects to Layer5 Cloud.

A role grants a permission, and the plan decides whether the capability exists for the organization. See Feature Availability by Plan. Custom roles 🔗 A custom role bundles keychains that the default roles do not combine. Only a Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a custom role. Roles and keychains are defined for the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment, not per organization. Only a Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a keychain, change its keys, or assign a keychain to a role. Changing the keychains of a role changes that role for every organization that uses it. See Roles.

body:
Kanvas saves a design for you. There is no Save button and no Save shortcut. Every change that alters the design, such as adding, moving, configuring, or deleting a component, renaming, editing a relationship, or merging, queues a save. The request is sent 3 seconds after your last change. Changes made while a save is in flight queue a new save when it finishes.
Saving needs a signed-in user or a guest session on kanvas.new, and an organization. It does not check a permission key.
What triggers a save, and what does not 🔗 A new design with no id is saved only once it has at least one component, or a name that is neither empty nor “Untitled Design”. A design that was saved before is always saved.
Kanvas does not save when you load a design, when the server assigns the id after the first save, when you open a component configurator, or when collaborators’ document updates arrive.
The first save creates the design, and the address bar updates to ?mode=design&design=<id>. If you edit again before the first save returns, Kanvas holds the second save until the id arrives, so no duplicate design is created.
Read the save indicator 🔗 The cloud icon in the top bar reports the state and doubles as a manual save trigger.
State Indicator Saving Animated icon and “Saving…” Saved “Saved” for 3 seconds, then a tooltip reading “All changes saved” with the time Failed Red cloud-off icon and “Unable to save. Retrying…” The tooltip on any saved design includes View Save History.
Save a copy 🔗 Save as saves the open design as a new design with a name you enter. It proposes <current name>-copy. The copy gets a new id, you as owner, your selected workspace, public visibility, and version 0.0.1, then Kanvas loads it. The original is unchanged. Save as is disabled on an empty canvas. The name is required but not checked for length or uniqueness.
A new blank design is named “Untitled Design” until you rename it.
Versions and history 🔗 Each save raises the patch number of the design’s version: the first save is 0.0.1, the next 0.0.2, and so on. Autosaves, visibility changes, and catalog data edits all count, so the version tracks how often the design was saved, not meaningful releases. Cloning and imports reset the version to 0.0.1. There is no way to bump the major or minor number.
View Save History opens a list titled “Design Version History”. It is an event log of who changed the design and when. You cannot restore, diff, or export an earlier version from it. If you need a version you can return to, export a copy at that point. See Export Designs.
Concurrent edits 🔗 Saving sends the whole design and the server overwrites the stored copy. The last save wins. Collaborators editing the same open design are reconciled live in the editor by the collaboration session, not at the storage layer.
Plan limit: components per design 🔗 The server rejects a save when the design has more components than your plan allows.
Plan Components per design Personal 100 Team Designer 200 Team Operator 100 Enterprise 300 These are the seeded plan values. A deployment can differ. The limit applies to every save, to Save as, to merges, and to URL imports. It does not apply to cloning. A cloned design that exceeds your limit opens normally but fails its first save.
The server answers 403 with the message “Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan” (the misspelling ships) and an upgrade remediation. Kanvas does not show that message. You see only “Unable to save. Retrying…” and the edits stay on the canvas, unsaved. Reduce the component count below the limit to save again. An organization with no active subscription that grants the feature gets “Org is not entitled to adding components to a design”.
For the other limits Layer5 lists per plan, see Feature Availability. Plan limits other than components per design are not enforced when you save.
When a save fails 🔗 Message Meaning Failed to reach the cloud. Any changes made may not be saved. The server was unreachable (HTTP 503). Failed to save Design with name: Any other failure, including the plan limit. Failed to save Design with name: Design is invalid or empty The design payload was empty or invalid. After a failure the editor enters an error mode: the top bar is tinted, and design-changing actions are ignored until the next command resets it. Autosave retries with exponential backoff, waiting 3 seconds times 2 to the power of the attempt number (6, 12, 24 seconds, and so on), up to 100 attempts. Any new edit resets the count.
Closing the tab or switching designs with unsaved changes asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?”
Who can save what 🔗 Anonymous users save normally into a guest account with its own organization and workspace. On sign-in, guest designs migrate to the account.
Updating an existing design keeps the original owner, visibility, and source type when the update does not state them. Operator mode blocks design edits, so it never saves a design. See Manage Designs for the defaults.

Every sign-in to Layer5 Cloud creates a session, on every browser, device, and Meshery Server you use. This guide reviews your sessions and ends the ones you do not want. For how long sessions last and what a session can reach, read the Sessions concept.
Before you start 🔗 You need the View Sessions permission to open the Sessions tab. Every default user role holds it. Ending another session from the tab requires the Delete Token permission, which Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold by default. Other roles see the Logout control disabled. This is how the interface works today. You can end only your own sessions. Review your sessions 🔗 Open the Sessions tab under Security. Each row is one sign-in and shows its ID, name, purpose, and creation date. Search filters by name or purpose, and the newest sessions appear first.
The list shows no device or location. Use the creation date to judge which sessions you started and which you did not. A creation date you cannot account for means someone else signed in with your credentials.
End a session 🔗 Choose Logout on the row and confirm. The session ends at once: the next request that carries its credentials fails. A confirmation reads Token "<name>" deleted, because a session is stored as a token.
The deleted session cannot be restored. Whoever used it must sign in again.
If you suspect your account is compromised 🔗 End every session you do not recognize. Change your password. Changing the password does not end other sessions, so complete step 1 first and check the list again afterward. Review your API tokens and revoke any you did not create. Tokens never expire and are not sessions, so signing out does not revoke them. If you cannot sign in, ask an Organization Admin or Provider Admin to help recover the account. Layer5 Cloud has no “sign out everywhere” action. End each session from the list.
What ends a session without your action 🔗 A session also ends when its access token expires, 24 hours after sign-in by default. See the Security Reference for the lifetimes.

An organization becomes useful when more than one person works in it. In this tutorial you invite a teammate by email, create a team, create a workspace, give the team that workspace, and move one of your designs into it. By the end you know which object controls what: the organization decides who is in, teams group people, and workspaces decide which shared resources those people reach.
Before you begin 🔗 You have a Layer5 Cloud account. If not, follow Create Your Layer5 Account. You work in My Organization, the organization Layer5 Cloud created for you, where you hold the Organization Admin role. Any organization where your role grants the permissions below works the same way. You own at least one design. If you do not, clone one first with Start from a Catalog Design. Each step in this tutorial needs a specific permission. The table shows which built-in roles hold each one:
Permissions used in this tutorial Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin Invite User to Organization Send a request for a user to join an organization. -Not granted -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Team Establish new team for organizing groups of users and resource access. -Not granted ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Add User to Team Directly create a new user account within a team. -Not granted ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Workspace Create new workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign team to workspace Add new team to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Designs to Workspaces Assign designs to workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed 1. Invite a teammate by email 🔗 Invite your teammate to the organization by email address. Your teammate does not need a Layer5 Cloud account first. An email invitation does all of the following at once:
Creates a pending account for the address. Adds that account to the organization, and to any teams you choose. Assigns the organization and team roles you choose. Sends an invitation email that names you, the organization, and the teams. Its sign-up link pre-fills your teammate’s name and address and carries your organization’s identifier. Layer5 Cloud refuses two kinds of invitation:
Situation Result The address already belongs to a Layer5 Cloud account Refused with HTTP 409 (“invite existing user”). No email address given Refused with HTTP 400 (“email is required”). To bring in someone who already has an account, share your organization’s open invitation link instead. Layer5 Cloud accepts that link on every sign-in, not only the first. See Using the open organization invitation link.
2. Create a team 🔗 Create a team for the people who will share the workspace you build next. A new team belongs to the organization you create it in.
Creating a team and adding people to it are separate actions. Once the team exists, add your teammate to it. When you invite more people later, you can choose this team in the invitation so they join it directly.
3. Create a workspace 🔗 Create a workspace in the same organization. A workspace groups shared resources such as environments, connections, credentials, and designs. Your My Workspace stays as it is; the new workspace is where you and your team collaborate.
4. Assign the team to the workspace 🔗 Assign your new team to the new workspace. Assignment is its own action, separate from creating either object. The relationship is many-to-many:
A workspace has zero or more teams. A team can be assigned to several workspaces. This is how you share access to a workspace’s resources: through the teams assigned to it, not person by person.
5. Move a design into the workspace 🔗 Assign one of your designs to the new workspace. You can assign only designs you own.
Assigning a design moves it. A design belongs to at most one workspace, so assigning it to the new workspace removes it from the workspace it was in before, such as My Workspace.
How the pieces fit together 🔗 Object What it controls What you did with it Organization Who is a member at all. Teams and workspaces belong to one organization. Invited a teammate into My Organization. Team A named group of organization members, each with a team role. Created a team and added your teammate. Workspace A set of shared resources, reached by the teams assigned to it. Created a workspace and assigned the team to it. Design A resource that lives in at most one workspace. Moved a design you own into the workspace. Roles determine what each person may do at each level, as the permission table above shows for the actions in this tutorial.
Check your result 🔗 Your organization is set up when all of the following are true:
Your teammate’s account appears in the organization. The new team lists your teammate. The new workspace lists the new team. The design you moved appears in the new workspace and no longer appears in its previous workspace. Go deeper 🔗 Organizations: organizations as the unit of tenancy. Teams: how teams group users. Workspaces: what a workspace holds and how it is shared. Organization management: editing your organization and managing invitations. Managing workspaces: editing, deleting, and organizing workspaces.
