The Kanvas Snapshot Helm plugin renders a Helm chart as a Kanvas design image from your terminal. Use it to see what a chart deploys before you install it, or to put a picture of a chart in a review, a ticket, or a README. It needs no repository, no cluster, and no Layer5 Cloud account.
You give the plugin the URL of a packaged chart. The plugin imports the chart as a design, starts a render, and then prints the image URL or emails you when the image is ready.
Before you start 🔗 Helm installed on your machine. A packaged chart (.tgz) at a URL that the snapshot service can download without credentials. The plugin submits the value of -f as a URL, so a local file path is not a supported input. For email delivery, an address in lowercase. Install the plugin 🔗 helm plugin install https://github.com/meshery/helm-kanvas-snapshot The install downloads a prebuilt binary for your platform. Confirm the install and update it later with:
helm plugin list helm plugin update helm-kanvas-snapshot The list shows the plugin as helm-kanvas-snapshot. Helm runs a plugin by its name, so the command is helm helm-kanvas-snapshot.
Generate a snapshot 🔗 helm helm-kanvas-snapshot -f <chart-url> [--name <name>] [-e <email>] For example:
helm helm-kanvas-snapshot -f https://meshery.github.io/meshery.io/charts/meshery-v1.0.20.tgz --name meshery-chart Flag Required Behavior -f, --file Yes URL of the packaged chart. --name No Name of the design that the plugin creates. Without it, the plugin uses the file name without its extension and prints a warning that it did. -e, --email No Email address to notify when the snapshot is ready. The plugin rejects any address that contains uppercase letters or does not look like an address, and exits with an error. What happens 🔗 The plugin imports the chart as a saved design and prints Successfully created Meshery design. ID: <id>. The plugin starts the rendering workflow. The plugin prints the result and exits. Without --email, the plugin prints the snapshot URL. The image takes three to five minutes to appear at that URL, so an immediate request can return nothing. With --email, the plugin prints a confirmation and the service emails you when the snapshot is ready.
Privacy and ownership 🔗 The plugin ships with Layer5’s service credentials, so it works without signing in. That has three consequences:
The service downloads your chart from the URL you give. Use only a chart that you are willing to expose to that service. The image sits at a public URL named after the design id. Anyone who has the URL can open it. The plugin saves the design with the service’s credentials, not under a Layer5 Cloud account of yours. To work on a chart as your own design, import it into Kanvas instead. See Import and Merge Designs. Errors 🔗 The plugin exits with status 1 and prints an error code.
Code Meaning kanvas-snapshot-900 The chart URI is invalid. kanvas-snapshot-901 The plugin could not create the design. kanvas-snapshot-902 The plugin could not start the render. kanvas-snapshot-903 An HTTP request failed. kanvas-snapshot-905 A response could not be decoded. kanvas-snapshot-906 A request returned an unexpected status. The message carries the status and the response body. kanvas-snapshot-907 A required field is missing. kanvas-snapshot-908 The email address is not valid. kanvas-snapshot-909 GitHub rejected the request to start the render with a 401 or 403 status. If the image never appears, check that the chart URL opens in a browser without signing in, then run the command again. For pull request snapshots, see Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot.
description: Generate a rendered image of a Helm chart from the command line with the Kanvas Snapshot Helm plugin, and receive it by URL or email.

Log streaming live-tails the output of a pod’s containers inside the Operator canvas. Each stream starts with the most recent lines and then follows new output as it is written, so you can watch a rollout, a crash loop, or a request path next to the topology that produced it.
Before you start 🔗 Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. A connected cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. MeshSync reads the logs and Meshery Server relays them through the broker, the same path the terminal uses. See Operator. Containers that exist. Logs come from the Kubernetes log API, so a container that has not started has nothing to stream. Start a stream 🔗 The action is named Initiate Log Session and is offered on Pod and Container resources only. Right-click the resource, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel. The stream opens in the same bottom-left panel as terminal sessions, as a tab.
You select Tabs opened A pod One tab for the pod that combines every container in its containers list. Each line is prefixed with [<pod>:<container>] in a per-container color. A container One tab for that container. Several pods, one after another One tab per pod. Kanvas does not merge different pods into one tab. Starting a stream for a pod that already has a tab does nothing. To stream only some of a pod’s containers, use the container selector in the panel header. Choosing different containers restarts that tab’s stream.
Read and control the stream 🔗 Backlog. Each container starts with its last 1,000 lines. Kanvas requests timestamps, so every line begins with an RFC 3339 time. Standard output and standard error arrive combined. Scrollback. The browser keeps the last 10,000 lines per tab. Search. The search icon in the panel header opens a search field with next and previous controls. It highlights and jumps between matches. It does not hide non-matching lines. Copy. Select text in the stream to copy it. There is no Clear, Copy-all, or Download control. Stop. The trash icon on a tab stops the stream and removes the tab. Closing the panel with its close button only hides it; streams keep running. Empty lines are dropped. Very long lines can be split across messages and display broken.
Limits and scope 🔗 Item Behavior Initial backlog 1,000 lines per container, fixed. Previous container logs Not available. Streams read the current container only. Follow Always on. Reconnect None. If the connection drops, the tab stops updating with no message. Close it and start a new stream. Container exits or pod is deleted The stream ends with no message. Resource names Pod, namespace, and container names must be valid Kubernetes DNS labels. Other names are rejected by the server. Changing the container selection Requests the 1,000-line backlog again, so lines can repeat in the tab. Who can use it 🔗 Kanvas does not hide or disable the action by role or plan. The permission model lists Stream container logs as an Operator capability for the Team Operator plan and above, granted to workspace administrators, organization administrators, and provider administrators. See Permissions by Role and Feature Availability.
Failure modes 🔗 Symptom Cause and fix Panel shows Failed to create terminal session with a reason The Kanvas extension could not be loaded by Meshery, for example because it was built for a different Meshery version. Install matching versions. Toast No container found to create log session The selected component lists no containers. Empty tab, no lines The pod has produced no output, or Meshery Server cannot reach MeshSync. Confirm the cluster shows as connected and that the broker is connected. Kanvas does not display the server’s error text for log streams. For cluster connection problems, see Troubleshoot Kanvas.
Related 🔗 Run a Performance Test to see how a service holds up under load while the stream is open. Operator explains the data path from the cluster to the canvas.

body:
A Kanvas tutorial is a guided path to a realistic outcome. You build something real, such as a shared design, a cloud architecture, or a running application, and you learn how Kanvas works by doing it. Each tutorial explains what Kanvas does at every step, so you finish with both the result and the mental model behind it.
Tutorials are for learning. When you already know what you want to do, other parts of the Kanvas docs serve you better:
New to Kanvas? Start with Getting Started to reach your first design quickly. How-to guides accomplish one specific task for a reader who knows the basics. Concepts explain how Kanvas works and why it behaves the way it does. Reference lists exact options, limits, permissions, and shortcuts. The scenario 🔗 The collaboration and GCP tutorials follow two fictional organizations: Orbital Labs, a cloud-native startup on the Team plan, and Stellar Dynamics, their enterprise client on the Enterprise plan. Both organizations are managed under the Constellation Cloud provider. A cast of named characters builds, shares, and reviews designs, so you see how permissions, workspaces, and cross-organization access work together in practice. The cloud deployment and Kubernetes tutorials do not use this scenario.
Collaborate on a design 🔗 These tutorials teach how people work together on one design. Neither deploys anything, so they run anywhere Kanvas runs.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Collaborative Editing A design that you and a teammate edit at the same time, ending with a review resolved in a comment thread. You learn the four mechanisms behind collaboration: the live session, access, comments, and saving. A Kanvas account and a teammate with their own account. Share a Design Across Organizations A private design that a reviewer in another organization can open, a review held in comments, and the removal of that access when the review ends. You learn what a grant gives someone and where Kanvas checks permissions. A Kanvas account in your organization and a reviewer with an account in a different organization. Model a cloud architecture without deploying 🔗 This tutorial teaches design as documentation. You model an architecture in Designer and share it, without connecting a cluster or a cloud account.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Build a GCP Data Pipeline Design A design of a GCP data pipeline: Pub/Sub ingests events, Dataflow processes them, BigQuery stores results, and Cloud Storage archives raw payloads, all on GKE. You place components, connect them with relationships or annotation lines, group them into sections, add labels, check the design with Validate, and share it. A Kanvas account and a workspace. No cluster and no GCP account. Deploy cloud resources from Kubernetes 🔗 These tutorials provision real cloud resources by deploying a cloud provider’s Kubernetes operator to your cluster and then deploying resource definitions that the operator turns into cloud infrastructure.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Deploy AWS EC2 Instances EC2 instances managed from Kubernetes through AWS Controllers for Kubernetes. A self-hosted Meshery with your own connected Kubernetes cluster, AWS credentials, and awareness of the cost of the instances you create. Deploy Azure Resources Azure resources managed from Kubernetes through Azure Service Operator. A self-hosted Meshery with your own connected Kubernetes cluster, Azure credentials, and awareness of the cost of the resources you create. Warning Never run the AWS or Azure tutorials on Meshery Playground. Both tutorials store real cloud credentials in a Kubernetes Secret, and Playground is a cluster shared with other users. Use your own cluster, and delete the cloud resources when you finish so they stop accruing charges. Run Kubernetes workloads 🔗 These tutorials teach core Kubernetes objects by building them in Kanvas, deploying them to a live cluster, and inspecting the result in Operator.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Kubernetes tutorials A learning path from a single Pod through Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps and Secrets, and CronJobs to complete multi-tier applications. Meshery Playground, or a self-hosted Meshery with at least one connected Kubernetes cluster. The Kubernetes request flow explanation describes what happens inside the cluster when those objects receive traffic. Read it before the Services tutorial.
Choose where to run 🔗 Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, Undeploy, and Operator prompt you to use Meshery Playground or self-host Meshery instead. Only the design-only tutorials run there in full. Meshery Playground is a shared live cluster for the Kubernetes tutorials. The AWS and Azure tutorials need your own cluster.
Tutorial group Hosted kanvas.new (designing only) Meshery Playground Self-hosted Meshery with your own cluster Needs cloud credentials Deploys to a cluster Collaborate on a design Yes Yes Yes No No Model a cloud architecture (GCP) Yes Yes Yes No No Deploy cloud resources (AWS, Azure) No No, never Yes Yes Yes Run Kubernetes workloads Drawing only, no deploy Yes Yes No Yes What every tutorial assumes 🔗 You can sign in to Kanvas. You have a workspace. Every design belongs to one workspace, the one selected in your current organization. Kanvas saves designs automatically. A design saves after a 3 second pause in editing, and a new design saves once it has a name or a component. Your plan limits the number of components in a design. Kanvas enforces the limit when it saves the design, and it cannot save a design that exceeds the limit.

GitHub Actions is how Layer5 Cloud meets your pull-request workflow. The Kanvas Snapshot action renders the infrastructure file in a pull request as a Kanvas design and posts the picture as a comment, so reviewers see the resources and their connections before they read the YAML. It runs on GitHub-hosted runners and never touches your cluster.
Choose how to install it 🔗 Path Use it when Where it is documented Layer5 GitHub App wizard You want Layer5 Cloud to commit the workflow and show you the API token to store as a secret. Connect GitHub and the snapshot guide. Your own workflow You want to pick the triggers, run snapshots from a workflow you already maintain, or authenticate with a personal access token. Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot Both paths produce the same pull request comment. The snapshot guide documents every action input, the workflow the wizard installs, token handling, and troubleshooting. It is the single reference for the action, so this page does not repeat it.
Decide when snapshots run 🔗 The workflow the wizard installs runs when a pull request is opened, synchronized, or reopened. In a workflow you own, you can use any GitHub event, such as push, schedule, or workflow_dispatch. Only pull request runs post a comment, because the comment needs a pull request number. Other runs still render the snapshot and expose its image URL as an output. See Choose other triggers.
What Layer5 Cloud provides 🔗 An API token that authenticates the action to Layer5 Cloud. You generate and revoke tokens in Layer5 Cloud. See Tokens. A GitHub App that installs the workflow file in the repositories you choose, through the Connect GitHub wizard. A generated design. Each comment links to the design the action produced and to an editable copy in the Playground. Availability depends on your plan. See Feature Availability by Plan.
Related automation 🔗 Performance testing from a workflow is a Meshery capability, not a Layer5 Cloud one. See GitOps with Meshery in the Meshery documentation.
The action is also available on the GitHub Marketplace.

This page states how keys, keychains, tokens, and sessions behave, exactly, as of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280. For the model, read the Keys, Keychains, Sessions, and Tokens concepts. For tasks, use the security guides. For base URL, authentication, and the organization header, see the Cloud API. All paths below sit under /api unless noted.
Permission keys 🔗 Provider Admin holds every key. The table lists the default holders of the other roles. “Interface” means the control or tab is disabled or replaced by a permission error screen. “Server” means the Layer5 Cloud server refuses the request with HTTP 403.
Key Governs Default holders besides Provider Admin Enforced by View Tokens The Tokens tab User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Interface Create Token Creating an API token Organization Admin Interface only Download Token Downloading a token file User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Interface; the server returns only your own tokens Delete Token Revoking a token, and the Logout control on the Sessions tab Organization Admin Interface only; the server deletes only your own tokens View Sessions The Sessions tab User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Interface Logout from a Session Seeded for ending a session User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Not checked. The interface uses Delete Token for Logout. View Keys Seeded for the Keys tab User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Not checked. Every signed-in user sees the Keys tab. Edit Key Creating and changing a key None Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. Delete Key Deleting a key None Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. View Keychains The Keychains tab User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Interface Create Keychain Creating a keychain None Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. Edit Keychain Renaming a keychain, adding or removing its keys None Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. Delete Keychain Deleting a keychain None Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. Assign Keychains to Roles Adding or removing a keychain on a role None Server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. Roles that hold the keys come from the default keychains: View keys sit in User View, Create Token and Delete Token in Security Management, Download Token in Security Management and User Edit, and the key and keychain management keys, including Assign Keychains to Roles, in Provider Management. Where the server requires the Provider Admin role, it checks the role across the whole deployment, not the role held in one organization. See Roles and Permissions for the full role-by-keychain mapping.
Visibility rules 🔗 Resource Who sees it Scope Keys System-owned default keys, plus keys you created Deployment-wide; not per organization Keychains System-owned default keychains, plus keychains you own Deployment-wide; not per organization API tokens Your own, never the token value in the list User account Sessions Your own User account Default keys and keychains are owned by the system. Deleting a key or keychain is a soft delete, and a deleted key or keychain stops granting access immediately.
Session and token lifetimes 🔗 The values are the defaults of the Layer5 Cloud deployment configuration. Operators of self-hosted deployments can change them.
Credential Lifetime Notes Browser session (access token) 24 hours Not extended by activity. The user signs in again after it lapses. Refresh token 1000 hours Single-use. Each refresh issues a new refresh token. Meshery Server uses it to renew without a new sign-in. API token No expiry Ends only when deleted. Sign-in flow 12 hours Time allowed to complete a sign-in. Privileged-action window 15 minutes in the packaged default After the window, sensitive account changes ask the user to sign in again. A deployment can set a different value. Anonymous Kanvas session 24 hours For use without signing in. It does not appear in the Sessions list. Cookies 🔗 Cookie Purpose Attributes provider_token The browser session credential HttpOnly, Secure over HTTPS, SameSite Lax has_session Tells the interface a session exists. Carries no secret and cannot authenticate a request. Readable by page scripts, SameSite Lax, expires with the session The cookie domain is shared across the platform’s hosts for organizations that use the platform sign-in provider. It is host-only for organizations that bring their own identity provider, and for custom domains outside the platform’s domain.
Endpoints 🔗 Success responses are JSON unless stated. Errors from the handlers below return a plain-text message. Refusals from the authorization layer return JSON. A missing or revoked credential returns 401 with {"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"}.
Keys 🔗 Method and path Who may call Behavior GET /auth/keys Signed-in user Lists keys you can see. Parameters: page, pageSize, order, search (matches the key name). Default order: most recently updated first. GET /auth/keys/{keyId} Signed-in user Returns one key. A malformed id returns 400. POST /auth/keys Provider Admin holding Edit Key Creates or updates a key. DELETE /auth/keys/{keyId} Provider Admin holding Delete Key Soft-deletes the key. Returns 204. GET /identity/orgs/{orgId}/users/keys Signed-in user Returns your effective keys in the organization. The interface uses it to enable controls. Keychains 🔗 Method and path Who may call Behavior GET /auth/keychains Signed-in user Lists keychains you can see. Parameters: page, pageSize, order, search (matches the keychain name). GET /auth/keychains/{keychainId} Signed-in user Returns one keychain. GET /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/keys Signed-in user Lists the keys in a keychain. search matches the key description. POST /auth/keychains Provider Admin holding Create Keychain Creates a keychain owned by the caller. Only the name in the body is used. PUT /auth/keychains/{keychainId} Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain Updates the keychain name. POST /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/{keyId} Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain Adds a key. DELETE /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/{keyId} Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain Removes a key. DELETE /auth/keychains/{keychainId} Provider Admin holding Delete Keychain Soft-deletes the keychain and its key mappings. POST and DELETE /identity/orgs/{orgId}/roles/{roleId}/keychains/{keychainId} Provider Admin holding Assign Keychains to Roles Adds or removes a keychain on a role. Roles are global, so the change applies in every organization. These key, keychain, and role writes refuse with 403 and a JSON error. A caller who lacks the route’s key receives code meshery_cloud-1108. A caller who holds the key but is not a Provider Admin for the whole deployment receives code meshery_cloud-3336, “Only a Provider Admin can change roles, keychains or permission keys”. Owning a keychain does not authorize a change to it. For a Provider Admin, a malformed keychain id on these routes returns 400 with a plain-text message.
Tokens and sessions 🔗 Tokens and sessions share one store. isOauth=false selects API tokens and isOauth=true selects sessions.
Method and path Who may call Behavior POST /identity/tokens?name=&purpose= Signed-in user Creates a token for the caller. name is required: an empty name returns 400 with Token name missing. purpose is optional. Writes a create event. GET /identity/tokens?isOauth= Signed-in user Lists your tokens or sessions. Default order: newest first. search matches name and purpose. The response never contains token values. GET /identity/tokens/{id} Token owner Returns the token for download. Returns 404 for an unknown or revoked token and 400 for a malformed id. Writes a download event. DELETE /identity/tokens?tokenId= Token owner Revokes the token or session. A malformed id returns 400 with invalid token id. An unknown or already-deleted id returns 400 with tokens does not exist. Writes a delete event. GET /identity/tokens/infinite?userId=&provider= Provider Admin Issues a non-expiring token for another account. The token is listed under that account. Others receive 403. POST /refresh (outside /api) Holder of a refresh token Exchanges a refresh token for a new session credential. Returns 400 with a JSON error if the token is missing, malformed, or already used. GET /logout (outside /api) Signed-in browser Ends the browser’s identity session. When Layer5 Cloud cannot read the revocation record, it refuses the request rather than accept a token it cannot check.
Audit events 🔗 Action Event Create a token <email> generated token <name> (category token, action create) Download a token Token <name> downloaded (category token, action download). A failed download is also recorded, with an error severity. Delete a token or log out a session <email> revoked token <name> (category token, action delete) Key and keychain changes do not write audit events.

body:
In Layer5 Academy, a Certification is a formal assessment designed to validate a learner’s professional skills in a specific domain. Unlike a Learning Path, which guides a user through a curriculum, a Certification’s primary goal is evaluation.
The successful completion of a Certification results in an official, shareable Certificate of Completion and a valuable badge, signifying a verified level of proficiency.
When to use a certification 🔗 Choose a certification when the goal is to test, not teach. It assumes prior knowledge. Compare the content types in Create Academy Content.
Certification: Focus on Assessment, Not Instruction A Certification is ideal when the main objective is to test, not teach. It assumes learners have prior knowledge and are ready to prove their expertise. If the objective is instead for the learner to solve a concrete, hands-on problem, build a Challenge rather than a Certification. How to Create Your Certification 🔗 Building a new certification involves setting up the correct directory structure and defining its properties through Markdown frontmatter.
Get your identifiers 🔗 Register the certification in the Instructor Console and choose Certification as the content type. The console generates the certification id and a ready-to-paste front matter block. Use your organization’s ID in the directory path. See Create Academy Content.
1. Set Up the Directory Structure 🔗 All content for a new certification must reside within the content/certifications/<your-organization-uuid> directory. To keep content organized, each certification has its own folder named with a descriptive, URL-friendly slug.
The final URL will follow this pattern: https://cloud.layer5.io/academy/content/certifications/<your-organization-uuid>/<certification-folder-name>/
Below is the standard file structure:
content/certifications/<your-organization-uuid> └── layer5-certification-exam/ <-- The <certification-name> directory ├── _index.md <-- Defines the certification's metadata ├── exam-1.md <-- (Optional) A standard content page for introduction ├── optional-exam-2.md <-- An optional supplementary exam └── exam-3.md <-- A mandatory exam, accessible after completing all previous required units. Key Files:
_index.md: The entry point for your certification containing all metadata (title, description, banner, etc.) Exam Files (*.md): Individual Markdown files containing the exams. Order and optional status are controlled by frontmatter, not filename. 2. Define the Certification with Frontmatter 🔗 The _index.md file’s frontmatter controls how the certification is presented to users..
Here’s a complete example of the YAML frontmatter for a certification’s _index.md file:
--- type: "certification" id: "<your-certification-uuid>" title: "Layer5 Network Certification" description: "Validate your expertise in Layer5 networking technologies through comprehensive assessment" banner: "images/layer5-icon.svg" weight: 1 tags: [layer5, cloud, infrastructure] level: "beginner" categories: [platform] badge: png: "https://images.credly.com/images/f28f1d88-428a-47f6-95b5-7da1dd6c1000/twitter_thumb_201604_KCNA_badge.png" svg: "https://images.credly.com/images/f28f1d88-428a-47f6-95b5-7da1dd6c1000/twitter_thumb_201604_KCNA_badge.png" title: "Layer5 Certified" description: "Earn the Certification badge to showcase your expertise in Layer5 cloud services." --- Frontmatter Fields Reference 🔗 In this table, fields marked with ✅ are required, while those marked with a hyphen are optional.
Field Required Description type ✅ Must be set to "certification" to identify this content correctly. id ✅ Crucial. A stable ID used to track learner progress. Do not change. title ✅ The human-readable title that will be displayed to users. description ✅ A comprehensive summary of the certification’s scope and objectives. weight - Controls the display order (lower numbers appear first). Items are sorted alphabetically by title if not specified. banner - Path to a banner image located in the same folder (Page Bundle). tags - Keywords for content discovery. Multiple tags can be selected. level - A string for the intended difficulty (beginner, intermediate, advanced). Default: beginner. categories - A string that assigns the certification to a specific category. badge - Defines the awarded digital badge. The png and svg fields accept either a full remote URL or a local file path for an image in the same folder (e.g., layer5-badge.svg). 3. Add Content and Exams 🔗 A certification is primarily composed of exams. However, you can also include standard content pages to provide context.
Exams: The core assessable components. A certification can contain one or multiple exams. Informational Pages: Standard Markdown pages that can serve as an introduction, a study guide, or a list of helpful resources. How to Create and Configure Exams Every “Exam” file within a certification follows the unified Academy assessment standard.
For detailed instructions on how to write an exam file, define various question types, set scoring and passing percentages, and use advanced options, please refer to our comprehensive Integrating Assessments in the Academy guide.
4. Manage question pools and test attempts 🔗 A test can include more questions than those presented to users in a single attempt, effectively turning it into a test bank, the collection of all possible questions available for that test. When users retry the test, a new set of questions is drawn from the test bank for each attempt.
This behavior is controlled by the numberOfQuestions property in the front matter.
If numberOfQuestions is not defined, all questions in the test are used in every attempt. If it is defined, the test is automatically divided into multiple sets, each containing the specified number of questions. To ensure even division, the total number of questions must be a multiple of numberOfQuestions.
By default, the number of retries is set to the number of generated sets. However, you can increase it, in which case the question sets will cycle through repeatedly across attempts.
Multi-Exam Certification Settings For certifications containing multiple exams, each exam may have its own test bank, question count, and retry settings.
These configurations are defined per test and may differ across exams within the same certification. Learner outcomes 🔗 Outcome When it is awarded Details Badge The learner passes the certification’s final test. Named by the content’s badge setting. A badge setting that points at a badge that no longer exists awards nothing, and the failure is logged. Certificate of Completion The same moment, when the certification defines a certificate. Free learning and exams; certificate issuance is an optional paid feature. Each certificate gets its own ID, the recipient’s name, the organization, and the issue date. It is served at a public certificate page, and the learner receives an email. A failed email does not undo the certificate. Registration status Becomes Completed. Visible to instructors in the console. Certificates do not carry an expiry date. Attempt limits and time limits come from each exam’s settings, covered in Add Assessments. You do not handle certificate payment; the platform does.
Academy Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Academy Theoretical Learning A comprehensive learning management system for creators and instructors on how to build, manage, and extend educational content like learning paths, challenges, and certifications. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Academy Practical Learning An inclusive, collaborative, hands-on learning environment for students. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Frequently Asked Questions 🔗 Can my certification have only one exam? Yes, it can. The simplest form of a certification consists of a single final exam. You can also include multiple independent exams if you wish to assess different skills.
When should I choose to create a "Certification" instead of a "Learning Path"? You should choose a Certification when your primary goal is to test and assess a learner’s existing knowledge, rather than teaching them from scratch. A Learning Path focuses on instruction, while a Certification focuses on assessment.
What does an "Optional" exam mean, and how does it affect a learner's progress? An optional exam is supplementary material. Learners can take it, but they do not have to pass it to earn the final certificate. Its score does not count towards the certification’s passing requirements. This is typically used for extra practice or to test non-core knowledge.
How do I set an exam as "Optional"? You need to add a specific field, isOptional: true, to the front matter of the exam’s .md file. This field tells the system that the exam is not a mandatory requirement to pass the certification.
Can I control the order of multiple exams within a certification? Yes, you can. Each exam file’s front matter has a weight field. Lower numbers result in an earlier display order. If you don’t set a weight, the exams will be sorted alphabetically by file title by default.

In this tutorial you follow Zara Osei, Team Admin of the Orbital Labs Infrastructure Team, as she models the team’s Google Cloud data pipeline in Kanvas. The pipeline ingests events through Pub/Sub, processes them with Dataflow, writes analytical results to BigQuery, archives raw payloads to Cloud Storage, and runs alongside a GKE cluster. The result is a design named data-pipeline-gcp: a reviewable, shareable model of the architecture that lives in the team’s workspace instead of in a slide deck.
This is a design-only tutorial. It ends with a validated design shared with a teammate, and it deploys nothing. Deploying Google Cloud resources from a design needs a controller running in the target cluster that reconciles those resources against Google Cloud, the same pattern the AWS and Azure tutorials walk through. Without that controller, a deploy creates objects that nothing acts on.
What you will learn 🔗 A Kanvas component is a resource definition from the Meshery registry, and its configuration form is generated from that definition’s schema. Relationships between components come from the registry. Where the registry defines none, an annotation line documents the flow without changing any configuration. Labels carry metadata on a component, while sections group components visually. Neither changes how the components are configured. Validate checks each component against its schema and reports problems as warnings that never block you. Sharing grants a named person full editing access, and collaborators see each other’s changes live. Before you begin 🔗 A Kanvas environment that supports Validate. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io) or a self-hosted Meshery. Validate runs entirely in your browser and needs no cluster, but hosted kanvas.new offers no cluster actions: its Validate opens a prompt to use Meshery Playground or self-host instead. Playground is shared with other users, so never enter real cloud credentials there. This tutorial needs none. A workspace. Kanvas creates a new design in your currently selected workspace in the current organization. Zara uses orbital-production. Select yours before you start. Permission to share designs. Sharing requires the Share Design permission in the organization that owns the workspace. The Organization Admin role carries it by default. See Permissions. A teammate with an account. You share with a named user. Zara shares with Five. Your plan’s component limit. Each plan limits the number of components in one design, and Kanvas enforces the limit when it saves the design. This design holds well under a dozen components, plus a few annotation objects. See Feature availability. You need a working knowledge of the Google Cloud services involved. You do not need a Google Cloud project or credentials.
The scenario 🔗 At the end, the design contains five Google Cloud components, grouped into four sections by layer, with the data flow drawn between them:
[ Ingestion ] [ Processing ] [ Storage ] Pub/Sub topic ---> Dataflow job ---> BigQuery dataset events-ingest stream-processor analytics-store | +-------------> Cloud Storage bucket raw-archive [ Compute ] GKE cluster pipeline-cluster Each component also carries a layer label (ingestion, processing, storage, or compute). The design is validated and shared with Five, who leaves a review comment.
A note on environments 🔗 The design does not name a cluster or an environment, and it does not need to. Kanvas stores no environment on a design. You choose environments when you deploy: the Deploy stepper asks which environments to target, and deploys to the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. That separation lets one design go to staging and production unchanged. See Environments.
Phase 1: Create the design 🔗 Create a new design and name it data-pipeline-gcp.
Kanvas saves the design automatically: a new design is saved once it has a name or a component, and every later change is saved after a short pause in editing. There is no Save button. The design lands in your selected workspace, orbital-production in Zara’s case.
What just happened. A design is a single document that holds every component, relationship, and annotation you add. Autosave writes that document after each pause, and the save is where your plan’s component limit is checked: a design over the limit cannot be saved. Placing the design in a workspace organizes it; it does not give the workspace’s teams access to it. Access comes from sharing, which you do in Phase 6.
Phase 2: Add the Google Cloud components 🔗 Add one component for each service in the pipeline:
Name Service Role in the pipeline events-ingest Pub/Sub topic Entry point for incoming event streams stream-processor Dataflow job Reads events and writes them downstream analytics-store BigQuery dataset Long-term store for processed records raw-archive Cloud Storage bucket Raw payloads kept for replay and compliance pipeline-cluster GKE cluster The team’s Kubernetes cluster for the pipeline’s supporting services Find each one by typing the service name into the component palette search. The search runs against the Meshery registry after you pause typing for about a second, and returns matching models and components. Pick the Google Cloud component for each service, not a similarly named component from another model. If a model offers several versions, the palette lists the newest first.
Give each component the name from the table, and arrange the components left to right in the direction data flows.
What just happened. Every component in the palette comes from a model registered in the Meshery registry. The component’s name, its available versions, and every field in its configuration form come from that model, so they can differ between registry versions and between Meshery deployments. That is why this tutorial names services rather than exact component kinds or fields: match what your registry shows. When a component lands on the canvas, its configurator opens with a form generated from the component’s schema.
Phase 3: Fill in required configuration 🔗 Open each component’s configurator (double-click the component) and fill in the fields its schema marks as required. Required fields carry a red asterisk. Set the values your team actually uses, such as the project, region, or resource name the form asks for.
You do not have to complete every field now. Phase 5 lists anything required that is still missing.
What just happened. Each edit is written to the design after a short pause. Kanvas checks the edited component against its schema and marks problems beside the field. Those marks are warnings: Kanvas never stops you from saving an incomplete component, because a design is often a work in progress.
Phase 4: Draw the data flow 🔗 Draw three connections: events-ingest to stream-processor, stream-processor to analytics-store, and stream-processor to raw-archive. How you draw them depends on what the registry defines for each pair.
Try a relationship first. Hover over the source component to reveal its edge handles, and open the handle menu. The menu lists only the edge relationships the registry defines that can start from that component. If one fits, pick it and drag to the target. Compatible targets in view get a green outline. Releasing on a compatible target creates the relationship; releasing anywhere else creates nothing.
Fall back to an annotation line. If the menu offers nothing that connects the two services, document the flow with the Pen tool (Ctrl/Cmd+E toggles it, Escape exits). Pen places points where you click and draws an annotation line between each consecutive pair, so you can trace the path from one component to the next.
Whichever kind you draw, select the line and use Rename in the edge toolbar to label it. Zara labels the first connection subscription-pull so reviewers see the consumption pattern at a glance, and the others processed-records and raw-payloads. The same toolbar sets line color, line style, and an animated marching-ants effect, which suits a data flow.
What just happened. The two kinds of line look alike but behave differently. A registry relationship is part of the model: Kanvas evaluates it after each change and can write values from one component’s configuration into the other’s. An annotation line is a drawing. It is saved with the design and seen by collaborators, but it changes no configuration and is never deployed. Whether the registry offers a relationship between two Google Cloud services depends on the models your registry holds, so check the handle menu rather than assuming either way. See Relationships.
Phase 5: Organize by architectural layer 🔗 Give the design two kinds of structure: metadata on each component and a visual grouping on the canvas.
Labels for metadata. In each component’s configurator, open the Labels tab and add the key layer with the value for that component: ingestion for events-ingest, processing for stream-processor, storage for analytics-store and raw-archive, and compute for pipeline-cluster. Labels are free-form key-value pairs, so add others your team relies on, such as an owner or cost center.
Sections for visual grouping. Press S to add a section, size it around a group of components, and name it for its layer. Create four: Ingestion, Processing, Storage, and Compute.
What just happened. Labels and sections answer different questions. A label is data on the component, carried in its configuration. A section is an annotation object on the canvas that groups components for the reader’s eye; like every annotation, it is saved with the design and never deployed. Kanvas does not filter the design canvas by label.
You may also see a translucent shaded region appear around components that share labels. That region is a TagSet, and Kanvas draws it automatically only when a registry relationship defines a label match for those components. You cannot draw a TagSet yourself, and many models define none.
Phase 6: Validate the design 🔗 Run Validate from the Actions menu. Kanvas opens a validation report for data-pipeline-gcp.
The report states how many components and annotations it found and how many errors. With no errors, it reads “No validation errors.” Otherwise it lists each component that has errors, with a count, and each error names the field path and the problem, for example a required property that is missing.
Resolve each required field the report lists by opening that component’s configurator and filling in the value, then run Validate again. Components with errors also show a warning badge on the canvas in Full render mode; selecting the badge opens the configurator at the offending field.
What just happened. Validate runs in your browser against each component’s schema from the registry. It checks configuration only: it skips annotation objects such as sections and Pen lines, and it does not check relationships, namespaces, cross-references, or any cluster. Its findings are warnings and never block saving or sharing. A clean report means every component’s configuration matches its schema. It does not mean the pipeline would deploy successfully; a Dry Run against a cluster tests that.
Phase 7: Share the design for review 🔗 Open Share and add Five by searching for his name or email. Share is not available until the design has content, so it appears once you have added components.
Five now has the same access to the design as any editor: he can open, edit, comment on, and clone it, and he can share it with others. Kanvas has no read-only or comment-only share level. When you and Five have the design open at the same time, each of you appears as an avatar in the toolbar, and you see each other’s cursors and changes live.
Five reviews the topology and presses M to place a comment next to stream-processor: “Do we need a dead-letter topic for events Dataflow cannot parse?” Zara replies in the same thread.
What just happened. A share is a grant to one named user, not to a team or a workspace, and it carries no permission level. Share only with people you trust to edit. Comments are Comment components stored in the design itself, so the review conversation is saved with the design, syncs live, and travels with it when someone clones or exports it. See Collaboration.
Verify 🔗 Open data-pipeline-gcp and confirm:
Components. Five Google Cloud components, named events-ingest, stream-processor, analytics-store, raw-archive, and pipeline-cluster. Data flow. Three connections from Pub/Sub to Dataflow and from Dataflow to BigQuery and Cloud Storage, each either a registry relationship or a Pen annotation line, labeled subscription-pull, processed-records, and raw-payloads. Sections. Four sections, Ingestion, Processing, Storage, and Compute, each enclosing its components. Labels. Each component’s Labels tab shows the layer key with the correct value. Validation. Validate reports “No validation errors.”, or lists only fields you have deliberately left for later. Sharing. The Share dialog lists Five among the people with access, and his comment thread appears beside stream-processor. Workspace. The design appears in orbital-production. Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix Palette search for a Google Cloud service returns “Sorry, no matching records found”. The registry in your Meshery deployment does not hold that model, or the search term does not match its name. Try another form of the service name. If nothing matches, the model is not registered in this deployment; ask your Meshery administrator to import it. The edge handle menu offers nothing that connects two components. The registry defines no edge relationship between that pair. Draw an annotation line with the Pen tool and label it. Releasing a drag on the target creates no edge. The target is not compatible with the relationship you picked. Release only on a component with a green outline, or use the Pen tool. Validate lists missing required properties. Required fields in a component’s schema are empty. Open the component’s configurator, fill in each listed field, and validate again. Validate opens a prompt instead of a report. You are on hosted kanvas.new, which has no cluster actions. Open the design in Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery. The Actions menu is disabled. The design is empty. Add at least one component. Share does not appear. The design is empty, or it is published to the catalog. Add components first. A published design is not shared from this dialog. Five cannot open the design. He was not granted access, or the grant failed. Workspace membership alone does not grant access. Share the design with Five by name and confirm he appears in the access list. Changes stop saving and Kanvas reports an error. The design exceeds your plan’s components-per-design limit. Annotation objects such as sections and comments are components in the design too. Remove components or annotations you do not need, or move to a plan with a higher limit. A shaded TagSet region appears or disappears as you edit labels. A registry relationship matches those labels, and evaluation redraws the group after each change. This is expected. Change the labels if you do not want the grouping, or hide TagSets in the Layers panel. Where to go next 🔗 Deploy AWS EC2 instances and Deploy Azure resources show the controller pattern you need before a cloud design like this one can be deployed. Configuring components covers the configurator, its tabs, and the Labels tab in depth. Whiteboarding covers the Pen tool, sections, text boxes, and other annotation objects. Relationships explains how the registry defines relationships and how Kanvas evaluates them. Designs explains how designs, workspaces, and autosave fit together.
description: Model a Google Cloud data pipeline as a Kanvas design, organize it by architectural layer, validate it, and share it for review.

Everything on a Designer canvas is an object, and every object answers to the same small set of actions: add, select, copy, duplicate, lock, restyle, resize and delete. This page lists each object kind, each action, every style option and the limits that apply. Edges - the lines that connect objects - have their own section at the end.
Designer mode only. In Operator mode you cannot add, edit, duplicate, delete or rename objects, and live nodes discovered from a cluster are read-only in every mode. See Designer for how the two modes differ.
Object kinds 🔗 Object What it is Configurable Added from Component A piece of infrastructure under management, such as a Deployment, an S3 bucket or a Lambda function. Yes. It carries configuration and is part of what gets deployed. The Components and Kubernetes pickers in the dock, a file import, or a drop Shape A visual primitive: a circle, an arrow, a flowchart symbol or a cloud-provider glyph. No The Shapes picker in the dock Section A labeled frame that fences off a region. Objects dropped inside it become its children and move with it. No The Section tool in the dock, or S Textbox A resizable box whose content is text. No The Textbox tool in the dock, or T Image A picture embedded in the design. No I, the Image tool in the dock, or a file drop Comment A threaded note pinned to the canvas. See Reviewing Designs. No M or the Comment tool in the dock Pencil stroke and pen point Freehand drawings and the joints of drawn lines. See Tool Modes. No The Pencil and Pen tools Every object except a component is an annotation. Kanvas stores annotations in the design alongside components, but treats them differently:
Behavior Annotation Configurable component Layers panel toggle Annotations Configurable Components Kind name appended to the on-canvas label No Yes Has configuration to edit No Yes Counts toward the components-per-design limit of your plan when the design is saved Yes Yes The plan limit counts every entry in a design, drawn objects included, so a heavily annotated design can reach the limit sooner than its infrastructure alone suggests. See Feature Availability by Plan.
Adding objects 🔗 Method Result Drag from a dock picker onto the canvas The object lands where you release it. Click an icon in a picker The object lands at a random position near the center of the canvas. M, T, S Adds a comment, textbox or section near the center of the canvas. A textbox opens ready for typing. I Opens a file picker for an image. Drop or paste a file See the file rules below. Paste a copied selection Adds the copied objects and the relationships between them at the pointer. A newly added component opens its configurator beside the node. A textbox starts inline text editing on double-click. Shapes accept body text too, so double-click a shape to type in it.
Shapes 🔗 The Shapes picker lists the shape libraries registered in Meshery, with search across all of them. A default installation includes libraries for cloud providers (Amazon Web Services, Azure, Google Cloud Platform), developer icons, arrows, flowchart symbols, general-purpose shapes and line icons. The libraries come from the registry, so the list can differ between installations. Pin a library to the dock to keep it one action away - see Pinning a Model to the Dock.
The Shapes picker lists every shape library available to your design A shape library expanded Sections 🔗 A section draws its label along its top edge instead of through its middle, so the region it encloses stays readable. Drop other objects inside it and they move with the section. Deleting the section does not delete them.
Textboxes 🔗 A textbox carrying a caption Files dropped or pasted on the canvas 🔗 File Result Limit Any image type the browser recognizes An image object. The picture is embedded in the design as data, not linked. 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) Plain text (.txt) A textbox holding the file text. 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) YAML, JSON, TAR, GZ, TGZ, ZIP, RAR, 7Z An infrastructure-as-code import at the drop position. See Importing Designs. Import rules apply Any other type Ignored with no message - Files over the size limit are rejected with an error message. The limit is fixed and is the same on every plan. A file with no browser-reported type is classified by its extension.
Selecting objects 🔗 Gesture Effect Click Selects one object and shows its style toolbar. Ctrl/Cmd + click Adds or removes one object from the selection. Ctrl/Cmd + drag on empty canvas Draws a selection box. Box selection is off in Pan, Pen and Pencil modes. Ctrl/Cmd + A Selects every component on the canvas. Dragging selected objects moves them together. Locked objects do not move.
Actions on objects 🔗 Right-click an object, or press and hold on it, to open its menu. Each entry appears only when its condition holds.
Action Shortcut Appears when Behavior Copy Ctrl/Cmd + C Designer mode, object is not a group Menu: copies that one object. Keyboard: copies the whole selection and every relationship whose two ends are both selected. Duplicate Ctrl/Cmd + D Designer mode, not a group Adds a copy to the same design. Lock - Designer mode, not a group, not locked Fixes the object’s position. Unlock - The object is locked Releases the position. Delete Delete or Backspace Designer mode, not a group Removes the object. The keys delete the whole selection. Reset styles - The object supports style changes Restores the object’s default styling. Group - A multi-selection Turns the temporary selection group into a permanent group. Ungroup - A permanent group Dissolves the group. Move Out of Parent - Designer mode, the object sits inside a parent Takes the object out of its parent. The context menu open on a selected object Every change an action makes, restyling included, is a change to the shared design, so Ctrl/Cmd + Z reverses it. See Canvas Actions.
Copy and paste 🔗 Copy writes the object data to your system clipboard. Paste with Ctrl/Cmd + V into the same design, a different design or another browser tab running Kanvas.
Pasted objects land at the pointer when it is over the canvas, otherwise at the canvas center, and keep their relative layout. Every pasted object receives a new identifier. Styling travels with the copy. The browser must allow clipboard access. If it refuses, nothing happens and no message appears. Duplicate 🔗 Duplicate skips the clipboard. It places the copy 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down from the original, gives it a new identifier and copies the relationships between members of the duplicated set. Duplicating a section together with its children reproduces the whole arrangement. Names are unchanged.
Lock 🔗 A lock fixes position only. A locked object can still be selected, restyled, configured and deleted, but it cannot be dragged, directly or inside a selection. The lock is stored with the object, so it survives a reload and applies to collaborators. Locking a section does not lock the objects inside it.
Delete 🔗 Deleting an object also removes the relationships that touch it. Kanvas marks those relationships as deleted rather than discarding them, so the next policy evaluation can undo any configuration they had applied. Deleting a section leaves its children on the canvas. Deletion is immediate and has no confirmation, but it can be undone.
Style options 🔗 Selecting one object shows a style toolbar above it. The toolbar edits the selected object; it does not apply a change to a multi-selection. Each control appears only when the object’s definition declares that capability, so the controls you see vary by object. The toolbar appears only when the canvas is zoomed in past a detail threshold; zoomed out, the canvas shows a hint to zoom in.
Property Options Shape 24 outlines: ellipse, triangle, round-triangle, rectangle, round-rectangle, bottom-round-rectangle, cut-rectangle, barrel, rhomboid, diamond, round-diamond, pentagon, round-pentagon, hexagon, round-hexagon, concave-hexagon, heptagon, round-heptagon, octagon, round-octagon, star, tag, round-tag, vee. Changing the outline keeps the content. Fill 13 swatches including transparent, and an opacity slider from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1. Border Color from the same swatches, style (solid, dotted, dashed, double) and thickness from 0 to 25. Layer order Move To Front, Move Forward, Move Backward, Move To Back. Label The name drawn with the object. Link An external URL. A link adds an External Link badge, which opens the URL in a new tab. See Component Badges. Image A background image, set by URL or by upload, with a reset to the default. Animation None, blink, ripple, bounce or pulse. Text Color, weight (Regular, Medium, Semi Bold, Bold, Black), decoration (none, underline, line-through), horizontal alignment (left, center, right), vertical alignment (top, center, bottom) and size. Configure Opens the configurator. Components only. See Configuring Components. The default text style is gray, 12 pixels, regular weight and centered. Sections carry their label on the top edge rather than body text.
Restyling changes only how an object is drawn. It never changes a component’s configuration or what gets deployed.
Reset styles 🔗 Reset styles re-applies the styling recorded in the object’s definition and discards every change made in the style toolbar. It restores the definition, not an earlier state, so it is not an undo. Position, lock state, configuration and relationships are untouched.
Resizing 🔗 Select a single object and Kanvas draws eight handles around it, one at each corner and one at the midpoint of each side.
Drag a corner or side handle to resize. Hold Shift while dragging to keep the aspect ratio. Objects that contain other objects, such as a parent component or a section with children, show no handles. Resizing needs the object’s definition to declare the resize capability. The new size is saved with the design.
Edges 🔗 An edge is a line between two objects. Each edge is a relationship in the design, and relationships come in two kinds.
Edge kind What it represents Effect Semantic A relationship defined in the registry, such as a network connection or a volume mount. Kanvas updates the configuration of the components it joins as you draw it, and re-evaluates it as the design changes. See Relationships. Annotation A line you draw with the Pen tool to explain a flow or a dependency. Visual only. It is non-binding and configures nothing. Select an edge to open the edge toolbar.
Control Options Line Color The same 13 swatches as fills. The arrowhead takes the same color. Line Style Dotted, Solid, Dashed. Arrow/Curve Style A curve style and an arrowhead, listed below. Name A text label drawn on the edge. Edge Animation None, or marching ants: a dashed line that travels along the edge. Delete Removes the edge. Works on any edge. Curve styles 🔗 Curve style Shape Bezier A smooth curve. The default. Straight A direct line. Segments A line with two bends. Round segments Segments with rounded corners. Taxi Right-angle routing. Round taxi Right-angle routing with rounded corners. Haystack A short line that starts and ends inside the nodes. Unbundled bezier A curve with one adjustable control point. Multi unbundled bezier A curve with two control points. Straight triangle A straight line drawn with a triangular profile. Choosing a curve style applies its default geometry. Choosing Round taxi does not apply its default corner radius.
Arrowheads 🔗 Vee (the default), triangle, circle, square, diamond, triangle-cross, tee, triangle-tee, circle-triangle, triangle-backcurve and chevron. An arrowhead is drawn at the target end only.
Edge defaults 🔗 A new edge uses a dotted line, a vee arrowhead, a bezier curve, a width of 1.5 pixels and a light gray color. A selected edge draws at 4 pixels. Edges that carry TCP traffic draw as a solid gold line with a triangle-cross arrowhead.
Permissions 🔗 Kanvas gates canvas actions by mode and by object capability, not by role. The permission catalog in Layer5 Cloud lists a key for each shape, section, textbox and component-styling action (add, copy, clone, lock, delete, configure styles, reset styles and resize), and a Provider Admin can include them in keychains and roles. Kanvas does not check those keys on the canvas today, so withholding one does not hide a control.
The permissions Kanvas does enforce on the toolbar are Validate Design, Deploy Design, Undeploy Design and Share Design. See Permissions by Role.
Action Gate When the gate fails Add, duplicate, copy, paste, delete, lock Designer mode The control is not offered in Operator mode. Edit a live cluster node Never allowed Live nodes are read-only in every mode. Style, reset styles, resize The object’s definition declares the capability The control is hidden. Pen and Pencil The Enable Pen and Enable Pencil options The dock icons are hidden. Limits 🔗 Item Limit Image file 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB), same on every plan Text file 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB), same on every plan Border thickness 0 to 25 Fill opacity 0 to 1 Components per design Set by your plan and enforced when the design is saved. Annotations count. Image count per design No limit Related reading 🔗 Tool Modes - select, pan, pencil and pen. Whiteboarding - a task guide to drawing on a design. Keyboard Shortcuts - every shortcut. Layout and Layers - arranging and hiding objects.

Cloning copies a design into your own workspace so you can change it freely. The clone is an independent record: later changes to the source never reach it, and edits to the clone never reach the source.
What you can clone 🔗 The server clones only designs whose visibility is public or published. A request for any other design fails with 403 “unauthorized to clone design”. That includes your own private designs. To copy one of those, open it and use Save as. See Save Designs. A missing source design returns 500 “could not find design”.
Where to start a clone 🔗 Kanvas has no Clone item for the design that is open. You clone from these places:
The catalog. The catalog modal’s Clone action, and catalog design cards in Layer5 Cloud. A catalog link. Opening a link with mode=design&type=catalog&id=<id> clones that design and opens your copy. Tutorials. Opening a tutorial’s design clones it. The client names a catalog clone <design name> (Copy), and a tutorial clone <tutorial title> (Copy). The server stores whatever name it receives and rejects an empty request body with 400. When the clone completes, Kanvas loads it. If the open design has unsaved changes, you confirm first.
Layer5 Cloud shows the Clone action only to roles with the Clone Design permission. The server checks visibility, not the key. See Permissions.
What carries over 🔗 Carried over Reset or changed Components, relationships, styles, configuration, annotations, and preferences, converted to the current design format New id The origin of the source design Version 0.0.1 Catalog data (compatibility, type, info, caveats, content class, published version, snapshot URLs) Owner is you Visibility private Workspace is your selected workspace Source file and usage counters are not copied Cloning is the only path that creates a private design. Every other new design is public.
Limits and failure behavior 🔗 Cloning does not check your plan’s components-per-design limit. A clone from a larger plan can exceed yours and then fail its first autosave with a plan-limit error. See Save Designs.
Kanvas shows Cloning design "<name>" while the clone runs. It shows no failure message. Because the clone copies the catalog data block, a private clone can display catalog metadata even though it is not published.

body:
A custom keychain bundles the keys that a custom role needs. This guide creates a keychain, changes its keys, and deletes it. It is written for Provider Admins and self-hosted operators, because only a Provider Admin can create, change, or delete a keychain, or include it in a role. For the model, read the Keychains concept.
Before you start 🔗 You need the Provider Admin role. The interface also checks the Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, and Delete Keychain permissions for the matching controls. Provider Admin holds all three. No other default role does. A keychain does nothing until a role includes it. Creating and editing roles is a Provider Admin action. On hosted Layer5 Cloud an organization cannot complete this path alone. On a self-hosted deployment, your Provider Admins can. Keychains are not organization-scoped. A role that includes your keychain grants its keys to every user who holds that role, in every organization. Create a keychain 🔗 Open the Keychains tab under Security and create a keychain. Give it a name and choose the keys it bundles. Layer5 Cloud creates the keychain and adds each key to it. If adding a key fails, the interface reports it as “Failed to add key to keychain”. Open the keychain and confirm every key you chose is present.
You are recorded as the keychain’s owner. The Keychains list shows system keychains and the keychains you own, so other administrators do not see it in their list. Any Provider Admin can still edit or delete it through the server, and ownership grants no right to change it.
Change the keys in a keychain 🔗 Needs: the Provider Admin role. The interface also requires Edit Keychain.
Open the keychain’s update dialog, rename it, or change the selected keys. The interface adds and removes only the difference. Removing a key stops that key flowing to every role that includes the keychain, immediately.
Use the keychain 🔗 Add the keychain to a role. See the Roles concept for how roles bundle keychains and how users receive roles. Only a Provider Admin can assign a keychain to a role. The change applies to the role in every organization, because roles are global.
Test with a user who holds the role: sign in as that user in a specific organization and confirm the controls the keys govern are enabled.
Delete a keychain 🔗 Needs: the Provider Admin role. The interface also requires Delete Keychain.
Delete the keychain from its row and confirm in the “Delete Keychain” dialog. Deleting removes the keychain’s key mappings. The keychain stops granting anything at once, for every role that included it.
As with every keychain, only a Provider Admin can edit or delete a default keychain. Do not change a default keychain unless you intend to change permissions for every user who holds a default role.
Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix The Keychains tab shows a permission error You lack View Keychains in the selected organization. Ask an Organization Admin to check your role. Create Keychain is disabled You lack the Create Keychain key. Use a Provider Admin account. 403 with code meshery_cloud-1108 or meshery_cloud-3336 You are not a Provider Admin for the whole deployment. Keychains and their assignment to roles apply across the whole provider. Ask a Provider Admin to make the change. A user still lacks a capability The keychain is not on the user’s role, or the user holds the role in a different organization. Add the keychain to the role, and check the role is held in the organization in use.
description: Group keys into a keychain, change its keys, and delete it. A role must include the keychain before it grants anything.

Layer5 Cloud calls an HTTP endpoint you choose when three things happen: a person asks for help, a Provider Admin decides a signup request, and a person gains Kanvas access. The calls let you route those events into your help desk, your chat, or your onboarding automation. On a self-hosted deployment you set the three endpoints; none is set by default, and an unset webhook does nothing useful.
The three webhooks 🔗 Chart value Fires when Payload env.webhookHelpAndSupport Someone submits the Help and Support form in Layer5 Cloud, or a support request raised in Kanvas reaches your deployment memberFormOne env.webhookSignupRequest A Provider Admin approves or denies a signup request signupData and newUser env.webhookKanvasEntitlement A new user registers, a user completes a first brokered social sign-in, or a role assignment gives a user Kanvas access signupData and newUser Set the endpoints 🔗 Add the three URLs to your Helm values and upgrade. The values are written into the server’s ConfigMap, so the pods restart when you change them.
env: webhookHelpAndSupport: "https://hooks.example.com/layer5/support" webhookSignupRequest: "https://hooks.example.com/layer5/signup" webhookKanvasEntitlement: "https://hooks.example.com/layer5/kanvas-access" helm upgrade layer5-cloud layer5/layer5-cloud -n layer5-cloud --values values.yaml Leave a webhook unset if you do not need it. The only way to add a fourth webhook is a change to Layer5 Cloud itself; the three names above are fixed.
How a call is made 🔗 Property Behavior Method and body POST with a JSON body and Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8. Authentication None. There is no signature and no shared secret header. Restrict the receiver by network policy, or put an unguessable token in the URL path. Success A 200 or 202 response. Any other status counts as a failure. Timeout None. The server waits until the receiver answers. Retries None. Each event is sent once. Respond quickly and do the work afterward: the support and signup webhooks run inside the request of the person who triggered them, so a slow receiver makes that person wait.
Payloads 🔗 Help and support 🔗 { "memberFormOne": { "firstname": "Ada", "lastname": "Admin", "email": "ada@example.com", "message": "I cannot connect my cluster.", "form": "support", "scope": "Layer5 Cloud", "subject": "Connection problem" } } Layer5 Cloud rejects a request that carries any field other than these seven, with a 400 error that names the problem. The same payload arrives whether the request came from the Layer5 Cloud form or from Kanvas. Kanvas relays a request through the person’s Meshery Server to the remote provider, so those users must be connected to your deployment for support to work. Under Meshery’s local provider the request is refused as not implemented.
Signup decisions 🔗 { "signupData": { "id": "3f0c1d1e-8f6e-4a57-9d0e-2f1f0b4a9c11", "firstName": "Grace", "lastName": "Hopper", "email": "grace@example.com", "occupation": "Platform engineer", "organization": "Example Corp", "role": "Engineer", "formType": "meshmap", "status": "approved", "taskId": "task-123", "taskLink": "https://tasks.example.com/task-123", "createdAt": "2026-01-15T09:30:00Z", "updatedAt": "2026-01-16T10:00:00Z" }, "newUser": true } A decision requires an email, a first name, a last name, and a valid taskLink URL; otherwise Layer5 Cloud refuses it with a 400 error before any call is made. When the webhook fails, the decision request returns a 500 error (unable to webhook) and an alert event is recorded against the person.
Kanvas entitlement 🔗 { "signupData": { "firstName": "Grace", "lastName": "Hopper", "email": "grace@example.com", "formType": "meshmap" }, "newUser": true } newUser is true for a first registration and a first brokered sign-in. For a role assignment it reflects whether the person is new to Kanvas. The formType value is the literal meshmap, the internal name of the Kanvas entitlement. A failure here never blocks the person: Layer5 Cloud records an event and continues.
Failure behavior 🔗 Webhook When the receiver fails What the person sees What you see Help and support The caller receives a 500 error. An error on the form. A logged error. Signup decision The decision request returns 500. The decision fails with an error. A logged error and an alert event. Kanvas entitlement The call is dropped. Nothing. A logged error and an error event. Because nothing retries, build the receiver to be reliable, and reconcile missed events from the signup request list and the audit events.
Test a webhook 🔗 Trigger each one through its real action: submit the Help and Support form, approve a test signup request, or register a test user. For a quick receiver check, point the URL at a request-capture service, perform the action, and confirm that the capture shows a POST with the payload above.
description: Send support requests, signup decisions, and Kanvas entitlement events from your self-hosted Layer5 Cloud to your own systems: the three webhooks, when each fires, the payloads, and how failures behave.
