body:
Deploying applies the components in a design to the Kubernetes clusters in the environments you choose. Meshery Server does the work with the kubeconfig it holds: it creates each object, or updates it in place when it already exists. Deploying the same design again is safe and idempotent.
Before you start 🔗 A Meshery you run, with a connected cluster. The hosted kanvas.new site does not deploy; it shows a self-hosted-feature prompt. Meshery needs at least one connected Kubernetes context that belongs to an environment in your organization. A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled for an empty design. An unsaved design deploys as it stands on the canvas. Permission. The Deploy Design permission gates the action. See Permissions by Role. Selecting environments from the empty state also needs the Create Environment and Edit Environment permissions. A provider session. Without a signed-in session the request fails before any event is raised. Deploying does not need Meshery Operator, MeshSync, or the broker. Those make the result visible in Operator mode.
Validate and dry-run the design first. See Validate a Design and Dry-run a Design. The deploy flow runs both for you.
The deploy flow 🔗 Choose Deploy from the design’s Actions menu. The Deploy design "<name>" stepper has five steps, with Back and Next throughout.
Step What it does 1. Validate Design Runs validation inline. Next is always enabled, because validation errors are warnings. 2. Identify Environments Lists your organization’s environments as cards. Ticking an environment selects all of its Kubernetes connections. You need at least one. 3. Dry Run Runs a deploy-type dry run against the selected clusters. Next stays disabled while it runs, or when errors exist and the bypass checkbox is off. 4. Finalize Deployment Shows the environments you chose and the component count, excluding annotations. The button reads Deploy. A Schedule Deployment checkbox is shown disabled. 5. Finish Starts the deployment and shows the results. Step 2 shows only Kubernetes connections. When your organization has no environments, it shows No environments found. Add a new environment. When an environment has no connections, it shows No connections configured. Add a connection to get started. Your selection persists for the session. A cluster that belongs to two selected environments is listed twice and targeted twice.
Targets 🔗 The stepper always sends the explicit clusters you selected. Where no selection exists, such as a one-click action or the mobile sheet, the target is all. The server expands a lone all to every connected Kubernetes context. Otherwise it keeps only the ids that match a connected context and silently drops unknown ones. If none remain, the request fails with meshery-server-1096.
Clusters are deployed in parallel.
How components are applied 🔗 Aspect Behavior Ordering Components form a dependency graph. A component starts when every component it depends on has succeeded. Independent components run in parallel. Kanvas applies no other ordering, so deploy custom resource definitions before the resources that use them. Failed dependency A component whose dependency failed is withheld: Withheld <component>: <dependency> did not deploy successfully (meshery-server-1480). Invalid dependencies A malformed, unknown, ambiguous, or circular dependency fails the whole request before anything is applied (meshery-server-1475 through 1479). Existing objects The object is replaced in place. An update to an immutable field, or an attempt to unset a Service’s cluster IP, is reported as success but does not take effect. Namespaces A missing target namespace is created before the object is applied. A namespaced component with no namespace goes to default. Annotation components Never applied. Dependencies of non-Kubernetes models 🔗 For a component whose model is not the built-in Kubernetes model and whose registrant is an Artifact Hub source, Meshery installs the model’s source Helm chart into the component’s namespace, creating the namespace if needed. This brings in the custom resource definitions and operators the component needs. The step is fail-forward: if the chart fails, Meshery still applies the component and adds a row to the results, error deploying dependent helm chart for <component>.
Meshery always processes these dependencies. The Include Dependencies checkbox in the dry-run step does not change this.
What Meshery marks on applied objects 🔗 Mark Value Label design.meshery.io/id The design’s id Annotation design.meshery.io/version The design’s version Annotation component.meshery.io/id The component’s id Operator’s per-design view filters on the design-id label. A component carrying it is shown as managed by Meshery.
Read the results 🔗 Every deployment raises an event from Meshery Server. It appears as a toast and as an entry in the notification center. In the Finish step, a summary lists one row per component and cluster: Deployed <Kind> "<name>", or Failed to deploy <Kind> "<name>" with an error card. When Operator is enabled, the step offers Open In Operator.
Outcome Event The request completed Deployment completed for design '<name>'. at informational severity The request failed before applying (cluster client, dependency graph, malformed design) Failed to deploy design '<name>'. at error severity, with an error card A deployment in which some components failed in Kubernetes still raises the completed event. Read the per-component rows in the Finish step to see which ones failed.
Each persisted deploy event, including an error event, adds 1 to the design’s deployment count in Layer5 Cloud. Dry runs and undeploys do not change it. The count drives the catalog sort Most Deployed.
Error cards 🔗 An error card shows the event description, then Details, then Probable Cause and Suggested Remediation side by side. In the notification center, the Error Docs menu item opens the matching entry in the Meshery error code reference.
Code Meaning Fix meshery-server-1073 Unable to deploy the design. Wraps most hard failures; Details holds the inner error. Confirm the connection’s status is Connected or upload a new kubeconfig, and assign the connection to the selected environment. meshery-server-1096 Kubernetes cluster is unavailable: no selected context resolved. Upload a new kubeconfig, check the network and the cluster, and verify the server’s credentials. meshery-server-1095 Invalid kubeconfig. Upload a new kubeconfig and make sure the server can reach the API server. meshery-server-1070 Failed to parse the design file. Check the design definition. meshkit-11190 Error applying a manifest. The Kubernetes API’s own reason and remediation replace the generic text. Make sure the manifest is valid. meshery-server-1475 to 1480 A dependency problem in the design. Open the design, fix, rename, or remove the dependency, and retry. For 1480, resolve the dependency’s failure first. When nothing happens 🔗 The Finish step waits for the next deploy event from the server. If the request fails before the server raises an event, such as an expired session, a proxy error, or no provider, Kanvas shows no error and the Finish step keeps spinning. The step has no timeout. Close it, sign in again if your session expired, and check the notification center and the Meshery Server logs.
Related 🔗 Undeploy a Design removes what a deployment created. Troubleshoot Kanvas covers connection and loading problems.

body:
In this tutorial you put three Services in front of running workloads: a ClusterIP Service in front of a Deployment, a NodePort Service in front of one Pod, and a LoadBalancer Service in front of another. Pods come and go and change IP addresses every time they are replaced. A Service gives a changing set of Pods one stable address and finds them by label, and its type decides who can reach that address. Building all three side by side makes the difference between the types concrete.
What you will learn 🔗 A Service selects its backend Pods by label, and any Pod whose labels match joins the Service automatically. A ClusterIP Service gets a virtual IP reachable only from inside the cluster. A NodePort Service adds a port on every node, and a LoadBalancer Service adds an external load balancer provisioned by the cluster’s cloud provider. In Kanvas, the Network relationship documents which workload a Service sends traffic to, while the selector is what Kubernetes acts on. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed environment. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. An environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. See Environments. Operator mode for the inspection phases, which needs Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster. Where Operator mode is turned off, its switch is disabled; the deploy summary still confirms each object. A unique prefix. Playground is shared. Use your own prefix in every name and label; this tutorial uses alex. The earlier tutorials. Explore Pods and Explore Deployments cover building, deploying, and inspecting workloads, which this tutorial uses without re-explaining. The scenario 🔗 You build one design with six components and deploy it in three rounds:
Service Type Selector Backend alex-api-cip ClusterIP app=alex-api Deployment alex-api, 2 replicas alex-np NodePort app=alex-np Pod alex-np-pod alex-lb LoadBalancer app=alex-lb Pod alex-lb-pod Every workload runs nginx:latest, which listens on port 80. Every Service listens on port 80 and forwards to target port 80.
What each type exposes, and what you can observe in Meshery Playground:
Type Reachable from Kubernetes allocates In Playground ClusterIP Pods inside the cluster A cluster IP Works fully NodePort Anything that can reach a node A cluster IP and a port on every node The node port is assigned; node IPs are often unreachable from your browser LoadBalancer Clients outside the cluster A cluster IP, a node port, and an external address from the cloud provider No external address is assigned; it stays pending Kubernetes request flow follows a single request from a client through a Service to a Pod, and Creating relationships covers every relationship you can draw between components.
Expose a Deployment with a ClusterIP Service 🔗 Create a new design named alex-services. Add a Deployment named alex-api with replicas 2, selector match labels app: alex-api, template labels app: alex-api, and one container named web with image nginx:latest and container port 80. Add the label app: alex-api to the Deployment itself in the Labels tab. Add a Service named alex-api-cip. Set its type to ClusterIP, add a port with port 80 and target port 80, and set its selector to app: alex-api. Add the label app: alex-api to the Service in the Labels tab so it shows up with the workload when you filter by label. Draw a Network relationship from the Service to the Deployment. Edge handles appear when you hover a component; choose the network option and drag to the Deployment. Compatible targets show a green outline while you drag, and releasing anywhere else creates nothing. Run Validate, Dry Run, and then Deploy from the Actions menu, selecting the environment that holds your cluster’s connection. What just happened. The Service’s selector, app=alex-api, matches the labels in the Deployment’s Pod template, so both Pods the Deployment creates become backends of the Service. The selector points at Pod labels, not at the Deployment: Kubernetes matches Pods, whoever created them. Port 80 is the port clients use on the Service’s address, and target port 80 is the container port that traffic is forwarded to.
The Network relationship records the same connection in the design so that anyone reading the diagram sees where traffic flows. Its edge shows the port values it reads from both components, and Kanvas evaluates relationships after every change; a relationship’s registry definition can copy designated fields from one component to the other. Kubernetes routes by the selector alone, so confirm the selector in the Service’s configurator after you draw the edge.
Check your work. The summary lists Deployed Deployment "alex-api" and Deployed Service "alex-api-cip". Switch to Operator, select the Service, and switch its details panel to Details. It shows the service type ClusterIP, a cluster IP, no external IP, and the selector app=alex-api. The cluster IP is reachable only from inside the cluster: any Pod can send requests to it, and the cluster’s DNS also resolves the name alex-api-cip.default.svc.cluster.local to it.
A selector that matches no Pods is not an error. The Service still deploys and gets a cluster IP, but it has no backends and requests to it fail. If you mistype the selector, nothing warns you; compare the selector with the Pod labels.
Expose a Pod with a NodePort Service 🔗 Switch to Designer and add a Pod named alex-np-pod with the label app: alex-np and one container named web, image nginx:latest, container port 80. Add a Service named alex-np. Set its type to NodePort, add a port with port 80 and target port 80, and set its selector to app: alex-np. Leave the node port empty so Kubernetes assigns a free one from the node port range (30000 to 32767 by default). Draw a Network relationship from alex-np to alex-np-pod. Run Deploy again with the same environment. What just happened. A NodePort Service is a ClusterIP Service plus one port opened on every node in the cluster. Traffic that arrives at any node on that port is forwarded to the Service’s backends, wherever they run. Deploying the design again created the two new objects; Kanvas also resubmitted the Deployment and the ClusterIP Service, which already exist, and those stay as they are.
Check your work. Switch to Operator and select alex-np. Its details show the service type NodePort, a cluster IP, the selector app=alex-np, and, under its connections, the ports including the node port Kubernetes assigned. The Service is reachable at http://<node IP>:<node port> from any machine that can reach a node; the Pod’s host IP is one node address. In Playground, node IPs are often not reachable from your browser, and the assigned node port still confirms that Kubernetes exposed the Pod. If you set a fixed node port and another user on the cluster already holds it, the dry run fails with a Field Value Invalid error on the node port; clear the field and let Kubernetes choose.
Expose a Pod with a LoadBalancer Service 🔗 Switch to Designer and add a Pod named alex-lb-pod with the label app: alex-lb and one container named web, image nginx:latest, container port 80. Add a Service named alex-lb. Set its type to LoadBalancer, add a port with port 80 and target port 80, and set its selector to app: alex-lb. Draw a Network relationship from alex-lb to alex-lb-pod. Run Deploy again. What just happened. A LoadBalancer Service builds on a NodePort Service: Kubernetes allocates a cluster IP and a node port, then asks the cluster’s cloud provider integration to create an external load balancer that forwards to those node ports. When the provider finishes, Kubernetes records the load balancer’s IP or hostname in the Service’s status. A cluster without such an integration, such as Playground, accepts the Service and never assigns an external address.
Check your work. In Operator, select alex-lb. Its details show the service type LoadBalancer, a cluster IP, and a node port under its connections. In Playground there is no external IP and no load balancer address, because no cloud provider fulfills the request. On a managed cloud cluster, an external address appears once the provider has created the load balancer; load a fresh snapshot to see it, because Operator does not update on its own.
Change a deployed Service 🔗 Deploy replaces an existing object in place, but Kubernetes rejects some changes to a Service, such as clearing the cluster IP it assigned. Kanvas reports those rejected changes as Deployed, and the Service stays as it was. To change a deployed Service’s type or ports reliably, undeploy the design and deploy it again.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu and select the same environment. Undeploy deletes each component’s object by kind, name, and namespace: the Deployment, both Pods, and all three Services. Kubernetes then removes the ReplicaSet and Pods the Deployment owned. Undeploy matches by name, not by the design label, so same-named objects that someone else created in the same namespace are deleted too. If the dry-run step reports objects as not found, they are already gone; select the bypass option to finish.
The design stays in your account until you delete it from the design’s file menu. Deleting a design never removes cluster objects.
What you learned 🔗 A Service gives a changing set of Pods one stable address and finds them by label selector, not by owner. ClusterIP serves clients inside the cluster, NodePort adds a port on every node, and LoadBalancer adds an external load balancer that only a cloud provider integration can supply. A selector that matches nothing deploys without error, so checking it is your job. The Network relationship documents traffic flow in the design; the selector is what Kubernetes routes by. Next steps 🔗 Continue with ConfigMaps and Secrets to configure workloads without rebuilding images. Read Deploying designs for every option in the Deploy workflow. Read Operator to understand views, filters, and snapshots.

The Instructor Console reports on your organization’s Academy content and learners. It answers three questions: how many people are learning, how far they get, and which assessments stop them. The console is also where you register new content and manage who can access it.
Availability and access 🔗 Academy Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Academy Theoretical Learning A comprehensive learning management system for creators and instructors on how to build, manage, and extend educational content like learning paths, challenges, and certifications. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Academy Practical Learning An inclusive, collaborative, hands-on learning environment for students. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Opening the console requires the View Academy Metrics permission in the selected organization. Without it, the console shows a missing-permission message that names the permission.
Role Opens the console Notes Academy Admin Yes Also holds team and workspace management, so it can assign content access to teams. Organization Admin Yes Provider Admin Yes Can view the combined “all organizations” scope. Academy Learner No Holds content access only. User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Billing Manager No Unless an operator has added the permission to the role. Role-to-permission assignments are seeded defaults and an operator can change them. See Roles and Permissions.
Organizations that are not configured 🔗 The console reports data only for an organization that has an Academy content module and version configured. Until your first content version is published, the console shows a “not configured” state that lists what you get after configuration: learner registration and progress tracking, content creation tools, test analytics, and reporting. Publishing is described in Create a Learning Path.
Views 🔗 The console has three views: Overview, Learners, and Curricula. “Curricula” is the console’s term for a learning path, challenge, or certification.
Overview 🔗 Metric Definition Total Learners Distinct learners who have registered for any of the organization’s content to date. Active Learners Distinct learners who registered, progressed, or were graded on content this calendar month. Shown with its share of all learners. Registrations Every registration in the organization, including registrations against draft or retired content. Also shown as an average per learner. Completion Rate Registrations with status Completed divided by all registrations. Quiz Pass Rate Passed quiz attempts divided by all attempts. Retakes by one learner each count. A rate below 60% is highlighted. A rate with nothing to divide displays as -, not 0%. No attempts and all attempts failed are different facts.
The Overview also charts:
Registrations by status, using the five registration statuses below. Final exams against practice quizzes. Tests marked as final gate completion of the content. Every other test is practice. Comparing the two shows whether learners who practice successfully fail the exam that counts. Test outcomes, with the lowest pass rate, highest pass rate, and most attempted test. The two pass-rate rankings consider only tests with at least five attempts, so one failure on a new quiz does not crown it the hardest test. While no test has five attempts, the ranking uses all tests. Content by type and level, and the content ranked by registrations. Learners 🔗 A table with one row per registration: learner, content, registration time, and status. Rows load 20 at a time by default. Filter by content type (learning path, challenge, certification) and by status.
Status Meaning Registered The learner enrolled and has not started. In Progress The learner started and has not finished. Completed The learner finished everything the content requires. Failed The learner did not pass the content. Withdrawn The learner left the content, or an instructor withdrew the registration. The Learners view does not export to a file.
Curricula 🔗 Lists the published content of the organization. Draft and retired content is excluded, so the registrations count here is normally smaller than the Overview total. Each row shows the registrations, completion rate, and pass rate. Content that nobody has registered for is marked Awaiting First Learner. The view also shows the content version your learners are using.
If you published a release and the version does not change, publishing is a two-stage process: your content repository release, then the next Layer5 Cloud release for production. See Create a Learning Path.
Actions 🔗 Action Where Effect Register new content Content creation flow Creates the content record and generates the configuration for your repository. See Create Academy Content. Update content access Curricula Changes the team that can access the content, the access end date, the access status, the workspace, and the awarded badge. Copy invite link Curricula Copies the link that registers a learner for the content. Delete content Curricula Removes the content record after confirmation. Withdraw a registration Learners Sets the registration to Withdrawn. Learners can also withdraw themselves. Any other learner needs an instructor with View Academy Metrics. Active Learner definition 🔗 Active Learners counts people, not registrations, over the current calendar month, and it resets each month. A learner who enrolled months ago and submits a quiz this month is active this month. A learner who both registers and takes a quiz counts once. Because it counts distinct people over a monthly window, it is not comparable with the registration totals beside it.
Limits and edge cases 🔗 Situation Behavior Quiz Pass Rate Counts attempts, not learners. A learner who fails twice and then passes contributes two failures and one pass. Registrations differ between views Overview counts all registrations. Curricula counts registrations against published content only. Provider “all organizations” scope The console skips the not-configured check and aggregates across organizations. Exporting Not available in the console. Related 🔗 Academy for how content types relate. Build a Challenge and Build a Certification for authoring.

Layer5 Cloud gives you four signals: two health endpoints, structured logs with stable error codes, a set of startup messages that tell you whether the deployment is fully working, and optional OpenTelemetry traces. It does not expose a Prometheus metrics endpoint, so build service-level indicators from ingress and Kubernetes metrics plus the signals below.
Health endpoints 🔗 Endpoint Answers Meaning GET /healthz 200 with the text Cloud is live The process is running. The chart uses it for the liveness probe. GET /readyz 200 when ready, 503 before The server finished startup and is serving. The chart uses it for the readiness and startup probes. Both endpoints are unauthenticated. The startup probe allows 20 failed checks at 10-second intervals, so a slow start gets about 200 seconds before Kubernetes restarts the pod. Database migrations run before the server reports ready, so an upgrade that carries a large migration can approach that limit.
Kratos and Hydra expose their own health endpoints through their subcharts. The chart configures Hydra liveness on /health/alive and readiness on /health/ready.
Logs 🔗 The server writes logs in syslog format. The chart sets the level to 4 (info). Set env.loglevel to 5 for debug and 6 for trace; use debug only while diagnosing, because it records more detail about requests and mail.
Errors carry a stable code of the form meshery_cloud-NNNN. Alert on the codes, not on message text. The codes that matter operationally:
Code Level Meaning Reference meshery_cloud-3301 Error, then the process exits The shared mail relay fails a startup screen. Troubleshoot Email Delivery meshery_cloud-3302 Error The mail relay is unreachable. No mail leaves until it clears. Same meshery_cloud-3304 Error The mail relay’s certificate does not verify. Same meshery_cloud-3300 Critical An organization’s own mail relay refused a message and fallback is off, so the message was dropped. Same meshery_cloud-3303 Critical An organization’s mail relay accepted a message and never confirmed it. Same Failures that the server survives are logged and, where a person acted, recorded as events that Provider Admins can read: an entitlement webhook that did not return 200 or 202, and a signup decision whose webhook failed. A failed support-request webhook is logged and returned to the person who sent the request, but not recorded as an event.
Startup messages worth alerting on 🔗 The server exits when a database connection fails or a migration fails. It logs and keeps running for these, so a green pod does not prove they succeeded:
Message What it means Failed to initialize Provider Admin And Provider Organization INIT_CONFIG was invalid or a step failed. The deployment runs without a provider administrator. IdP seed warnings The default Google or GitHub sign-in credentials were not stored. Sign-in on custom domains that use the defaults fails. A credential encryption key error env.cloudCredentialEncryptionKey is missing or malformed. Stored credentials cannot be read or written. Failed to initialize OpenTelemetry tracing The tracing configuration was rejected. The server runs without traces. Traces 🔗 Set env.otelConfig to send OpenTelemetry traces to an OTLP gRPC collector:
env: otelConfig: | service_name: layer5-cloud service_version: "1.0.278" environment: production endpoint: otel-collector.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:4317 insecure: true Field Required Meaning service_name Yes Name that identifies the service in traces. endpoint Yes Collector address in host:port form, without a scheme. insecure No true sends without TLS. Defaults to false. service_version No Version reported with each trace. environment No Deployment environment reported with each trace. Each request produces one trace with a span for the whole HTTP request, a span for each middleware that ran (domain resolution, authentication, authorization), and a span for the handler. Leave otelConfig empty to turn tracing off.
What to monitor 🔗 Concern Signal The server is up /healthz, pod restarts The server is serving /readyz, ingress 5xx rate and latency by route Sign-in works Ingress 5xx on /kratos and /hydra, Kratos and Hydra pod health Mail flows Error codes 3301 to 3304, and a periodic send through the email test endpoint Webhooks deliver Recorded webhook failure events The database is healthy PostgreSQL connection count, storage, and replication, from your database’s own metrics Co-editing works Ingress WebSocket connection counts on /collaboration Restrict access to logs: they carry user email addresses, and at debug level they include request detail. Provider initialization also logs the configuration it reads, including the initial administrator password, so treat startup logs as secret and remove env.initConfig after the first successful start.

body:
Evaluation is how a design stays consistent. After you change a design, Kanvas runs it through the policy engine, which applies the registry’s relationship definitions: it identifies relationships, writes configuration across related components, and drops relationships that no longer hold. The engine returns the whole evaluated design, and Kanvas applies it back to the canvas. This is why a value you did not touch can change a moment after you edit a related component.
Evaluation never blocks editing. You can keep designing while it runs, and a new edit supersedes the evaluation in progress.
What triggers evaluation 🔗 Evaluation runs after any of these changes:
A configuration value or a display name changes. A relationship is added or removed. A component is added, removed, duplicated, or merged. A design loads, or an import or merge completes. Kanvas waits until changes stop for about one second, then evaluates. Another change during evaluation restarts the cycle. Selecting the indicator icon forces an evaluation, and a new design resets evaluation state.
Two interchangeable engines 🔗 Engine Where it runs Properties Meshery server In your Meshery server Always available. Client-side (WASM) In a background worker in your browser No round trips to the server, so it is typically faster. A WASM evaluation times out after 10 seconds. Both engines apply the same policy engine and the same definitions. The choice changes where the work happens.
Choosing the engine 🔗 The Relationship Evaluation Engine preference lives in the Options dialog, which you open from the canvas right-click menu.
Value Behavior Automatic (recommended) The default. At load, Kanvas tries to start the WASM engine and waits up to 30 seconds for it to report ready. If it starts, WASM is used. If not, the Meshery server is used. Meshery server Always uses the server. Client-side (WASM) Always uses WASM. The preference is saved to your user preferences, so it applies on all your devices and designs. Kanvas chooses the engine once, when Designer loads, so reload Kanvas for a change to take effect.
Two behaviors to know:
Forcing Client-side (WASM) gives no fallback. If the engine fails to start, evaluations fail silently and relationships stop updating. Switch to Automatic or Meshery server and reload. Automatic checks only that the engine initializes. It does not fall back to the server later if the WASM engine fails after a successful start. Reading the indicator 🔗 The top toolbar shows an icon for relationship evaluation. Its state is in the tooltip.
State Tooltip Running “Evaluating relationships…” with a spinning icon Done “Relationships evaluated” and the time elapsed, a summary of the actions the evaluator applied, and a View Evaluation History button Nothing evaluated “No relationships evaluated yet” There is no error state. A failed evaluation clears the last-evaluation details, so the tooltip returns to “No relationships evaluated yet”, and the failure is logged to the browser console only. If relationships stop updating, check the engine first.
When Kanvas applies an evaluation result and decides to skip it, it shows the notice “Skipping evaluation application”, with a reason when one is known. A successful evaluation shows no message.
Diagnosing unexpected results 🔗 Turn on Enable Debugger in the Options dialog. It is off by default. Open the debugger and go to its Evaluation Engine tab. Read the status: Initialized, Not Initialized, or Not Available. Read the engine type, WASM or SERVER, and any initialization error. The tab refreshes every second. If WASM is not initialized, or results look wrong, set the engine to Meshery server, reload, and compare. Make any change to re-trigger evaluation. If the server engine also gives wrong results, file an issue that includes the engine type, any initialization error, the relationships you expected, and the design or a minimal version of it.
Large designs 🔗 Evaluation covers the whole design regardless of which relationship layers you hide. In Adaptive render mode, Kanvas can suggest cost-saving changes when a design grows: disabling TagSets when there are more than 5, collapsing parents when there are more than 10, hiding unused components when there are more than 200, and using Wireframe mode when there are more than 100 relationships. Each suggestion appears at most once per 60 seconds.
Related pages 🔗 Relationships: the kinds that evaluation applies. Create Relationships: what you create by hand.

Operator mode shows a live picture of your clusters. A performance test adds the missing signal: how a service responds under load. You select a Service or Ingress on the canvas, Kanvas seeds a test from it, and Meshery runs the load and keeps the result as a reusable performance profile.
Before you start 🔗 Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. A target Meshery Server can reach. Meshery Server generates the load, not your browser and not the cluster. The address you test must be routable from wherever Meshery Server runs. A ClusterIP address is reachable from inside the cluster only. Performance permissions. The form needs View performance profiles to appear, and the Run Test button needs Run test. See Permissions by Role. Start a test 🔗 The action is named Initiate Performance Test and is offered on Service and Ingress resources only, the kinds that expose an endpoint. It is not offered on pods, deployments, or any other kind. Right-click the resource, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel.
The Performance panel opens on the canvas at 400 px wide, floating and minimizable. Only one performance panel exists: starting a test from a second resource replaces the target of the open panel. The panel hosts the Meshery performance test form, so the fields, profiles, and results are the same ones Meshery provides. Opening the panel generates no load. Nothing runs until you press Run Test.
What Kanvas pre-fills 🔗 Setting Seeded value Profile name <Kind> - <component name>, for example Service - checkout URL to test The first endpoint derived from the resource, or empty Concurrent requests 10 Queries per second 20 Duration 30s Load generator fortio Change any value before you run. The form also accepts request headers, cookies, content type, request body, additional load generator options as JSON, and a certificate for TLS endpoints.
How the URL is derived 🔗 For a Service, Kanvas builds an endpoint from the service’s type and ports and seeds the first one. A service with several ports yields several endpoints; edit the URL to test another port.
Service type Seeded URL ClusterIP (also when no type is set) http://<clusterIP>:<port> LoadBalancer http://<ingress IP or hostname>:<port>. Empty until the cloud assigns an address. ExternalName http://<externalName>:<port> NodePort Empty. Kanvas does not know node addresses. Enter http://<node address>:<nodePort>. Headless (clusterIP: None) Seeds http://None:<port>. Replace it with a real address. For an Ingress, the URL is always empty. Enter the host and path you want to test. The seeded scheme is always http; change it to https for TLS endpoints.
Run it and read the result 🔗 Edit the seeded values. Press Run Test. Meshery first saves the settings as a performance profile (the toast reads Performance profile <name> has been created), then submits the load test (Load test has been submitted). A countdown runs for the test duration. The results then render in the same panel, with a way back to the form. The same profile can be selected and re-run later, which is what makes a test repeatable before and after a change. Results are stored in Meshery’s performance results history, not in Kanvas. Profiles, schedules, comparisons between runs, and how results are interpreted are covered in Performance Management in the Meshery documentation.
Validation and failure modes 🔗 Message Meaning Please enter a valid URL along with protocol The URL needs a scheme such as http://. Please enter a valid JSON string The additional options field is not valid JSON. Duration rejected Duration must be positive and end in h, m, or s. Failed to create performance profile The profile could not be saved, so the test did not start. Load test did not run with msg: <message> The load generator reported a failure. The message names the cause, often an unreachable endpoint. Connection to the server got disconnected. Load test might be running in the background. Please check the results page in a few. The result stream dropped. The test may still finish; check the results page in Meshery. Permission denied block or disabled Run Test Your role lacks View performance profiles or Run test. Empty panel The host Meshery did not supply the performance form. Use a Meshery release that includes it. Kanvas does not pre-check that the endpoint is reachable.
Related 🔗 Resource Details shows the live state of the resource you are testing. Performance Limits covers the limits of Kanvas itself on large designs.

The fastest way to a working design is to start from one someone has already published. The catalog is a public collection of designs for cloud native infrastructure. In this tutorial you browse it, try a design without changing anything, and then clone it. You finish with your own private copy in your workspace and a clear picture of what a clone is and what it is not.
Before you begin 🔗 Browsing the catalog needs no account. Cloning does: if you do not have one, follow Create Your Layer5 Account. Cloning needs the Clone Design permission. The table shows which built-in roles hold it: Catalog permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin Clone Design Clone any published design to customise it according to your use cases ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View Designs View all public and published designs of other team members and private of signed-in user ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed 1. Browse the catalog 🔗 Open the catalog and search by technology or type. Sort by Most Cloned or Most Downloaded to see what other people rely on most. Each design card shows a summary, and opening a design shows its full details. You can also download a design to work with it outside Layer5 Cloud.
2. Try a design in the Playground 🔗 Before you commit to a copy, open the design in the Playground. Open in Playground opens the design in a new browser tab in Kanvas on the Meshery Playground, loaded straight from the catalog. Nothing is cloned and nothing lands in your workspace, so this is the safe way to explore a design.
3. Choose where the copy will go 🔗 A clone lands in the workspace you have selected, in the organization you have selected. Pick both before you clone, for example My Workspace in My Organization.
You must have one specific organization selected. Cloning in the all-organizations scope is refused.
4. Clone the design 🔗 Clone the design from its catalog entry. If your role lacks the Clone Design permission, the clone action is shown disabled.
Layer5 Cloud then creates your copy:
Property of the clone Value Name The original name followed by " (Copy)", for example “My App (Copy)” Owner You Visibility Private to you Location Your selected workspace in your selected organization Content The original’s catalog data and file location, converted to the current design format Cloning also counts toward the original: Layer5 Cloud records a clone event on the original design, which feeds the catalog’s Most Cloned sort and the catalog leaderboard. If this is the first design you own, your profile earns the first-design badge.
When cloning is refused 🔗 Situation Result The design is not Published or Public Refused with HTTP 403 (“unauthorized to clone design”). Only published or public designs can be cloned. The all-organizations scope is selected Refused with HTTP 400 (“Creating designs is not allowed for orgID all”). No organization is selected Refused with HTTP 400 (“orgID is not provided”). Your role lacks Clone Design The clone action is disabled. What a clone is 🔗 A clone is a separate, private design that you own. It starts from the original’s content and lives in your workspace, where you work on it like any other design you own. Opening a design in the Playground, by contrast, creates nothing in your account: it is a preview.
Check your result 🔗 Your copy is ready when a design named after the original with " (Copy)" appended appears in the workspace you selected, owned by you and private.
Next steps 🔗 Kanvas: design and edit infrastructure visually. Catalog: how the catalog works. Set Up Your Organization: move your copy into a workspace your team shares.

body:
A subscription connects an organization to a Layer5 plan and bills for it. This guide covers what you can see and do with subscriptions, who can do it, and how the amount you pay follows your membership. For what each plan includes, read Feature Availability by Plan. Current prices are on the pricing page.
Who can manage a subscription 🔗 A subscription belongs to an organization, not to a person. Layer5 Cloud checks the caller against the subscription’s own organization, so administering one organization gives you no access to another organization’s billing.
Action Organization Owner Organization Admin Provider Admin Other members See the organization’s subscriptions Yes Yes Yes No Start a paid subscription Yes Yes Yes No Upgrade a subscription Yes Yes Yes No Cancel a subscription Yes Yes Yes No The Subscription and Plans tabs open for any user who holds View Subcription or View Plans. The default user role holds both. A member who is not an owner or Organization Admin can open the tab, but Layer5 Cloud refuses the data behind it, so the subscription table cannot load. For subscriptions that belong to another organization, Layer5 Cloud answers “subscription not found”, the same answer it gives for an id that does not exist.
The Subscription and Plans tabs belong to the Layer5 Cloud interface. When the account page is shown inside a Meshery UI that uses Layer5 Cloud as its provider, only the Profile tab appears.
Read your subscriptions 🔗 The Subscription tab lists each subscription with these columns:
Column Meaning Plan The plan the subscription is on. Cadence Monthly or annual billing. Status The subscription’s state, from the table below. Users Billable The number of billable users counted for the subscription. Forecasted Amount Users Billable multiplied by the plan’s price per user, in US dollars. Start Date, Created At, Updated At When the subscription started, was created, and last changed. Three summary cards sit above the table: your current plan, the forecasted bill (“Based on current usage”, or “No billable usage” when the amount is zero), and the next payment due.
Status Meaning active Paid and in good standing. trialing In a trial period. Layer5 Cloud’s own checkout starts no trial. incomplete Created, but the first payment has not completed. past_due A payment failed. unpaid Payment attempts for the period have been exhausted. canceled Ended. expired, inactive No longer in effect. incomplete_expired The first payment never completed. The row is hidden from the list. Layer5 Cloud takes the status from the payment processor. Status changes arrive when the processor reports them, so the tab can trail a payment by a short time. Use the refresh control to reload.
Start a paid subscription 🔗 The Plans tab lists the Personal plan (“Free Forever”), Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise, each with monthly and annual prices and a currency selector.
Personal is free and needs no subscription step. Team Designer and Team Operator start in the tab. Review the plan, apply a coupon if you have one, and enter your billing address and payment details. The payment form is hosted by the payment processor, and Layer5 Cloud does not store card details. Enterprise does not use self-service checkout. Its subscribe action opens a contact form, and the Layer5 team arranges the subscription. Layer5 Cloud creates the subscription as incomplete, counts your billable users, and asks the payment processor to start billing. The status becomes active when the first payment succeeds. Checkout starts no free trial.
Upgrade a subscription 🔗 Upgrade moves a subscription to a higher plan on the same ladder. Each ladder is separate:
Monthly core plans, in order: Team Designer, Team Operator, Enterprise. Annual core plans, in the same order. Academy theory and lab bundles, each with its own monthly and annual ladder. You cannot move down a ladder, and you cannot switch between monthly and annual billing on an existing subscription. To change cadence or move to a lower plan, contact Support.
Before you confirm, the upgrade shows an invoice preview with the prorated line items. Layer5 Cloud prorates the change: you pay for the new plan’s price for the rest of the current period, less credit for the unused part of the old plan. The confirmation reads “Subscription upgraded to” followed by the plan name.
Upgrade is unavailable for subscriptions that are canceled, inactive, incomplete, or on the free plan.
Cancel a subscription 🔗 Cancel asks you to confirm and then tells the payment processor to end the subscription at the end of the current billing period. The plan stays in force until the period ends. Because the plan runs to the end of the period, canceling issues no refund.
Cancel is unavailable for subscriptions that are already canceled or inactive, that never completed, or that are on the free plan.
How the billable user count works 🔗 Plans bill per user. The count is the number of distinct people who are members of the organization, with these rules:
The account must be active. A person who has been invited but has not accepted is not counted. A deleted account is not counted. A member whose only role is academy learner is not counted. A member added without any role is not counted. The count never falls below the plan’s minimum number of users. Academy plans that bill per learner count active learners instead of organization members. Layer5 Cloud recalculates the count when it creates a subscription, and then every 2 hours for subscriptions that are active, trialing, past due, incomplete, or unpaid. It sends the new count to the payment processor each time. No plan blocks you from adding users: the count changes what you pay, never what you can do.
What a change in the count costs 🔗 The count rises mid-period. The payment processor charges a prorated amount for the added users for the rest of the period. At renewal, the full amount reflects the new count. The count falls mid-period. The processor issues a prorated credit for the unused part. The credit stays on the organization’s account balance, does not expire, and reduces future invoices. It is not refunded automatically. Renewal date. A change in the count never moves the renewal date. At renewal, the organization pays for the count as of that date. Removing a user from the organization, or deleting their account, lowers the count at the next recalculation.
What a plan enforces 🔗 Plans record several limits, but Layer5 Cloud enforces only the number of components in a design. See Feature Availability by Plan. Saving or importing a design that exceeds the component limit of the organization’s active plan is refused, and an organization with no active subscription cannot add components to a design at all. Reduce the design or upgrade the plan.
Failure modes 🔗 What you see Cause What to do The subscription table does not load You are not an Organization Owner or Organization Admin of the selected organization Ask an owner or Organization Admin to manage billing, or switch to the right organization. “Payment Error” during checkout The payment processor declined the payment Correct the payment details and retry. Status stays incomplete The first payment has not completed Complete the payment. An incomplete subscription that never completes becomes incomplete_expired. Cancel and Upgrade are disabled The status or plan rules above Check the status column. See also 🔗 Feature Availability by Plan lists what each plan includes. Organizations explains organization owners and Organization Admins. Manage Your Account covers your own profile and sign-in.

Whiteboarding in Kanvas (3:41) follows one late-night incident from page to postmortem on a single live design. Its page has chapters and a transcript.
Whiteboarding lets you diagram freely on the same canvas as your infrastructure. You draw shapes, text, freehand strokes, and lines to explain intent, and they sit beside real components in one design. It is on by default and available on every plan.
Drawn objects are saved with the design and shared live with collaborators. They are components marked as annotations, so they count toward your plan’s components-per-design limit. See Designs and Components.
This guide covers the drawing tools. For per-object operations such as copying, locking, and resizing, see Working with Canvas Objects.
The dock 🔗 The dock sits at the bottom of the canvas in Designer mode. Its tools, left to right:
Tool Shortcut What it does Select V Select, move, and configure objects. Hand H, or hold Space Pan the canvas. Components - Open the component palette. Kubernetes - Open every Kubernetes component. Shapes - Browse shape categories. Comment M Drop a comment thread. Image I Pick an image file and place it. TextBox T Add a text box. Section S Add a labeled, dashed region that holds other objects. Pen Ctrl/Cmd+E Draw annotation lines. Pencil Ctrl/Cmd+P Draw freehand. Help Center Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+/ Open help. The Pen and Pencil icons turn green while their mode is active. Press Esc to leave a mode. Pinned models appear after a divider at the right end. See Pin Models to the Dock.
The dock scrolls horizontally when it overflows, and it is greyed out while the app is in an error state, for example after a failed save. In Operator mode only the Select and Hand tools, Help Center, and minimized panels remain.
Turn tools on or off 🔗 The canvas right-click menu opens an Options dialog with these toggles, all on by default:
Enable Dock hides or shows the entire dock, including component pickers, not only the drawing tools. Enable Pencil and Enable Pen hide or show those two icons. Each change saves to your user preferences, so it applies to all your designs and devices. The toggles hide icons only. The keyboard shortcuts for Pen, Pencil, M, T, S, and I keep working.
No permission key gates drawing. Tier listings show Pencil, Pen, and 500 built-in shapes on Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise.
Draw freehand with the Pencil 🔗 Each stroke becomes one filled shape. Defaults are caribbean green, thickness 1, and opacity 1. There is no color or thickness control before you draw. Afterward, select the stroke and use its style toolbar to change fill color, opacity, and border.
Draw lines with the Pen 🔗 The Pen is Connector mode. Click empty canvas to place a small terminal point, then click elsewhere to place another and join them with a line. Repeated clicks draw a connected polyline. Starting from a component’s edge handle also works. Cancelling mid-draw removes the dangling point.
Pen lines are annotation edges. They explain flow and do not change any component’s configuration. Style them like any edge: color, line style, arrow and curve style, label, and animation.
Pan and box selection are off while you draw with the Pen or Pencil.
Add shapes, text, sections, images, and comments 🔗 Shapes. Choose from the shape categories. A shape carries no configuration and is never deployed. You can swap any object’s outline for one of 24 shapes while keeping its content, position, and size. Text boxes. Double-click to edit text inline. Text options include color, weight (regular, medium, semi bold, bold, black), underline or strikethrough, alignment, and font size. Sections. A section groups the objects dropped inside it, and they move with it. Images. Images up to 512,000 bytes are embedded in the design. Larger files are rejected. Comments. A comment opens a discussion thread on the canvas. Resolved threads disappear from the canvas until reopened. See Review a Design with Comments. Style objects and lines 🔗 Select an object to open its toolbar. Controls appear only when the object supports them.
Control Options Fill 13 swatches including transparent, with opacity from 0 to 1 Border Color, style (solid, dotted, dashed, double), thickness from 0 to 25 Layer order Move to front, forward, backward, to back Animation None, blink, ripple, bounce, pulse Line style Solid, dashed, or dotted; ten curve styles; eleven arrow heads Line animation Marching ants, which shows the direction of flow Collaborate 🔗 Every change, including drawn objects, syncs live between everyone in the design through a shared document over a peer-to-peer session. Each collaborator appears as an avatar in the toolbar, and live cursors and selections are shared. Undo and redo cover the shared document: components, configuration, styles, relationships, drawn objects, and layer toggles.
Limits and behavior 🔗 Drawn objects are saved with the design. Kanvas never deploys annotations. Images and text files over about 500 KB are rejected, whatever your plan.

This page states how workspaces and environments behave, exactly. For the model, read the Workspaces and Environments concepts. For tasks, use the workspace guides. For every endpoint’s schema, see the REST API Reference, and for base URL and authentication see the Cloud API. All paths below sit under /api.
Fields, defaults, and limits 🔗 Property Workspace Environment Name Up to 255 characters. Not required or unique on the API. Up to 255 characters. Not required or unique on the API. Description Up to 255 characters. May be empty. Up to 255 characters. May be empty. Organization Required on create. Fixed for the life of the workspace. Required on create (organizationId is required). Fixed for the life of the environment. Owner The user who created it. Not recorded on create. Starting state No teams, environments, designs, or views. No connections, in no workspace. Kind Single kind. Ordinary when created through the API. Platform-provisioned environments exist and are protected. Update Only the fields sent change. Name and description are both replaced; an omitted field becomes empty. Plan check None. None. The feature matrix lists environments under Enterprise. Count limits None. An organization must keep at least one workspace. None. Layer5 Cloud creates My Workspace in any organization that has no workspace.
Scope and visibility 🔗 Question Answer Who sees a workspace or environment in a list? Every member of its organization. Team membership does not narrow the list. How is the organization chosen? A list request carries one organization identifier. The all-organizations value needs View All Organizations and otherwise returns HTTP 403. What does a missing or foreign identifier return? HTTP 404, workspace not found or environment not found. Can a workspace or environment move to another organization? No. Which relationships can cross organizations? None for teams and environments: both must share the workspace’s organization (HTTP 403 otherwise). A design assigned to a workspace takes on that workspace’s organization. Permissions by operation 🔗 Layer5 Cloud checks each key in the organization that owns the workspace or environment. Operations marked UI only are hidden in the interface but not checked by the server.
Operation Permission POST /workspaces Create Workspace (organization from the request body) GET /workspaces, GET /workspaces/{id} UI only (View Workspace); organization scoping applies PUT /workspaces/{id} Edit Workspace DELETE /workspaces/{id} Delete Workspace POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/teams/{teamId} Assign team to workspace, Remove team from workspace POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/environments/{environmentId} Assign environment to workspace, Remove environment from workspace POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/designs/{designId} Assign Designs to Workspaces, Remove Designs from Workspaces POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/views/{viewId} Assign Views to Workspace, Unassign Views from Workspace GET /workspaces/{id}/views, GET /workspaces/{id}/events View Workspace GET /workspaces/{id}/teams, /environments, /designs None POST /environments Create Environment (organization from the request body) GET /environments, GET /environments/{id} UI only (View Environment); organization scoping applies PUT /environments/{id} Edit Environment DELETE /environments/{id} Delete Environment POST, DELETE /environments/{id}/connections/{connectionId} Assign connections to environment, Remove connections from environment GET /environments/{id}/connections View Environment Default holders by role:

body:
Assessments gate progress and trigger completion in Academy content. A learner who passes an assessment unlocks the next level of the content, and a learner who passes the final assessment completes the content and receives its badge and, where defined, its certificate. Layer5 Cloud scores every submission on the server and records the result in the learner’s grade history.
This page shows how to write an assessment file and explains how the server treats it. It assumes you have a content repository with a learning path, challenge, or certification.
Place assessments at each level 🔗 Each level of the content hierarchy takes its own kind of assessment. The kinds differ in name only. All three use the same file format.
Level Assessment Typical file Scope Learning path, challenge, or certification Exam exam.md Validates the whole content item Course Test test.md Validates one course Module Quiz quiz.md Checks one module Learning path ├── Course 1 │ ├── Module A │ │ └── quiz.md │ ├── Module B │ │ └── quiz.md │ └── test.md ├── Course 2 │ ├── Module A │ │ └── quiz.md │ └── test.md └── exam.md Challenges and certifications place their exams directly under the content item. You may use any file names that keep the levels distinguishable, for example test-for-course.md.
Each mandatory section needs at least one assessment. A course with no test, or a learning path with no exam, has no event that can mark it complete or award its badge.
Write an assessment file 🔗 An assessment is a Markdown file whose front matter holds the questions. Text after the front matter appears above the questions as orientation for the learner.
--- title: "Kubernetes Basics Quiz" id: "quiz-kubernetes-basics" type: "test" layout: "test" passPercentage: 70 timeLimit: 15 maxAttempts: 3 final: false isOptional: false questions: - id: "q1" text: "Which object runs one or more containers as a unit?" type: "single-answer" marks: 2 options: - id: "a" text: "Pod" isCorrect: true - id: "b" text: "Namespace" - id: "q2" text: "Which kubectl command lists all pods?" type: "short-answer" marks: 2 correctAnswer: "kubectl get pods" --- Answer every question. You can retake this quiz. Front matter keys are camelCase. The theme still accepts older snake_case keys such as pass_percentage and is_optional for existing content, but new content should use camelCase.
Assessment fields 🔗 Field Required Behavior type Yes Must be test. layout No Must be test when set. passPercentage Yes Minimum percentage of total marks needed to pass, for example 70. questions Yes The list of questions. title No Name shown to the learner. id No Unique identifier. When omitted, the build generates one from the file path. Set a readable, globally unique value such as quiz-containers so grade history stays traceable. isOptional No When true, the assessment does not block progress. See Required and optional assessments. Default false. final No When true, passing completes the parent section. See Final assessments. timeLimit No Minutes allowed per attempt. 0 (the default) means no limit. maxAttempts No Attempts allowed per learner and registration. 0 means unlimited. numberOfQuestions No Number of questions served per attempt when the file holds a larger question bank. The bank size should be a multiple of this value. Question fields 🔗 Field Required Behavior id Yes Identifier, unique within the assessment, for example q1. text Yes The question prompt. type Yes single-answer, multiple-answers, or short-answer. marks Yes Points awarded for a correct answer. options For choice questions List of options. Each has an id, text, and optional isCorrect: true. correctAnswer For short-answer The expected text. instructions No Replaces the default hint shown with the question. Question types 🔗 Type Learner action Scored correct when Default hint single-answer Selects one option Exactly one option is selected and it is correct Select one answer multiple-answers Selects any number of options Every correct option is selected and no incorrect option is selected Select all that apply short-answer Types text The text equals correctAnswer after trimming whitespace, ignoring case Type your answer below Scoring is all or nothing per question. A multiple-answers question gives no partial credit. An unanswered question scores zero.
Short-answer matching is always case-insensitive. Layer5 Cloud has no case-sensitive mode, so write correctAnswer as the one canonical form you accept and avoid questions with several valid phrasings.
For a true or false question, use single-answer with two options:
questions: - id: "q3" text: "A Kubernetes pod can contain multiple containers." type: "single-answer" marks: 1 options: - id: "true" text: "True" isCorrect: true - id: "false" text: "False" Use only the supported types The scoring service evaluates single-answer, multiple-answers, and short-answer. A question with any other type is shown but never scores, so a learner cannot earn its marks. Required and optional assessments 🔗 Assessments are required by default. A learner must pass every required assessment in a section before the next level unlocks.
Pass all module quizzes to unlock the course test. Pass all course tests to unlock the learning path exam. Set isOptional: true to exclude an assessment from these prerequisite checks. Optional assessments never block progress, and a learner can skip them. If every module in a course is optional, learners go straight to the course test.
When a learner submits a test whose prerequisites are incomplete, the server rejects the submission with Prerequisites not completed.
Final assessments 🔗 The final assessment of a section decides when that section is complete. The build selects it with these rules:
A section with a single exam treats it as final. A section with several exams uses the one marked final: true. Mark at most one per section. When no exam is marked, the last exam by file path is final. A final exam cannot be optional, even when it is the only exam. The build orders by file path and not by weight, because weight can be missing or duplicated across files. Name the file that must come last so that it sorts last, or mark it final: true.
A learner can take a final exam only after completing every mandatory sibling and child item.
What passing does 🔗 Result Effect Pass any assessment That assessment is marked completed in the learner’s progress. Pass a final assessment The parent section is marked completed. Pass the final assessment of a learning path, challenge, or certification The registration becomes Completed, the content’s badge is awarded when one is set, and a certificate is issued and emailed when the content defines one. Pass a non-final assessment Only that assessment completes. Passing a course test that is not final does not complete the course. Mark the assessment that closes each course or content item final: true when a section holds more than one exam, so completion does not depend on file ordering.
A learner can retake an assessment after passing it, subject to maxAttempts. The server never blocks a retake because of an earlier score.
Attempts, time limits, and question banks 🔗 Layer5 Cloud applies these limits when a learner starts and submits an attempt.
Behavior Rule Attempt counting Starting an attempt counts against maxAttempts, whether or not the learner submits it. Attempt limit reached Starting another attempt fails with Maximum attempts reached for this test. Time limit The attempt expires timeLimit minutes after it starts. A submission after expiry fails with Test submission has expired. Resubmission A submitted attempt cannot be submitted again. Ownership A learner can submit only their own attempt, and only against their own registration. Payload size A submission larger than 1 MiB is rejected. With numberOfQuestions set, the learner receives the next window of questions from the bank on each attempt. Attempt 1 gets questions 1 to N, attempt 2 gets N+1 to 2N, and so on. After the last window, the sequence restarts at question 1. When the bank size is not a multiple of N, the final window is shorter, so keep the bank an exact multiple.
The server never sends correct answers to the learner’s browser.
Do not rename or move assessment files after launch The server identifies an assessment by its published path. Renaming or moving the file makes the new path a different assessment. Earlier attempts and passes recorded against the old path no longer count, so attempt limits reset and prerequisites that depended on the old path stay unmet. Scoring 🔗 The build sums the marks of the questions into the assessment’s total marks. The server computes:
percentage = learner's score / total marks * 100 The attempt passes when the percentage is greater than or equal to passPercentage. The saved result holds the score, the percentage, the pass or fail outcome, and which questions the learner got right. Instructors see pass rates in the Instructor Console.
Test your assessment 🔗 Local preview renders the assessment layout. It does not score. Submission, grading, attempt counting, and completion run on the server, so you must publish a version of your content to test them end to end. Use a dedicated test learner registration in a non-production organization so that pass and completion states do not appear in your real metrics.
Answers to common questions 🔗 Is the id required? No. The build generates one from the file path when you omit it. Set one yourself for traceability.
Why does every course and learning path need an assessment? Completion is triggered by passing the final assessment. Without one, nothing marks the level complete or awards its badge.
How are multiple-answers questions scored? All or nothing. Selecting a wrong option or missing a correct one scores zero for the question.
Can a learner retake an assessment after scoring 100%? Yes, until maxAttempts is reached. When maxAttempts is 0, retakes are unlimited.

The Layer5 Cloud REST API lets you build integrations, retrieve data, and automate your infrastructure. This page states the conventions every endpoint shares: base URL, authentication, organization context, pagination, and errors. For the list of endpoints, see the REST API Reference.
Base URL 🔗 Every endpoint lives under /api on the host of your Layer5 Cloud deployment.
Deployment Base URL Hosted Layer5 Cloud https://cloud.layer5.io/api Self-hosted https://<your-cloud-host>/api Authentication 🔗 Authenticate with a security token. Send it as a bearer token in the Authorization header:
curl https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/users/profile \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" When a request has no Authorization header, Layer5 Cloud reads the browser session cookie instead. Scripts and integrations always send the header.
A token belongs to your user account, not to an organization. One token reaches every organization you are a member of, the way a GitHub personal access token reaches every repository its owner can. A request with a missing or invalid credential receives HTTP 401.
What a token can do is the same as what you can do: every guarded endpoint checks that you hold the required permission in the organization the request runs in. See Roles and Permissions.
Organization context 🔗 A guarded request runs in one organization. Layer5 Cloud resolves the organization from these sources, in this order:
The request’s host. A request that arrives on an organization’s custom domain runs in that organization, and the sources below are not consulted. Requests to the deployment’s own address skip this step. The X-Current-Orgid request header. The organization saved in your user preferences. The organization saved in your browser session (browser clients only). Header names are case-insensitive. The first source that holds a value wins.
Condition Result The value is the ID of an organization you belong to The request runs in that organization. The value is not a valid ID, or names an organization you do not belong to Layer5 Cloud ignores it and runs the request with no organization scope. This is not an error by itself. The endpoint decides what to return. The value is all The request spans every organization, but only for callers who hold the View All Organizations permission (Provider Admin by default). For everyone else Layer5 Cloud ignores all. A Provider Admin names an organization they do not belong to The request runs in that organization. Check the header name Layer5 Cloud reads X-Current-Orgid only. A header with any other name, including layer5-current-orgid, has no effect, and the request silently falls back to your saved organization. cURL JavaScript Python curl -X GET "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <Your-Token>" \ -H "X-Current-Orgid: <Your-Organization-ID>" const res = await fetch("https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "X-Current-Orgid": orgId, }, }); const data = await res.json(); import requests res = requests.get( "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments", headers={ "Authorization": "Bearer <Your-Token>", "X-Current-Orgid": "<Your-Organization-ID>", }, ) print(res.json()) Save a default organization and workspace 🔗 To make an organization the default for every request that omits the header, save it in your user preferences:
curl -X PUT "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/users/preferences" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <Your-Token>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "selectedOrganizationId": "<Your-Organization-ID>", "selectedWorkspaceForOrganizations": { "<Your-Organization-ID>": "<Your-Workspace-ID>" } }' selectedOrganizationId is the default organization. The key is case-insensitive. selectedWorkspaceForOrganizations maps an organization ID to the workspace that receives the designs you save in it. When an organization has no saved workspace, Layer5 Cloud uses the first workspace available. A preference key that the request does not mention keeps its stored value. A key the server does not recognize, such as selectedOrganization, is ignored. You cannot change your badges through this endpoint. Pagination 🔗 List endpoints that paginate accept these query parameters.
Parameter Default Behavior page 0 Zero-based page number. A negative value becomes 0. pageSize 10 Items per page. The maximum is 100; a larger value becomes 100, and zero or a negative value becomes 10. order Endpoint-specific Sort field and direction, for example updated_at desc. search None Filters items by text. The response carries the current page, the page size, the total count, and the array of items.
Errors 🔗 An error response is identified by its HTTP status code. The body takes one of three shapes, depending on the endpoint.
Shape Where you see it Example JSON with message Authentication failures and some middleware refusals {"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"} JSON with error Permission refusals and endpoints that report structured errors. May also carry code, severity, probableCause, and suggestedRemediation. {"error": "You do not hold the permission this action requires in this organization", "code": "..."} Plain text Endpoints that report a short message, for example a malformed request body malformed request body Status Meaning 400 The request is malformed or a required parameter is missing. 401 The credential is missing, invalid, or expired. 403 You do not hold the permission the endpoint requires in the organization of the request. 500 The server could not complete the request. Branch on the status code first, then parse the body defensively. The generated REST API Reference documents 401 responses as plain text, but the authentication layer answers with JSON.
Example: count Academy registrations 🔗 The Academy curricula endpoint is public. It needs no token. It returns curricula, each with its registration count.
cURL Python curl -s "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/academy/curricula" \ | jq '[.data[].registration_count] | add' import requests res = requests.get("https://cloud.layer5.io/api/academy/curricula") total = sum(item["registration_count"] for item in res.json()["data"]) print(total) The result is a single number, the total registrations across the curricula returned.

A design is one record with one owner. These guides cover how other people reach it and how you discuss it with them. Access is per person and has no access level: everyone who can open a design can edit it. Comments are part of the design, and they work in Designer mode.
Goal Guide Give specific people access, change visibility, copy a link, or revoke access Share a Design Leave threaded comments, mention people, resolve threads, and control email Review a Design with Comments Live co-editing needs no setup. When two people have the same saved design open, they see each other’s cursors, selections, and edits. Collaboration Model explains how live editing, access, and comments fit together. To try all three with a teammate, follow the Collaborative Editing tutorial.
Sharing and comments run under your permissions. Sharing needs the Share Design permission, and the people picker needs View All Users. See Permissions by Role.
