A workspace is a named grouping inside an organization that brings together the teams who do a piece of work, the environments they deploy to, and the designs and views they work on. Workspaces exist so an administrator can draw a boundary around a project or a stage of a pipeline, such as staging or production, and decide in one place which teams reach which infrastructure connections.
A workspace does two separate jobs, and keeping them apart is the key to the model:
It organizes resources. Designs and views live in a workspace, and the workspace decides which organization they are listed under. It grants connection access. Assigning a team to a workspace gives that team’s members read-only access to the connections in the workspace’s environments. That is the only access a team assignment grants. Workspaces and environments appear together in the Spaces area of Layer5 Cloud, which also shows counts of your organization’s environments, workspaces, and connections.
What a workspace contains 🔗 A workspace belongs to exactly one organization for its whole life. Editing a workspace changes its name, description, or metadata, never its organization. To have a workspace in another organization, create one there.
A workspace holds zero or more of each of the following:
Member How many workspaces it can be in What assigning it means Team Any number Members of the team gain read-only access to the connections in this workspace’s environments. The team must belong to the workspace’s organization. Environment Any number The environment’s connections become reachable by the workspace’s teams. The environment must belong to the workspace’s organization. Design At most one The design moves here. Assigning a design to a workspace removes it from the workspace it was in. View At most one The view moves here, the same way a design does. Assigning a team or environment that is already in the workspace changes nothing. Creating a workspace assigns no team and no environment; you add them afterward.
Designs live in one workspace at a time 🔗 Because a design sits in at most one workspace, assigning it to a workspace is a move, not a copy. The workspace a design sits in decides two things:
The organization under which the design is listed. The organization in which the Share Design permission is checked when someone shares the design. Moving a design requires the Assign Designs to Workspaces permission in the destination workspace’s organization. Layer5 Cloud does not also require access to the workspace the design leaves. When you list the designs you can add to a workspace, the list shows only designs you own that are not already in it.
Who sees a workspace and what a team assignment grants 🔗 Workspace visibility is organization-wide by design. Every member of an organization can list and open every workspace in that organization, whether or not one of their teams is assigned to it. Team assignment does not narrow what you see. The Workspaces, Environments, and connection areas of the Cloud UI appear only to people who hold the matching View Workspace, View Environment, and View Connections permissions.
Team assignment grants exactly one thing: read-only access to the connections, and their credentials, in the workspace’s environments.
It does not grant access to designs. Placing a private design in a workspace and assigning a team to that workspace does not let the team read the design. To give people access to a design, share it with them; see Share a Design.
The access chain for connections 🔗 A member of a team reaches a connection through a chain of four live links. Breaking any one of them ends the access.
Link Created by Broken by 1. User is a member of a team Adding the user to the team Removing the user from the team 2. Team is assigned to a workspace Assign team to workspace Removing the team from the workspace, or deleting the workspace 3. Environment is assigned to the workspace Assign environment to workspace Removing the environment from the workspace, or deleting either one 4. Connection is assigned to the environment Assign connections to environment Removing the connection from the environment, or deleting the environment The result is read-only. Modifying or deleting a connection still requires owning it. Two other routes reach a connection independently of this chain: owning it, and holding the View All Organizations key. See Environments for the full access rules.
Lifecycle 🔗 Default workspace. Every organization receives a workspace when it is created, so designs always have somewhere to live. Names. A name and description are each limited to 255 characters. Names are not unique: two workspaces in one organization can share a name. Editing. Only the fields you change are updated; the others keep their values. The last workspace stays. An organization always keeps at least one workspace. Deleting the last one is refused with cannot delete workspace: at least one workspace must exist for the organization. Two simultaneous deletes cannot both succeed and leave the organization empty. Deleting a workspace ends every team, environment, design, and view assignment it holds, in one step. The teams, environments, designs, views, and connections themselves remain. Designs and views that were in the workspace are left in no workspace until you assign them to another one. Team members lose any connection access that flowed through the deleted workspace. Recent activity 🔗 Each workspace records an activity log: creating, editing, and deleting the workspace, and assigning or removing teams, environments, designs, and views. Every entry carries the email address of the person who acted. Reading the log requires the View Workspace permission.
Permissions 🔗 Every workspace action is checked in the organization that owns the workspace. Creating a workspace is checked in the organization you create it in.
Workspace permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Workspace See all workspaces within an organization ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Workspace Create new workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Edit Workspace Edit workspace and it's team and environment membership -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Delete Workspace Dissolve workspace and all team and environment memberships. Leave associated resources intact -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign team to workspace Add new team to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove team from workspace Remove team from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign environment to workspace Add new environment to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove environment from workspace Remove environment from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Designs to Workspaces Assign designs to workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove Designs from Workspaces Remove designs from workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Views to Workspace Add new views to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Unassign Views from Workspace Remove views from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Plan availability 🔗 Workspaces Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise My Workspace My Workspace is your always available, primary space for storing designs, views, and models that you own. ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included Shared Workspaces Shared Workspaces are collaborative spaces that you can use to store and collaborate on files within and between teams. Easily share files with customizable permissions (edit, comment, view). Create up to 10 shared workspaces per organization. -Not included ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included The matrix shows how workspaces are packaged across plans. Layer5 Cloud enforces no plan check on workspace actions: creating, editing, deleting, and assigning work the same on every plan, governed only by the permissions above.
Related 🔗 Manage Workspaces covers creating, editing, and deleting workspaces and assigning their members. Environments explains the deploy targets a workspace exposes. Teams explains how teams group people.

Right-clicking an empty part of the canvas - anywhere no component sits - opens the Canvas Actions menu. Where the component context menu acts on one component, this menu acts on the canvas as a whole: undoing and redoing, pasting, selecting everything, capturing the canvas as an image, and reaching help.
The menu adapts to the mode you are in. Commenting and pasting, for example, are offered in Designer mode but not in Operator mode, where the canvas reflects discovered infrastructure rather than a design you are authoring.
Editing actions 🔗 Action Shortcut Behavior Add Comment M Drops a comment at the point you right-clicked. Designer mode only. See Review a Design with Comments. Undo Cmd/Ctrl + Z Reverses the last change to the design: components, configuration, styles, relationships, annotations and layer toggles. A message confirms the change was reverted, or reports that no changes remain. Redo Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + Z or Cmd/Ctrl + Y Re-applies the last undone change. Paste Cmd/Ctrl + V Pastes the clipboard contents at the cursor position. Designer mode only. Select All Cmd/Ctrl + A Selects every component on the canvas. Reset Design Clears every component from the canvas. Designer mode only, and destructive - see below. Reset Design 🔗 Reset Design removes everything currently on the canvas. Kanvas asks you to confirm before it does, and the confirmation reminds you that undo is usually the better tool if you only want to step back a few changes. The confirmation dialog carries a “don’t show this again” checkbox; ticking it stores that preference against your user settings, and the reset then happens immediately on every subsequent use.
Screenshot Canvas 🔗 Take Screenshot captures the canvas as drawn - components, relationships and annotations - and downloads it to your machine as a PNG. The file is named Kanvas-<timestamp>.png, so repeated captures of the same design do not overwrite one another.
The capture is of the canvas, not your browser window: panels, the dock and the toolbar are not included. It records the canvas as currently viewed, so pan and zoom to frame what you want before you capture. Object controls and badges appear only when the canvas is zoomed in far enough, so zoom in first if you want them in the image.
This is the quickest way to put a design into a pull request, an incident write-up or a slide. When you need the design as data rather than as a picture - to hand to another tool, or to re-import later - use Exporting Designs instead.
Options 🔗 Options opens the canvas settings drawer. Each change saves to your user preferences on the server after a short pause, applies to every design you open and shows a confirmation message. Preferences belong to you, not to a design.
Option Default Effect Dark Theme - Switches the canvas between light and dark themes. Snap to Grid On Snaps objects to the grid as you drag. Hide Gridlines On Gridlines are hidden by default. Enable Dock On Off hides the whole bottom dock, including the drawing tools and pickers. Keyboard shortcuts still work. Show Reset Canvas Confirmation On Off makes Reset Design act immediately. Enable Pencil On Shows the Pencil tool in the dock. Enable Pen On Shows the Pen tool in the dock. Auto-pan on Drag Off Pans the view while you drag an object past the canvas edge. Kanvas turns it off on large designs, with a limit for each render mode. See Auto-pan on Drag. Max Canvas Zoom 30 Upper zoom limit, from 0.1 to 30. Min Canvas Zoom 0.1 Lower zoom limit, from 0.1 to 5. Enable Debugger Off Shows debugging aids. Relationship Evaluation Engine Automatic (recommended) Chooses how relationships are evaluated. Show Tutorial On Shows the in-app tutorial. Show Walkthrough On Shows the walkthrough. Render Fidelity - Sets how much detail the canvas draws, from full fidelity down to a wireframe, and can adapt as a design grows. See Render Modes. Operator mode offers only Show Tutorial and Show Walkthrough.
Shortcuts 🔗 Shortcuts (Cmd/Ctrl + /) opens the keyboard shortcut reference in the help drawer, listing the shortcuts available in both Designer and Operator modes.
View help center 🔗 Help Center (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + /) opens the in-app help modal. It gathers, in one place, every route by which you can learn more about Kanvas or reach someone who can help:
Card What it opens Documentation Guides, references and how-tos for Kanvas and Meshery. Video Tutorials Walkthroughs and demos in the Layer5 video library. Quick Tips An in-app tour of core Kanvas features, shown in a drawer beside the canvas. Academy Structured learning paths in Layer5 Cloud. Discussion Forum The Layer5 discussion forum, for questions and shared knowledge. Slack The Layer5 community Slack, for real-time conversation. Keyboard Shortcuts The same shortcut reference the Shortcuts action opens. Support A form for contacting the Kanvas team with a problem or a piece of feedback. Quick Tips and Keyboard Shortcuts open in a drawer alongside the canvas, so you can keep working while you read them. Support opens its form in a modal over the canvas. The remaining five cards open in a new tab. The Help Center is also reachable from the help button at the right-hand end of the dock.

body:
In this tutorial you design a CronJob that runs a small container every minute, deploy it, and watch Kubernetes turn the schedule into Jobs and the Jobs into Pods. Then you change the schedule in place and clean up. Scheduled work such as backups, report generation, and cache warming runs this way, and understanding the CronJob to Job to Pod chain is what lets you answer the two questions that matter in production: did it run, and where is its output.
What you will learn 🔗 How a CronJob creates a Job for each scheduled time, and how each Job creates a Pod that runs to completion. Why a Job’s Pod must use restartPolicy OnFailure or Never. How the history limits decide how many finished Jobs stay in the cluster, and what concurrencyPolicy and suspend control. Why the objects a controller creates are not part of your design, and how to find them in Operator anyway. Before you begin 🔗 A Kanvas environment with a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use Meshery Playground, a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a self-hosted feature prompt. Familiarity with Pods and the Kanvas Designer. If this is your first Kanvas tutorial, complete the Kubernetes Pods tutorial first. A short unique suffix for names and labels, such as your initials plus a number (jd42). Playground is shared with other users; replace <suffix> everywhere with yours. About 15 minutes, most of it waiting for scheduled runs. The scenario 🔗 You build one component. Kubernetes builds the rest:
CronJob hello-<suffix> schedule "*/1 * * * *" (in your design) | at each scheduled minute, the CronJob controller creates v Job hello-<suffix>-<n> (not in your design) | the Job controller creates v Pod hello-<suffix>-<n>-<random> runs busybox, prints the date, exits Design the CronJob 🔗 Start a new design and name it, for example cronjobs-<suffix>. Kanvas saves the design automatically a few seconds after each change; see Save Designs for how saving and versions work. Add a CronJob component from the Kubernetes model. Set its name to hello-<suffix> and, on the Labels tab, add the label owner with your suffix as the value. Set the schedule to */1 * * * *, which means every minute. Under the job template, set the Job’s metadata label owner: <suffix>, and set the same label on the Pod template’s metadata. Labels on the CronJob itself are not copied to the Jobs and Pods it creates; the template labels are. In the Pod template spec, set the restart policy to OnFailure and add one container: Name: hello Image: busybox:1.36 Command: /bin/sh, -c, date; echo Hello from the Kubernetes cluster What just happened. A CronJob is a Job factory. Its schedule uses standard cron syntax (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and is evaluated in the time zone of the cluster’s controller manager unless you set timeZone, such as Europe/Berlin. Its jobTemplate is a complete Job spec, and the Job’s template is a complete Pod spec. A Job runs its Pod to completion, so the Pod’s restart policy must be OnFailure (retry in the same Pod) or Never (create a new Pod on failure); the Pod default, Always, is rejected.
Check your work. The CronJob is on the canvas with no warning badge. If a yellow triangle badge appears, select it to jump to the field that does not match the schema.
Validate, dry run, and deploy 🔗 Run Validate from the Actions menu. It checks the component against its schema in your browser and does not contact the cluster. Its findings are advisory. Run Dry Run. The cluster’s API server checks the CronJob with its full validation without persisting it. Run Deploy, select the environment that holds your cluster connection, and deploy. What just happened. The dry run is the first check that applies Kubernetes rules beyond the schema, such as the allowed restart policies and the cron syntax. Deploy creates the CronJob and labels it with the design’s id. Nothing runs yet: the CronJob controller creates the first Job at the next scheduled minute.
Check your work. The deploy summary lists Deployed CronJob "hello-<suffix>". If the dry run reports an error on the restart policy, set it to OnFailure. An error on the schedule means the cron expression is malformed. Select a dry-run error to open the configurator at that field.
Observe the Jobs and Pods 🔗 Wait two or three minutes, then switch to Operator. With the design loaded, Operator opens a view scoped to the design, and that view shows only the CronJob: Kanvas puts the design’s id label on the objects it applies, and the Jobs and Pods are created by Kubernetes, not by Kanvas. To see the whole chain, filter the view by the label owner=<suffix>, or search for hello-<suffix>, and include the kinds CronJob, Job, and Pod. Search matches part of a resource name, and Job and Pod names start with the CronJob’s name. Select one of the Pods. Its status chip reads Succeeded: the container printed its message and exited with code 0. Read the output of a run. Open a log session on one of the Pods (Initiate Log Session), or with kubectl access run kubectl logs job/<job-name>. The output is the date followed by Hello from the Kubernetes cluster. Operator shows a snapshot of the cluster, fetched when you open a view, change a filter, or change the selected cluster. To see Jobs created since the last fetch, change a filter or reopen the view.
What just happened. Every minute the CronJob controller created a Job named after the CronJob and the scheduled time, and the Job controller created a Pod for it. Wait five minutes and fetch again: no more than three completed Jobs remain. The CronJob keeps successfulJobsHistoryLimit (default 3) successful Jobs and failedJobsHistoryLimit (default 1) failed Jobs, and deletes older ones together with their Pods. Keep these limits low on a busy schedule: finished Jobs and Pods stay in the cluster and count toward any object-count quota in the namespace.
Three more fields shape a CronJob’s behavior:
Field Default Effect concurrencyPolicy Allow What happens when a run is due while the previous one is still running: Allow starts another, Forbid skips the new run, Replace stops the old run and starts the new one. suspend false true stops new runs without deleting the CronJob. Runs already started finish. startingDeadlineSeconds none How late a missed run may still start. A run that misses its deadline is skipped and counted as missed. Check your work. If no Jobs appear after several minutes, check the schedule and confirm the CronJob is not suspended. A Pod in Error or a Job that keeps retrying means the container failed: read its logs. A Pod stuck in Pending means the cluster could not schedule it or pull the image.
Change the schedule and redeploy 🔗 Return to Designer and change the schedule to */2 * * * *, every second minute. Set successfulJobsHistoryLimit to 1. Deploy again. What just happened. Deploy replaces an existing object in place, so the CronJob keeps its name and history and the controller uses the new schedule from the next run. After a few minutes Operator shows a new Job every two minutes and only one completed Job at a time. To pause the CronJob instead of changing its schedule, set suspend to true and deploy.
Changes to the job template apply only to Jobs created after the redeploy. Jobs and Pods that already exist keep the spec they were created with.
Check your work. In Operator, the CronJob’s newest Jobs are two minutes apart, and older successful Jobs disappear after the next run.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu in Designer. Undeploy deletes each component in the design by kind and name, which here is only the CronJob hello-<suffix>. The Jobs and Pods are not in the design. They are owned by the CronJob, and Kubernetes garbage collection removes owned objects after their owner is deleted. Fetch the Operator view again to confirm they are gone. If any remain, delete them with kubectl delete jobs -l owner=<suffix>.
Undeploy deletes any CronJob with the same name in that namespace, whoever created it, which is another reason to use unique names on a shared cluster. The design itself stays saved; delete it if you no longer need it.
What you learned 🔗 A CronJob creates a Job at each scheduled time, and each Job creates a Pod that runs to completion with restart policy OnFailure or Never. The history limits decide how many finished Jobs stay in the cluster; concurrencyPolicy, suspend, and startingDeadlineSeconds decide which runs start. Your design contains only the CronJob. Objects that controllers create carry the template labels, not the design’s id, so you find them in Operator by label or name. Deploying a changed design replaces the CronJob in place; the new schedule and template apply to future runs. Next steps 🔗 Deploying WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes - keep data across Pod restarts with PersistentVolumeClaims. Deploy a Design - the full Validate, Dry Run, Deploy, and Undeploy reference for everyday use. Operator - how Operator discovers cluster resources and what its views show.

In this tutorial you install Azure Service Operator (ASO) in your own Kubernetes cluster, then design an Azure resource group and a storage account inside it, deploy both from Kanvas, and find them in the Azure portal. You manage real Azure infrastructure with the same design, validate, and deploy loop you use for Kubernetes workloads, and the cluster keeps that infrastructure matched to the design.
The trade-off is indirection. Kanvas never calls Azure. It applies Kubernetes objects to your cluster, and ASO turns those objects into Azure resources in the background. A successful deploy means the cluster accepted the objects; the Azure resources follow a little later, and Azure-side failures surface on the objects in the cluster, not in the deploy summary.
What you will learn 🔗 ASO is a Kubernetes operator that turns custom resources into Azure resources, authenticating to Azure as a Service Principal whose credentials live in a Kubernetes Secret. Kanvas components from the Azure model are those ASO custom resources in design form, and their configurator forms come from the ASO schemas in the Meshery registry. Deploy applies custom resources to the cluster in one pass; ASO then reconciles each one with Azure on its own schedule. Azure resources have owners: a storage account belongs to a resource group, so the resource group must exist in Azure before the storage account can be created. Deleting a custom resource is how you delete the Azure resource it manages, which makes cleanup order matter. Before you begin 🔗 Your own cluster, never Meshery Playground. This tutorial puts real Azure credentials into a Secret in the cluster. Playground is a shared cluster, so anyone with access to it could read them. Use a self-hosted Meshery with a Kubernetes cluster you control. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. To install Meshery, see https://docs.meshery.io/installation. A connected cluster assigned to an environment. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them, so your cluster must be a connected Kubernetes connection that belongs to at least one environment. An Azure subscription and the Azure CLI. You need rights to create a Service Principal with the Contributor role on the subscription. Sign in with az login before you start. kubectl access to the same cluster. You install cert-manager and check ASO from the command line. Operator mode for verification (optional). Operator reads the cluster through Meshery Operator and MeshSync. Deploy does not need them; Operator does. A unique prefix. Storage account names are global across all of Azure. Pick a short prefix, such as your handle, and use it in every name. This tutorial uses alex. You need basic familiarity with Kubernetes and the Azure portal. You do not need to write YAML.
The scenario 🔗 You work with two designs. The first installs ASO; the second describes the Azure resources ASO creates.
Design 1: Azure Service Operator (cloned from the catalog) ASO operator, its custom resource definitions, and Secret aso-controller-settings ---- Service Principal credentials Design 2: alex-azure-resources (built by you) Resource Group alex-aso-rg location eastus ^ | owner | Storage Account alexasodemo01 location eastus, access tier Hot Kanvas Deploy --> Kubernetes custom resources --> ASO --> Azure subscription At the end, the portal shows resource group alex-aso-rg containing storage account alexasodemo01.
Phase 1: Create the Service Principal 🔗 ASO needs an Azure identity to act on your subscription. Create a Service Principal with the Contributor role scoped to the subscription:
az ad sp create-for-rbac -n azure-service-operator --role contributor --scopes /subscriptions/<AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID> Keep the output; you need three of its fields plus your subscription ID:
Output field Use it as appId AZURE_CLIENT_ID password AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET tenant AZURE_TENANT_ID (your subscription ID) AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID What just happened. You created a non-human identity in Microsoft Entra ID and granted it Contributor on the subscription. Everything ASO later does in Azure, it does as this identity, so its role assignment is the upper bound on what your designs can create. The password is shown only once; treat it like any other secret.
Phase 2: Install cert-manager 🔗 ASO serves admission webhooks that need TLS certificates, and it relies on cert-manager to issue them. Install cert-manager in the cluster before you install ASO:
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/jetstack/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.14.1/cert-manager.yaml Wait until the pods in the cert-manager namespace are running (kubectl get pods -n cert-manager) before you continue.
What just happened. cert-manager is now ready to issue certificates for any workload that asks. If ASO starts before cert-manager can serve its requests, the ASO webhooks have no certificates and the operator does not become ready.
Phase 3: Install ASO from the catalog 🔗 Find the Azure Service Operator design in the catalog and clone it. The clone is a private copy named Azure Service Operator (Copy), owned by you, in your selected workspace, and independent of the catalog original. Open the clone and select its aso-controller-settings Secret. Enter your four values under the keys AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, AZURE_CLIENT_ID, and AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET. Follow the format the Secret already uses: Kubernetes expects base64-encoded values under data and plain text under stringData. Deploy the design to the environment that holds your cluster. The Deploy stepper validates the design, asks for target environments, runs a dry run against the cluster, and then applies every component. Confirm the operator is running: its pod reaches the Running state in the operator’s namespace (azureserviceoperator-system in ASO’s standard install). What just happened. Deploy turned each component of the cloned design into a Kubernetes object and applied it: the operator’s workloads, the custom resource definitions that teach Kubernetes the Azure kinds, and the Secret. On startup ASO reads aso-controller-settings and uses those credentials for every Azure call. From now on, creating one of its custom resources in the cluster is a request to create the matching Azure resource.
The Secret now lives inside your design as well as in the cluster. Do not publish the design, and do not share it: anyone you share a design with can read, edit, clone, and re-share it, credentials included.
Phase 4: Design the resource group and storage account 🔗 Create a new design and name it alex-azure-resources. Kanvas saves it automatically once it has a name or a component. Search the component palette for Resource Group from the Azure model and add it. Its configurator opens as soon as it lands on the canvas. Name the resource group alex-aso-rg and set its location to eastus. Search the palette for Storage Account from the Azure model and add it. Name the storage account with your prefix, for example alexasodemo01. Azure requires storage account names to be globally unique, 3 to 24 characters, lowercase letters and digits only. In the storage account’s configuration, set the owning resource group to alex-aso-rg, set the location to eastus, and set the access tier to Hot (frequently accessed data) or Cool (infrequently accessed data, lower storage cost). Run Validate from the Actions menu. It lists every required field you have not set, per component. Fill each one in the configurator and validate again until the list is empty. What just happened. Each component is an ASO custom resource. Its configurator form is generated from that resource’s schema in the Meshery registry, which is why the fields are ASO’s fields and required ones carry a red asterisk. ASO uses the custom resource’s name as the Azure resource name by default. The owner field on the storage account is what places it inside the resource group in Azure; it is a reference by name, not a drawing on the canvas. Validate runs entirely in your browser against those schemas. It catches missing and malformed fields, never blocks you, and does not check Azure rules such as name uniqueness.
Phase 5: Deploy and let ASO reconcile 🔗 Deploy alex-azure-resources through the stepper to the same environment you used for ASO. On the Dry Run step, the cluster checks each custom resource against the ASO definitions installed in Phase 3. Fix any errors it reports before you continue. Finish the deployment. The summary lists a row per component and cluster, such as Deployed ResourceGroup "alex-aso-rg". What just happened. Deploy applied both custom resources in one pass. Kanvas orders components only by dependencies a design declares, so the storage account can reach the cluster at the same moment as the resource group. That is safe: ASO retries a resource whose owner is not ready yet until the owner exists in Azure, then creates it. The deploy summary reports what the cluster accepted. The Azure resources appear a minute or more later, once ASO has completed its calls to Azure. Every object Deploy applies carries a label with the design’s ID, which is how Operator finds them.
Deploy is idempotent: if you change the access tier and deploy again, Kanvas replaces the custom resource in place and ASO updates the storage account in Azure.
Verify 🔗 Check three places, from closest to the design to closest to Azure.
Operator. Open the design-scoped view from the design’s file menu (View in Operator). It filters on the design’s ID label, so it shows only the objects this design applied. Kinds outside the built-in Kubernetes lists appear under Custom Resources in the Layers panel. Operator draws a snapshot, not a live stream; reload the view or change a filter to fetch a fresh one. The cluster. kubectl get resourcegroups.resources.azure.com,storageaccounts.storage.azure.com -n default lists both custom resources. ASO reports progress through each resource’s Ready condition; kubectl describe shows the reason when a resource is not ready. The Azure portal. Open resource group alex-aso-rg and confirm that storage account alexasodemo01 is in it, in East US, with the access tier you chose. Clean up 🔗 These resources cost money while they exist. Remove them in this order.
Undeploy alex-azure-resources. Undeploy deletes each component’s custom resource from the cluster. ASO deletes the Azure resource when its custom resource is deleted.
Confirm in the portal that the storage account and the resource group are gone. Azure deletions take a few minutes.
If Undeploy reports an error, or the custom resources are still in the cluster, delete them directly and confirm in the portal again:
kubectl delete storageaccounts.storage.azure.com alexasodemo01 -n default kubectl delete resourcegroups.resources.azure.com alex-aso-rg -n default Undeploy the Azure Service Operator design last. It removes the operator and its custom resource definitions. If you remove the operator first, nothing is left to delete the Azure resources, and you must remove them in the portal yourself.
Remove the credentials. Delete the Service Principal in Azure if you no longer need it, and delete your cloned operator design so the credentials no longer live in your workspace.
Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix Dry Run or Deploy fails with meshery-server-1096 Kubernetes cluster is unavailable. None of the selected targets resolves to a connected Kubernetes context. Confirm the cluster’s connection status is Connected and that the connection is assigned to the environment you selected. Upload a fresh kubeconfig if the credentials changed. Deploy fails with meshery-server-1073 Unable to deploy the selected design. This error wraps most hard deploy failures. A common cause is a connection that is not assigned to the selected environment. Open the error’s Details to read the inner error. Assign the connection to the environment and confirm it is Connected. The resources design fails dry run or deploy because the cluster does not recognize the Resource Group or Storage Account kind. ASO’s custom resource definitions are not installed, or the operator design has not finished deploying. Deploy the Azure Service Operator design first and confirm the operator pod is running, then deploy the resources design again. Operator shows Uh-oh. Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster? Operator has no MeshSync data for the selected cluster. Confirm Meshery Operator and MeshSync are running in the cluster. Deploy does not depend on them; verify with kubectl and the portal in the meantime. The deploy succeeded, but nothing appears in Azure and the custom resource’s status reports an authorization error. The Service Principal lacks rights on the subscription, or the Secret holds wrong values. Check the Contributor role assignment and the four Secret values. Correct the Secret in the operator design and deploy it again; if ASO keeps reporting the old error, restart the operator pod so it rereads the Secret. The storage account never becomes ready and its status reports a name error. The name is taken elsewhere in Azure or breaks the 3 to 24 lowercase letters and digits rule. Choose another name with your prefix, update the component, and deploy again. Where to go next 🔗 Deploying designs covers the Deploy stepper, targets, and the deploy summary in full. Undeploying designs explains what Undeploy removes and what it leaves in place. Cloning a design describes how catalog clones are owned and stored. Operator explains how Operator draws what runs in your cluster. Deploy AWS EC2 instances applies the same operator pattern to AWS. The official ASO documentation at https://azure.github.io/azure-service-operator/ lists every Azure resource kind ASO supports and its fields.

An embedded design is an interactive picture of a design on your own page. Readers can pan and zoom it, but cannot edit it. It is a static export: Kanvas gives you a JavaScript module file and a snippet that loads it. How an embed works 🔗 It is a snapshot. The file holds the canvas as it was at export time: node positions, element styles, and inline background images converted to data URLs where the fetch succeeded. Later edits to the design do not change an exported file. Re-export to refresh it. It needs no Layer5 Cloud at view time. The page makes no request to Layer5 Cloud, so the embed works for private designs and keeps working if the design is deleted. Anyone who can read your page can read the embedded design data. It is view only. Layout is fixed to the exported positions. Selection and box selection are disabled, zoom is limited to 0.5x to 6.6x, and there is no editing, component configuration, relationship evaluation, or live cluster data. It loads one library. The page fetches the Cytoscape library (version 3.27.0) from a public CDN, so viewers need outbound access to it. A Meshery logo link, which opens meshery.io, is drawn at the bottom right of the canvas. No option removes it. It has no parameters. Width, height, theme, background, and zoom are not options. The container’s CSS sets the size. There is no iframe embed. Kanvas offers no embed URL for the app itself. Embedding needs no permission key and no paid plan. Embed a design in an HTML page 🔗 Open the design, choose Export, and select Embed Design. Kanvas loads the design if it is not the open one, waits for it to render plus 3 seconds, and then generates the file. A failure shows “Failed to generate Embed Code for ”. Download the JavaScript file, then copy the embed code. Place the file next to your page, or anywhere your page can reference, and paste the snippet:
The container id is embedded-design- plus the design id, lowercased, with spaces replaced by hyphens. The script file name is embedded-design- plus the design name, lowercased, with spaces replaced by hyphens, plus .js. Other characters in the name are not changed, so avoid unusual characters in design names. Keep the id in the snippet equal to the id the script expects. Two requirements follow from this snippet: Serve the page over HTTP or HTTPS. Module scripts do not load from file://. Give the container a real height. The div fills 100 percent of its parent, which collapses to zero in a parent with no height. Embed in WordPress 🔗 WordPress has no Kanvas-specific plugin. You add the script to your theme and the snippet to a Custom HTML block. Create a js folder in your active theme and copy the downloaded file into it. Enqueue the file as a script module from the theme’s functions.php, replacing design.js with your file name: function kanvas_design_script() { $script_uri = get_template_directory_uri() . '/js/design.js'; wp_enqueue_script_module('kanvas-design', $script_uri, array(), '1.1.0'); } add_action('wp_enqueue_scripts', 'kanvas_design_script'); In the post, add a Custom HTML block containing only the
from the snippet. Because the theme already loads the module, leave out the Parameter Required Meaning src Yes Path to the exported JavaScript file. id Yes Unique container id for this embed on the page. size No full (default, 80 percent wide) or half (50 percent wide). Ignored when style is set. style No Inline CSS for the container. Overrides size. Place the exported file near the page and reference it: {{< meshery-design-embed src="../path/to/your-design.js" id="your-unique-design-id" size="half" >}} A live example, rendered from a design exported from Kanvas: Open Design Related 🔗 Export Designs covers the other formats. Share Designs covers live access to a design for specific people.

An environment is a named group of connections, such as Kubernetes clusters, together with the credentials those connections use. Environments matter for two reasons:
An environment is a deploy target. When you deploy a design, you choose the environment to deploy it to, and the design deploys to that environment’s connections. An environment is how a workspace exposes connections. A workspace never holds connections directly. It holds environments, and teams assigned to the workspace reach the connections inside them. Group connections the way you deploy: one environment per pipeline stage, region, or purpose, so that choosing a target means choosing one environment instead of a list of clusters.
Scope and membership 🔗 An environment belongs to one organization for its whole life. Editing an environment never changes its organization.
Relationship Rule Connection in environments A connection can be in any number of environments. Adding it to one does not remove it from another. Environment in workspaces An environment can be in any number of workspaces in its organization. Who sees an environment Every member of the organization can list and open every environment in it. Team membership does not narrow the list. Names and descriptions are limited to 255 characters. Names are not unique: two environments in one organization can share a name.
Choosing an environment at deploy time 🔗 Deploying a design happens in Kanvas. The deploy action offers environments from your organization’s whole list at the moment you deploy. The workspace the design sits in does not limit that choice, so a design in a staging workspace can still be deployed to a production environment. Choose the target deliberately. See Deploy a Design.
Access to connections and credentials 🔗 A user can read a connection, and the credential it uses, when any one of these holds:
Route What it grants How it ends You own the connection Read, modify, and delete - You belong to a team assigned to a workspace that contains an environment that contains the connection Read only Removing you from the team, the team from the workspace, the environment from the workspace, or the connection from the environment, or deleting the workspace or environment You hold the View All Organizations key Read access to every connection and credential in every organization Losing the key Only ownership allows changes. Access through a workspace is always read-only, however many workspaces lead to the same connection.
This chain governs connections and credentials only. Designs and views are not opened by environment or workspace assignment; share a design to give someone access to it. See Workspaces for the full access chain.
Platform-provisioned environments 🔗 Some environments are created by Layer5 Cloud itself to hold organization configuration, such as sign-in providers or the mail server. They appear in your organization’s environment list, but they are not deploy targets you manage:
They cannot be deleted. The attempt is refused with this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be deleted here. Connections cannot be assigned to them or detached from them through the normal environment controls. They cannot be added to a workspace. If one is already in a workspace, you can remove it. Every environment you create is an ordinary environment.
Deleting an environment 🔗 Deleting an environment ends its connection assignments and its workspace assignments in one step. The connections remain, and keep their membership in any other environment. Teams that reached a connection only through the deleted environment lose that access.
Limits and behavior 🔗 Editing replaces both fields. An environment edit sets both the name and the description. A field left out of the request becomes empty, so always send both. Organization is fixed. An edit never moves an environment to another organization. Removing a connection that was never assigned is refused with no such connection assignment. Permissions 🔗 Every environment action is checked in the organization that owns the environment. Creating an environment is checked in the organization you create it in.
Environment permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Environment See all environments within an workspace. ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create Environment Create a new environment -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Edit Environment Edit environment and it connection membership -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Delete Environment Dissolve environment and all connection memberships. Leave associated resources intact. -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign connections to environment Add new connections to environments -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove connections from environment Remove connections from environment, -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign environment to workspace Add new environment to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove environment from workspace Remove environment from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Plan availability 🔗 The feature matrix lists environments under the Enterprise plan. Layer5 Cloud does not refuse environment actions by plan: creating, editing, deleting, and assigning environments are governed only by the permissions above.
Related 🔗 Manage Environments covers creating environments and assigning connections. Workspaces explains how environments reach teams. Promote a Design from Staging to Production puts environments and workspaces to work together.

Integrations connect Layer5 Cloud to systems outside it. Today that means GitHub, for importing infrastructure files and posting pull-request snapshots, and the infrastructure connections that Meshery Servers register. This page lists every integration the product offers, what each one does, and where to configure it, so you can tell quickly whether Layer5 Cloud can connect to the tool you use.
Integration matrix 🔗 Integration What it does Where to start GitHub (Layer5 GitHub App) Reads the repositories you grant, imports Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Docker Compose files, and Meshery designs as private designs, and can commit a snapshot workflow to a repository. Connect GitHub GitHub Actions (Kanvas Snapshot) Posts a picture of your infrastructure on every pull request. Use GitHub Actions Meshery Server Registers each Meshery Server as a connection, so you can see and manage the servers in your organization. Listed under Meshery on the Integrations tab. Kubernetes Lists the clusters your Meshery Servers manage, so you can assign them to environments. Manage Environments Prometheus Lists Prometheus connections that Meshery Servers report. Listed under Prometheus on the Integrations tab. Meshery Servers register Meshery, Kubernetes, and Prometheus connections. Layer5 Cloud has no setup wizard for them. The Integrations tab shows what the servers in your organization registered, and you assign those connections to environments to decide which teams reach them.
Not available 🔗 Layer5 Cloud does not offer these integrations:
Slack, PagerDuty, and Datadog. Cloud has no outbound connector for chat, paging, or alerting tools. It notifies people by email, subject to each user’s notification preferences, and records activity in the event log. Grafana and Helm. The Integrations tab shows cards for both, but they cannot be opened. GitLab, Bitbucket, and GitHub Enterprise Server. GitHub on github.com is the only supported source host. Who can use integrations 🔗 The Integrations tab appears for roles that hold the View Connections permission. Deleting a connection needs Delete a connection, and you can delete only connections you own.
Integration permissions by role Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Connections View all connections within an environment ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Delete a connection Delete a connection -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign connections to environment Add new connections to environments -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed The GitHub connection is personal: each user connects their own GitHub account, and no one else in the organization can use it. See Connect GitHub for details.
Next steps 🔗 Connect GitHub to import designs from your repositories. Use GitHub Actions to add pull-request snapshots. Feature Availability by Plan shows which plans include GitOps integrations.

body:
Kanvas Snapshot turns an infrastructure-as-code file into a picture of the design it describes. It runs as a GitHub workflow or as a Helm plugin, not in the Kanvas canvas, so reviewers see the shape of a change (which components exist and how they connect) without reading YAML or opening Kanvas.
A snapshot is standalone. It never connects to your cluster and never deploys anything. It reads the file you point it at, builds a design from it, and renders that design to an image.
What a snapshot does 🔗 Reads a Kubernetes manifest, a Docker Compose file, or a Helm chart. Builds a Kanvas design from it. The design imports the same way any file imported into Kanvas does. Renders the design to an image. The render runs on Layer5’s hosted Meshery Playground when it is reachable. Otherwise the workflow starts a temporary local Meshery on a KinD cluster inside the GitHub runner. Delivers the image: as a comment on the pull request, or as a URL printed in your terminal. The pull request comment links the image to a copy of the design in the catalog and a copy you can edit in the Playground. Each later run of the workflow updates the same comment instead of adding another.

body:
A key is a named permission for exactly one action, such as Create Organization, Approve Catalog Request, or Download Token. Every authorization decision in Layer5 Cloud comes down to one question: does this user hold the key this action requires, in this organization? Understanding keys tells you why a user can or cannot do something, and whether the model fits the access rules you need.
How a key reaches a user 🔗 Keys roll up in three layers. A keychain groups related keys, a role groups keychains, and a user holds roles in an organization or a team. A user never receives a key directly: granting a key means placing it in a keychain that belongs to a role the user holds.
Keys, keychains, and roles are defined once for the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment. They are not copied or customized per organization. What varies per organization is which roles a user holds there. A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys from every role they hold in that organization, so the same person can hold a key in one organization and lack it in another. Holding an additional role only adds keys; it never removes any. Provider Admin holds every key and passes every check in every organization. Security Boundaries explains why the organization is the authorization boundary.
A default installation ships more than 240 keys grouped into 30 default keychains. The system account owns every default key and keychain.
Anatomy of a key 🔗 The Keys tab of the Security page lists each key with these fields:
Field Meaning Key ID A UUID that identifies the key. Name The action the key grants, for example Create Token. Description What the action does. Category The resource the key acts on, for example Token or Keychains. Subcategory The default keychain family the key belongs to, for example Security Management. Owner The account that owns the key. Default keys are owned by the system. Created At, Deleted At When the key was created and, if deleted, when. Most keys follow one of four shapes. A few grant an action that is not a simple change to a resource.
Type Grants Example Create Creating a resource Create Organization View Seeing a resource or a list View Keys Edit Changing a resource Edit Keychain Delete Removing a resource Delete Token Action A workflow step Approve Catalog Request Where a key takes effect 🔗 A key has an effect only where something checks it. Two places do:
The server. On a guarded action, the server resolves the organization of the request and tests whether the user holds the required key there. A missing key returns HTTP 403 with a JSON body. This check is what actually protects the action. The interface. The Layer5 Cloud UI reads your effective keys for the organization in context and disables or hides controls for actions you cannot perform. Not every key is checked in both places. Some security keys are enforced only by the interface: the server does not test Create Token or Delete Token. Changes to keys, keychains, and roles are checked on the server, which also requires the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. The Security reference lists which security keys the server enforces.
Because a key grants nothing unless a check names it, a custom key is only a record. Adding one to a keychain and a role changes no behavior anywhere.
Who can see and change keys 🔗 Every signed-in user can open the Keys tab. It lists the system’s keys plus any keys you created, and searches by key name. Viewing keys requires no key on the server.
Creating or editing a key, including changing which keychains carry it, requires the Edit Key key. Deleting a key requires the Delete Key key. Both belong to the Provider Management keychain, which only Provider Admin holds by default, and the server also requires the caller to hold the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. Only a Provider Admin can change which keys a keychain carries or which keychains a role includes. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, Layer5 operates the Provider Admin role, so organizations cannot change keys. On a self-hosted deployment, the operator’s Provider Admins can.
Deleting a key is a soft delete. The key stops granting access immediately and disappears from every keychain that contained it. Because keys are deployment-wide, editing or deleting one changes access for every organization at once.
Auditing key use 🔗 Keys do not carry a usage counter; the Keys tab has no “last used” column. What a key’s use leaves behind is the event the action produced, and those events are what you audit. The Audit Logs page answers who did what, and when:
User ID - the account that performed the action, which is the account whose key was exercised. Category and Action - what was done, for example a workspace being created or a team being deleted. These correspond to the capability the key grants. Acted Upon - the resource the action affected. Description and Created At - the detail of the event and when it occurred. Filter by actor to follow one user’s activity, or by category and action to see everyone who exercised a capability over a period. The log you read belongs to the organization you currently have selected.
Tracing a missing permission 🔗 When a user cannot perform an action, work from the key outward:
Identify the key the action requires. A 403 response or a disabled control both point to a missing key. Find the default keychain and the roles that carry that key in the Roles and Permissions reference. Check which roles the user holds in the organization the request ran in, not in the organization they usually work in. Grant a role that carries the key in that organization. Do not add the keychain to a shared role unless every holder of that role in every organization should gain it. Limits 🔗 Keys do not rotate or expire. A key grants its action until it is deleted or removed from the user’s roles. Keys have no per-key usage counter. Use the Audit Logs page instead. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, only Provider Admins edit or delete keys. A key and its keychains are deployment-wide. Organizations tailor access by assigning roles, not by changing keys.

This guide covers the administrator tasks for teams. For what a team is and how it grants access, read the Teams concept.
Team permissions Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin Create Team Establish new team for organizing groups of users and resource access. -Not granted ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Edit Team Edit a team and add new members to it. -Not granted ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Delete Team Dissolve a team and all user memberships. Leave associated resources intact. -Not granted ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View All Teams See all teams within an organization. See all members of all teams. ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Add User to Team Directly create a new user account within a team. -Not granted ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove User from Team Discontinue user membership of a team and team resources. -Not granted ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Leave Team Leave a team ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed -Not granted ✓Allowed Assign team to workspace Add new team to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Create a team 🔗 Needs: the Create Team permission in your current organization.
A team takes a name and a description. The name is required on the Teams page; Layer5 Cloud does not check it for uniqueness or length beyond 255 characters. You can pick initial members from the organization’s users in the same step.
The creator becomes the team’s owner, a member, and a Team Admin. Members chosen at creation are added as plain members with no role.
The team is created in the organization you have selected. Confirm the organization switcher shows the organization you intend before you create it.
Add members 🔗 Needs: Team Admin or owner of the team, or Provider Admin.
Make sure each person is already a member of the organization. Add them first if not. Add them to the team. Added people receive an email unless they have turned off organization and team user-management notifications. Adding an existing member is harmless and changes nothing.
Adding someone to the team does not give them a role in it. A member with no role holds only what they receive through their organization roles and the team’s workspace assignments.
Make a member a Team Admin 🔗 Needs: Team Admin of the team, Organization Admin or a holder of Assign User Roles, or Provider Admin.
Team Admin is the only role offered for team scope. Assigning it sets the person’s role list in that team: the roles you submit replace the roles they held there, and an empty list removes every team role while keeping the membership. The person must belong to the organization. Granting the role to someone not yet on the team also adds them to it.
Team Admin permissions apply across the whole organization, not just this team. See How a team grants access.
Remove a member or leave a team 🔗 You are You can Team Admin removing someone else Remove them A member without Team Admin Leave the team (remove yourself) A Team Admin Not remove yourself; another Team Admin or a Provider Admin removes you The owner Not leave; delete the team instead Provider Admin Remove anyone except the owner removing themselves Removal ends the person’s membership and all their roles in the team. It leaves their organization membership and other teams unchanged. A removed owner remains the owner of record.
Give a team access to a workspace 🔗 Needs: Assign team to workspace in the workspace’s organization (Organization Admin, Workspace Admin, Academy Admin, Provider Admin).
Assign the team to the workspace. The team and the workspace must belong to the same organization. Unassigning needs Remove team from workspace. See Workspaces.
Delete a team 🔗 Needs: Organization Admin or Owner, Provider Admin, or the person who is both owner and Team Admin of the team. Team Admin alone and owner alone are refused.
Deleting is irreversible and removes only the team record: members keep their user accounts, and resources remain. Before you delete, do these so no access remains:
Remove every member from the team. Unassign the team from each workspace it has access to. Limits and failure modes 🔗 Deleting the team does not remove its members’ team roles or workspace assignments on its own; do the steps above. Updates that fail partway can leave a team without its creator as member. If the creator is not listed, add them to the team. A team cannot be moved to another owner. Plan to keep at least one other Team Admin so someone can administer the team if the owner leaves the organization.

Operator mode is Kanvas’s view of what is running. Designer mode works on what you intend to run. Operator draws the Kubernetes resources found in your connected clusters on the same canvas, shows each one’s recorded state, and gives you actions against the live workloads: open a shell, follow logs, run a load test, or jump back to the design that produced a resource.
Operator with no Kubernetes context selected. Choose one or more clusters to draw resources. Where Operator data comes from 🔗 Kanvas does not talk to your clusters directly. Four pieces sit between a cluster and the canvas:
Meshery Operator runs in each connected cluster. It deploys MeshSync and a message broker. MeshSync discovers the cluster’s resources and records them. It also carries out terminal and log requests inside the cluster. Meshery Server stores the discovered inventory and relays terminal and log traffic through the broker. Kanvas runs inside the Meshery you operate. Kanvas queries Meshery Server and draws the result. This is why Operator mode needs a Meshery deployment that can reach your clusters, and why the hosted kanvas.new site does not offer it. Design, validate, and deploy do not depend on Meshery Operator. Operator mode does, and so do the terminal and log actions. See How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud for the wider picture.
The canvas is a snapshot 🔗 Operator draws a snapshot of Meshery Server’s inventory, not a continuous feed. MeshSync keeps that inventory current in Meshery, but Kanvas re-reads it only when you:
load or create a view, change a filter, or change the selected clusters. Resources that appear, change, or disappear in the cluster show up on the canvas after one of those triggers. The Details panel works the same way: it fetches a resource once when you open it. When you need current state, change a filter or reselect the cluster.
What one snapshot contains 🔗 Meshery turns the inventory into a design: each resource becomes a component, and Meshery evaluates relationships between them to draw edges. Kanvas then lays the result out with a force-directed layout. Each snapshot is limited to 100 resources, the first page, with no paging and no notice that anything was left out. The Layers panel counts every matching resource, so a count can exceed what is drawn. Narrow the filters, or use a view for one slice, until the resources you need are within 100.
Resources deployed from a Kanvas design carry a design identity label. Those nodes show a Meshery badge that opens the source design. Container nodes with an open terminal or log session show a terminal badge.
Choosing what to draw 🔗 Cluster selection comes from the Meshery context selector, not from Kanvas. Everything else is a filter, set in the Layers panel or in the typing filter at its top.
Filter Matches search Resource names containing the text namespaces Resources in those namespaces kinds Resources of those kinds models Resources of those models labels Resources carrying any of those key=value labels Filter types combine with AND, and values within a type combine with OR. A new view starts with kinds Node and Namespace so the first snapshot is small. The Layers panel groups kinds, each with a count, so you can toggle them without typing:
Group Kinds Cluster Namespaces, Nodes, ResourceQuotas, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, LimitRanges Workloads Deployments, Pods, ReplicaSets, ReplicationControllers, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs Configurations ConfigMaps, Secrets, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings, PodDisruptionBudgets, PriorityClasses, RuntimeClasses, Leases, MutatingWebhookConfigurations Networking Services, Ingresses, IngressClasses, NetworkPolicies, Endpoints, EndpointSlices Storage PersistentVolumeClaims, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, VolumeAttachments Monitoring Events, HorizontalPodAutoscalers, VerticalPodAutoscalers Custom Resources Every other kind MeshSync has discovered The filter menu: search, namespaces, kinds, models, and labels. Every filter change refetches the snapshot and autosaves the open view. Selecting a resource opens the Details panel; search narrows what is drawn and does not select anything. See Resource Details for the panel.
When the canvas is empty 🔗 What you see Meaning Please select one or more Kubernetes clusters. No cluster is selected in the context selector. No data available for the current view, with removable filter chips The filters match nothing. Remove or loosen a chip. Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster? or No MeshSync data available for the selected cluster The selected cluster returned no inventory. Check that Meshery Operator and MeshSync are running and connected. Kanvas shows no separate notice when a cluster disconnects or MeshSync is missing. An empty canvas is the signal. While a snapshot loads, a Fetching resources notice shows; a failure shows Failed to fetch resources.
Operating on running workloads 🔗 Three actions send requests back down the same path. Each is offered on specific kinds.
Action Kinds Guide Interactive terminal Pod, Container Open an Interactive Terminal Log streaming Pod, Container Stream Container Logs Performance test Service, Ingress Run a Performance Test For a terminal or log session, Kanvas asks Meshery Server, which signals MeshSync through the broker. MeshSync opens the shell or log stream in the cluster and sends output back over the broker. Meshery Server preprocesses it and delivers it to your browser over a WebSocket subscription. Input travels the opposite way. Each session has its own identifier, so streams for several open sessions stay separate.
A performance test is different: Meshery Server generates the load itself against the URL you give it. It does not go through MeshSync.
Why terminal and log errors are quiet 🔗 Meshery Server reports failures such as an unready broker or a missing container, but Kanvas does not request or display those error fields for terminal and log sessions. A failed start looks like an empty tab. When a session is blank, check the cluster connection, Meshery Operator, and MeshSync first.
Views 🔗 A view saves a set of filters so a slice of your infrastructure comes back on demand. The Operator view for a design shows only the resources that design deployed. See Operator Views.
Where Operator is available 🔗 Environment Operator mode Self-hosted Meshery or Meshery you run, with Meshery Operator in the cluster Available Hosted kanvas.new Not available. Kanvas shows a self-hosted-feature prompt. Meshery Playground Disabled by the Playground’s capability configuration. Kanvas gates Operator mode on the provider enabling the Operator capability. It does not apply role or plan checks to the mode switch itself. See Feature Availability and Permissions by Role for the role and plan matrix.
What Operator does not do 🔗 It does not stream continuous updates to the canvas. It does not show live CPU or memory utilization, per-pod metrics, or time series. It does not change cluster resources. Deploy and undeploy run from Designer. See Validate and Deploy. Related 🔗 Operate Infrastructure Resource Details Operator Views
