Layer5 Cloud sends two kinds of mail. Application mail (invitations, notifications, welcome mail) leaves the Layer5 Cloud server, through an organization’s own mail server when one is turned on, and otherwise through the shared mail server you configure in the chart’s smtp values. Identity mail (email verification and account recovery) is produced by Kratos and reaches the same server only when you select the HTTP courier. See Plan a Deployment. This guide helps you find which of those paths is failing and why.
Read this before upgrading to v1.0.253 or later The shared mail server you configure with SMTP_HOST and SMTP_PORT is screened the same way an organization’s own mail server is, and the server refuses to start when it fails that screen. If SMTP_HOST points at an in-cluster relay, at a non-submission port such as mailpit on 1025, or at a plaintext MTA, this deployment stops on upgrade and says so at startup. See Constraints on the shared mail server. Debug Log Levels 🔗 To enable email debugging, set env.loglevel in your Helm values to 5 (debug) or 6 (trace) and upgrade. The chart default is 4 (info). Return it to 4 when you finish, because debug logs record more detail.
env: loglevel: 5 Testing Email Configuration 🔗 1. Email Configuration Test Endpoint (Provider Admin Only) 🔗 Check that the four SMTP_* values are configured, without sending an email. Both verbs of this endpoint require authentication and the provider admin role, so the GET must carry a credential. It validates configuration only - it does not dial the SMTP server.
curl -X GET "https://your-domain.com/api/system/email/test" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN" Expected Response (Success):
{ "status": "success", "message": "Email configuration is valid", "timestamp": "1695312000" } The response carries the verdict only. It does not report smtp_host, smtp_port or smtp_username: those are the deployment’s own relay settings, and SMTP_USERNAME is an email address. Read the configured values from your deployment configuration instead.
Expected Response (Error): 500 Internal Server Error, as plain text rather than JSON. The body is the error’s short description alone - the full error, which names the relay, stays in the log:
SMTP configuration error for field 'SMTP_HOST' Expected Response (Unauthenticated): 401 Unauthorized
{ "message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation" } Expected Response (Authenticated, not a provider admin): 403 Forbidden
{ "message": "user you@example.com must be Provider Admin to perform this operation" } 2. Send a test email 🔗 Send an actual test email to verify delivery end to end. The endpoint requires authentication and the Provider Admin role:
curl -X POST "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/system/email/test" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN" \ -d '{ "to": "test@example.com", "subject": "Layer5 Cloud Email Test" }' Request Body:
{ "to": "test@example.com", "subject": "Layer5 Cloud Email Test (optional)" } Expected Response (Success):
{ "status": "success", "message": "Test email sent successfully", "timestamp": "1695312000", "sentTo": "test@example.com" } Expected Response (Unauthenticated / not a provider admin): the same 401 and 403 JSON bodies as the GET above - both verbs carry the same provider-admin gate.
Expected Response (Error - Invalid Email): 400 Bad Request, as plain text:
Invalid email address format Expected Response (Error - Email Configuration): 500 Internal Server Error, as plain text. The configuration is checked before anything is sent, so this is the same verdict the GET gives:
SMTP configuration error for field 'SMTP_HOST' Expected Response (Error - the send itself failed): 500 Internal Server Error, as plain text, carrying the short description only. The relay’s own reply, the resolved endpoint and the SMTP username stay in the log:
Failed to send email with subject 'Layer5 Cloud Email Test' to recipients: test@example.com 3. Required Environment Variables 🔗 Either set all four values or leave all four empty. A deployment that leaves them empty is a supported state - it simply sends no mail - but a deployment that sets some of them and not others does not start.
Variable Chart value Requirement SMTP_HOST smtp.smtphost Must resolve to a publicly routable address SMTP_PORT smtp.smtpport One of 25, 465, 587, 2525 SMTP_USERNAME smtp.smtpusername A full address: it becomes the From: header SMTP_PASSWORD smtp.smtppassword The mailbox password or app password SMTP_PORT also decides how the session is encrypted, because the four keys carry no mode of their own: 465 means implicit TLS, and every other permitted port takes STARTTLS. Read Constraints on the shared mail server before you change either value.
Constraints on the Shared Mail Server 🔗 Since v1.0.253, mail is routed per Organization: an Organization that has brought its own mail server sends through that server, and everyone else sends through the shared mail server your deployment configures. Both now go through one send primitive, so the shared mail server is screened exactly as a tenant’s is.
That screening is new. The previous send path applied none of it, so a deployment that has been sending mail happily can be refused after an upgrade. A self-hosted install that points SMTP_HOST at an internal, plaintext, or non-submission relay can be refused.
What is refused 🔗 Constraint What is refused How to fix it Submission port allowlist any port other than 25, 465, 587 or 2525 - for example mailpit on 1025 move the relay onto a submission port, or put a submission-port listener in front of it Internal-address screen an SMTP_HOST that resolves to loopback, RFC 1918 private, IPv6 unique-local, RFC 6598 carrier-shared or link-local space - for example an in-cluster mailhog.default.svc point SMTP_HOST at a publicly routable relay. There is deliberately no allowlist or opt-out setting STARTTLS is required a relay that answers but does not advertise the extension - a plaintext internal MTA enable STARTTLS on the relay. It is refused rather than downgraded, because a downgrade would put the mailbox password on the wire in the clear SMTP_PORT parses as a number a stray character or space in the value, such as "587 " correct the value in your Secret or environment file SMTP_USERNAME parses as an RFC 5322 address a bare mailbox name such as no-reply with no domain - it becomes the From: header use the full mailbox address Every address SMTP_HOST resolves to is screened, not just the one a connection happens to use. A host publishing both a public and a private record is refused.
Port 465 is the exception to STARTTLS: it speaks TLS from the first byte, and the deployment selects that mode automatically from the port. You do not configure the encryption mode separately.
What happens at startup 🔗 The server validates the shared mail server once, at startup, rather than waiting for somebody’s password reset to fail silently. Only the first row below stops the deployment:
At startup Verdict What you see The configuration fails one of the constraints above the server exits meshery_cloud-3301 at Error, then exit code 1 The relay could not be reached at all - DNS did not answer, or the connection did not complete the server starts meshery_cloud-3302 at Error The relay answered but its certificate did not verify - expired, wrong host name, or an untrusted issuer the server starts meshery_cloud-3304 at Error, naming the relay host None of the four SMTP_* values is set the server starts a warning naming the first unset key The relay answered and the screens passed the server starts INFO The shared mail relay answered on smtp.example.com:587 over starttls The two non-fatal failures are still failures: no mail leaves over the shared mail server until they clear. Treat 3302 and 3304 at startup as a page, not a note. They are separate codes because the remedy is different - 3302 is the network, 3304 is the relay’s certificate.
A refusal is fatal on purpose. The alternative is a deployment that comes up green and drops every message silently, which is the failure this check exists to convert into a refusal to start.
The startup check does not authenticate and sends no message. A rotated password is not a reason a deployment will not start, and an authentication failure is not one of the verdicts this check acts on.
The configuration test endpoint does not dial GET /api/system/email/test now applies everything above that can be decided without a connection - the presence of all four keys, the port allowlist, the shape of the host, and the two parse rules. It still opens no connection, so whether the relay offers STARTTLS is the startup check’s answer to give, not this endpoint’s. Flow Emails (Kratos Integration) 🔗 Identity mail reaches Layer5 Cloud only when Kratos uses the HTTP courier, which posts each message to /api/identity/flow/emails. Layer5 Cloud then renders it with the signup organization’s branding and sends it like other application mail. Under the HTTP courier there is no SMTP fallback. When Layer5 Cloud answers anything but a success, Kratos retries the message (five times by default) and then abandons it, with no visible error to the user, so an unreachable or misconfigured Layer5 Cloud silently stops verification and recovery mail. With the default SMTP courier, Kratos sends the mail itself through kratos.kratos.config.courier.smtp.connection_uri, and none of the shared-relay rules on this page apply to it.
Only two Kratos template types are dispatched: verification_code_valid and recovery_code_valid. Every environment runs the code strategy for recovery and verification, so those are the only two Kratos emits - and the unknown-recipient notices (recovery_code_invalid, verification_code_invalid) are deliberately not sent. Any other type is acknowledged with a 200 and logged as unsupported rather than mailed; a 200 for one of those means the request was accepted and no message was sent.
DEBUG Flow email attempt. subject_template: email-templates/valid/email-recover-subject.body.gotmpl , body_template: email-templates/valid/email-recover.body.gotmpl , organization_id: 0e6b7ba0-... , recipient: user@example.com DEBUG Flow email delivery failed. error_type: *errors.Error , template_type: recovery_code_valid , organization_id: 0e6b7ba0-... , recipient: user@example.com INFO Flow email sent. template_type: recovery_code_valid , recipient: user@example.com Which Mail Server a Message Left Through 🔗 Every message this deployment sends is routed by the reader’s Organization. An Organization that has configured its own mail server, verified its from domain and turned it on sends through that server; every other message takes the shared mail server configured by SMTP_HOST.
That routing produces its own log lines, and a self-hosted operator will meet them without having configured anything themselves:
The Organization’s mail server was used and the message was accepted. No operator action; the verdict is recorded against that Organization’s delivery health, which its administrators read on the Email tab.
The Organization’s mail server refused the message and fallback is on. The message is re-sent over the shared mail server, arriving from this deployment’s address with the Organization’s name and a (via ...) suffix. Logged as meshery_cloud-3299.
The Organization’s mail server refused the message and fallback is off. The message is dropped, logged as meshery_cloud-3300 at Critical. This is that Organization’s own setting working as documented, not a fault in this deployment - but a dropped verification or recovery message locks a user out of their account, so it is worth alerting on.
The Organization’s mail server took the whole message and never answered. Delivery is unknown, so the message is deliberately not re-sent over the shared mail server - re-sending it could deliver it twice. Logged as meshery_cloud-3303 at Critical.
The Organization’s stored configuration could not be read - a database read failed, or a stored password would not decrypt, usually after CLOUD_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY was rotated. The message takes the shared mail server whatever that Organization’s fallback setting says, because the fault is this deployment’s rather than a delivery policy the tenant chose. Logged as meshery_cloud-3298.
The full behavior an Organization administrator sees is documented in Bring Your Own Mail Server.
Common Issues and Solutions 🔗 1. SMTP Configuration Errors 🔗 Issue: SMTP configuration error: SMTP_HOST is empty
Solution:
Verify all SMTP environment variables are set Check that environment variables are properly loaded in your deployment Use the test endpoint to validate configuration 2. Authentication Failures 🔗 Issue: SMTP authentication was refused by the mail server
Solution:
Verify SMTP username and password are correct For Gmail, use App Passwords instead of regular passwords Check if 2FA is enabled and properly configured The identity that was refused and the endpoint it was presented to are in the log’s long description (authenticating as <username> at <host:port>), never in the response - an SMTP username is an email address.
3. Template Errors 🔗 Issue: Email template missing or inaccessible
Solution: the templates ship inside the Layer5 Cloud image. If you built a custom image or mounted a volume over its configuration directory, restore the bundled templates, and confirm that the image tag matches the release you run.
4. Recipient Validation Errors 🔗 Issue: Email recipient validation failed
Solution:
Verify email addresses are valid and properly formatted Check for empty recipient lists Validate email addresses contain @ symbol Check for a carriage return or line feed in an address. An address carrying one is refused, not sanitized: recipient addresses are written as SMTP protocol verbs and into the header block, so a line break in one would start a header of its own. This applies to Cc addresses as well as To Subjects are the deliberate asymmetry: a line break in a subject is stripped rather than refused, because a subject is display text and dropping a notification over a design name containing a newline would turn a cosmetic problem into a lost message.
5. Network Connectivity Issues 🔗 Issue: meshery_cloud-3302 at startup, or dial tcp: lookup smtp.example.com: no such host
Solution:
Check network connectivity to SMTP server Verify egress from this cluster to the relay’s submission port is allowed Test DNS resolution for SMTP host No mail leaves over the shared mail server while this is outstanding, even though the deployment started.
6. The Server Will Not Start After an Upgrade 🔗 Issue: meshery_cloud-3301 at Error, then exit code 1.
Solution: the shared mail server fails one of the constraints. The logged cause names which screen refused it:
Cause code The screen that refused What to change meshery_cloud-3297 a key is unset, SMTP_PORT is not a number, or SMTP_USERNAME is not an RFC 5322 address correct the named key meshery_cloud-3262 the host is empty, or carries whitespace or a line break correct SMTP_HOST meshery_cloud-3263 the port is not a submission port, or the host resolved into internal address space correct SMTP_PORT, or point SMTP_HOST at a publicly routable relay meshery_cloud-3265 the relay answered and does not offer STARTTLS. Only reachable on a port other than 465, which never negotiates STARTTLS enable STARTTLS on the relay, or move it to 465 for implicit TLS 7. The Server’s Certificate Is Not Trusted 🔗 Issue: meshery_cloud-3304 at Error; the deployment starts.
Solution: the relay answered, and its certificate did not verify against the trusted roots - it has expired, was issued for a different host name, or is self-signed or from an issuer this server does not trust. Fix the certificate; this is not a network fault and not something egress rules will clear. Every send fails identically until it verifies.
Development Mode 🔗 In development environment (ENVIRONMENT=development), the rendered email content is logged in addition to being sent, so the body can be read without opening the recipient’s mailbox:
INFO Development mode - Email details recipients=user@example.com subject="Test Email" body="<html>...</html>" The message still goes out over the shared mail server, which still has to satisfy the constraints above. Pointing a development deployment at a local catch-all mailbox on port 1025 does not work.
Error Codes Reference 🔗 Error Code Description Common Causes meshery_cloud-1092 Failed to send email Network issues, SMTP server down meshery_cloud-1144 SMTP authentication was refused by the mail server Invalid credentials. The refused identity and the endpoint reach the log only meshery_cloud-1145 SMTP send mail error Server rejection, quota exceeded meshery_cloud-1146 SMTP configuration error Missing environment variables meshery_cloud-1147 Email template missing Template files not found meshery_cloud-1148 Email recipient validation failed Invalid email addresses, an empty recipient list, or an address containing a carriage return or line feed Mail routing and the shared mail server 🔗 These codes arrived with per-Organization mail routing in v1.0.253. The four marked send path describe a message that belonged to an Organization with its own mail server; the rest describe the shared mail server this deployment configures.
Error Code At startup Meaning meshery_cloud-3297 cause of 3301 The shared mail server is not usable as configured: a key is unset, SMTP_PORT is not a port number, or SMTP_USERNAME is not an address. The log names the key, never its value. The same faults are reported under this code by /api/system/email/test and by a send meshery_cloud-3298 send path An Organization’s mail server configuration could not be read, so the message went over the shared mail server meshery_cloud-3299 send path A delivery over an Organization’s own mail server failed. The endpoint is in the log only meshery_cloud-3300 send path Nothing was sent: an Organization’s mail server refused the message and its fallback is turned off meshery_cloud-3301 exits The shared mail server fails one of the constraints - port, address, or no STARTTLS. The cause names which screen refused it meshery_cloud-3302 starts DNS or the connection did not complete. Genuine unreachability only; no mail leaves over the shared mail server until it clears meshery_cloud-3303 send path An Organization’s mail server took the whole message and never acknowledged it. Recorded as uncertain and not re-sent, because re-sending could deliver it twice meshery_cloud-3304 starts The shared mail server’s certificate failed verification - expiry, host name or issuer. Check the certificate, not the network Monitoring 🔗 Alert on the error codes in the tables above, in particular meshery_cloud-3301, 3302, 3304, 3300, and 3303. See Monitoring.
Troubleshooting Checklist 🔗 Set env.loglevel to 5 for debug logging while you diagnose Verify all SMTP environment variables are configured Confirm SMTP_PORT is one of 25, 465, 587, 2525, and that SMTP_USERNAME is a full address Confirm SMTP_HOST resolves only to publicly routable addresses, and that the relay offers STARTTLS (or is on 465) Read the startup log for meshery_cloud-3301, -3302 or -3304 before looking anywhere else Test the configuration with the Provider Admin-only /api/system/email/test endpoint, authenticating the request If only identity mail is missing, check which Kratos courier you use and, for the HTTP courier, that Kratos can reach /api/identity/flow/emails Check network connectivity to SMTP server Confirm the image still carries its bundled email templates Verify recipient email addresses are valid Check SMTP server logs for additional error details Monitor email service provider quotas and limits

The Content Template Creator is the five-step flow in the Instructor Console that registers a learning path, challenge, or certification and hands you the front matter to start writing it. One run does three things:
Creates the content’s record in Layer5 Cloud, with status not ready, public visibility, and a generated slug. Creates the invitation that governs who can enroll. Generates the front matter, the content ID, and the organization ID that tie your repository files to that record. The record is what learners enroll in, what progress and grades attach to, and what the Instructor Console reports on. The front matter is how your repository declares the same content, so the two must carry the same ID.
Prerequisites 🔗 The View Academy Metrics permission, held by Academy Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin. See Roles and Permissions. A workspace and a team to assign. You can type a new workspace name instead of picking an existing one. The team must already exist. Optional: a badge to award on completion. The Recognition step can create one. Run the creator 🔗 The field list, with the behavior of each field, is in Create Academy Content. Three details matter when you run it.
Team accepts one value. The team you pick is added to the invitation, and learners join it when they enroll. Access status sets the invitation to enabled or disabled. It defaults to enabled. A disabled invitation blocks enrollment. See How the invitation controls enrollment. Content Access End Date sets the invitation’s expiry. Leave it empty for no expiry. The creator writes the record when you advance from Recognition to Generate Template. You can go back to earlier steps and the entries you made stay in place, but advancing to the last step again creates another record with a new content ID and a new invitation. Use the ID on the final screen of your last run, and treat any earlier record as unused.
The generated front matter 🔗 The last step shows the front matter with a copy button, followed by the content ID and your organization ID. For a certification titled “Meshery Contributors Certification”, the output has this shape:
--- type: "certification" title: "Meshery Contributors Certification" description: "A certification for developers who contribute to Meshery" weight: 1 banner: "images/meshery-contributors-banner.svg" id: "7c0f6a3e-2b1d-4c58-9d0e-5a1b2c3d4e5f" tags: ["meshery", "kubernetes", "golang"] categories: "open-source, cloud-native" level: "beginner" # competencies: # - title: "Domain Name" # percentage: 25 # items: # - "Competency item 1" # prerequisite_knowledge: # - title: "Prerequisite Title" # url: "https://example.com/resource" # description: "Brief description of the prerequisite" --- A certification for developers who contribute to Meshery. <!-- Add your Academy content here --> Key Source Notes type Content type learning-path, challenge, or certification. title, description Basic Information Also appear on the catalog card. weight Fixed at 1 Change it to order the content among its siblings. banner Content Details Present only when you entered a banner. The path is relative to the folder that holds the content’s index file. id Generated The content ID. It links your files to the record. tags, categories Content Details Present only when you entered values. level The content record Always reads beginner at creation, whatever difficulty you picked. Set it to beginner, intermediate, or advanced yourself. competencies, prerequisite_knowledge Commented samples Uncomment and fill them in to describe what an exam covers and what learners should know first. Paste the output into the content’s index file in your repository, inside the directory named for your organization ID. Then write the content as described in Create a Learning Path.
Never change the content ID after learners enroll Registrations, progress, grades, and certificates are recorded against the content ID. Changing the id in your repository orphans the existing learners’ progress. How the invitation controls enrollment 🔗 Every content record created in an organization other than the provider organization has an invitation attached. Enrolling in the content accepts that invitation for the learner, and acceptance is where access is decided.
Invitation setting Value the creator sets Effect on a learner who enrolls Name Academy Invitation for <slug>, using the generated slug Identifies the invitation in the organization’s invitation list. Role Academy Learner Assigned in the organization if the learner does not hold it. Team The team you picked The learner is added to it if not already a member. Status Your Access status A disabled invitation blocks enrollment. Expiry Your Content Access End Date Checked at enrollment. Once it passes, new learners cannot enroll. Learners who already enrolled keep their role and team membership. Email list Empty Anyone who is signed in can accept. Add exact addresses or @domain entries to restrict it. Quota Empty Unlimited. A quota blocks enrollment once that many people have accepted. Acceptance is idempotent. A learner who accepts twice gains no duplicate membership or role, and the invitation counts them once.
When an enrollment hits a disabled, expired, full, or email-restricted invitation, the request fails with a server error. The registration is recorded before the invitation is evaluated, so the learner appears in the Learners view without having joined the organization or team. Fix the invitation, then have the learner enroll again.
You can change the team, access status, and end date later from the Curricula view of the Instructor Console. Editing the invitation itself, to set a quota or restrict the email list, follows the invitation guide. To bring in a co-instructor, create an invitation with the Academy Admin role instead of Academy Learner.
Content owned by the provider organization 🔗 Content created while the console is scoped to all organizations belongs to the provider organization. It has no attached invitation, so enrollment accepts nothing and grants no team or role.

Tags are the key-value labels and annotations on a component. When components share matching labels, Kanvas groups them in a TagSet, a shaded region drawn around the matching components. Use tags to see which components belong together, such as the Service and Deployment of one application.
Add labels and annotations 🔗 Open a component’s configurator and go to its Labels tab. It holds two key-value maps:
Labels identify and select Kubernetes components. Annotations attach extra metadata to a component. Values are strings and default to empty. The form checks only the type, so it does not enforce Kubernetes label syntax. Edits are written 300 ms after you stop typing and trigger a relationship evaluation. See Add and Configure Components.
How grouping works 🔗 Grouping is automatic. No button creates a TagSet. After you change labels, Kanvas evaluates the design, and where the registry’s relationship definitions say labels match, it creates a TagSet and draws a translucent steel-blue region around the group. The Layers panel lists these as hierarchical TagSets.
To remove a TagSet, change the labels so they no longer match. To hide TagSets, switch off their toggle in the Layers panel. Evaluation continues. Limits 🔗 Limit Behavior Render fidelity TagSets draw only in Full render fidelity. Maximum drawn 30. Past that, Kanvas warns “Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30”. Region outline Kanvas builds the outline from the first 10 members of a group. Later members are still inside the region. Adaptive mode TagSets disappear when Adaptive mode steps below Full. What tags do not do 🔗 Designer has no filter that shows only components with a given tag. Operator mode filters live resources by namespace, kind, model, label, and free-text search. Palette search matches model and component names, not labels. See also 🔗 Relationships: how TagSets fit with the other kinds. Create Relationships: hiding relationship kinds.

body:
Layer5 Academy is the learning platform built into Layer5 Cloud. Organizations use it to publish structured training on cloud native infrastructure, assess what learners know, and award verifiable badges and certificates. Layer5 Cloud tracks every learner’s enrollment, progress, and test results, and gives instructors a console to measure how their content performs.
Academy is an Enterprise-tier capability. An organization needs an Academy configuration from Layer5 before it can publish its own content.
Content types 🔗 Academy content comes in three types. All three share the same lifecycle, enrollment model, and test engine. They differ in intent.
Learning path Challenge Certification Structure A guided sequence of courses that breaks a broad topic into modules A focused, scenario-based exercise built around one problem A formal assessment of skills the learner already has Outcome Systematic understanding of a subject from the ground up Hands-on experience solving a specific, realistic problem Proof of professional competence Assessment Tests throughout; final tests gate completion, practice tests do not Tests that verify the solution; final tests gate completion Exams; the final exam gates completion Credential Completion badge Completion badge Completion badge, plus a certificate when the content defines one Every test, in every content type, follows the same rules for scoring, attempt limits, time limits, and prerequisites. The Learner Guide describes them in full.
Audiences 🔗 The Academy serves three audiences, each with its own guide.
Learners browse the catalog, enroll, work through content, pass tests, and earn credentials. Start with the Learner Guide. Content creators and instructors write and publish content for their organization and track learner outcomes. Start with Creating Content, then see Creating Your Learning Path, Building Challenges, Building Certifications, and the Instructor Console Guide. Platform developers extend and maintain the Academy platform itself. Start with Platform Development. How content flows 🔗 Academy content is not written inside Layer5 Cloud. Authors keep it as Markdown in their organization’s own Git repository, and Layer5 Cloud holds the registry of that content and every learner’s record against it.
Author. A content creator registers a new piece of content in Layer5 Cloud, choosing its type, title, level, categories, tags, workspace, team, access end date, and the badge it awards. New content starts as Public, Beginner level, and not ready. The creator then writes the content as Markdown in the organization’s Git repository. Publish. An organization admin or owner publishes a version of the content. The publish workflow in the content repository sends the organization ID and version to Layer5 Cloud, which builds that version into the Academy site. Content counts as published once its status is ready. Catalog. Published content appears in the Academy catalog. The catalog is public: anyone can browse it without signing in. An organization’s own Academy domain shows only that organization’s content. Enroll. A signed-in learner enrolls, which creates a registration with status Registered. If the content carries an invitation, enrolling also accepts it and adds the learner to the invitation’s team. Learn and test. As the learner works through the content, Layer5 Cloud records the current item, completed items, quiz grades, and time spent. Each test attempt is a timed session scored on the server. Credential. Passing the final test marks the registration Completed, awards the content’s badge, and issues a certificate if the content defines one. A certificate has a public verification page and arrives by email. Measure. Instructors watch registrations, completion rates, and test pass rates in the instructor console, and can withdraw learners or update the content’s team, access, expiry, workspace, and badge. Layer5 Cloud records each Academy event in the organization’s audit log: content created, updated, or deleted; registration and withdrawal; progress updates and completion; content marked ready; test started and evaluated; and certificate issued.
Roles and capabilities 🔗 Access to Academy features follows the role a user holds in the organization that owns the content. The Learner role grants access to Academy content. The instructor console requires the View Academy Metrics permission, which the Academy Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin roles hold by default.
Capability Anonymous Learner Academy Admin Organization Admin Provider Admin Browse the catalog Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Enroll, take tests, earn badges and certificates No (sign-in required) Yes Yes Yes Yes Withdraw your own registration No Yes Yes Yes Yes Withdraw another learner’s registration No No Yes Yes Yes Use the instructor console No No Yes Yes Yes Create, update, and delete content No No Yes Yes Yes Publish a content version No No No Yes (organization admin or owner) Yes

The catalog is the library of designs that their owners have published for everyone to use. It turns a design that worked for one team into a reusable starting point for every other team: anyone can find it, read it, and see how often others open, deploy, and clone it, and any signed-in user can clone it into their own workspace and adapt it.
The catalog works on a simple contract. Publishing makes a design readable by the world and clonable by any signed-in user, a review step decides what gets in, and a class label tells readers who stands behind each entry. The rest of this page explains each part of that contract and where it stops.
What the catalog holds 🔗 The catalog is every design whose visibility is published. It is not tied to an organization: entries come from publishers in every organization, and one listing shows them all. You can narrow the listing by organization, workspace, team, or owner, but by default you see everything.
The catalog is readable without signing in. A signed-out visitor can browse entries, open them, and read their metadata. Each entry shows the publisher’s name and avatar. The publisher’s email address is not included in what anonymous visitors receive.
Every catalog entry carries metadata that the publisher supplies at publish time:
Metadata What it tells a reader Type The kind of design, such as deployment. Stored in lower case. Technology tags The technologies the design is compatible with. Stored in lower case, and used by the technology filter. Description The purpose and intended use of the design. Caveats Known limitations or conditions a reader should weigh before using it. Class Who produced the design and who stands behind it. See Classes. Published version The design version that was approved for the catalog. Snapshot images Light and dark preview images of the design. WebAssembly filters 🔗 The catalog serves a second content type, WebAssembly filters, through the same API. Published filters are available to Meshery and to API clients, but the Cloud UI has no tab for browsing them. To manage filters, see Filter Management in the Meshery documentation. The rest of this page covers designs.
Visibility 🔗 Every design has one of three visibility levels. Visibility decides who can read a design and who can clone it.
Visibility Who can read it Who can clone it Listed in the catalog Private The owner, provider administrators, and users the design is shared with Nobody, not even the owner No Public Anyone with the link, signed in or not, including downloads Any signed-in user No Published Anyone, signed in or not Any signed-in user Yes Published is public plus a catalog entry. A design saved for the first time is public by default, while designs imported through the GitHub integration start private.
Once a design is published, its visibility cannot be changed from the publish dialog. The only way out of the catalog is to unpublish, and unpublishing returns the design to private, not public. If you want the design to stay readable by link after it leaves the catalog, set it to public again afterward. The catalog metadata stays on the design after unpublishing.
Classes 🔗 A class tells a reader who produced an entry and who supports it.
Class Meaning Official Produced and fully supported by Meshery maintainers. Verified Produced by partners and verified by Meshery maintainers. Community Produced and shared by Meshery users. Publishers do not choose their own class. The class is set by who publishes and who reviews:
A publisher without the Approve Catalog Request permission creates a publish request with the class Community. The request waits in the review queue. A publisher with the Approve Catalog Request permission skips the queue. The design is approved immediately with the class Official. An approver deciding a queued request chooses the class, Official, Verified, or Community, at the moment of approval. This keeps the Official and Verified labels in the hands of the people who review catalog content.
Publication lifecycle 🔗 A design moves through the catalog in these stages:
Stage What happens Who is notified 1. Request A signed-in user publishes a design with its catalog metadata. Without the Approve Catalog Request permission, this creates a pending request and the design’s visibility does not change yet. The catalog maintainers receive an email, and the requester receives a copy. 2. Review queue Pending requests wait in the queue. Reviewers see the author, the author’s email, the content name and type, the status, the class, and when the request was created. The queue shows requests from the reviewer’s current organization, or from all organizations for holders of View All Organizations. - 3. Approve or deny A reviewer approves, choosing the class, or denies. Approval publishes the design and records its published version. Denial leaves the design’s visibility unchanged. Only pending requests can be decided; a request that was already approved or denied cannot be decided again. The owner receives an approval or denial email, unless their notification preferences turn approval emails off. 4. Published The design is in the catalog, readable by anyone and clonable by any signed-in user. - 5. Unpublish The design’s creator, or a holder of Approve Catalog Request, removes it from the catalog. The design becomes private and an event is recorded. - The publish form asks for a type, at least one technology, a description, and caveats. Cloud does not reliably reject an entry with empty fields, so a reviewer should confirm they are filled in before approving.
Denying a request is checked against the Approve Catalog Request permission, the same as approving. Holding Deny Catalog Request alone does not let you deny a request.
One request per design 🔗 Each design can have only one publish request, ever. A design that already has a request, whether pending, approved, or denied, cannot be submitted again. Unpublishing does not clear the earlier request, so a design that was unpublished, or whose request was denied, cannot be published through a new request. Plan the metadata and timing of a submission with this in mind.
The Meshery catalog website 🔗 The Cloud catalog and the public Meshery catalog website are separate listings. When a holder of Approve Catalog Request publishes a design directly, Layer5 Cloud triggers a refresh of the Meshery catalog website. If that refresh cannot be triggered, the publish still succeeds and an error event is recorded for the publisher.
Approving a request from the review queue does not refresh the Meshery catalog website. A design approved from the queue appears in the Cloud catalog immediately but is not pushed to the website at that moment.
Unpublishing triggers removal of the design from the Meshery catalog website. A failure to trigger that removal is logged but not shown to the user.
Cloning 🔗 A clone is a private copy of a catalog design that you own and can change freely. Cloning is how a catalog entry becomes your own working design. The original stays untouched, and its owner keeps control of it.
When you clone a design:
The copy is private and owned by you. The copy is placed in the workspace you have selected in your current organization. Cloning requires a selected organization; it is refused when you are viewing all organizations. See Workspaces for how workspaces organize designs. The copy starts at a fresh version, and keeps the original’s catalog metadata and record of where it came from. The source design’s clone count goes up by one. Any signed-in user can clone a published or public design, provided they hold the Clone Design permission, which the Cloud UI requires before it enables the clone action. Signed-out visitors cannot clone. Private designs cannot be cloned by anyone, including their owner. To duplicate one of your own private designs, save a copy from Kanvas instead.
Metrics 🔗 Every design keeps five counters. They appear on catalog cards and in the leaderboard, and they give readers a rough sense of how widely an entry is used.
Metric What it counts Opens Each time the design is loaded, whether from the catalog, from Kanvas, or from a direct link. Downloads Each time the design is downloaded. Deploys Each time the design is deployed. Clones Each time someone clones the design. Shares Each time the design is shared. Reading the counters 🔗 The counters are lifetime totals. Keep these properties in mind when you compare entries:
No deduplication. One person opening a design ten times adds ten Opens. The counters measure activity, not distinct people. Signed-out activity counts. Opens from anonymous visitors are included. No time window and no reset. A counter only grows. An older design has had more time to accumulate counts than a newer one. Edits do not reset them. Changing a design keeps its counts. Best effort. If recording a count fails, the action itself still succeeds, so a counter can undercount slightly. Treat a high count as a signal of attention, and use the description, caveats, and class to judge fitness for your use.
Leaderboard 🔗 The leaderboard is the catalog sorted by one of these counters. It is not a separate ranking or score. By default it sorts by Opens, highest first, and you can sort by any of the other counters instead. You can filter it by type and by class, one choice each, and search it by design name. The catalog page shows the top performers in a summary panel, and the dashboard shows the leaderboard as a widget.
Permissions and plans 🔗 Browsing the catalog requires no permission and no account. Publishing, reviewing, unpublishing, and cloning are governed by the permissions below.
Catalog permissions by role Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Catalog Requests View the catalog publication request queue -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Approve Catalog Request Approve catalog publication requests -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Deny Catalog Request Deny catalog publication requests -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Publish Design Publish a design ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Unpublish Design Unpublish a design ✓*Allowed on resources the user owns ✓*Allowed on resources the user owns ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Clone Design Clone any published design to customise it according to your use cases ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View Designs View all public and published designs of other team members and private of signed-in user ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Users and Team Admins can unpublish only designs they created. Workspace Admins, Organization Admins, and Provider Admins can unpublish any design. Reviewing requests requires a selected organization, and a reviewer cannot decide a request from outside their current organization. For the complete role defaults, see Roles and Permissions.
Catalog Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Public Catalog: 400 Cloud Native Patterns A library of pre-built design patterns and operational templates for common deployment scenarios, simplifying the configuration process and ensuring best practices. ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included Organization Private Catalog Privately publish and share reusable design patterns and operational templates within your organization. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Share Design Share design with anyone within your organization, and make your design easily accessible to all relevant team members. ✓Included ✓Included -Not included ✓Included Clone Design Clone any published design to customise it according to your use cases ✓Included ✓Included -Not included ✓Included Publish Design Publish a design -Not included -Not included -Not included -Not included View Designs View all public and published designs of other team members and private of signed-in user -Not included -Not included -Not included -Not included View Filters View all public and published filters of other team members and private of signed-in user -Not included -Not included ✓Included ✓Included Approve Catalog Request Change management for the curation of content published in the catalog. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Single and multiple approvers -Not included -Not included -Not included -Not included Import Filter Import a publish WASM filter -Not included -Not included -Not included -Not included The plan matrix lists what each plan includes. Layer5 Cloud does not check your plan when you publish, review, or clone a design: those actions are governed only by the permission matrix above, which is what the product enforces.
Limits and edge cases 🔗 Search matches design names only. It does not search descriptions, caveats, or technology tags. Use the type, technology, and class filters to narrow by metadata. One publish request per design. A design with any earlier request, including a denied one or one that was later unpublished, cannot be submitted again. Unpublishing makes a design private. It does not return to public. The Meshery catalog website is a separate listing. It is refreshed on direct publish by an approver, not on approval from the review queue. Filters are not browsable in the Cloud UI. The catalog API and Meshery still serve them. Private designs cannot be cloned, even by their owner. Next steps 🔗 Find and Use Catalog Designs shows how to find, filter, and use catalog entries. Publish Designs covers submitting a design to the catalog from Kanvas. Clone a Design covers making your own copy of a design. Roles and Permissions lists every permission by role. Workspaces explains where your clones land.

body:
Collaboration in Kanvas, whether at kanvas.new or inside Meshery, rests on three separate layers that work together:
Live co-editing (presence) - people who have the same design open see each other’s cursors, selections, and edits as they happen. Access - the design’s visibility and its grant list decide who can open and change the design. Conversation (comments) - comment threads that live inside the design itself. The three layers are independent. A live session forms between whoever has the design open at the same time. Access decides who can open the design in the first place. Comments are part of the design’s content, so they follow the design wherever it goes. Keeping these layers apart in your head explains most of what you see when a team works on one design.
The live session 🔗 When you open a saved design, your browser joins a live session for that design. Layer5 Cloud acts only as an introducer: it tells the browsers that have the same design open how to reach each other. From then on, edits flow directly from browser to browser over WebRTC. Your edits do not pass through Meshery Server or Layer5 Cloud.
The design is the session key. A session needs a design that has been saved at least once, because only a saved design has an id. A brand-new, unsaved design has no session until its first save. The session ends when you open a different design, when the design is deleted, or when you leave the editor.
The session shares some things and keeps others yours:
Shared with everyone in the session Stays in your browser The design: components, relationships, and annotations, including comments Layout state Editor filters Viewport and zoom Render mode and adaptive mode Your selection Presence shows who else is working with you. The Designer toolbar shows an avatar for each other participant, with a ring in that person’s color. Each person’s cursor appears on your canvas as an arrow labeled with their first name, and any component they select carries a border in their color. Kanvas picks each person’s color at random from a fixed palette when the session starts, so two people can end up with the same color. A second browser tab signed in to your own account appears as another collaborator.
Kanvas tries a direct network path between browsers first and falls back to a public relay. It uses public STUN servers and one public relay, and this network configuration is built in and not configurable. Networks that block WebRTC traffic or those public hosts can prevent browsers from connecting.
A failed session is silent If a live session cannot open, for example because Layer5 Cloud is unreachable, Kanvas keeps working in single-user mode. It shows no on-screen warning and offers no reconnect control. If collaborators cannot see your cursor, assume the session did not open. Joining a live session requires an authenticated session. Layer5 Cloud rejects a connection without a valid token.
Live editing versus saving 🔗 The live session and the saved design are two different things. Each person’s own changes autosave from their own browser a few seconds after they stop editing, and each save writes the whole design. Changes that arrive from other people do not trigger a save on your side. No live copy of the session exists on the server.
The saved design follows last-write-wins. When two people edit at once, the stored design is whatever the most recent save wrote. Anyone who opens the design later, after the session has ended, loads that last saved version, not the live session state.
The access model 🔗 Visibility sets the baseline for who can open and change a design:
Visibility Who can open it Who can change it Private Owner, provider administrators, and users granted access Owner, provider administrators, and users granted access Public Anyone, including anonymous visitors Any signed-in user Published Anyone, including anonymous visitors Owner, provider administrators, and users granted access A grant gives one user access to one design. A grant carries no access level. Everyone who can open a private design through a grant can edit it, comment on it, clone it, and download it, and can change its visibility between private and public. Kanvas has no view-only or comment-only access.
Granting and revoking access requires the Share Design permission, checked in the organization that owns the design’s workspace. When the design has no workspace, Kanvas checks it in an organization the owner belongs to. Layer5 Cloud refuses to check a design that belongs to workspaces in more than one organization. Ownership is not required: a collaborator who holds the permission can share the design further, and by default the Organization Admin role carries it. Anonymous sessions cannot grant or revoke access.
A few rules hold regardless of permissions:
The owner cannot be granted access or have access revoked. Deleting a design stays with the owner and provider administrators. Ownership cannot be transferred. Sharing is not limited to your organization. You can grant access to any user on the platform. Teams do not open private designs. Assigning teams to a workspace that contains a design does not give those teams access, and Kanvas shares with individual users only. To give a team member access to a private design, grant it to that person.
Capabilities by role 🔗 Capability Owner Collaborator (user grant) Any other signed-in user Provider administrator Open a public design Yes Yes Yes Yes Open a private design Yes Yes No Yes Edit a private design Yes Yes No Yes Edit a public design Yes Yes Yes Yes Comment Yes Yes Public designs only Yes Grant or revoke access With Share Design With Share Design Public designs only, with Share Design With Share Design Change visibility Yes Yes Public designs only Yes Delete Yes No No Yes Anonymous visitors can open public designs. They cannot grant or revoke access, and they cannot open a private design.
A published design cannot have its visibility changed. For the full role and permission catalog, see Permissions.
Comments in the model 🔗 A comment is a component of the design. It saves with the design, syncs live to everyone in the session, and travels with the design when you clone, export, or copy it. Anyone who can open the design sees its comments, and hiding comments on your canvas does not stop them from syncing.
Each comment holds one thread. The thread records its state (open or resolved), when it last changed, its messages, and the list of people who muted it. Messages cannot be edited or deleted one at a time; deleting the comment removes the whole thread. Resolving a thread removes it from the canvas, and adding a message to a resolved thread reopens it. Muting a thread is stored in the thread itself, so every collaborator can see who muted it, and the mute saves with the design.
Kanvas sends comment notifications by email only when someone adds a message. Resolving and reopening a thread send nothing. When a message is added, Kanvas emails:
users mentioned in the new message earlier participants in the thread, meaning past authors and people mentioned in past messages, except the author of the new message the design owner, when the author is someone else Muting a thread stops mention and participant emails to you. The owner’s email ignores the owner’s own mute, and Kanvas skips it when the commenter has muted the thread. Each recipient’s account notification preferences also apply. A first comment that mentions nobody sends no email to anyone, including the design owner. Kanvas does not check that a recipient can open the design, and the mention picker searches all users on the platform, not only people with access.
The role catalog lists separate permissions for individual comment actions such as add, resolve, and delete. Kanvas does not enforce them. Anyone who can edit a design can perform every comment action.
Design trade-offs and limits 🔗 This model favors low friction over fine-grained control. For a team, it means:
No view-only reviewers. Every person with access can edit. To gather feedback, use comments with people you trust to edit. To circulate a read-only copy, publish a copy or have reviewers clone the design. A clone is independent of the original, so changes to it never reach the original. Public means editable. Any signed-in user can change a public design, change its visibility, and share it. Keep a design private until you intend that. The grant list protects private designs. Only the owner, provider administrators, and granted users can open a private design. Review the grant list when a project changes hands, because ownership cannot move. Collaborators can re-share. A collaborator who holds the Share Design permission can grant access to anyone on the platform. The last save wins. Live co-editing does not merge saves on the server. The stored design reflects the most recent save. Related 🔗 Sharing designs Reviewing designs with comments Collaborative editing tutorial Saving designs Publishing designs Kanvas architecture Permissions Designs and Components
description: How live co-editing, design access, and comments work together in Kanvas, and what each layer does and does not control.

Academy content is Markdown in your organization’s Git repository, built with Hugo into your organization’s Academy. Markdown covers most lessons. When a lesson needs a custom layout, a reusable component, or a live design, you extend the content in your own repository without touching the shared theme. This page covers what you can extend and the limits of each extension. It assumes a working content repository. If you do not have one yet, start with Create a Learning Path. Availability 🔗 Publishing your own Academy content is an Enterprise-tier capability. Your organization also needs an Academy configuration from Layer5 before it can publish. Without one, the Instructor Console shows its “not configured” state and the extensions below have nowhere to deploy. See Roles and Permissions for who can use the console. What you can extend 🔗 Extension Where it lives Scope Inline HTML and CSS Your Markdown pages The page that contains it Custom shortcode layouts/shortcodes// in your repository Every page in your organization’s content Embedded Kanvas design A shortcode in your page The page that contains it Branded award emails Organization settings in Layer5 Cloud Every badge and certificate email your organization sends You cannot replace the theme’s layouts, archetypes, or site-wide styles from a content repository. You can customize shortcodes only. Request theme changes through the theme’s issue tracker. Keep your files in your organization’s directory 🔗 Each organization’s files live under a directory named for its organization ID, which the Template Creator shows on its final step. The Academy build keeps organizations apart by that directory name, so content or shortcodes placed outside it are not part of your Academy. Use the same ID for the content directory and for the shortcode directory. Mix HTML and CSS with Markdown 🔗 Markdown pages accept raw HTML. Use it for layout that Markdown cannot express, such as columns, callout boxes, or styled tables. ## Why this matters Standard **Markdown** works above and below the block.
Note: Use inline HTML for one-off layout.
Leave a blank line between a raw HTML block and the Markdown that follows it. Without the blank line, Hugo does not parse the next Markdown element and it renders as literal text. Markdown inside an HTML element is parsed only when blank lines separate it from the tags, so write short content inside HTML elements in HTML. Style with inline style attributes, with CSS classes you define in a shortcode’s
{{ .Get "title" | default "Note" }}: {{ .Inner }}
Call it from a page by its file name, without the extension. The tags below are escaped for display. Write them as {{< callout title="Heads up" >}} and {{< /callout >}}. {{< callout title="Heads up" >}} Back up the design before you scale it down. {{< /callout >}} Hugo reads {{ .Get "title" }} as a named parameter and {{ .Inner }} as the content between the opening and closing tags. A shortcode written without a closing tag cannot use .Inner. The Academy supports the full Hugo shortcode feature set. See the Hugo shortcode documentation. Name collisions Choose names that do not match a shortcode the theme already provides. Use a prefix that is specific to your organization. Embed a Kanvas design 🔗 The Academy renders live Kanvas designs inside a lesson with the meshery-design-embed shortcode, so learners inspect a real topology instead of a screenshot. See the publishing diagram in Create a Learning Path for a working embed. Award emails 🔗 When a learner earns a badge or a certificate, Layer5 Cloud sends an email on behalf of your organization. Both messages draw their branding from your organization’s settings, including your logo, colors, and contact links. See White-label Layer5 Cloud for how to set them. Badge email Certificate email Sent when A badge is awarded The learner passes the final assessment of content that defines a certificate Subject Names the organization that awarded the badge Congratulations on receiving your certificate title certificate from organization name Recipient The learner The learner, addressed by first and last name Learner can turn it off Yes, through the badge assignment and updates notification preference No Links Learner’s public profile The certificate’s public page on your organization’s Academy The certificate link points to your organization’s custom domain when one is set. Otherwise it points to the deployment’s base address. If the branding settings cannot be read when the email is sent, the email still goes out with default branding. A failure to send the certificate email is logged and does not undo the completion or the certificate. Anonymous users never receive a badge email.
description: Go beyond plain Markdown in your Academy content with inline HTML and CSS, organization-specific Hugo shortcodes, embedded Kanvas designs, and branded award emails.

body:
A keychain is a named bundle of keys. It sits between the single permission and the role a person holds:
A key allows one action, such as Create Token. A keychain groups related keys, such as everything needed to manage teams. A role groups keychains, and users hold roles in an organization or team. A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys in every keychain of every role the user holds there. A keychain grants nothing by itself. It takes effect only through a role that includes it.
Why keychains exist 🔗 Keychains make permissions reusable. Many roles need the same set of keys: every default user role, for example, needs to view tokens, sessions, keys, and keychains. Instead of attaching those keys to each role one by one, Layer5 Cloud puts them in one keychain and includes that keychain in each role. The same keychain can belong to many roles, and a role can include many keychains.
Reuse also means one change propagates. Adding a key to a keychain grants it to every role that includes the keychain, and removing a key withdraws it from all of them at once.
Keychains are defined for the whole deployment 🔗 Keys, keychains, and roles are records of the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment, not copies inside each organization. What is scoped to an organization is the role assignment. As a result, a change to a keychain, or to the keychains a role includes, applies to every user who holds an affected role in every organization. Roles explains this from the role side.
Default keychains 🔗 Layer5 Cloud ships 30 default keychains, each grouping the keys for one area. The system account owns them. Representative examples:
Keychain What it groups User View Viewing keys every user needs, including View Tokens, View Sessions, View Keys, and View Keychains User Management Managing users and their roles Team Management Managing teams and team membership Organization Management Managing organizations, their teams, and their users Security Management Token administration, including Create Token, Delete Token, and Download Token Provider Management Deployment administration, including Edit Key, Delete Key, Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, Delete Keychain, and Assign Keychains to Roles The remaining default keychains cover workspaces, environments, the catalog, lifecycle actions, extensions, settings, performance, views, collaboration, infrastructure, curation, the Academy, events, and the Kanvas action sets. The Roles and Permissions reference lists them and shows which roles hold which keys.
Only a Provider Admin can change a default keychain, as with every other keychain. See Who can change a keychain.
Custom keychains 🔗 A Provider Admin can create keychains beyond the defaults. The Provider Admin who creates a keychain is recorded as its owner, and a custom keychain appears only in its owner’s keychain list. Other administrators, including other Provider Admins, do not see it in their list, although any Provider Admin can still change or delete it on the server. Ownership only decides that list: it grants no right to change the keychain. A custom keychain does not belong to an organization.
Who can change a keychain 🔗 Keychains and their assignment to roles apply across the whole provider, not to one organization. Only a Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a keychain, add or remove its keys, or include it in a role or remove it from one. This is the rule as of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280.
Layer5 Cloud enforces keychain operations in two places. The interface enables or disables each control based on the keys you hold. The server checks the matching key and then confirms that the caller holds the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. Holding the Provider Admin role inside one organization does not satisfy that check.
Operation Who can do it Where it is enforced View the keychain list and a keychain’s keys Anyone holding View Keychains, which every default user role holds through User View. The list shows system-owned keychains and the viewer’s own. Interface: the Keychains tab requires View Keychains. Server: returns only system-owned keychains and the caller’s own. Create a keychain Provider Admin. The interface also requires Create Keychain. Server and interface Rename a keychain, add keys, remove keys Provider Admin. The interface also requires Edit Keychain. Server and interface Delete a keychain Provider Admin. The interface also requires Delete Keychain. Server and interface Include a keychain in a role, or remove it Provider Admin Server When the server refuses a change to a keychain, it answers HTTP 403 with a JSON error. A caller who lacks the route’s key receives code meshery_cloud-1108. A caller who holds the key without being a Provider Admin for the whole deployment receives code meshery_cloud-3336, “Only a Provider Admin can change roles, keychains or permission keys”.
Note Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, Delete Keychain, and Assign Keychains to Roles belong to the Provider Management keychain, so by default only Provider Admins see these controls enabled. Everyone else can still view keychains. A keychain takes effect only through a role 🔗 Creating a keychain changes no one’s permissions. The keychain grants its keys only when a role includes it, and including it in a role changes that role for every holder in every organization.
Creating and editing roles is a Provider Admin action on the server. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, Layer5 operates the Provider Admin role, so an organization cannot build its own custom role from custom keychains. On a self-hosted deployment, the operator’s Provider Admins can create custom keychains and the custom roles that use them. To give people a role, see Roles and Users.
What changes take effect, and when 🔗 Deleting a keychain removes its key mappings, so the keychain stops granting anything immediately, in every role that included it. Removing a key from a keychain stops that key flowing to every role that includes the keychain. Adding a key to a keychain grants it to every holder of every role that includes the keychain. Authorization is evaluated on every request, so users gain or lose access on their next action, without signing in again.
Change keychains deliberately 🔗 Default roles carry the default keychains, and every new user receives a default role. A change to a default keychain therefore changes permissions for users across the deployment, regardless of organization. Leave default keychains as shipped unless that is the intended outcome. On a self-hosted deployment, to grant a different combination of keys, a Provider Admin creates a new keychain and includes it in a new role, and then the role is assigned to the users who need it. Keychains and roles are shared by every organization, so per-organization differences come from which roles a user holds in that organization.
The custom keychains guide covers creating, editing, and deleting a keychain and including it in a role. To browse keychains in your account, open Keychains in Layer5 Cloud.
Related 🔗 Keys - the individual permissions and how they are enforced. Roles - how roles bundle keychains and who assigns them. Roles and Permissions - the default roles, keychains, and keys. Security reference - security permissions, token and session lifetimes, and endpoints.
description: How keychains group keys into reusable bundles for roles in Layer5 Cloud, who owns and can change a keychain, and what a change to a keychain affects.

These tutorials teach core Kubernetes objects by building them in Kanvas, deploying them to a live cluster, and inspecting the result. Each one ends with real objects running in a cluster, so you learn both the Kubernetes concept and the Kanvas workflow that takes a design from the canvas to the cluster and back into view.
The learning path 🔗 Work through the tutorials in order. The first five each introduce one kind of object. The last three combine many objects into complete applications and assume you know the earlier material.
Tutorial You build Concept it teaches Do first Explore Pods A standalone NGINX Pod exposed by a NodePort Service Pods, labels, your first deploy, and inspecting a running container Nothing Explore Deployments A replicated NGINX Deployment that you scale and roll to a new image Controllers, ReplicaSets, scaling, and rolling updates Explore Pods Explore Services ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Services in front of a Deployment and Pods Label selectors and what each Service type exposes Explore Deployments ConfigMaps and Secrets A Pod that reads configuration and credentials from the cluster Separating configuration and sensitive data from container images Explore Pods CronJobs A job that runs on a schedule Jobs, cron schedules, and run-to-completion workloads Explore Pods PHP guestbook with Redis A web frontend backed by a Redis datastore Multi-tier applications and service discovery between tiers Explore Services WordPress and MySQL with persistent volumes A WordPress site and its MySQL database with durable storage PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, and Secrets in a real application ConfigMaps and Secrets Cassandra with a StatefulSet A Cassandra ring StatefulSets, stable network identity, and per-replica storage WordPress and MySQL The single-object tutorials build every object by hand in the component configurator, so you see each field Kubernetes requires. The multi-object tutorials start from published Kubernetes example manifests that you import into Kanvas, which is how most teams bring existing applications into a design.
What every tutorial requires 🔗 Every tutorial deploys to a real cluster, so you need a Kanvas environment backed by one:
Meshery Playground at https://play.meshery.io, a shared live cluster that you use from your browser. Other people use the same cluster, so give every object a unique name and label. A self-hosted Meshery with at least one connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new has no cluster actions. You can draw the designs there, but Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy open a prompt to use Meshery Playground or self-host Meshery instead.
How the pieces fit together 🔗 Each tutorial repeats the same loop: you configure components in Designer, check them with Validate and Dry Run, Deploy them to the cluster, and then inspect the live objects in Operator. The Kubernetes request flow explanation describes what happens inside the cluster when those objects receive traffic, and it is useful background before the Services tutorial.
description: Hands-on Kubernetes tutorials using Meshery Playground and Kanvas.

body:
Two controls decide how a design reads on screen. Layout arranges the components - where they sit relative to one another. Layers decide which of them are drawn at all.
Both are recorded in the design rather than in your browser, so they travel with it: a layout writes the components’ positions, and the Layers panel writes their visibility into the design’s preferences. Anyone else opening the design sees the same arrangement and the same components hidden. What neither touches is configuration - a hidden component is still part of the design and is still deployed, and re-running a layout changes only where components sit.
Change design layout 🔗 The layout control sits in the bottom-left corner of the canvas, showing the icon of the layout currently in use. Clicking it fans out the available layouts; picking one re-arranges every component on the canvas with an animated transition, so you can see where things moved to. The zoom controls sit at the opposite corner, bottom-right.
Layout Shape it produces Suits Constrained A force-directed arrangement that respects grouping and containment The default, and the best general-purpose choice Grid Even rows and columns Inventories and flat sets of similar components Hierarchical A layered, top-down tree following the direction of relationships Designs with a clear flow, such as ingress to service to workload Star Concentric rings around the most connected components Finding the hubs in a design Bus A breadth-first arrangement fanning out from a root Tracing what a component reaches, level by level Ring A single circle Small designs, and comparing components at a glance Constrained is the layout selected by default.
When Kanvas lays a design out for you 🔗 Kanvas arranges a design automatically on open only when every component has no saved position, or sits at the origin. That is the case for a design imported from a file that carries no coordinates. Any other design opens with its saved positions untouched, and nothing re-arranges it until you choose a layout.
Once you drag components by hand, those positions are what the design stores. Choosing a layout overwrites them for everyone who opens the design. Use undo (Ctrl/Cmd + Z) if an arrangement was not what you wanted: positions are part of the shared design, so undo restores them.
The layout control, bottom-left of the canvas Layouts on large designs Re-running a layout across a very large design is the most expensive operation on the canvas. If a design is slow to arrange, see Performance Limits. Configure visible layers 🔗 The Layers panel controls what the canvas draws. Open it with the Layers button in the toolbar above the canvas, or press \ (backslash). Every entry has an eye toggle: switch it off and that entity disappears from the canvas until you switch it back on.
The Layers panel in Designer mode: By Type, Component Badges and Components In Designer mode the panel is organized into four sections:
By type - a single toggle each for Annotations (comments, shapes, text and other non-semantic components) and Configurable Components (the semantic components that actually get deployed). Turning annotations off is the fastest way to see the deployable shape of a design on its own. The count beside each is the number of components of that type in the design. Component Badges - Validation Warnings, Deployment Errors and Inventory badges. These are the small markers Kanvas draws on components; hiding them declutters a design that is mid-review. See Component Badges. Components - every kind present in the design, grouped by model. Expanding a group lists the individual components, each with its own visibility toggle, so you can hide one Deployment without hiding the rest. Clicking a component’s name selects it on the canvas and zooms the view to it. Relationships - each relationship kind, type and subtype found in the design, with its own toggle and a count. TagSet relationships appear here under that name. The header of the panel expands or collapses every section at once.
A resolved comment is not drawn at all until its thread is reopened, whatever the toggles say. A parent component can be collapsed to hide its children; see Component Badges.
Because visibility travels with the design, the Layers panel is a way of presenting a design as much as a way of reading one - hide the noise before you hand a design to someone else and they will open it the way you left it.
Layers in Operator mode The Layers panel is present in Operator mode too, but it filters rather than hides: instead of design components it lists the Kubernetes resource kinds MeshSync has discovered - Cluster, Workloads, Configurations, Networking, Storage, Monitoring and Custom Resources - and choosing among them changes which resources are fetched and drawn. Those choices are what a saved view records. Render mode 🔗 Layout and layers decide what is drawn and where. Render mode, in the Options drawer and the Designer toolbar, decides how much detail each component is drawn with - from full fidelity down to a wireframe - and can be set to adapt automatically when the canvas slows down. Reach for it when a design has become large enough that panning and zooming feel heavy. Render Modes explains the trade-off, and Performance Limits lists what each mode draws.
description: Reference for the six automatic layouts and the Layers panel - what each layout produces, when Kanvas lays a design out on its own, and what each layer toggle hides.
