body:
In this tutorial you build the Kubernetes guestbook: a PHP frontend that writes entries to a Redis leader and reads them from Redis followers. Six manifests from the Kubernetes examples become one Kanvas design, which you deploy, inspect in Operator, scale, and remove. The application is small, but it carries the pattern behind most multi-tier systems: each tier runs as a Deployment, each tier is reached through a Service, and tiers find each other by Service name, never by Pod address.
What you will learn 🔗 How a Service selects Pods by label, and why the selector decides where traffic goes. How one tier finds another through cluster DNS, using the Service name as the hostname. How several manifests become one design that you deploy and remove as a unit. How a design acts as desired state: you change the design, deploy again, and Kubernetes converges. How Operator shows the live objects your design created. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed Kanvas environment. Deploying needs a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use Meshery Playground, a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new does not run cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. Operator views and log streaming also need Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster. Kubernetes basics. You know what Pods, Deployments, and Services are. If Services are new to you, complete Exploring Kubernetes Services first. A namespace of your own. Playground is shared with other users. Deploy replaces any existing object with the same kind, name, and namespace, and Undeploy deletes by kind and name, so two readers deploying the guestbook into default would overwrite and delete each other’s objects. This tutorial uses the namespace guestbook-ada; substitute a unique name of your own, and give your design a unique name too. The scenario 🔗 You build six objects in three tiers:
frontend (Service, port 80) | frontend (Deployment, 3 replicas, PHP + Apache) / \ writes / \ reads v v redis-leader (Service, 6379) redis-follower (Service, 6379) | | redis-leader (Deployment, 1) redis-follower (Deployment, 2) \________ replication ____________/ Each manifest holds one object. The labels on each Deployment’s Pod template are what its Service selects:
Manifest Object Pod labels or Service selector redis-leader-deployment.yaml Deployment redis-leader, 1 replica app: redis, role: leader, tier: backend redis-leader-service.yaml Service redis-leader selects app: redis, role: leader, tier: backend redis-follower-deployment.yaml Deployment redis-follower, 2 replicas app: redis, role: follower, tier: backend redis-follower-service.yaml Service redis-follower selects app: redis, role: follower, tier: backend frontend-deployment.yaml Deployment frontend, 3 replicas app: guestbook, tier: frontend frontend-service.yaml Service frontend selects app: guestbook, tier: frontend The frontend connects to Redis at the hostnames redis-leader and redis-follower. Those names resolve only because Services with exactly those names exist in the same namespace. Renaming a Service breaks the frontend, which is why this tutorial isolates you with a namespace instead of with new object names.
Import the manifests into one design 🔗 Start from an empty canvas and open the Import Design dialog from the file menu. Import the first manifest by URL. Set the name to your design name (for example guestbook-ada), choose URL Import, and enter https://k8s.io/examples/application/guestbook/redis-leader-deployment.yaml. On an empty canvas the dialog offers Import, which loads the result as the open design. Import the other five manifests the same way, naming each import after its file. With a design open, the dialog offers Import as new and Merge into current; choose Merge into current every time so each object joins the open design. Drag the components apart, or apply a layout, until each tier is readable. Merged components keep their internal layout and land slightly offset, so they can overlap what is already on the canvas. If a URL import fails, Kanvas shows Failed to import design "<name>" without a reason. Download the file and import it with File Upload instead, keeping the .yaml extension, because the server identifies a Kubernetes manifest by its .yaml or .yml extension. Dragging a downloaded file onto a non-empty canvas also works: Kanvas asks whether to merge it into the open design or open it as new.
What just happened. Each import sent one manifest to Meshery Server, which recognized it as a Kubernetes manifest, converted the object into a component, and saved the result as a new design in your account. Merge then copied that design’s components into the open design with fresh ids. Merge never matches or de-duplicates, so merging the same manifest twice gives you two copies. The single-manifest designs stay saved in your account after the merge; you can delete them at the end. Kanvas saves the open design automatically a few seconds after each change, and new designs are saved with public visibility.
Check your work. The canvas holds six components: three Deployments and three Services. Seven or more means a manifest was merged twice; delete the duplicate.
Place every object in your namespace 🔗 Open each of the six components in turn and set its namespace to guestbook-ada. What just happened. The example manifests do not set a namespace, so without this step every object would go to default. The namespace field appears only on namespaced kinds such as Deployments and Services. You do not need to create the namespace: Deploy creates a missing namespace before it applies the objects. Because the frontend uses short hostnames, it still finds redis-leader and redis-follower; short Service names resolve within the caller’s own namespace.
Check the wiring before you deploy 🔗 Open the frontend Service and compare its selector with the Pod template labels of the frontend Deployment. Do the same for both Redis pairs. Each selector must match its Deployment’s labels exactly. Run Validate. Run Dry Run. What just happened. Validate runs in your browser. It checks each component’s configuration against that component’s schema and reports problems as advisory warnings; it never contacts the cluster and never checks whether a selector matches anything. Dry Run sends every object to the cluster API server as a server-side dry run: the API server runs its own validation and admission checks but persists nothing.
Check your work. Validate reports No validation errors. On the first deployment into a new namespace, Dry Run reports a not-found error for every component, because a dry run does not create namespaces and guestbook-ada does not exist yet. That error is expected here. Any other dry-run error names the field at fault; selecting it opens the component’s configurator at that field.
A mismatched selector passes both checks. The Service deploys, selects no Pods, and silently routes traffic nowhere. Matching selectors to labels is your job, and the comparison in step 1 is how you do it.
Deploy and verify 🔗 Run Deploy. The deploy dialog steps through validation, the deployment target, a dry run, and a final review. At the target step, select the environment that holds your cluster connection. At the dry-run step, the namespace errors from the previous phase appear again. Select Bypass errors and initiate deployment to continue. Confirm the deployment and read the summary. What just happened. Meshery Server applied each component to the cluster. For each object it creates the object, or replaces it in place if one with the same kind, name, and namespace already exists, so deploying the same design twice updates rather than duplicates. Kanvas applies independent components in parallel and does not order them, so the frontend can start before Redis is ready; Kubernetes restarts what fails until the dependencies answer. Every applied object carries a label with your design’s id. Kubernetes, not Kanvas, then creates the ReplicaSets and Pods that each Deployment asks for.
Check your work. The summary lists six rows, such as Deployed Deployment "frontend". A row that reads Failed to deploy carries an error card with the probable cause and a suggested remediation. Read the rows even when the notification says the deployment completed: that notification also appears when some components failed. An error that the Kubernetes cluster is unavailable means no connected cluster was selected.
Inspect the application in Operator 🔗 Open the design in Operator, either from Open In Operator in the deploy summary or from the design’s View in Operator action. Operator opens a view scoped to your design. In the Layers panel, filter by your namespace to see every object in it, including the ReplicaSets and Pods that the Deployment controller created. Select the frontend Service. The details panel shows its type, cluster IP, and selector. Select a frontend Pod. The status chip shows its phase, and the details list the node it runs on, its IP, and its containers. What just happened. Operator draws a snapshot of the cluster as MeshSync last reported it. The design-scoped view filters on the design-id label that Kanvas put on the objects it applied. Operator does not stream changes: it refetches when you open a view, change a filter, or change the selected clusters. To see Pods that were still starting, change a filter or reopen the view.
Check your work. Six Pods are Running: three frontend, one redis-leader, two redis-follower. A Pod stuck in Pending usually means the cluster lacks room to schedule it; check its conditions in the details panel. If the canvas reads Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster?, Operator has no inventory for the cluster.
Scale the frontend 🔗 Switch back to Designer, open the frontend Deployment, and set its replicas to 5. Run Deploy again. The dry run passes cleanly this time, because the namespace now exists. Return to Operator and refresh the view by changing a filter. What just happened. Deploy replaced the existing frontend Deployment with the version in your design. The Deployment controller saw a desired count of five and started two more Pods. The design is your desired state: any change made directly in the cluster, for example with kubectl scale or kubectl set image, is overwritten the next time you deploy the design. Change the image tag the same way when you need to roll out a new version.
Keep changes to fields Kubernetes allows you to update, such as replicas and images. A change to an immutable field, such as a Deployment’s selector, is rejected by Kubernetes, yet the deploy summary reports it as deployed and the old value stays in the cluster.
Check your work. Operator shows five frontend Pods. The Deployment’s details read 5 / 5 once all Pods are available.
Read the logs 🔗 In Operator, right-click the redis-leader Pod and start a log session (Initiate Log Session). Read the session in the panel that opens. What just happened. A log session follows the Pod’s output, starting with its most recent 1,000 lines. Each line carries a Kubernetes timestamp and a [pod:container] prefix; a Pod with several containers shows all of them in one tab. The leader’s log shows Redis accepting connections and the two followers requesting replication, which confirms that the followers found the leader through the redis-leader Service name. Search in the panel highlights matches without hiding other lines. Closing the tab stops the stream.
Check your work. Lines appear within a few seconds. An empty tab means the stream did not start; the panel does not display stream errors, so confirm that MeshSync is healthy on the cluster and start the session again.
Clean up 🔗 In Designer, run Undeploy, select the same environment, and confirm. Delete the guestbook design and the five single-manifest designs from your account if you no longer need them. See Deleting a design. Undeploy deletes each component’s object by kind and name, in that component’s namespace, on the clusters you select. It removes the three Deployments and three Services; Kubernetes then garbage-collects the ReplicaSets and Pods those Deployments owned. Undeploy acts only on components in the design, and it matches by kind and name, not by label, so it also deletes a same-named object in your namespace that Kanvas did not create. The namespace guestbook-ada remains, empty, because the design has no Namespace component for Undeploy to delete. The design itself is unchanged; you can deploy it again at any time.
What you learned 🔗 A Service routes to whatever Pods its selector matches. Labels and selectors are the wiring of a multi-tier application, and neither Validate nor a dry run checks that they agree. Tiers address each other by Service name through cluster DNS, so names are part of the application’s contract and namespaces are the safe way to isolate copies. Six manifests imported and merged into one design deploy and undeploy as a unit. Deploy creates or replaces each object, so the design is the desired state and redeploying is how you scale and update. Operator shows a snapshot of what is running, scoped to your design or filtered by namespace, and streams Pod logs on demand. Next steps 🔗 Add storage and secrets to a two-tier application in Deploy WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes. Review every deploy option and failure mode in Deploying designs. Learn how Operator discovers and draws cluster resources in Operator.

body:
Publishing makes a design discoverable in the Layer5 Cloud catalog, where anyone can view and clone it. Publishing is separate from visibility: making a design public does not publish it.
Visibility and publication states 🔗 State Who can read it How it gets there Private Owner, provider administrators, and users with a share grant Cloning, unpublishing, or switching a public design to private Public Anyone, including anonymous callers, who has the design’s id or link The default for every newly saved design Published Everyone through the catalog An approved publish request, or a direct publish by an approver The owner can toggle a design between private and public until it is published. A published design cannot be toggled. The toggle saves through the normal save path, so it raises the version and re-checks the components limit.
Publish a design 🔗 Publishing needs a signed-in account. Anonymous users see a “Sign in to publish” prompt. The Publish to Catalog action sits in the design’s details, and is available from the Share menu. It is disabled until the design has loaded.
The form asks for:
Type: the design category used for catalog browsing. Compatibility: the technologies the design applies to. Select at least one, or the form stops with “Please select at least one technology.” Pattern info: the purpose and intended use. Pattern caveats: limitations, assumptions, and operational warnings. Write for a reader who clones the design without your context. The form shows “Upon submitting your catalog item, an approval flow will be initiated.” Once the design is published, the button reads “Published” and is disabled. Save stores catalog data and visibility without publishing.
Publishing needs the Publish Design permission in the interface. The server accepts any caller who passes the checks below.
What happens on submit 🔗 The server requires a catalog data object, lowercases the type and compatibility values, and sets the light and dark snapshot image URLs from the design id. A design that already has a publish request in any state (pending, approved, or denied) is rejected with catalog request for content with id "<id>" already exist from user <name>. That includes a design whose earlier request was denied or whose publication was later removed.
Then the outcome depends on your role:
Your permission Outcome Approve Catalog Request The design publishes at once. Visibility becomes published, the content class is “official”, and the published version is the design’s current version. A workflow adds it to the public catalog repository. If that workflow fails, the publish stands and an error event is recorded. Anyone else A request is created with status pending and content class “community”. Visibility does not change. The catalog maintainers receive an email titled “New Catalog publish request”, and you receive a copy. Content classes are official, verified, and community. A direct publish by an approver is always official.
Review a request 🔗 Users with the View Catalog Requests permission see the queue in Layer5 Cloud. Users with Approve Catalog Request or Deny Catalog Request decide each request.
Only a pending request can be decided. Deciding any other request returns 409 “publish request already exists with status: ”. A caller without the key gets 403 “unauthorized to approve catalog publish request”. Approving sets visibility to published, records the approver’s chosen content class, and records the published version. It does not start the workflow that adds the design to the public catalog repository, which only a direct publish by an approver starts. Denying sets the request to denied and leaves visibility unchanged. The design owner receives an approval or denial email unless their notification preferences turn it off. Server-side validation of catalog data is minimal. The interface form enforces the required fields.
Unpublish a design 🔗 The design’s creator, or any user with Approve Catalog Request, can unpublish it. The Unpublish Design permission controls the action in the Layer5 Cloud interface. Others get 403 “unauthorized to unpublish to catalog”.
Unpublishing sets visibility to private (not public), starts a delete-from-catalog workflow, and records an event. Catalog data stays on the design. The earlier publish request record is not cleared, so submitting the same design again hits the existing-request rule above.
Deleting a published design also starts the delete-from-catalog workflow. See Delete a Design.
Publish to Artifact Hub 🔗 Kanvas has no direct Artifact Hub publishing. To list a design there, export it as a Helm chart and publish that chart to a Helm repository, then register the repository in Artifact Hub using its own documentation. See Export Designs. Exporting to a Helm chart drops layout and annotations.
Tiers 🔗 No plan feature is checked when you publish. Publishing is governed by the permissions above. See Permissions.

body:
A self-hosted deployment runs the same Layer5 Cloud that Layer5 operates, on infrastructure you control. Your users sign in against your identity services, your organizations and designs live in your database, and Meshery Servers in your network connect to your deployment as their remote provider. Your data stays in your database.
Self-hosting is part of the Enterprise plan.
Identity & Access Management Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Cloud as an IDP Own and control the user accounts of your enterprise members with Cloud your identity provider (IdP). -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Support and Deployment Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Managed Service Provider White Label: Customize the appearance and branding of your engineering platform powered by Cloud. Multi-tenancy: Hierarchical organizations, teams, users and customizable permissioning. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Self-hosted Deployment Self-hosted Cloud for on-prem appliances or self-managed cloud tenants. Keep your designs internal to your workplace. Get remote support when you need it. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included What you deploy 🔗 One Helm chart, layer5-cloud, installs the identity-aware application and its two identity services. You supply the database, the ingress, and the TLS certificate.
Component Provided by What it does Layer5 Cloud server layer5-cloud chart Serves the web UI and the API, enforces organizations, teams, roles, and keys, and runs the signaling endpoint for real-time co-editing. Listens on port 9876. Kratos Subchart Owns accounts: password sign-in, social sign-in, email verification, and account recovery. Hydra Subchart Issues OAuth2 tokens to the UI, to Meshery Servers, and to API clients. PostgreSQL You Holds three databases on one server: meshery, kratos, and hydra. Ingress controller and TLS You Publishes one hostname. Routes / to the server, /kratos to Kratos, /hydra to Hydra, and passes WebSocket upgrades on /collaboration. SMTP relay You Sends invitations, notifications, and identity mail (verification and recovery). Webhook receivers You Optional endpoints that receive support requests, signup decisions, and Kanvas entitlement events. Meshery Server is deployed separately and is not part of this chart. See Meshery Server registration for how a Meshery Server attaches to a provider.
What changes when you host it 🔗 Area On your deployment Provider administration Your operators hold the Provider Admin role. They create the first organization, assign custom roles, and approve signup requests. See Roles and Permissions. Default sign-in providers You register the Google and GitHub OAuth applications that every organization without its own credentials uses. See Identity Services. Mail The shared relay is yours. Organizations can still register their own. See Troubleshoot Email Delivery. Branding and domains Organizations apply their own theme and domain; you set the provider-level defaults. See White-label Layer5 Cloud. Upgrades You choose when to upgrade. The server applies database migrations at startup. Billing Plan entitlements are not enforced by the deployment beyond the component limit. See Feature Availability. Plan, deploy, operate 🔗 Plan a deployment. Decide on the database, hostname, identity providers, mail relay, provider administrator, and network paths. Deploy Layer5 Cloud. Install with Helm, create the Hydra client, and confirm the deployment is ready. Configure. Set chart values, provider initialization, and webhooks. Operate. Watch health and logs and diagnose mail delivery. Real-time co-editing has one network dependency outside your cluster: browsers must reach public STUN and TURN hosts to connect to each other. See Networking before you deploy into a restricted network.

body:
A badge is a small marker Kanvas draws on the edge of a component to report something about it: errors waiting to be fixed, components held inside it, a link, or where it came from. Badges are status, not decoration. A count on a badge tells you there is something to read, and clicking it shows what.
Which badges appear depends on the mode. Designer mode draws badges that help you build a valid design. Operator mode draws badges about live resources.
Badges in Designer mode 🔗 Badge Position Appears when Click Error count Bottom-left, red, shows a number The component has at least one schema validation warning or deployment error. The number is the sum of both. Opens a summary with one count per category. Each count opens the matching details: the validation results or the deployment results. Inventory Bottom-right, shows a number The component holds other components inside it. The number is how many. Lists the held components. Choosing one opens its configurator. External Link Top-right You set a Link on the component in its style options. Opens the URL in a new tab. Parent model icon Left edge, above the error count The component is a parent that contains other components. None. It shows the parent’s model icon in the component color. Expand and collapse Inside the component, top-right The component is a parent with children. Hides the children, or shows them again. Section label Top-left, inside the section The object is a section. None. It carries the section name, shortened with an ellipsis when it does not fit the width. Error count 🔗 The error count joins two checks into one number:
Validation warnings come from checking the component’s configuration against its schema, such as a missing required field or an invalid value. Deployment errors come from a dry run of the design against a cluster. See Validating Designs. A component with no errors shows no badge. Fix the field the warning names and the count drops, and the badge disappears at zero. Opening a validation warning from the badge takes you to the offending configuration field.
Inventory 🔗 An inventory badge appears on a component that holds other components, such as a workload that holds its configuration objects. The held components are drawn inside the inventory rather than as separate nodes on the canvas. The relationship between them is created by the policy engine; see Relationships.
Badges in Operator mode 🔗 Badge Position Appears when Click Managed by Meshery Top-left, green The resource was created from a design and Kanvas knows which one. Opens the source design in Designer mode. Terminal Bottom-right, black The resource is a container that has a terminal session open. Opens the terminal panel. See Interactive Terminal. Operator mode draws no health, performance or policy badge. Resource state is on the resource itself; see Resource Details.
Showing and hiding badges 🔗 The Layers panel has a Component Badges section with separate switches for Validation Warnings, Deployment Errors and Inventory. Switching one off removes its share of the error count, or the inventory badge, from the canvas without changing the design’s contents. The setting is saved with the design. See Layout and Layers. Badges draw only at Full render fidelity. In Medium and the lower fidelity modes Kanvas leaves them out to keep large designs responsive. Badges, like object controls, draw only when the canvas is zoomed in far enough to read them. Practical use 🔗 Clear the error count on every component before you deploy. A design with no badges is a design that passes both checks. Use the Managed by Meshery badge to jump from a live resource to the design that produced it when you need to change its configuration. Hide badges before you take a screenshot for a review if you want a clean image. See Canvas Actions.

body:
Deleting a design removes the design record and its workspace mappings in one transaction. There is no trash and no restore. Export a copy first if you might need it. See Export Designs.
Who can delete 🔗 The server allows the design’s owner or a provider administrator. Organization administrators, workspace owners, and collaborators with a share grant cannot delete a design (403 “unauthorized for the operation”). Layer5 Cloud hides its Delete action for roles without the Delete a Design permission, but the server decides by ownership, not by the key. To remove a design from a workspace without deleting it, use the workspace’s remove action instead.
Delete from Kanvas 🔗 Delete is a File menu action, disabled on an empty canvas. A confirmation reads Delete <name> design with the text Are you sure you want to delete <name>?. You confirm with a single button. There is no type-to-confirm step.
If you delete the open design, the editor resets to a new blank design. Deleting a different design from a list does not change the canvas. Kanvas shows no success message for a delete, while Layer5 Cloud shows <name> deleted.
What deletion affects 🔗 Item Effect Deployed resources None. Deleting does not undeploy anything from clusters. Undeploy first if you want the resources gone. Clones, Save as copies, merged-in components Untouched. They are independent. Share grants Removed with the design. Collaboration session Ends when the canvas resets. Published design A delete-from-catalog workflow runs against the catalog repository. If it fails, the failure is logged only. The catalog request record stays. Catalog clones made by others Remain. An event records who deleted which design.
Delete several designs 🔗 Layer5 Cloud’s catalog designs table offers multi-select delete with the prompt Are you sure that you want to delete <N> designs?. It issues one delete per selected design, so a partial failure shows per-design errors. Kanvas has no multi-select delete.
Errors 🔗 Response Cause 400 “please provide a valid design ID” The id is invalid. 404 “design not found” The design does not exist. A missing row can also surface as 500 “failed to get design from database”. 403 You are not the owner or a provider administrator.

body:
Render mode sets how much detail Kanvas draws for a design. It works as a fidelity dial for your current session, not a property of the design. Switching modes never changes components, relationships, configuration, or layers, and the mode is not saved with the design. Every session starts in Full unless the URL sets a different mode. The switcher appears in the Options dialog and in the Designer toolbar.
What each mode trades away 🔗 Kanvas has four render modes. Each of the first three gives up something the mode above it draws.
Full draws everything: component images and gradient fills, every badge, TagSets, mount animations on new components, and animated layouts on designs that are small enough. Medium keeps component images and relationship styling but drops gradient fills, TagSets, animations, and most badges, including validation and dry-run error badges. It keeps expand and collapse badges so you can still navigate compound components. Wireframe reduces the design to its structure. Component images, all badges, and text-box overlays disappear, and edges become thin, straight, light gray lines with simple arrowheads. You can still edit everything. View-only draws as sparsely as Wireframe but keeps relationship styling on edges. It also removes interaction: components are locked, and nothing can be grabbed, dragged, selected, resized, or double-clicked. The exact element-by-element breakdown is on Performance Limits.
Why less detail is faster 🔗 Panning and zooming move the viewport, and every visible element must follow. In Full, that means repositioning badges, redrawing images and gradients, and tracing curved, colored edges on every frame of the gesture. Each mode below Full removes some of that per-frame work, so the same design responds faster as fidelity drops. The design’s size does not change; the cost of looking at it does.
Adaptive mode 🔗 Adaptive mode lets Kanvas turn the dial for you. Turning it on in the switcher shows an AUTO chip, and the mode you pick from then on becomes the ceiling: the highest fidelity Adaptive mode may use. The default ceiling is Full, and the canvas switches to the ceiling as soon as Adaptive mode turns on.
What it measures. While Adaptive mode is on, Kanvas measures how long the canvas takes to show the next frame after each pan or zoom. It keeps the last 20 measurements and acts on the 95th percentile, so a single slow frame does not trigger a change. It measures nothing while the canvas is idle.
The ladder. Adaptive mode moves one step at a time between Full, Medium, and Wireframe. It never enters or leaves View-only; that mode is always your choice.
Down fast, up slow. When the 95th percentile exceeds 80 ms, Kanvas drops one step, and it can drop another step 3 seconds later if the canvas is still slow. Climbing back requires 10 consecutive fast measurements (under 30 ms), at least 5 seconds since the last change, and a next mode no higher than the ceiling. The asymmetry is deliberate: lag is an immediate problem, and returning too early causes the canvas to flicker between modes.
How it behaves today:
Each automatic change shows a notification, such as “Switched to Medium mode for better performance” or “Performance improved - switched to Full mode”. The switcher shows the ceiling, not the mode currently drawn. Use the notifications to tell which mode is active. After a slowdown, Kanvas climbs back at most one step. It stays at that mode until the next slowdown, even when the canvas is fast again. Changing the ceiling while Adaptive mode is on updates the switcher, but the new ceiling takes effect the next time you turn Adaptive mode on. Turning Adaptive mode off leaves the canvas in whichever mode Adaptive mode last chose. You can also start a session in a given mode or with Adaptive mode on through the URL. When a URL sets both, Adaptive mode starts with a Full ceiling and the URL’s mode as the starting mode. See URL Parameters.
How render mode interacts with other features 🔗 Size gates. Some features turn themselves off on large designs, and render mode moves the threshold. Auto-pan on drag, which is off by default, runs only while the design’s component and edge counts stay under a per-mode limit that rises as fidelity drops. Kanvas re-checks the limit whenever you add or remove elements or change modes, so the feature returns without a reload. Animated layout runs only in Full and only on small designs; in every other case, layouts apply instantly. See Auto-pan on Drag and Performance Limits for the numbers.
Zoom. Feasibility evaluation and component style editing depend on zoom level, not render mode. They become available only once you zoom in past a fixed level, in every mode.
Layers. Layer visibility is saved with the design and applies in every mode. A hidden layer stays hidden in Full, and switching modes never brings it back. TagSets need both conditions: the TagSets layer must be visible and the mode must be Full. See Layout and Layers.
Designer and Operator 🔗 Render mode works the same way in Designer and Operator. Operator’s badges, which show resources managed by Meshery and terminal sessions, appear only in Full, like the other decorative badges.
Choosing a mode 🔗 Full - reviewing, presenting, or capturing a design when every badge and TagSet matters. Medium - everyday editing on a design large enough that Full feels slow. Wireframe - layout passes and heavy panning on large designs where structure matters more than appearance. View-only - showing a design to others when nobody should move anything by accident. Adaptive, Full ceiling - general work when you would rather not manage the dial. Turn it off for screenshots, recordings, and side-by-side comparisons, where a mode change in the middle would mislead. Related pages 🔗 Performance Limits: render-mode matrix, size gates, and limits. URL Parameters: set the render mode and Adaptive mode on load. Auto-pan on Drag: the setting and its per-mode thresholds. Layout and Layers: layer visibility and layout behavior.

body:
A session is the credential Layer5 Cloud issues each time someone signs in. It is what keeps a browser tab, a second device, or a connected Meshery Server signed in, and it is what you end when you want one of those sign-ins to stop working. Sessions expire on their own; API tokens do not.
One session per sign-in 🔗 Every sign-in creates its own session. Each browser, device, and Meshery Server that signs in through Layer5 Cloud holds a separate session with its own expiry, and any number of them can be active at once. Ending one session leaves the others untouched.
A session acts as the user who signed in. What it can do in an organization is whatever the roles that user holds there allow, checked on every request. See Keys for how roles grant permissions.
Users see their own sessions on the Sessions tab of the Security page, which lists each session’s ID, name, purpose, and creation date. The tab requires the View Sessions key, which every default user role holds. The list shows no device, browser, or location for a session.
How long a session lasts 🔗 These are the Layer5 Cloud deployment defaults. Operators of a self-hosted deployment can change them.
Credential Default lifetime Behavior Access token 24 hours The browser session ends when it lapses. Activity in the interface does not extend it, so a browser user signs in again after 24 hours. Refresh token 1000 hours (about 41 days) Clients such as Meshery Server use it to obtain a new access token. Each refresh token works once; every refresh issues a new one. A failed refresh returns an error. Privileged-action window Set by the deployment; 15 minutes in the packaged default Sensitive actions, such as profile changes, ask you to authenticate again once this window has passed since sign-in. Anonymous Kanvas use, without signing in, lasts 24 hours and does not appear on the Sessions tab.
What ends a session 🔗 A session ends in one of three ways:
Expiry. The access token lapses at its lifetime, as described above. Logout from the Sessions tab. The session’s token is revoked immediately; the next request that presents it fails. The action records the same audit event as deleting a token. Signing out of the app. Signing out ends the browser’s identity session and revokes its stored grant. Changing your password does not end your other sessions. Layer5 Cloud has no sign-out-everywhere action and no idle timeout setting. To end your other sessions, log each one out from the Sessions tab. Review and sign out sessions covers the task.
Who can use Logout The Logout action on the Sessions tab requires the Delete Token key, which only Organization Admins and Provider Admins hold by default. Users, Team Admins, and Workspace Admins see Logout disabled, even though their roles hold the Logout from a Session key. Layer5 Cloud lets each user log out only their own sessions; no role can end another user’s session from this tab. How the browser stores a session 🔗 The browser keeps the session in a cookie that page scripts cannot read (HttpOnly), that is sent only over HTTPS, and that uses SameSite Lax, so other sites cannot send it along with their own requests except on ordinary top-level navigation. A second, companion cookie tells the interface that a session exists. It carries no secret and lapses with the session.
The cookie’s scope depends on how the organization signs users in:
Platform sign-in provider. The cookie is shared across the platform’s hosts, so one sign-in covers them. Organization’s own identity provider, or a custom domain outside the platform’s domain. The cookie is host-only and is never sent to any other host. See Organizations for how custom domains and identity providers decide where a user signs in.
Sessions and API tokens 🔗 Sessions and API tokens both authenticate as you, and Layer5 Cloud revokes them through the same mechanism. They differ in how they start and how long they live.
Session API token Created by Signing in from a browser, device, or Meshery Server Creating it on the Tokens tab with a name and purpose Lifetime 24-hour access token, renewable by clients for up to about 41 days No expiry Ended by Expiry, Logout on the Sessions tab, or signing out Deleting it on the Tokens tab Used for Interactive use and connected Meshery Servers Scripts and API clients sending a Bearer token The Tokens tab never lists sessions, and the Sessions tab never lists API tokens. See Tokens for how API tokens behave.
What Layer5 Cloud does not offer 🔗 No organization-level session policy. Lifetimes are set for the whole deployment. No idle timeout setting in the product interface. No device, browser, or location detail on a session. No action that ends every session at once. The security reference lists the session keys, default lifetimes, and cookie attributes in one place.

body:
In this tutorial you deploy WordPress backed by a MySQL database, and you give both tiers storage that outlives their Pods. You import the two Kubernetes example manifests into one design, add the Secret that holds the database password, and add the PersistentVolumes that the claims bind to. Stateless Pods can be replaced at any moment; a database cannot lose its files when that happens. This tutorial shows how Kubernetes separates the data from the Pod, and exactly which pieces a deploy creates and an undeploy removes.
What you will learn 🔗 How a PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage and how Kubernetes binds it to a PersistentVolume. Why data on a volume survives Pod restarts, and where it physically lives with a hostPath volume. How a Secret passes a password to containers without writing it into the Deployment, and what a Secret does not protect. How labels and sections organize a design without changing what it deploys. What Undeploy removes and what it leaves in place. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed Kanvas environment. Deploying needs a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use Meshery Playground, a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new does not run cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. Operator views and terminal sessions also need Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster. The multi-tier pattern. You have completed Deploy a PHP Guestbook with Redis, or you already know how to import and merge manifests and how Services select Pods. Understanding Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets covers Secrets in more depth. Unique names. Playground is shared. Deploy replaces any object with the same kind, name, and namespace, and Undeploy deletes by kind and name. This tutorial uses the namespace wordpress-ada and the prefix ada for cluster-wide names; substitute your own. The scenario 🔗 You build nine objects. Two of them, the PersistentVolumes, are cluster-scoped; the rest live in your namespace.
wordpress (Service, LoadBalancer, port 80) mysql-pass (Secret) | / \ wordpress (Deployment) ---- WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD --' '-- MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD | \ | | '-- connects to host "wordpress-mysql" --> wordpress-mysql (Service, headless, 3306) | | wp-pv-claim (PVC, 20Gi) wordpress-mysql (Deployment, Recreate) | | ada-wp-pv (PV, hostPath) mysql-pv-claim (PVC, 20Gi) | ada-mysql-pv (PV, hostPath) The two manifests, mysql-deployment.yaml and wordpress-deployment.yaml, each hold a Service, a PersistentVolumeClaim, and a Deployment. They do not include the Secret or any PersistentVolume: both Deployments expect a Secret named mysql-pass, and the claims expect the cluster to provide storage. You add those pieces yourself.
Import and merge the manifests 🔗 On an empty canvas, import https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/wordpress/mysql-deployment.yaml with the Import Design dialog (URL Import). Name it after your design, for example wordpress-ada. Import https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/wordpress/wordpress-deployment.yaml and choose Merge into current. Set the namespace of all six components to wordpress-ada. What just happened. Each import converted one multi-document manifest into components and saved it as its own design; merging copied the second design’s components into the open one. The open design now holds six components, and your account also holds the single-manifest WordPress design, which you can delete at the end. Deploy creates the wordpress-ada namespace if it does not exist.
Check your work. The canvas shows two Deployments, two Services, and two PersistentVolumeClaims. If an import fails with Failed to import design "<name>", download the file and import it with File Upload, keeping the .yaml extension.
Add the Secret for the database password 🔗 Both Deployments read the password from the Secret mysql-pass, key password:
env: - name: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: mysql-pass key: password Encode a throwaway password in base64, for example echo -n 'tutorial-only' | base64. Add a Secret component from the Kubernetes components in the dock. Set its name to mysql-pass, its namespace to wordpress-ada, and its type to Opaque. Add one data entry with the key password and your base64 value. What just happened. The Deployments refer to the password by Secret name and key, so the password never appears in either Deployment, and you can change it without editing them. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. The value is stored in your design, and new designs are saved with public visibility, so anyone who can open the design can decode it. Use a password that protects nothing else. In Operator, the details panel shows a Secret’s type but not its values; the resource download from the details panel does include them.
Check your work. The Secret’s name and key match the secretKeyRef exactly. A mismatch does not fail Validate or the dry run; it shows up after deployment as Pods that never start, with a status such as CreateContainerConfigError.
Add PersistentVolumes and bind the claims 🔗 The claims in the manifests request 20Gi each and name no storage class, which means “use the cluster’s default dynamic provisioner”. Instead, you provide the volumes yourself and bind each claim to them through a storage class name of your own.
Add two PersistentVolume components. They are cluster-scoped, so they have no namespace field, and their names must be unique across the whole cluster: name them ada-wp-pv and ada-mysql-pv. On both, set the storage class name to ada-manual, add the access mode ReadWriteOnce, and set the capacity to storage: 20Gi. Give each a hostPath volume source with type DirectoryOrCreate: path /mnt/data/ada-wp-pv for the WordPress volume and /mnt/data/ada-mysql-pv for the MySQL volume. Set the storage class name of both claims, wp-pv-claim and mysql-pv-claim, to ada-manual. What just happened. A claim is a request: “20Gi, mounted read-write by one node, from class ada-manual.” The Kubernetes control plane binds each claim to an available volume of the same class with a compatible access mode and at least the requested capacity. The class name needs no StorageClass object behind it; it only has to match. A class name unique to you keeps another reader’s claim from binding your volume. A hostPath volume is a directory on the node where the Pod runs, so the data belongs to that node. That is acceptable for learning and wrong for production, where a node failure takes the data with it.
Check your work. You have two PersistentVolumes and two claims, all with the class ada-manual, and each volume’s capacity is at least its claim’s request.
Label and group the components 🔗 Add the label tutorial: wordpress-ada to every component in its Labels tab. Add two sections (the Section tool in the dock, or press S). Name one web tier and the other database tier, and drag the WordPress and MySQL components into their sections. What just happened. Labels on a component become labels on the object it deploys, so you can filter for all of your objects at once in Operator, across kinds. These labels change object metadata only. They do not change any Deployment’s Pod template or any Service’s selector, so they do not affect traffic. Sections are annotations: a section is saved with the design, components inside it move with it, and Deploy skips it because annotations are never applied to the cluster.
Check your work. The design has nine Kubernetes components inside two sections, and each component lists the new label.
Deploy and verify 🔗 Run Validate, then Deploy. Select the environment that holds your cluster connection. At the dry-run step, expect a not-found error for each namespaced component on the first deployment: a dry run does not create namespaces, and wordpress-ada does not exist yet. Select Bypass errors and initiate deployment. Any other error names the field at fault. Confirm the deployment and read the summary. What just happened. Meshery Server created the namespace, then created each object, or replaced it in place if it already existed. Independent components are applied in parallel, with no ordering. Kubernetes reconciles the rest: a Pod waits for its claim to bind, a container that starts before its Secret exists retries, and WordPress restarts until MySQL accepts connections. The MySQL Deployment uses the Recreate strategy so that an update stops the old Pod before the new one mounts the same ReadWriteOnce volume.
Check your work. The summary lists nine Deployed rows. A Failed to deploy row carries an error card with the cause and remediation. Read the rows even when the notification says the deployment completed, since it also says so when some components failed.
Inspect storage in Operator 🔗 Open the design in Operator. The view is scoped to the objects your design created. In the Layers panel, open the Storage group and turn on PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims, or filter by the label tutorial=wordpress-ada. Select ada-mysql-pv. Its details show capacity, the bound claim and its namespace, access modes, and storage class. Select the wordpress Service. Its type is LoadBalancer. Optional: right-click the MySQL Pod, start a terminal session, and run ls /var/lib/mysql to see the database files on the mounted volume. What just happened. Operator shows a snapshot of the cluster from MeshSync, refetched when you open a view, change a filter, or change clusters; it does not stream. Change a filter to see Pods that were still starting. A LoadBalancer Service receives an external address only when the cluster has a load balancer integration, so on Playground the load balancer field stays empty and WordPress is reachable only inside the cluster.
Check your work. Both claims and both volumes show Bound, and both Pods are Running. A claim stuck in Pending means no volume matched its class, access mode, or size; compare the claim’s storage class with the volume’s. A Pod stuck in Pending is usually waiting for that claim.
What persistence means here 🔗 MySQL writes its files to /var/lib/mysql, which is the mounted claim, which is bound to ada-mysql-pv, which is the directory /mnt/data/ada-mysql-pv on a node. When the Pod is replaced, for a crash, an update, or a rescheduling, the new Pod mounts the same claim and finds the same files. The data’s lifetime is tied to the volume and the directory, not to any Pod.
The limit of this setup is the node. A hostPath directory exists on one node only. If the replacement Pod lands on a different node, it gets a different, empty directory. Production clusters use a storage class backed by network or cloud storage, which can follow a Pod from node to node. The Kubernetes documentation on Persistent Volumes covers binding, reclaim policies, and dynamic provisioning in full.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy and select the same environment. Delete the design and the single-manifest WordPress design if you no longer need them. See Deleting a design. Undeploy deletes each component’s object by kind and name. This design has a component for every object you built, so Undeploy removes both Deployments, both Services, the Secret, both claims, and both PersistentVolumes. Kubernetes holds a claim’s deletion until no Pod uses it, and a volume’s until no claim is bound to it, so the order resolves itself. Sections were never deployed, so there is nothing to remove for them. Undeploying designs describes removal in full.
Undeploy does not remove:
The data. Deleting a manually created PersistentVolume object does not delete the files under /mnt/data/ada-wp-pv and /mnt/data/ada-mysql-pv. If you deploy again and the Pods land on the same node, MySQL starts with its old database. The namespace. wordpress-ada remains, empty, because the design has no Namespace component. Anything not in the design. Undeploy acts only on components it finds in the design. Had you removed the PersistentVolume components before undeploying, the volumes would stay in the cluster. What you learned 🔗 A claim requests storage by class, access mode, and size; the control plane binds it to a matching volume, and a unique class name keeps the binding yours. Data lives on the volume, not in the Pod, so it survives Pod replacement; with hostPath it is also tied to one node. A Secret decouples a password from the Deployments that use it, but base64 is not encryption, and a Secret component stores its value in the design. Labels and sections organize a design. Labels also mark the deployed objects; sections never reach the cluster. Undeploy removes exactly the components in the design, by kind and name, and leaves volume data and unlisted objects in place. Next steps 🔗 Give each replica its own identity and its own volume in Deploy Cassandra with a StatefulSet. Review every deploy option and failure mode in Deploying designs. Learn how Operator discovers and draws cluster resources in Operator.
description: Build a stateful two-tier application in Kanvas with a Secret and PersistentVolumes, deploy it, and learn what persists, where, and what Undeploy leaves behind.

body:
In this tutorial you deploy Apache Cassandra as a three-node ring. A Deployment treats its Pods as interchangeable; Cassandra cannot, because each node owns part of the data and other nodes must find it at a known address. A StatefulSet gives every replica a fixed ordinal, a fixed DNS name, and its own volume, and starts the replicas one at a time. You import the Kubernetes example manifests into a Kanvas design, adapt them to your cluster, deploy, and watch the ring form.
What you will learn 🔗 How a headless Service gives each StatefulSet Pod its own DNS name. Why ordinals and stable network identity let a clustered database find its peers. How a StatefulSet starts replicas in order and why that matters for a seed node. How volume claim templates give each replica its own persistent storage, and why that storage outlives the StatefulSet. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed Kanvas environment. Deploying needs a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use Meshery Playground, a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new does not run cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. Operator views and terminal sessions also need Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster. Dynamic storage. The cluster needs a default StorageClass that provisions volumes on demand, because each Cassandra node claims its own volume. Capacity. Each Cassandra Pod requests half a CPU and 1Gi of memory, three Pods in total. Persistence basics. You have completed Deploy WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes, or you know how claims bind to volumes. A namespace of your own. Playground is shared, and Deploy and Undeploy act on objects by kind and name. This tutorial uses the namespace cassandra-ada; substitute your own. The scenario 🔗 cassandra (Service, clusterIP: None, port 9042) | gives each Pod a DNS name: <pod>.cassandra.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local | cassandra (StatefulSet, 3 replicas, serviceName: cassandra) | +-- cassandra-0 --> cassandra-data-cassandra-0 (PVC, 1Gi) seed node, starts first +-- cassandra-1 --> cassandra-data-cassandra-1 (PVC, 1Gi) starts when cassandra-0 is Ready +-- cassandra-2 --> cassandra-data-cassandra-2 (PVC, 1Gi) starts when cassandra-1 is Ready cassandra-service.yaml holds the headless Service. cassandra-statefulset.yaml holds the StatefulSet and a StorageClass named fast. The Pods and claims in the diagram are not in either manifest: the StatefulSet controller creates them from the StatefulSet’s Pod template and volume claim template.
Import and merge the manifests 🔗 On an empty canvas, import https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/cassandra/cassandra-service.yaml with the Import Design dialog (URL Import), named after your design, for example cassandra-ada. Import https://kubernetes.io/examples/application/cassandra/cassandra-statefulset.yaml and choose Merge into current. What just happened. Each import converted a manifest into components and saved it as its own design in your account; the merge copied the StatefulSet manifest’s components into the open design. If an import fails with Failed to import design "<name>", download the file and import it with File Upload, keeping the .yaml extension.
Check your work. The canvas shows three components: a Service, a StatefulSet, and a StorageClass.
Adapt the manifests to your cluster 🔗 The example targets a single-node minikube cluster in the default namespace. Three changes make it portable.
Namespace. Set the namespace of the Service and the StatefulSet to cassandra-ada. Seed address. In the StatefulSet’s container environment variables, change CASSANDRA_SEEDS from cassandra-0.cassandra.default.svc.cluster.local to cassandra-0.cassandra.cassandra-ada.svc.cluster.local. Storage. Delete the fast StorageClass component, and clear the storage class name in the StatefulSet’s volume claim template so each claim uses the cluster’s default StorageClass. What just happened. The seed address is the heart of this tutorial. A new Cassandra node joins the ring by contacting a seed, so the seed’s address must be known before any Pod exists. A StatefulSet makes that possible: its Pods are named <statefulset>-<ordinal>, and the headless Service named in serviceName gives each one the DNS name <pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. cassandra-0 therefore always answers at the same name, even after it is rescheduled to another node with a new IP address. The name includes the namespace, which is why the seed must change with it.
The fast StorageClass uses the minikube host-path provisioner, which provisions nothing on other clusters; claims against it stay Pending, and so do the Pods. A StorageClass is also cluster-scoped, so on a shared cluster its name can collide with another reader’s. If you run minikube and keep the StorageClass, expect the dry run to report a not-found error for it even though the object is valid; bypass that error at the dry-run step.
Check your work. The design holds two components, both in cassandra-ada, and the seed address names your namespace.
Deploy the ring 🔗 Run Validate, then Deploy, and select the environment that holds your cluster connection. At the dry-run step, expect a not-found error for both components on the first deployment, because a dry run does not create namespaces and cassandra-ada does not exist yet. Select Bypass errors and initiate deployment. Confirm the deployment and read the summary. What just happened. Meshery Server created the namespace and applied both objects, in parallel and in no particular order. Kanvas applies only the two objects in your design. Everything after that is the StatefulSet controller’s work: it creates cassandra-0 and its claim, waits until that Pod is Running and Ready, then creates cassandra-1, then cassandra-2. Ordered start matters here because cassandra-0 is the seed; the later nodes join a ring that already exists instead of racing to form separate ones. The readiness probe in the Pod template tells the controller when a node is ready.
Check your work. The summary lists two Deployed rows: Service cassandra and StatefulSet cassandra. A Failed to deploy row carries an error card with the cause and remediation.
Watch ordered startup in Operator 🔗 Open the design in Operator, then filter by your namespace in the Layers panel so the view includes the Pods and claims the controller created. Change a filter every minute or so to refresh the snapshot, and watch cassandra-0, cassandra-1, and cassandra-2 appear in turn. Cassandra takes a few minutes to bootstrap each node. Select the StatefulSet. Its details show available Pods out of replicas, the selector, the image, and the update strategy. Open the Storage group in the Layers panel and select cassandra-data-cassandra-0. Its details show the requested size, storage class, and access modes. Right-click cassandra-0, start a terminal session, and run nodetool status. What just happened. Operator draws a snapshot from MeshSync and refetches only when you open a view, change a filter, or change clusters, which is why you refresh to follow the rollout. Each claim is named <template>-<pod>, so cassandra-0 always mounts cassandra-data-cassandra-0. Ordinal, DNS name, and volume form one identity: if cassandra-0 is deleted, its replacement gets the same name, the same address, and the same data.
Check your work. Three Pods are Running and Ready, three claims are Bound, and nodetool status lists three nodes with status UN (up, normal). If only cassandra-0 exists after several minutes, it has not passed its readiness probe, so the controller is holding the others back; read its logs with a log session. If cassandra-0 is Pending, its claim is Pending: the cluster has no default StorageClass, or it is out of CPU or memory.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy and select the same environment. Delete the design and the single-manifest Cassandra design if you no longer need them. See Deleting a design. Delete the claims, if you have kubectl access to the cluster: kubectl delete pvc -l app=cassandra -n cassandra-ada. Undeploy deletes each component’s object by kind and name, so it removes the Service and the StatefulSet; Kubernetes then deletes the StatefulSet’s Pods. It does not remove the three claims. They are not components in the design, and Kubernetes keeps volume claims when a StatefulSet is deleted, by design, so that a database’s data is never lost by accident. If you deploy the design again, the new cassandra-0 mounts the old cassandra-data-cassandra-0 and finds its data. The namespace also remains, because the design has no Namespace component. See Undeploying designs for the full removal behavior.
What you learned 🔗 A headless Service plus a StatefulSet gives every replica a DNS name built from its ordinal, so peers can be configured before they exist. Stable identity means name, address, and volume travel together across rescheduling. The StatefulSet controller starts replicas in order and waits for readiness, which lets the seed node form the ring before others join. Volume claim templates give each replica its own claim, and those claims outlive both the StatefulSet and Undeploy. Kanvas deploys and removes only the objects in the design; controllers create and own the rest. Next steps 🔗 Review every deploy option and failure mode in Deploying designs. Learn how Operator discovers and draws cluster resources in Operator. Revisit storage binding and reclaim behavior in Deploy WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes.

body:
Kanvas is not a standalone service. It is an extension that runs inside Meshery, relies on Meshery Server to reach your clusters, and relies on a remote provider, Layer5 Cloud, to store and share designs. Knowing which part does what explains why some features need a cluster connection, why others need an account, and why the hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new offers a subset of what a self-hosted Meshery deployment offers.
Read the diagram from left to right. Providers sit on the left: Meshery runs with either a remote provider (Layer5 Cloud for Kanvas), which stores designs and handles identity and sharing, or a local provider. Meshery sits in the middle and mediates every request. Your clusters sit on the right, where Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and Meshery Broker to report live state back to Meshery. Kanvas is a Meshery extension 🔗 Kanvas has two parts, and both run inside Meshery:
The Kanvas interface loads into Meshery UI at runtime. Designer and Operator modes are screens of Meshery UI supplied by the extension. A server-side plugin is loaded by Meshery Server and adds Kanvas behavior to it. Because Kanvas lives inside Meshery, it inherits Meshery’s connections to your clusters and Meshery’s choice of provider.
Every request goes through Meshery Server 🔗 Kanvas sends every request to Meshery Server. Meshery Server then does one of two things:
Answers local requests itself. Requests about your connected clusters and their resources stay within Meshery. Forwards provider-bound requests to the remote provider. Requests for designs, views, the catalog, sharing, and support go to Layer5 Cloud, and Meshery Server relays the response back to Kanvas. Kanvas never calls Layer5 Cloud directly, with one exception: real-time collaboration, described below.
The provider also decides which features Kanvas offers. Each provider publishes a capability document that lists the features it supports, and Kanvas enables only those features. The hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new ships its own capability document.
Where designs live 🔗 The remote provider persists your designs. Layer5 Cloud stores each design and every version of it, records who a design is shared with, hosts the catalog of published designs, and keeps the event log. For example, when Kanvas completes a validation of a whole design, it publishes a validation event to the Layer5 Cloud event log.
What talks to your clusters 🔗 Meshery Server, not your browser, talks to your Kubernetes clusters. It reaches them through components it deploys into each cluster:
Meshery Operator runs in the cluster and deploys MeshSync and Meshery Broker there. MeshSync records the state of the cluster in Meshery Server. Meshery Server feeds that inventory into Operator mode. Operator draws a snapshot of it each time you load a view, change a filter, or change clusters, so it reflects the cluster as of the last refresh. When you dry-run, deploy, or undeploy a design, Meshery performs the operation against the Kubernetes contexts you selected, or against all connected contexts when you select none. Meshery can also connect to adapters, which Kanvas does not require for designing or deploying.
Every resource Kanvas deploys carries a label with the id of its source design and annotations with the design version and component id. Operator’s per-design view uses that label to show exactly what one design produced. See Designs and Components.
Real-time collaboration: the one direct path 🔗 Real-time collaboration is the only path from your browser straight to Layer5 Cloud. When you edit a design with others, your browser connects to a signaling service hosted by Layer5 Cloud, which introduces the participants to each other. After that, edits synchronize directly between participants’ browsers, peer to peer over WebRTC, rather than through Meshery Server.
Hosted kanvas.new versus self-hosted Meshery 🔗 The hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new is for authoring designs. Every capability that needs a cluster is reserved for Meshery deployments: the Meshery Playground or your own self-hosted Meshery.
Capability kanvas.new, anonymous kanvas.new, signed in Meshery Playground or self-hosted Meshery, signed in Author and edit designs Available Available Available Import designs Available Available Available Share and publish designs Requires sign-in Available Available Validate Not available Not available Available Dry-run Not available Not available Available Deploy and undeploy Not available Not available Available Operator mode Not available Not available Available Connect clusters Not available Not available Available Every action in the table also requires the matching permission in your organization. Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy are disabled while the design is empty.
What you see when you reach a boundary:
A cluster-bound capability on kanvas.new opens a prompt that explains Operator mode is not available on kanvas.new and directs you to the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery deployment. Sharing or publishing while anonymous opens a “Sign in to” prompt that names the feature and offers a single Sign in action. You are anonymous when no user is signed in or the signed-in user has anonymous status. Signing in navigates the whole page to the provider and returns you to the page you started from. If the provider address is malformed, sign-in does not start and Kanvas shows the error “Sign-in could not start:” followed by the reason. The local provider limitation 🔗 Meshery can run with a local provider instead of a remote one. Under the local provider there is no remote service to forward requests to, so every provider-bound feature, including views, the catalog, sharing, and support requests, returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. Use a remote provider such as Layer5 Cloud for any feature that depends on it.

body:
Kanvas binds every shortcut to both modifier keys. On Windows and Linux use Ctrl. On macOS use Cmd. The tables write the modifier as Ctrl/Cmd.
Kanvas ignores shortcuts while you type in a text field, so typing a label, a comment or a search never triggers one. Open the same list inside the app with Ctrl/Cmd + /.
Modes and navigation 🔗 Shortcut Action Designer Operator V or Esc Switch to the Select tool. Esc also closes open menus and dialogs. Yes Yes H Switch to the Pan tool. Yes Yes Space (hold) Pan while the key is down, then return to the Select tool. Yes Yes Ctrl/Cmd + P Turn the Pencil tool on or off. Yes No Ctrl/Cmd + E Turn the Pen tool on or off. Yes No Ctrl/Cmd + + Zoom in. Yes Yes Ctrl/Cmd + - Zoom out. Yes Yes \ (backslash) Open the Layers panel. Yes Yes Ctrl/Cmd + / Open the shortcut reference in the help drawer. Yes Yes Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + / Open the Help Center. Yes Yes The tools are described in Tool Modes.
Adding objects 🔗 Shortcut Action M Add a comment near the center of the canvas. T Add a textbox near the center of the canvas and start typing. S Add a section near the center of the canvas. I Open the image picker to place an image. Adding objects works in Designer mode only. See Canvas Objects.
Editing 🔗 Shortcut Action Ctrl/Cmd + Z Undo the last change. Ctrl/Cmd + Y or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Z Redo the last undone change. Ctrl/Cmd + A Select all components. Ctrl/Cmd + C Copy the selection and the relationships between its members. Ctrl/Cmd + V Paste at the pointer. Ctrl/Cmd + D Duplicate the selection, 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down. Delete or Backspace Delete the selection. Undo and redo work in both modes. Copy, paste, duplicate and delete change the design, so they apply in Designer mode only. Cut has no shortcut because Kanvas has no cut action.
Mouse and wheel 🔗 Input Action Right-click, or press and hold Open the object menu on an object, or the canvas menu on empty canvas. Drag on empty canvas (Select tool) Draw a selection box. Ctrl/Cmd + click Add an object to the selection or remove it. Scroll wheel Pan vertically. Shift + scroll wheel, or horizontal scroll Pan horizontally. Ctrl/Cmd + scroll wheel Zoom toward the pointer. In Operator mode, drag on empty canvas and Ctrl/Cmd + click select resources in the topology. Esc closes the interactive terminal while it has focus.
Zooming the page itself, rather than the canvas, is left to your browser. Kanvas binds no shortcut for it.
Shortcuts that are not bound 🔗 The interactive terminal has no keyboard shortcut. Open it from the terminal badge on a container or from the resource’s details. See Interactive Terminal.
Filtering resources in Operator mode is done in the view filters, not with a shortcut. See Operator Views.

body:
A recognition is a badge that an organization defines and awards to its members. Recognitions mark milestones such as completing training, contributing to a project, or reaching a team goal. An awarded badge appears on the recipient’s public profile, where the recipient can share it.
Two kinds of badges exist, and they come from different places:
Organization recognitions are created and awarded by an organization’s administrators. This guide covers them. Layer5 community badges belong to the Layer5 community recognition program. Browse them in the Badge Gallery and read how they are earned in the Recognition section of the Layer5 Community Handbook. Who can do what 🔗 Task What it needs Create, edit, or delete a recognition The Manage Recognitions permission in the organization that owns the recognition. Organization Admin, Provider Admin, and Academy Admin hold it by default. The Manage Recognitions control on the Organizations page is enabled for holders of Edit Organization. Award a recognition to a member The permission to update that member’s profile, held in an organization you share with the member. View a badge Anyone who can open the recipient’s public profile. Two limits apply to every award:
You cannot award a badge to yourself. Layer5 Cloud refuses the request with a 403 error, including for a Provider Admin. A badge is a public claim about what its holder completed, so someone else must grant it. The recipient is notified, and an event records who awarded which badge to whom. Create a recognition 🔗 Open Manage Recognitions from the Organizations page to see every recognition and to create, edit, or delete the ones your organization owns.
Each recognition follows these rules:
The name must contain at least one letter or number. The label must be unique. A label that another organization has already reserved is refused with a 409 conflict. Choose a different name. Ownership is fixed. A recognition belongs to the organization where it was created. You can edit or delete it only while that organization is selected. A recognition owned by another organization stays visible in the list, but its edit and delete controls are disabled, with the message that it belongs to another organization. The recognition list itself is not private. The recognition catalog read is unauthenticated and not scoped to an organization, so any recognition’s name and label can be read by anyone. Do not put sensitive text in a recognition’s name or description.
Award a recognition 🔗 Administrators award a recognition to one member at a time, or set a member’s full badge list from the member’s profile editor. Both paths apply the same rules: the recipient is never the person awarding, and the awarder needs permission to update the recipient’s profile.
Some badges are awarded automatically. Completing an Academy quiz awards the badge tied to that quiz. Layer5 Cloud awards no other badge automatically.
Removing a badge uses a separate request from awarding and needs the same permission to update the member’s profile.
Share a badge 🔗 A member opens a badge from the Badges tab of their public profile. The badge detail offers:
Share buttons for X, LinkedIn, and Facebook. An HTML snippet that embeds the badge image and links to the badge on the member’s profile. A profile badge link has the form https://cloud.layer5.io/user/<profile-id>?tab=badges&badge=<label>.
description: Create recognitions for your organization, award them to members, and let members share them from their public profile.

An API token lets software act as you. Scripts, CI/CD pipelines, mesheryctl and other Meshery clients present it to Layer5 Cloud instead of signing in through a browser. Because a token carries your full authority and never expires, deciding how many tokens to create, who holds them and when to delete them is a security decision. This page explains how tokens behave so you can make it.
What a token is 🔗 A token is a credential bound to your user account. A client sends it as a bearer token in the Authorization header of each request; the Cloud API reference shows the exact form.
A token is not scoped to an organization. One token reaches every organization you belong to. Each request chooses the organization it runs in, so a single pipeline token can act in several organizations if you are a member of each. See Organization context for how Layer5 Cloud selects it.
What a token can do 🔗 A token can do exactly what you can do, no more and no less. Layer5 Cloud does not record permissions inside the token. It evaluates your roles at the moment of each call, in the organization of that request.
Role changes apply at once. When an administrator grants or removes a role, the next request made with your token reflects the change. Removing the user ends the token. If your account is disabled or deleted, Layer5 Cloud refuses every request that presents your tokens. There are no token scopes. You cannot limit a token to read-only access, to one organization or to a subset of your permissions. To give automation narrower authority, give it a token from an account whose roles are narrower. Lifetime 🔗 Tokens never expire. Layer5 Cloud offers no expiry setting, and a token remains valid until it is deleted. This differs from sessions, which Layer5 Cloud creates at each sign-in and which lapse on their own. A token is the right credential for unattended automation; a session is the right one for a person at a browser.
Name, purpose and retrieval 🔗 Every token has a name, which is required. The Tokens tab also asks for a purpose. Both are labels: they appear in your token list and help you recognize each token later, and they have no effect on what the token can do.
The token list never shows a token’s value. Instead, you can download any live token you own as a JSON file at any time after creation. The file uses the Meshery provider format, so Meshery clients read it directly. Anyone who obtains the file can act as you, so protect it like a password.
Creating, downloading and deleting a token each write an audit event, so your organization’s audit trail records who generated a token, who retrieved it and who revoked it.
Revocation 🔗 Deleting a token revokes it. Revocation takes effect immediately and cannot be undone.
Layer5 Cloud removes the stored credential, so a deleted token cannot be downloaded again. Every request that presents the deleted token fails. Layer5 Cloud checks revocation on every request. If it cannot complete that check, it refuses the request rather than accept a token that might be revoked. To rotate a token without downtime, create the replacement first, switch each consumer to it, then delete the old token. The API tokens guide walks through creating, downloading, rotating and deleting tokens.
Who can manage tokens by default 🔗 Each action on the Tokens tab is governed by a key. With the default roles:
View Tokens, which opens the Tokens tab, is held by every default user role. Download Token is held by User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin and Organization Admin. Create Token and Delete Token are held by Organization Admin and Provider Admin only. For every other role, the interface disables the create and delete controls. Every token action applies only to your own tokens. You cannot list, download or delete another user’s token.
Current behavior: Create Token and Delete Token are enforced in the interface only The Layer5 Cloud server allows any signed-in user to create and delete their own tokens through the API. It does not itself check the Create Token or Delete Token keys. Withholding those keys hides the controls in the interface; it does not prevent a user from minting a token. The security reference lists every security key and the roles that hold it.
A Provider Admin can mint a token on behalf of another account; that token appears in the account holder’s token list, and the account holder can revoke it.
Practices that limit risk 🔗 Create one token per consumer. A separate token for each pipeline, script or Meshery Server lets you revoke one without breaking the others. Name each token after its consumer. The name is the only way to tell tokens apart in the list. Delete a token when its consumer is retired. A token never expires, so an unused token remains a live credential until you delete it. For storing a token as a pipeline secret, see GitHub Actions. Manage your tokens at cloud.layer5.io/security/tokens.
description: An API token is a long-lived credential that authenticates scripts, pipelines and Meshery clients to Layer5 Cloud as your user account. It never expires and ends only when you delete it.
