body:
A request to an application in Kubernetes passes through several objects before it reaches a process in a container, and none of those objects is wired to the next by a fixed address. Each layer finds the next one by name or by label at the moment the request arrives. Knowing that path, and what each layer is responsible for, turns “why am I not getting a response?” into a short list of places to look. This page walks the path from the client to the container, explains why labels and selectors are what hold it together, and shows how the same path appears in a Kanvas design.
The path at a glance 🔗 The prebuilt design below models the in-cluster part of the path: a user, a ClusterIP Service, a Deployment, and a Pod running two containers. Select the image to open the design in Kanvas.
The full path, including the entry layer the design leaves out, is:
Layer Kubernetes object Responsibility Entry Ingress, or a Service of type LoadBalancer or NodePort Accept traffic from outside the cluster Stable address Service (ClusterIP) Give a changing set of Pods one name and one virtual IP Routing kube-proxy rules on every node, EndpointSlices Translate the virtual IP to the IP of one ready Pod Backends Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod Keep the right number of matching Pods running Process Containers in the Pod Listen on a port and serve the request Getting into the cluster 🔗 A ClusterIP Service is reachable only from inside the cluster. Traffic from outside enters through one of three doors:
NodePort. Kubernetes opens the same port, by default in the range 30000-32767, on every node. A request to any node’s IP on that port is forwarded to the Service. LoadBalancer. The cluster’s cloud integration provisions an external load balancer and points it at the Service’s node ports. Until the provider assigns an address, the Service’s external address stays pending. Ingress. An Ingress is a set of HTTP routing rules (host and path to Service). The rules do nothing on their own: an Ingress controller, itself exposed through a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service, reads them and proxies each request to the matching Service. Every door ends in the same place: a Service.
The Service: a stable name and address 🔗 Pods are disposable. They are replaced on every rollout, rescheduled when a node fails, and receive a new IP each time. A Service gives clients something that does not change: a DNS name (<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, or just <service> from the same namespace) and a virtual IP, the ClusterIP. Clients talk to the Service and never need to know which Pods exist right now.
The ClusterIP is not attached to any machine. On every node, kube-proxy (or a replacement that fills the same role) programs packet-forwarding rules that rewrite traffic sent to the ClusterIP and Service port into traffic to one backend Pod’s IP and target port. The list of backends comes from EndpointSlices, which Kubernetes keeps current with the IPs of the Pods that match the Service’s selector and report Ready. A Pod that fails its readiness probe drops out of the list and receives no new traffic until it recovers.
Labels and selectors are the glue 🔗 No layer of this path holds a reference to a specific Pod. Each layer describes the Pods it wants with a label selector, and Kubernetes evaluates the selector continuously:
The Service selector (for example app: web) decides which Pods receive traffic. The Deployment selector decides which Pods the Deployment, through its ReplicaSet, counts and replaces. The Pod template in the Deployment stamps labels onto every Pod it creates. For traffic to flow, the Pod template’s labels must satisfy both selectors. The Service does not route to the Deployment: it routes to whatever Pods carry matching labels, whoever created them. That design is what lets a rollout replace every Pod without touching the Service, and it is also the most common cause of a silent failure. A one-character difference between a selector and a label produces a Service with no endpoints and no error message.
The ports follow the same pattern. A Service’s targetPort must be the port the process in the container actually listens on. The container’s declared containerPort is informational; declaring a port does not make a process listen on it.
Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod: who keeps the backends alive 🔗 A Deployment does not carry traffic. It declares how many Pods you want and what they look like. The Deployment creates a ReplicaSet for each version of its Pod template, and the ReplicaSet creates and replaces Pods until the count matches. During a rolling update the old and new ReplicaSets both own Pods, and because both sets carry the labels the Service selects, the Service sends traffic to old and new Pods alike until the rollout finishes.
Inside the Pod: one network namespace 🔗 All containers in a Pod share one network namespace. They have the same IP address and the same port space, and they reach each other on localhost. In the prebuilt design, the application container can reach the database-layer container at localhost on that container’s port, and two containers in the same Pod cannot both listen on the same port. A request that arrives at the Pod’s IP is delivered to whichever container listens on the target port.
How the path maps to a Kanvas design 🔗 In a Kanvas design, each Kubernetes object on the path is a component, configured with the same fields as its manifest: the Service’s type, selector, and ports; the Deployment’s replicas, selector, and Pod template; each container’s image and ports. The connection between a Service and the workload it fronts is a Network relationship, drawn as an edge labeled with the ports and protocols on each side. A relationship definition can also write a value from one component into the other, such as a Service port into a container port. See Relationships for the kinds of relationships and what each one changes.
The edge documents intent; the selector and labels decide behavior. When you deploy, the cluster routes traffic according to the selector and labels in the components’ configuration, so check those fields whenever the edge and the running system disagree.
After a deploy, Operator shows the same objects as they exist in the cluster. Its resource details show what you need to follow the path: a Service’s type, ClusterIP, and selector; a Deployment’s available and desired Pods and its selector; a Pod’s IP and status; and each container’s status, ports, and restart count. Operator can also list EndpointSlices, open a terminal or a log session on a Pod, and filter the view by any label, which shows at once whether a selector’s label matches the Pods you expect. Operator reads a snapshot of the cluster, so fetch again after a change by reopening the view or changing a filter.
Debug a failing path layer by layer 🔗 Work from the client inward and stop at the first layer that does not behave:
Symptom Layer to check What to look at External clients get no answer, but requests from inside the cluster work Entry An Ingress controller is installed and the Ingress names its class; the LoadBalancer has an external address; the NodePort is open in the node firewall The Service name does not resolve Service The Service exists in the namespace you are calling; use the full name <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local across namespaces The name resolves, but connections time out Routing The Service has endpoints. No endpoints means the selector matches no Pods or no matching Pod is Ready The Service has no endpoints Labels and selectors Compare the Service selector with the Pod labels key by key, and check that the matching Pods pass their readiness probes Endpoints exist, but connections are refused Ports targetPort equals the port the container process listens on, and the process listens on all interfaces, not only 127.0.0.1 Fewer Pods than replicas, or Pods stuck in Pending Deployment and ReplicaSet Pod events for scheduling and image-pull failures, resource requests, and quotas Pods restart repeatedly Container Container logs and exit codes, and liveness probe settings One container cannot reach the other on localhost Pod Both containers are in the same Pod, the target container listens on the expected port, and no two containers use the same port Related 🔗 Explore Kubernetes Services - build ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Services and inspect them in Operator. Explore Kubernetes Pods - build, deploy, and inspect a Pod. Relationships - what each relationship in a design means and changes.
description: How a request travels from a client through Ingress or a Service to a Pod and its containers, why labels and selectors hold the path together, how the path maps to a Kanvas design, and how to debug it layer by layer.

body:
A view is to Operator mode what a design is to Designer mode: a named, saved definition you reopen later. A view stores which resources to show, not the resources themselves. Opening a view re-applies its filters to the current inventory of your connected clusters.
What a view stores 🔗 Field Content Name Defaults to Untitled View. Up to 255 characters. Not required to be unique. Filters Kinds, models, namespaces, labels, and the name search text. See Filters. Visibility public or private. Notes Free text (Markdown) in the view’s metadata, edited in View Info. Owner, created, updated Set by Layer5 Cloud. A view does not store layout, zoom, pan, or the selected resource. It does not store cluster selection either: the clusters selected in the Meshery context selector at the time you open the view always win. A copied link includes your current pan and zoom as URL parameters, but they are not saved in the view.
Filters 🔗 Filter Matches kinds Resources of any listed Kubernetes kind. models Resources belonging to any listed model. namespaces Resources in any listed namespace, plus the Namespace objects themselves. labels Resources carrying any listed key=value label. search Resources whose name contains the text. Different filter types combine with AND. Values within one type combine with OR. A new empty view starts with kinds Node and Namespace.
Design-scoped views 🔗 Choosing View in Operator from a design opens an unsaved view named <design name>-View whose only filter is the label design.meshery.io/id=<design id>. It shows exactly the resources that design deployed. The view is saved on your first filter or name change.
Saving 🔗 Saving is automatic. Any filter change, cluster selection change, or rename saves the view after a three second pause. The first save creates the view; later saves update it. The toolbar shows Saving..., then Saved, or Unable to save. Retrying.... A failed save retries with doubling delays, up to 100 attempts.
Creating a view requires a concrete organization selected. Layer5 Cloud refuses creation when the organization selector is set to all organizations. Every view is created public, owned by the caller, and placed in the workspace you have selected for that organization (or your first workspace).
Save as… creates a new view with the same filters and the name <current name>-copy by default, owned by you, in your selected workspace, and opens it. The original is unchanged. The copy is created public; change its visibility afterward if you need it private. A Clone command and an Import command appear in the code but are not implemented, so Save as is the only way to duplicate a view.
Opening and finding views 🔗 Where Result File menu, Open… Opens the Meshery workspace browser in Operator mode. It offers Recents (Global), My Views, Shared With Me, and each workspace’s Views tab. Layer5 Cloud workspace Views belong to exactly one workspace. Open the workspace and select the view. Design file menu, View in Operator Opens the design-scoped view. Non-administrators see views shared with them, public views, and their own private views. Provider administrators also see private views. Moving a view to another workspace needs the Assign Views to Workspace permission and is offered while browsing a workspace.
Visibility and access 🔗 Action Public view Private view Open Any user Owner, users granted access, provider administrators Edit filters, name, visibility, notes Any signed-in user Owner, users granted access, provider administrators Share and unshare Owner only Owner only Delete Owner or provider administrator Owner or provider administrator Public views are editable by every signed-in user Layer5 Cloud does not check ownership or organization when a public view is updated. Anyone who can reach a public view can change its filters, name, and visibility. Keep a view private, or use Save as… and set the copy private, when others should not change it. “Provider administrator” is the platform-level administrator role. It is not the organization administrator role.
Sharing 🔗 The toolbar Share button opens the share dialog, the same one designs use. It has a General Access selector, a People with Access list, a user picker, and Copy Link.
General Access setting Visibility Meaning Anyone with the link can edit public Anyone with the link can open and edit. Only people with access can open with the link private Only listed users can open it. Sharing offers a single implicit access level; there are no separate viewer and editor roles. Only the owner can change general access. Sharing sends email to new recipients, and is refused for anonymous sessions. The server requires the Share Views permission in the view’s organization. Kanvas’s own Share button checks the Share Design permission, so a role can see the button and still be refused by the server. See Share a Design for the dialog and its messages.
In Operator mode, the file menu’s Share… item creates a new empty view instead of opening the dialog. Use the toolbar Share button.
Export 🔗 Export… in the file menu downloads <view name>.json, containing the complete stored view: id, name, visibility, filters, metadata, owner, and timestamps. It is disabled for an unsaved view. Views cannot be imported back.
View info 🔗 Details in the file menu (or View Info in a view list) shows Owner, Visibility, Notes, Created, and Updated. Everyone can read the notes. Only the owner can change visibility and notes, and only the owner sees Save. Copy Link is available to everyone.
Delete 🔗 Delete removes the view with a soft delete. The server allows the owner and provider administrators. Anyone else receives a “no view with the requested id” error. The Meshery view list offers Delete View to the owner who holds the Delete View permission. Kanvas confirms with Are you sure you want to delete <name>? and shows no success or failure message afterward; the editor resets to a new empty view either way.
Permissions and plans 🔗 The permission names for views are View Views, Open view, Save Views, Clone Views, Share Views, Export views, Delete View, and Assign Views to Workspace. Public and private views, view sharing, view export, and assigning views to workspaces are Team Operator plan features and above. Layer5 Cloud does not check most view permission names on the create, update, and delete routes; the access rules in the table above are what the server enforces. See Permissions by Role and Feature Availability.
Related 🔗 Operator explains where the resources a view filters come from. Resource Details covers what you see when you select a resource in a view.
description: What an Operator view stores, how views are saved, shared, opened, exported, and deleted, and who can do what.

body:
Kanvas separates two kinds of failure. A design action that fails, such as a dry run or a deployment, produces an event with an error code and a remediation. A Kanvas that fails to load, or an Operator view with no data, produces an in-product message. This page covers both.
Ask for help from within Kanvas The Get Help action opens the Help and Support form. It needs a remote provider and a signed-in identity. See Help and Support. Kanvas does not load 🔗 If an unhandled error occurs, or the extension fails to load in the Meshery shell, Kanvas shows Uh-oh! Something went wrong.. (Uh-oh! Please pardon our mesh. in the shell) with the error text. The screen offers:
Troubleshooting Guide, a dialog with the checks below. Get Help, which opens the Help and Support form. Switch To Designer, when Designer mode is available. Symptom Cause Fix The Kanvas bundle fails to download, or the error says the bundle has no default component The Meshery shell downloads the Kanvas UI from the provider. A failed download, or a bundle that was built incorrectly, leaves nothing to render. Reload. If you build Kanvas yourself, rebuild it and confirm the provider serves the new bundle. Missing or stale data after an update The browser holds a previous version. Hard-reload the page, or open Kanvas in a private window. Features missing, or errors after upgrading Meshery or Kanvas The Kanvas version and the Meshery version are out of step. Kanvas has no version-mismatch screen. Update Meshery, mesheryctl, and Kanvas together. The Help Center footer shows the installed Kanvas version. Operator backend fails to start on a self-built Meshery The server-side plugin is loaded from the provider’s package path. A missing file, or dependency versions that differ from your Meshery build, make Meshery reject it. Build the plugin from the same version as your Meshery server and place it in the provider package path. Designer mode does not depend on a connected cluster. Designing, saving, and validating work with none connected.
A deployment fails 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix Dry run, deploy, or undeploy fails with meshery-server-1096 No selected context resolved to a connected cluster. Connect a cluster in Meshery, check that its status is Connected, and select an environment that contains it. meshery-server-1073 with a note about the environment The connection is not assigned to the environment you selected, or it cannot reach the cluster. Assign the connection to the environment, or upload a new kubeconfig. meshery-server-1095 The kubeconfig is invalid. Upload a new kubeconfig. Step 2 shows No environments found Your organization has no environment. Create an environment and assign a connection to it. This needs the Create Environment and Edit Environment permissions. The Finish step spins and never reports The request failed before the server raised an event, for example when your session expired. Sign in again and retry. Check the notification center and the server logs. A prompt titled SELF-HOSTED FEATURE opens You are on kanvas.new, which does not run validate, dry run, deploy, undeploy, or Operator. Use a Meshery you run. Every component fails an undeploy dry run The objects are not on the cluster. Check that the design was deployed, or bypass the errors. Error cards, codes, and remediations are described in Deploy a Design. The notification center’s Error Docs entry opens the Meshery error code reference.
Operator mode shows no data 🔗 Operator reads the cluster inventory that MeshSync reports through the Meshery broker. Designer keeps working when this is down.
Message Cause Fix No Kubernetes context selected, Please select one or more Kubernetes clusters. No cluster is selected in the context picker. Select one or more clusters. No data available for the current view The view’s filters or the search hide every object. Change the filters or the search. Uh-oh. Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster? or No MeshSync data available for the selected cluster MeshSync has reported no objects for the cluster. The broker may be unreachable. Check that the Meshery broker service has an external address with kubectl get svc -n meshery, and check firewalls and VPN software. Docker Desktop commonly fails to give the broker an address. Toast Failed to fetch resources: <reason> The request for cluster resources failed. Read the reason, then check the connection and MeshSync as above. Toast No container found to create <type> session A terminal or log session needs a container and the object has none. Pick an object that runs a container. The Troubleshooting Guide dialog repeats the data checks. It also suggests removing the local Meshery configuration folder as a last resort when stored data is corrupt. That step deletes your local Meshery configuration, so use it only when nothing else restores the data.
description: Find the symptom you see, learn what causes it, and apply the fix. Covers loading failures, missing cluster data, and failed deployments.

Selecting a resource on the Operator canvas opens the Details panel. It shows the resource as Meshery last recorded it from the cluster, and it carries the actions that apply to that kind. Fields with no value are omitted, so each kind shows only what applies.
Node Details Example: Kubernetes Node details.
Container Details Example: Kubernetes Pod Container details.
How the panel behaves 🔗 Opens on a single click. Selecting several resources does not change this: the panel always shows the last resource you clicked. Not live. The panel shows the canvas snapshot immediately, then fetches the resource’s full record once. It does not update while open. Close and reselect the resource to refresh it. See Operator for how the snapshot is built. Two views. Summary (the default) shows the key fields. Details adds the collapsible sections and tables, each titled with its item count, for example Labels (4). Status chip. Shows the resource’s phase when it has one (Running, Pending, Failed, Succeeded, Active, Terminating, Bound, Available, and so on). Otherwise it shows Ready whenever the resource has a Ready condition, whatever that condition’s value. Do not read Ready as a health check. Load failures. While loading you see a loader. If the fetch fails the panel shows Error loading instance details. Fields by kind 🔗 Kind Fields shown All kinds Age (hours below 24 hours, otherwise days), kind, API version, labels, annotations, condition type names (not their True or False values), and deep links Node Kubelet version, three capacity gauges, and Capacity and Allocatable tables Pod Pod IP, host IP, QoS class, node selector, priority, container count, total restarts, init containers, containers, volumes by type, tolerations Container Status, ports, start time, image pull policy, restarts, image, container id, environment variables, volume mounts (read-only or read-write), command, arguments, liveness, readiness, and startup probes, resource requests and limits Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet Available and total pods, ready and total replicas, selector, container images from the pod template, update strategy (StatefulSet) DaemonSet Selector, images, update strategy. Replica counts may be blank. Service Service type, cluster IP, external IP, selector, load balancer ingress addresses, the remaining spec as an expandable tree Ingress Rule hosts, the rules as an expandable tree, load balancer addresses PersistentVolume Capacity, claim, claim namespace, access modes, storage class PersistentVolumeClaim Requested size, storage class, access modes Namespace Phase and finalizers Secret, ConfigMap Secret type. Secret values are not rendered. Event and all other kinds The fields under All kinds only Container environment variables show their plain values. Values drawn from another source appear as source(apiVersion: fieldPath).
Labels and annotations 🔗 Labels render as key=value chips in the Details view. Selecting a chip toggles that label in the open view’s labels filter and the chip turns green. The filter matches resources carrying any selected label, and the view autosaves. Annotations are listed without actions.
Deep links 🔗 A resource that references a Node, Namespace, or ServiceAccount shows a link for each. Selecting one replaces the view’s kinds filter with that kind and sets the name search to the value, keeping other filters. Use it to walk from a failing pod to the node it landed on.
Node capacity gauges 🔗 For a Node, three gauges show how much of the node’s capacity Kubernetes holds back from Pods.
Gauge title Resource System Reserved Cpu CPU Memory Usage Memory Disk Usage Ephemeral storage Each value is (capacity - allocatable) / capacity as a percentage, rounded to two decimals, using the node’s reported capacity and allocatable. The gauge color follows the value:
Value Color 0 to 30 percent Teal-green Over 30 to 60 percent Amber Over 60 to 90 percent Orange Over 90 percent Red Reserved capacity, not utilization Despite the titles Memory Usage and Disk Usage, these gauges show reserved capacity, the share of the node unavailable to Pods. They do not show what Pods request or consume. Operator mode shows no live CPU or memory utilization, no per-pod metrics, and no time series. Use your metrics stack for those. Memory and storage parsing assumes the node reports values in Ki units. Actions 🔗 The panel header carries these actions. The same actions are in the canvas right-click menu, except Open Source Design and Download.
Action Offered on Result Initiate Terminal Session Pod, Container Opens shells. See Open an Interactive Terminal. Initiate Log Session Pod, Container Streams logs. See Stream Container Logs. Initiate Performance Test Service, Ingress Opens the load test form. See Run a Performance Test. Open In Design Resources deployed from a design Opens the source design in Designer with this component focused. Open Source Design Resources deployed from a design Opens the source design. Download All kinds Saves the resource record as indented JSON. The file name is the resource name with no .json extension. A resource counts as deployed from a design when it carries the design identity label that Meshery adds at deploy time. Resources created outside Meshery have no such label and do not offer the design actions. The header also shows Expand and Collapse buttons for every kind; they currently render without an icon.
Events 🔗 Kubernetes Event objects appear on the canvas when you enable Events under Monitoring in the Layers panel. It is a plain kind toggle, grouped with the autoscalers. Selecting an event shows the generic fields only. Because events are short-lived and numerous, filter to a namespace first.
Secrets 🔗 The panel does not render Secret values. The stored values still reach your browser: Meshery keeps the Secret and ConfigMap data MeshSync discovers and returns it with the resource, and Download writes it to the JSON file. Treat downloaded files as sensitive, and restrict who can use Operator mode against clusters whose Secrets matter.
Related 🔗 Operator Views save the filters you build with labels and deep links. Kubernetes events and the Layers panel describes the Layers panel in both modes.

body:
This page lists exactly what Kanvas accepts and produces. For the steps, see Import and Merge Designs and Export Designs.
Import 🔗 Kanvas accepts the extensions .yml, .yaml, .json, .tar, .tar.gz, .tgz, .gz, and .zip. Detection is by content and takes the first match in the order below.
Order Format Extensions Detected when Notes 1 Meshery design .yml .yaml .json The schema version is a supported design version Lossless round trip of a design file export 1 Meshery design as OCI image .tar .tgz .tar.gz .zip The archive’s layers contain a design file Only the first design is taken. Other layer files are ignored. No design file means failure. 2 Kubernetes manifest .yml .yaml One or more valid Kubernetes documents Multi-document files work. Unknown kinds are kept as generic objects. 3 Helm chart .tgz .tar.gz .gz .tar .zip A valid packaged chart An uncompressed .tar is reported as needing gzip. No values overrides. 4 Docker Compose .yml .yaml Converts as a Compose file The result is Kubernetes components. 5 Kustomize .yml .yaml (kustomization), or an archive containing kustomization.yaml The project builds Archive must contain every referenced file. If nothing matches, the import fails and lists why each format was rejected. The interface shows only the generic failure message.
Import sources 🔗 Source Supported Limits Local file in the import dialog Yes One file at a time. No size limit in the client. Single-file http or https URL in the import dialog Yes 16 MiB body, 5 redirects, 10 second connect, 30 second request. Internal addresses are refused. Drag or paste on the canvas Yes One design per file. Images and .txt files become canvas objects, limited to 500 KB on every plan. Catalog clone or open Yes Public or published designs only. Files and folders in a repository connected through the GitHub integration Yes One private design per valid file. Git clone URL, Helm repository URL, oci:// reference, directory, or pasted text No RAR and 7Z archives No The drop check lets them through and the import fails. Export 🔗 Output Keeps layout, annotations, metadata Re-importable Notes Design file (YAML) Yes Yes, lossless Downloads as <design name>.yml. Design (OCI image) Yes Yes Archive of an OCI image. Push it with a registry tool. Kubernetes manifest No Resources only Plain Kubernetes YAML. Helm chart No Resources only .tar.gz chart archive. Embeddable JavaScript module Canvas snapshot No Static snapshot for web pages. See Embed Designs. View as JSON Not applicable No Operator mode only. Downloads as <view name>.json. The canvas screenshot (a PNG picture, not a design file) is a separate action. See Canvas Actions. Not available: Docker Compose export, SVG image export, export of an earlier version, and per-format export options. The catalog’s light and dark snapshot images are produced by an automated workflow after publishing and are not user exports.
Format by operation 🔗 Format Import Export Meshery design (YAML or JSON) Yes Yes (YAML) Meshery design (OCI image) Yes Yes Kubernetes manifest Yes Yes Helm chart Yes Yes Docker Compose Yes No Kustomize Yes No JavaScript embed No Yes

body:
Kanvas reads its starting state from the query string of its address. A link can open a specific design, open Operator on a view, choose how much detail the canvas draws, and restore a zoom and pan position. The links produced by the Share dialog and by Copy Link are built from these parameters.
Append parameters to the Kanvas route of the Meshery you are using. On the hosted app that route is https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap; on the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery it is /extension/meshmap on that host.
https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap?mode=design&design=<design-id>&render=wireframe What to open 🔗 Parameters Result mode=design&design=<design-id> Opens the design in Designer. This is the form the Share dialog produces. name=<design-name> is optional. mode=design&type=design&id=<design-id>&name=<design-name> Opens the design. An older form that Kanvas still accepts. mode=design&type=catalog&id=<catalog-id>&name=<name> Clones the catalog design into the opener’s workspace and opens the copy. catalog-design=<catalog-id> Opens the catalog dialog focused on that design. mode=operator Opens Operator. mode=operator&type=view&id=<view-id>&name=<view-name> Opens Operator on a saved view. mode=operator&type=view&design_id=<design-id>&design_name=<design-name> Opens Operator on a view scoped to a design. A link to a private design opens only for people who can read the design. For anyone else the load fails with the message “Failed to render design”, followed by the reason. Public designs open for anonymous visitors. See Collaboration Model for who can read what.
How to draw it 🔗 Parameter Values Default Effect render full, medium, wireframe, view-only full Sets the render mode when the canvas loads. adaptive true off Turns on Adaptive mode when the canvas loads. Spell the render value exactly. The accepted value for the read-only mode is view-only, with a hyphen. Kanvas does not validate the value, and behavior with any other value is unsupported - for example, auto-pan stays off. Full is the default. A link with no render parameter opens in Full, which already draws TagSets, badges and animations. Add render to draw less, not to draw more. adaptive=true always starts with a Full ceiling. Adaptive mode may never exceed its ceiling, and a link cannot set it. Combine the two parameters and render sets the starting mode while the ceiling stays Full. Choose a different ceiling in the render mode switcher after the canvas loads. Both parameters survive navigation inside Kanvas. Kanvas keeps them in the address when it rewrites it, for example when it changes the mode or the open design. Neither parameter is stored. Render mode is session state. It is not saved in the design, not shared with collaborators, and not remembered the next time you open Kanvas without the parameter. What each mode draws, and what Adaptive mode measures, is on Performance Limits. The reasoning behind the modes is in Render Modes.
Where to restore the view 🔗 Parameter Value Effect viewport An encoded zoom and pan position Restores that zoom and pan on load. Copy Link adds it so the person who opens the link sees the same region you were looking at. The value is produced by Kanvas. Copy it from a link rather than writing it by hand.
Common links 🔗 Goal Link Open a large design without waiting for badges and overlays ...?mode=design&design=<id>&render=wireframe Open a design for review and let Kanvas manage fidelity ...?mode=design&design=<id>&adaptive=true Share a design that nobody should edit by accident ...?mode=design&design=<id>&render=view-only Give a reader a catalog design as a starting point ...?mode=design&type=catalog&id=<catalog-id>&name=<name> View-only is a display choice, not an access control render=view-only locks the components on the canvas for that session. It does not change who may edit the design. Anyone with edit access can switch the mode back. Control who can edit with design access.

body:
Auto-pan on Drag scrolls the canvas for you while you drag a component toward the edge of the view. Without it, moving a component to a part of the design that is off screen takes a drag, a manual pan, and another drag. With it, one continuous drag carries the component there.
Auto-pan is off by default. You turn it on as a personal setting, and Kanvas still switches it off while a design is too large for the current render mode.
Behavior 🔗 Property Value Default Off Scope Per user. The setting is stored in your Kanvas preferences on the server and follows you across browsers and devices. It is not stored in the design and is not shared with collaborators. Trigger Dragging a component to within 50 pixels of the edge of the visible canvas. Pan speed Fixed. It is not configurable. Acts on Component drags. Applies in Designer. The setting is listed with the Designer canvas settings in the Options dialog. Takes effect Immediately. Changing the setting needs no reload and no reopened design. Check where the component lands Auto-pan ships off because, while it is on, panning during a drag can move the dragged component lower than you intended. Review the final position after a long drag, and turn the setting off if components drift. Undo (Ctrl/Cmd + Z) restores the previous position. When Kanvas turns it off 🔗 Every pan moves the whole canvas, and every layer that depends on the viewport redraws with it: the grid, badges, overlays and the drawing surface. The work grows with the number of components and relationships, so auto-pan on a large design makes dragging lag instead of helping it.
Kanvas therefore allows auto-pan only while both the number of components and the number of relationships drawn on the canvas are at or below a limit set by the render mode:
Render mode Auto-pan limit (components and relationships) Full 100 Medium 500 Wireframe 1,000 View-only 1,000 The limit rises as the mode draws less, because fewer layers redraw on each pan.
Auto-pan runs only when your setting is on and the design is within the limit for the current mode. Kanvas re-checks this continuously:
The design grows past the limit. Pasting a large group, importing a fragment, or receiving a collaborator’s bulk change turns auto-pan off. Kanvas checks once per animation frame, so a burst of changes causes one decision, not many. The design shrinks under the limit. Deleting components turns auto-pan back on. You change the render mode. Moving from Full to Wireframe raises the limit from 100 to 1,000, so a design that blocked auto-pan in Full can allow it in Wireframe. You change the setting. The change applies at once. Nothing on the canvas shows that auto-pan has been turned off by size. If it is on in your settings but does not scroll at the edge, count the components and relationships against the table for your current mode.
Regain auto-pan on a large design 🔗 Switch to a lower-fidelity render mode. Wireframe and View-only allow 1,000. Reduce what draws. Hiding layers in the Layers panel takes their components and relationships off the canvas, which lowers the counts Kanvas compares against the limit. Deleting components does the same. Split the design. A design that regularly passes the limit of the mode you prefer is a candidate for several smaller designs. Known discrepancies 🔗 The setting’s description in the Options dialog says auto-pan is disabled “outside Full render mode”. Kanvas does not behave that way: it allows auto-pan in Medium, Wireframe and View-only within the limits above.

body:
Kanvas draws a design on a canvas and redraws it on every pan, zoom and edit. The cost grows with the number of components and relationships and with how much detail each one carries. Kanvas controls that cost in four ways: the render mode you choose, gates that turn expensive features off past a design size or below a zoom level, Adaptive mode, which changes the render mode for you, and a small number of enforced limits.
For the reasoning behind render modes, see Render Modes.
What each render mode draws 🔗 Switching render mode never changes the design. Components, relationships, configuration and layers stay as they are. Only what Kanvas draws changes. Full is the default.
Drawn element Full Medium Wireframe View-only Component images Yes Yes No No Gradient fills Yes No No No Relationship styling (color, curves, arrow style) Yes Yes No. Thin, straight, light gray lines Yes TagSets Yes No No No Expand and collapse badges Yes Yes No No Compound-component, label and external-link badges Yes No No No Validation and dry-run error badges Yes No No No Managed-by-Meshery and terminal-session badges (Operator) Yes No No No Text-box content Yes Yes No No Animation when a component is added Yes No No No Animated layouts Yes, on designs within the limit below No No No Editing and selecting on the canvas Yes Yes Yes No. Components are locked and take no pointer input Layer visibility from the Layers panel applies in every mode. A layer you hide stays hidden.
Render mode applies to Designer and Operator alike, and to the whole canvas at once. It is session state: it is not saved in the design, not shared with collaborators and not remembered across sessions. Set it from the render mode switcher, which appears in the Options dialog and in the Designer toolbar, or from the render URL parameter.
Size and zoom gates 🔗 A gate turns a feature off while a condition holds and turns it back on when the condition clears. Kanvas re-checks gates as the design changes, as you change render mode, and as you zoom, so you never reload to recover a feature.
Feature Gate Applies in Auto-pan on Drag Needs your setting on, and at most 100 components and 100 relationships drawn in Full, 500 in Medium, 1,000 in Wireframe and View-only Designer Animated layout Full mode only, and only while the design has no more than 50 components, no more than 50 relationships and no more than 100 edges drawn. Past that, a layout still applies its positions, without the animation Designer TagSets Full mode only, and at most 30 drawn. Past 30, Kanvas skips the rest and shows the warning “Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30” Designer Feasibility evaluation Zoom above 0.5 divided by the display pixel ratio. That is 0.5 on a standard display and 0.25 on a display with a pixel ratio of 2 Every mode Component style toolbar The same zoom threshold Every mode TagSets are the only relationship type with a rendering limit. See TagSets.
Adaptive mode 🔗 Adaptive mode lowers the render mode when the canvas becomes slow and raises it again when the canvas recovers.
Property Value Turn on The Adaptive switch in the render mode switcher, or adaptive=true in the URL Default Off Ladder Full, Medium, Wireframe. View-only is never entered or left automatically Ceiling The highest mode Adaptive may use. It starts at Full. While Adaptive is on, the switcher shows the ceiling, labeled AUTO, not the mode currently in use Signal How long the canvas takes to produce the next frame after each pan or zoom, taken as the 95th percentile of the last 20 samples Idle cost None. Kanvas samples only when you pan or zoom Step down When the 95th percentile exceeds 80 ms. After a step down, Kanvas ignores samples for 3 seconds Step up When the 95th percentile stays under 30 ms for 10 consecutive samples, more than 5 seconds after the last change, and the next mode is not above the ceiling Notification “Switched to mode mode for better performance” on a step down. “Performance improved - switched to mode mode” on a step up Behavior to plan around:
Turning Adaptive on sets the canvas to the ceiling at once. With the default ceiling, that is Full. Recovery is one step. After a step down, Adaptive recovers at most one step on its own. It steps down again if the canvas slows again, and it does not climb further until then. To return to a higher mode, turn Adaptive off and choose the mode. A new ceiling applies the next time you turn Adaptive on. Choosing a ceiling in the switcher while Adaptive is already on updates the label but does not change the running behavior. Turn Adaptive off and on to apply it. Turning Adaptive off keeps the current mode. The canvas stays in whichever mode Adaptive last chose, and manual selection resumes. The thresholds are fixed. You cannot set them per user or per design. Enforced limits 🔗 Limit Value Where it is enforced Components per design Set by the organization’s plan: 100, 200, 100 and 300 for Personal, Team Designer, Team Operator and Enterprise Layer5 Cloud, when a design is saved or imported. See Components per design Image or text file added to a design 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) each, the same on every plan The Kanvas canvas, when a file is dropped, pasted or uploaded. Images are embedded in the design, so each one adds to its size TagSets drawn 30 The canvas, as described above Canvas zoom Minimum 0.1 (adjustable from 0.1 to 5), maximum 30 (adjustable from 0.1 to 30) The Options dialog. Each person sets their own Kanvas enforces no cap on the number of relationships in a design or on how many images it holds. Large designs and embedded images still enlarge what Kanvas saves and synchronizes with collaborators, so loading, saving and live editing slow down as a design grows.
What to change when a design is slow 🔗 Work from the cheapest change to the most disruptive.
If Then Panning and zooming feel heavy Switch to Medium, or turn on Adaptive. Switch to Wireframe for a layout pass on a very large design Dragging a component to the edge does not scroll Count components and relationships against the auto-pan limit for your mode Only part of the design matters right now Hide the layers you do not need in the Layers panel. Hidden components and relationships come off the canvas, and the design keeps them TagSets are missing Check the mode is Full, the TagSets layer is on, and the design has no more than 30 The design saves slowly or collaboration lags Remove unused embedded images, and prefer SVG or WebP images over PNG, JPEG and GIF files The design keeps outgrowing the mode you prefer Split it into several designs Screenshots or demos need a steady picture Turn Adaptive off and choose Full, so the mode cannot change mid-capture Experimental WebGL renderer 🔗 Kanvas can draw the canvas with WebGL instead of the standard 2D canvas. It is an advanced option for diagnosing rendering, off by default, and available only from the Debug Mode panel, which appears when Enable Debugger is on in the Options dialog.
Scope. The choice is stored in your browser, not your account, and applies the next time a canvas loads. Reload after changing it. Trade-offs. The WebGL path draws dashed and dotted relationship lines as solid lines, draws every arrowhead as a triangle, and does not hide labels at low zoom. Fallback. Above a zoom of 7.99 Kanvas draws with the standard canvas. After a browser loses its WebGL context, Kanvas uses the standard canvas for the rest of the browser session. Browser support. The panel reports when the browser does not support WebGL 2.

body:
Kanvas gives you two ways to get help without leaving the canvas: the Help Center, a single place for documentation, learning material and community channels, and the support form, which sends a request to the Layer5 team. This page lists what each one contains, which support channels each plan includes, and the conditions the support form needs to work.
Help Center 🔗 The Help Center is a dialog with eight entries. Open it from the canvas context menu or from the help control in the whiteboard dock. It also opens from the Get Help action in the troubleshooting panel.
Entry What it gives you Documentation These docs, opened in a new tab. Video Tutorials The Layer5 video library, opened in a new tab. Quick Tips An in-app tour of the core Kanvas workflow: placing and configuring components, connecting and grouping them, loading and combining designs, sharing, validating, deploying and undeploying, and collaborating. In Operator mode it covers filtering the resources under observation, health and details, quick operations, performance tests, the terminal and log streaming. Academy Structured learning paths in Layer5 Cloud, opened in a new tab. Discussion Forum The community forum at discuss.layer5.io. Slack The Layer5 community Slack at slack.layer5.io. Keyboard Shortcuts A side panel listing shortcuts for Designer and Operator modes. The full list is in Keyboard Shortcuts. Support Opens the support form described below. The Help Center footer shows the installed Kanvas version and links to that version’s release notes.
Support channels by plan 🔗 Every plan includes community support. Standard and Premium support add direct contact with the Layer5 team. The table below is rendered from the product feature list and updates with it.
Support and Deployment Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Community Support Get help with most of your questions and issues in our Community Forum. ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included Standard Support Support can help you troubleshoot issues you run into. Get support via email. -Not included ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included Premium Support With Premium, get a 2-hour SLA and 24/7 web and phone support. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included For the channels themselves, see Layer5 Cloud support.
How a support request is delivered 🔗 A support request never leaves your browser for a third party. Kanvas submits the form to Meshery Server, which forwards it to your provider’s support intake:
Kanvas (browser) -> Meshery Server extension proxy -> Remote provider support webhook For Layer5 Cloud that intake is Layer5’s support queue, the same one the Layer5 Cloud Help and Support form uses, so a request raised from Kanvas is triaged exactly like one raised from Layer5 Cloud. For a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud deployment it is whatever endpoint the operator has configured - see Customizing Webhooks.
Requirements 🔗 A remote provider 🔗 Because the submission travels through Meshery Server’s extension proxy, the support form only works when Meshery is connected to a remote provider. Under the local provider, Meshery Server has no support intake to forward to, and the extension proxy returns 501 Not Implemented. This matches every other provider-bound Kanvas capability, including sharing, the catalog and views.
If the form fails under the local provider, switch Meshery to a remote provider and submit again. If you cannot switch, reach the Layer5 team through the community forum or Slack.
A signed-in identity 🔗 Every request carries the requester’s name and email so the team can reply. Kanvas resolves your signed-in profile when you open the form instead of asking you to retype it:
While the profile loads, the dialog shows a loading state and the form is unavailable. When the profile resolves, the form appears addressed with your identity. When the profile cannot be resolved, for example because the session expired, the form does not appear and nothing is submitted. A request with no way to reply has no value. If the form does not appear, sign in to your provider again and reopen it. If it still does not appear, see Troubleshooting Kanvas.
Type of inquiry 🔗 Each request carries a type that the support intake uses to route it.
Type Default Support Yes Community No Account No Commercial No If a submission fails, Kanvas keeps your subject, description and type so you can retry without retyping them.

body:
Hotfix - custom-domain orgs with anchored-fallback credentials hit 1722 at callback 🔗 Custom-domain orgs without their own BYOC IdP credentials (e.g. exoscale.layer5.io) ran into meshery-cloud-1722 \state validation failed\ immediately after GitHub redirected back to /oidc/callback/github. The W2 state binding stamped the request host (exoscale.layer5.io), but the callback legitimately lands at the canonical host (cloud.layer5.io) because the fallback chain anchors redirect_uri there. The validator’s strict host-binding equality refused the cross-host bounce.
What changed 🔗 OIDCStart now stamps the effective callback host into the state payload, mirroring composeCallbackURL’s precedence:
BYOC (cred.CallbackHost empty) -> stamp req.Host Anchored fallback (cred.CallbackHost set) -> stamp cred.CallbackHost So the state’s host-binding holds whether the callback lands on the same custom domain or on the canonical Provider Org host. body:
Hotfix - production sign-in restored on cloud.layer5.io (v1.0.97 regression) 🔗 Fixes a regression introduced in v1.0.97 where sign-in via GitHub / Google on cloud.layer5.io failed with meshery-cloud-1729 \direct OIDC sign-in without a Hydra login_challenge is not yet supported\ (Cloudflare shows this as 502 from some POPs). The legacy Kratos selfservice OIDC flow initiated the Hydra login challenge internally; W2’s /oidc/start had no equivalent, so the React /login page’s \Sign in with…\ button forwarded to W2 without a login_challenge and OIDCCallback fell into its fail-closed branch.
What changed 🔗 OIDCStart now bounces server-side through Hydra’s /oauth2/auth endpoint when the inbound URL lacks ?login_challenge=, parses the freshly minted challenge out of the 302 Location header, and feeds it into the W2 state binding. The callback then has a valid challenge for accept_login, Hydra returns a code-carrying redirect to /oauth/callback, and HandleRedirect closes the loop via its existing code exchange + cookie issuance. The off-eTLD guard moved ahead of the new bounce so off-eTLD-custom-domain misconfigs surface the correct meshery-cloud-1725 error instead of being masked by a bounce failure. PR: #5392

body:
Hotfix - production sign-in restored on cloud.layer5.io 🔗 Fixes a regression where clicking Sign in with GitHub / Sign in with Google on cloud.layer5.io/login redirected users to the upstream OAuth provider with a redirect_uri of https://cloud.layer5.io/kratos/self-service/methods/oidc/callback/{provider}, which GitHub / Google rejected as edirect_uri is not associated with this application\ after the production OAuth App callback URL was updated to the W2 native path /oidc/callback/{provider}.
What changed 🔗 OrgAuthData exposes a new UseCloudNativeOidc boolean that is true for both registered custom-domain hosts AND for the canonical Provider Org host (SERVER_BASE_URL’s host). The React login / registration pages now gate the W2 cloud-native redirect on this field, so canonical-host sign-in no longer falls through to the legacy Kratos OIDC flow. A new resolveOIDCOrgID(req) helper in the server handlers prefers the middleware-resolved org and falls back to ProviderOrgID when the request lands on the canonical host. Both OIDCStart and OIDCCallback consume the helper so the state binding’s orgId is symmetric across the round trip on the canonical host. Rollout notes 🔗 The Layer5 production GitHub OAuth App’s Authorization callback URL is already https://cloud.layer5.io/oidc/callback/github and this deploy restores canonical-host sign-in without further OAuth App changes.
The staging GitHub OAuth App (1065875) must mirror this with https://staging-cloud.layer5.io/oidc/callback/github for staging sign-in to work after this deploys to staging. If that has not yet been updated, staging will exhibit the same symptom until it is.

body:
Layer5 Cloud is the identity, tenancy, and collaboration service behind Kanvas and Meshery. It signs users in, organizes them into organizations, teams, and workspaces, decides what each of them may do, and stores the designs they create and share. Layer5 Cloud runs as a hosted service and as a self-hosted deployment.
Understanding the Layer5 Ecosystem 🔗 5-light-bg Layer5 Cloud is the identity provider and remote provider for Kanvas and Meshery. It owns accounts, organizations, teams, workspaces, roles, and the catalog, and it stores every design and design version. It is available as a hosted service or self-hosted. Kanvas is a visual designer and operator for Kubernetes and multi-cloud infrastructure. It runs as an extension inside Meshery and uses Layer5 Cloud to store, share, and publish designs. What Layer5 Cloud does 🔗 Sign-in and identity. Users create an account with an email address and password, with GitHub, or with Google. An organization that configures its own identity providers, including a generic OIDC provider, offers those instead. A signed-in user can link a GitHub or Google account to an existing profile, so either method signs in to the same profile. Email sign-ups verify their address before password sign-in works.
Tenancy. Organizations own teams and workspaces. A team belongs to the organization it is created in, a workspace can hold any number of teams, and a team can belong to several workspaces. At first sign-in, every new user receives a default organization, team, and workspace: they hold the Organization Admin role on the organization, the Team Admin role on the team, and own the workspace, so they can start working immediately.
Authorization. Roles, keys, and keychains decide what each user may do. A key is a single permission, a keychain groups keys, and a role carries keychains. Users hold roles within an organization, so the same person can have different permissions in different organizations. Built-in roles cover the provider, organization, team, and workspace levels, and organization admins invite users and assign their roles. See Identity and Security.
Design storage and sharing for Kanvas. Layer5 Cloud persists every Kanvas design and every version of it, records who each design is shared with, and keeps the event log. A design belongs to at most one workspace at a time. Real-time collaboration in Kanvas starts with a signaling service that Layer5 Cloud hosts; after participants connect, edits synchronize directly between their browsers.
The catalog. The catalog publishes reusable designs. Anyone can browse it. A signed-in user with the right permission can clone a published or public design into their own workspace, download it, or open it in Kanvas on the Meshery Playground.
Remote provider for Meshery Server. Meshery Server connects to Layer5 Cloud as its remote provider. Users sign in to Meshery through Layer5 Cloud, Meshery Server registers itself as a connection owned by the signed-in user, and Layer5 Cloud returns a capabilities document that tells Meshery which features to enable for that user. Every new user holds the Kanvas role, which enables the Kanvas extension when their Meshery Server connects.
Academy. Academy delivers learning paths, challenges, and certifications, and gives content creators the tools to build and publish their own.
What Layer5 Cloud does not do 🔗 It does not deploy to or manage your clusters. Meshery Server, running in your environment, talks to your Kubernetes clusters through Meshery Operator and MeshSync, and performs every dry-run, deploy, and undeploy. It does not run Kanvas. Kanvas is an extension that runs inside Meshery. Kanvas sends its requests to Meshery Server, which forwards design, catalog, and sharing requests to Layer5 Cloud. Real-time collaboration signaling is the only direct path from the browser to Layer5 Cloud. How Layer5 Cloud works explains these boundaries in depth, and How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud covers them from the Kanvas side.
Choose your path 🔗 Section Go here to Getting Started Create an account and learn what Layer5 Cloud sets up for you at first sign-in. Tutorials Work through end-to-end examples that build a working mental model. How-to Guides Complete a specific task: manage organizations and workspaces, connect integrations, or self-host. Concepts Understand organizations, teams, workspaces, roles, the catalog, and how they relate. Reference Look up default permissions by role and the API. Academy Take learning paths and certifications, or create and publish your own content. To design infrastructure with what Layer5 Cloud stores, go to the Kanvas documentation.

Use comments to offer feedback to team members, take detailed design notes, capture helpful tips for your team members, and include justification as to your infrastructure and application configuration decisions. Pay it forward to your future self by leaving historical record for reference later.
Lessons learned in this Peer Review module:
Collaboration is Key: Kanvas facilitates collaborative design through peer reviews. It emphasizes both asynchronous (commenting, notifications) and synchronous (real-time discussion) methods. Clear Workflow: The script outlines a defined workflow for peer reviews, from requesting a review to providing feedback and reaching completion. Specific Feedback: Kanvas allows users to provide feedback on specific components of a design, making the review process more targeted and effective. Centralized Review: All feedback is stored within the Kanvas design, creating a centralized location for review and discussion. Benefits of Peer Review: The script highlights the advantages of using Kanvas for peer review, such as improved collaboration, reduced errors, and faster design cycles. Flexibility: The script allows for different methods of adding comments (drag and drop, toolbar icon, hotkey, right-click) to accommodate user preferences. Notifications: Users receive notifications for review requests and comments, ensuring they stay updated. Both Asynchronous and Synchronous Collaboration are Important: The demo covers both types of interaction.

Transcript:
Five has found that he frequently references the same set of models while designing. If you know that you’ll be using components from a model frequently, you can pin that model for easy retrieval of its components. To pin a model to the dock in Layer5 Kanvas, click the pin icon next to the model. The model will now be accessible in the dock for quick use.
There is no limit to the number of models that you can pin to the dock.
When a model is pinned you can still browse all components or search for a specific component. Drag and drop or click to place a new component into your design.
When you no longer want a model pinned to the dock, you can remove the pin by revisiting the model in its original location and choosing to “remove from dock”.

body:
At 2:47 AM, checkout latency is climbing and the architecture diagram cannot be trusted. Five, Mia, and Raj open the live checkout design in Kanvas and work the incident together on one canvas, using the whiteboarding tools that are on by default in every design. By morning, that same canvas is the incident record, the postmortem starting point, and the onboarding guide. (The incident and its telemetry are a demo scenario.)
Chapters 🔗 0:00 Three sources of truth 0:37 Kanvas becomes the war room 1:12 Sketch the blast radius 1:48 Style without changing configuration 2:17 Put the evidence in context 2:47 Find, fix, and remember 3:22 The whiteboard that never goes stale What You Will See 🔗 Three tool modes. Default mode selects, moves, and configures; Pencil mode draws freeform notes without connecting components; Connector mode (Command+E or Ctrl+E) draws annotation edges that explain relationships and flow. See Understanding Tool Modes. Shapes. A warning shape dropped from the shapes palette, then switched to a different outline without rebuilding it. See Working with Canvas Objects. Annotation edges. The request flow traced with edges, then styled with a dashed line, arrowheads, and the marching ants animation. See Whiteboarding. Styling is not configuration. Fill, borders, text, edges, and animation change how the design looks, never how it is configured. Evidence on the canvas. A Grafana panel image and the runbook text placed beside the affected path, so the metric, the guidance, and the architecture share one frame. The fix, made in the design. A connection-pool setting raised in the component’s configuration, then validated and deployed. See Configuring Components, Validating Designs, and Deploying Designs. Annotations as a layer. Hide the annotations and the infrastructure stays; show them again and the context is intact. See Layout and Layers. Real-time collaboration. Every cursor and every edit stays visible to the whole team. See Collaborative Editing. Transcript 🔗 Narrator: Whiteboarding in Kanvas, through one late-night alert on the billing system’s checkout service.
Narrator: At 2:47 AM, Five gets the page every SRE dreads: checkout latency is climbing, but the architecture diagram cannot be trusted. The runbook is in a wiki, the evidence is buried in Slack, and the deployment lives across walls of YAML. The team has plenty of information - just no shared context.
Five: Three sources of truth, and none of them agree.
Narrator: Five opens the live design in Kanvas. Whiteboard is on by default for everyone, so the tools are already waiting in the bottom dock. Mia and Raj join; now everyone can investigate on the same canvas.
Narrator: Default mode is for selecting, moving, and configuring. Pencil mode draws freeform notes without connecting components. And Connector mode - Command-E or Control-E - creates annotation edges that explain relationships and flow.
Five: Default to arrange. Pencil to think. Connector to explain.
Narrator: Five circles the failing path with the Pencil. Mia drops a warning shape from the palette and switches its outline without rebuilding it. Raj traces the request flow with annotation edges, then adds a dashed line, arrowheads, and marching ants to make direction and movement unmistakable.
Raj: The flow slows after checkout hands off to fraud-check.
Narrator: Five inspects the fraud-check Deployment and marks it red. Styles can change fill, borders, text, edges, and animation - but styling never changes configuration. All the while, every cursor and edit stays visible to the whole team.
Mia: That matches the alert window.
Narrator: Mia drops the Grafana image beside the affected path, then adds the runbook text directly to the canvas. The metric, the operational guidance, and the architecture finally share one frame.
Narrator: The animated trail points to an exhausted connection pool on the fraud-check sidecar. Five updates the setting in the design; the team validates and applies the fix through its normal deployment controls; latency recovers.
Narrator: By morning, the same canvas is the incident record, the postmortem starting point, and the onboarding guide. The reasoning stays attached to the infrastructure instead of disappearing into yesterday’s screen share.
Narrator: Kanvas gives engineers one visual place to investigate, decide, and remember - together and in real time. This is Infrastructure as Design: the whiteboard that never goes stale.
